papers.title: Prompt-agnostic Language Models
papers.abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.

papers.title: Coherent control and high purity single-photon emission from telecom quantum dots on metamorphic InGaAs
papers.abstract: Semiconductor quantum dots emitting in the telecommunication O- and C-bands are promising candidates as single-photon sources for fiber-based quantum communication. In this work, we show how coherent quasi-resonant and phonon-assisted excitation help reveal the intrinsic optical properties of InAs quantum dots embedded in relaxed InGaAs matrices on top of metamorphic InGaAs layers for achieving emission in the telecom bands. By systematically comparing excitation schemes, we separate excitation-induced effects from intrinsic emitter properties. This allows us to observe linewidths as narrow as 21 $\mu$eV, the disappearance of slow decay channels, and single-photon purity reaching second-order autocorrelation values in the order of $10^{-2}$. Photoluminescence excitation reveals higher excited states, enabling coherent control of trion transitions and the observation of Rabi-like oscillations in both telecom bands. These results confirm the promising potential of these quantum dots for applications in quantum technologies.

papers.title: What Hallucinations Have We Measured? Semantic Illusion, Confabulation, and Expressed Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Hallucination remains one of the most critical challenges in deploying large language models (LLMs) reliably and safely. Yet the term is used inconsistently across the research community. We argue for a strict definition of hallucinations in LLMs. First, hallucinations should be confident incorrectness, kept separate from expressed uncertainty (UNK)1. UNK reveals that the model may be wrong, whereas a hallucination does not reveal it and is therefore more dangerous in practice. Conflating the two obscures their distinct behaviors and makes them hard to study. Second, hallucinations should be split by a simple re-elicitation test: does any semantically equivalent prompt recover the correct response? This test probes whether the relevant knowledge2 is accessible. If none does, the knowledge is likely absent or inaccessible, and the error type is a confabulation (CF) that likely requires external knowledge or retraining; if some does, the knowledge is accessible from the model but applied inconsistently, and the error type is a semantic illusion (SI) that simple prompt or decoding changes can mitigate3. Re-evaluating 14 recent hallucination methods under this taxonomy yields three findings. (1) Detection methods flag UNK more often than hallucinated responses (i.e., SI and CF). (2) Mitigation methods are far more effective for SI than for CF. (3) Latent signals are more informative than output-level signals for CF. An audit of recent hallucination papers shows that most conflate these categories. We recommend reporting CF, SI, and UNK separately, and introduce a practical labeling protocol that needs only a modest number of semantically equivalent prompts.

papers.intro:
Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a central concern for both researchers and practitioners. Yet there is surprisingly little consensus on what the term actually means. Across the literature, it is applied to a broad and heterogeneous set of model failures—factual inaccuracies [82, 3, 2], faithfulness errors [45, 117], reasoning inconsistencies [39, 12], and uncertain outputs [117, 39, 102]—often without distinction or explicit definition. This conceptual ambiguity is not merely terminological but obscures the underlying causes of model incorrect responses, undermines evaluation validity, and hinders the development of targeted mitigation strategies.

Hallucinations then split by whether the knowledge is behaviorally accessible. If some paraphrase, instruction or decoding setting recovers the correct answer, the error is a semantic illusion (si); if none does, it is a confabulation (cf) (see §4 for terminological motivations). The test is an operational proxy for knowledge accessibility, and it makes a sharp prediction that si should yield to inexpensive inference-time mitigation, while cf should need new, additional knowledge.

papers.title: Detecting Fine-Grained Differences between Image Datasets
papers.abstract: Detecting whether and in particular how two data distributions differ is a fundamental statistical problem. For example, we might be interested in which concepts (expressed in natural language) differ between two classes, the outputs of different generative models, or the same model with different prompt specifications. When working with large and complex image datasets, we intuitively think that first selecting concepts from a broad list using fine-grained patch embeddings, and then optimizing the concepts to better fit the data is an effective workflow. However, prior work instead uses MLLMs to propose concepts and image-level embeddings to select them. Therefore, we systematically compare these techniques and find that selecting concepts from broad lists can replace MLLM-proposals at obviously lower cost. MLLM inference can then be spent on optimizing selected concepts instead to achieve substantial improvements. Additionally, by designing a new benchmark that focuses on low-prevalence and multi-concept distinctions, we find that selecting nonredundant concepts instead of only the most distinguishing concepts matters, and we introduce techniques for how to effectively do this. Finally, we show how our methods address important problems like detecting spurious correlations and biases. Overall, our work presents a fundamental perspective shift on how we analyze interpretable distributional differences between datasets.

papers.title: The Reality Gap in Automated Driving Systems Testing: Landscape, Challenges, and Research Directions
papers.abstract: Simulation is essential for testing automated driving systems (ADS), but discrepancies between simulation and reality can undermine testing conclusions. It remains unclear which discrepancies the literature addresses and what evidence supports correspondence claims. We present a systematic mapping of 235 primary studies that measure or mitigate the reality gap in ADS testing, selected from 4,195 publications. We characterise objectives, targets, approaches, experimental setups, and evaluation evidence. Our classification distinguishes simulated and real-world execution across six ADS test components, separately for each approach and its evaluation reference. This distinguishes real-world information used to construct an approach from evidence used to evaluate its claims. Of the included studies, 76% address mitigation, primarily targeting scenario and actor realism and perception, while 94% report validation or measurement procedures. Only 61 studies report metrics from multiple families covering sensor/perception correspondence, ADS behaviour, vehicle dynamics, or safety outcomes; this coverage does not establish causal links between discrepancies and test verdicts. The synthesis highlights that real-world content and physical execution must be interpreted against the claim evaluated. The findings motivate claim-specific evaluation and component-level reporting to establish which discrepancies affect testing conclusions and when simulation evidence supports conclusions about real-world ADS behaviour.

papers.intro:
Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) and automated driving systems (ADS) operate in an open and largely unconstrained environment (Yurtsever et al., 2020). Their behaviour depends on learned perception components, planning and control software, and physical actuators. On-road testing alone cannot establish that such a system is acceptably safe. Demonstrating a fatality rate comparable to human drivers with statistical confidence would require hundreds of millions of kilometres of testing (Kalra and Paddock, 2016). Software changes can require renewed evidence, while on-road testing exposes road users to the failures that the campaign aims to find. Simulation makes rare and hazardous situations reproducible, less expensive to test, and executable in parallel. It is therefore widely used in ADS research and scenario-based safety assessment (Zhong et al., 2021; International Organization for Standardization, 2019; Koopman, 2022; Borg et al., 2022).

Simulation makes rare and hazardous situations reproducible, less expensive to test, and executable in parallel. It is therefore widely used in ADS research and scenario-based safety assessment (Zhong et al., 2021; International Organization for Standardization, 2019; Koopman, 2022; Borg et al., 2022).

Simulation introduces a different problem. A simulated test relies on models of the road, traffic, sensors, and vehicle dynamics, each approximating reality. The difference between a simulated execution and the corresponding real-world execution is the simulation-to-reality gap, or reality gap. This gap can undermine a test verdict in two ways. A simulator that is more benign than reality can create false confidence by failing to expose failures that occur in the real system. Conversely, it can create false alarms by reporting failures that do not reproduce in reality, directing engineering effort towards simulator artefacts rather than defects of the system under test. These concerns are supported by empirical observations. Offline and online evaluations can disagree on which inputs cause failures (Haq et al., 2020; Haq et al., 2021; Codevilla et al., 2018). Failures found in simulation may transfer only partially to the corresponding physical platform (Stocco et al., 2023a; Lambertenghi et al., 2025a). Different simulators can produce different results for the same ADAS and differ from reality (Borg et al., 2020; Sorokin et al., 2026; Biagiola et al., 2024). Simulator non-determinism can introduce further differences (Amini et al., 2024).

These terms can concern the faithfulness of a sensor signal, the plausibility of a traffic scenario, the accuracy of a dynamics model, or the transferability of a control policy.

These combinations must be interpreted against the research target and evaluation claim. Reducing a discrepancy or including real-world content does not by itself establish correspondence of ADS behaviour or agreement between simulated and physical test verdicts.

papers.title: Pinpointing Pivot Points: The DECIDE Framework for Data Analysis Decision Importances
papers.abstract: Human judgment calls made throughout the data science life cycle can change the conclusions drawn from data. Independent analysts often make different choices when given the same data, leading to often unacceptable variations in results and contributing to the ongoing reproducibility crisis across scientific disciplines. The rapid adoption of agentic tools threatens to amplify this crisis. Several approaches have been developed to address this variation by following the same strategy: repeating an analysis under different combinations of analytical decisions and inspecting the distribution of outcomes. Examples include multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and vibration of effects. More broadly, the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework assesses how documented judgment calls across the data science life cycle affect conclusions, with predictability serving as a reality-check that a model captures signal. Each of these approaches results in a "multiverse" object. While the distribution of outcomes reflects the overall variability of conclusions, estimating the influence of each individual decision requires additional tools. A common heuristic is to train a model to predict the outcome from these decisions and treat its coefficients or feature importances as proxies for each decision's influence. Although this strategy may work in certain cases, it assumes the model is correctly specified and accurately predicts the outcome, which we show is not always the case. In this work, we introduce DECIDE, a model-free framework that quantifies each decision's importance from the actual outcomes across the plausible decision space, avoiding issues of predictability by design. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DECIDE by applying it to real-world multiverse analyses. We further provide what is, to our knowledge, the first formal definition of the multiverse.

papers.intro:
While conclusions drawn from data are often treated as infallible, analysts answering the same research question using the same dataset can make different methodological choices and arrive at conflicting results [1, 2]. This calls into question the robustness of empirical findings. A striking illustration of this is a recent study by Aczel et al. [3], in which 100100 published social science findings were independently reanalyzed at least five times by analysts using the original data. Only 34%34\% of the independent reanalyses closely matched the original result, with 26%26\% either finding no effect or reaching the opposite conclusion. This sensitivity of results to analytical choices is not a new observation [4, 5, 6], nor is it unique to the social sciences, as the natural sciences face the same challenge [7]. Furthermore, the rapid adoption of agentic programming tools threatens to exacerbate this issue by introducing methodological decisions that analysts accept without full scrutiny. Conventional statistical inference largely ignores this source of variability, leaving practitioners ill-equipped to measure and explain it, thus contributing to overconfident conclusions and irreproducible findings. Understanding the drivers of this variation is crucial not only for achieving accurate findings, but also for informing real-world decisions that rely on these findings.

Understanding the drivers of this variation is crucial not only for achieving accurate findings, but also for informing real-world decisions that rely on these findings.

To address this unacknowledged uncertainty and combat the reproducibility crisis, researchers have developed several parallel lines of work over the past decade. The Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) framework [4, 8, 9, 10] applies across the entire data science life cycle, from data collection to communicating results. It requires conclusions to pass a predictability “reality-check” and to be stable under reasonable perturbations to judgment calls at each step. PCS calls for these judgment calls and their perturbations to be documented in domain context and satisfy computational resource constraints. Independently, multiverse analysis [11], specification curve analysis [12], and vibration of effects [13] enumerate “reasonable” options for each analytical decision to examine a combinatorial set of plausible data analyses and mostly differ in how they analyze or visualize the results of this set. Multiverse analysis [11] has emerged as the predominant framework for exploring the consistency of results and has been proposed as the umbrella term for enumeration-based approaches [14, 15]. By computing the outcome of every plausible analysis, practitioners can observe the entire distribution of potential results. While the multiverse contains the exact structural information needed to explain analytical instability, current methods fail to fully exploit this, an issue explicitly highlighted by Short et al. [14]. A multiverse with highly variable outcomes tells an analyst that something is fragile, but additional tools are necessary to infer which particular decisions are responsible. This leaves practitioners without the targeted guidance needed to understand the root causes. Our work seeks to bridge this gap by providing a principled method for pinpointing the specific decisions that drive analytical variability. Specifically, we combine the strengths of PCS and multiverse analysis to directly analyze the stability of a multiverse with respect to each individual decision.

Independently, multiverse analysis [11], specification curve analysis [12], and vibration of effects [13] enumerate “reasonable” options for each analytical decision to examine a combinatorial set of plausible data analyses and mostly differ in how they analyze or visualize the results of this set. Multiverse analysis [11] has emerged as the predominant framework for exploring the consistency of results and has been proposed as the umbrella term for enumeration-based approaches [14, 15]. By computing the outcome of every plausible analysis, practitioners can observe the entire distribution of potential results. While the multiverse contains the exact structural information needed to explain analytical instability, current methods fail to fully exploit this, an issue explicitly highlighted by Short et al. [14]. A multiverse with highly variable outcomes tells an analyst that something is fragile, but additional tools are necessary to infer which particular decisions are responsible. This leaves practitioners without the targeted guidance needed to understand the root causes. Our work seeks to bridge this gap by providing a principled method for pinpointing the specific decisions that drive analytical variability. Specifically, we combine the strengths of PCS and multiverse analysis to directly analyze the stability of a multiverse with respect to each individual decision.

To distill actionable insights from the descriptive complexity of a multiverse, savvy researchers may fit a variety of different surrogate models (e.g., linear regression, random forest, etc.) to the multiverse output and interpret the model’s feature importances as proxies for decision importances [16, 14]. Whether or not these models fit the data is seldom reported and, as we demonstrate in Section 4, these surrogate models often fit the multiverse poorly. Consequently, practitioners should be highly cautious in using surrogate models, as the relationships derived from them are frequently unfaithful to the true dynamics of the analysis. Global sensitivity analysis (GSA), which quantifies the contributions of each input to the observed variation in the output of a system, presents a principled alternative. Recent work has applied variance-based GSA to multiverse analysis [17]. However, the structure of analytical decisions in multiverses is different from the setting standard GSA methods were designed for. In particular, decisions are categorical and can be restricted or branch-dependent. Furthermore, analysts may be interested in quantities other than average-case importance, such as how a decision can influence the tail of an outcome distribution.

This model-free design yields a more robust interpretation of decision importance, achieving actionable insights without sacrificing the full coverage provided by the multiverse. papers.title: Early warning of critical transitions: Distinguishing supercritical and subcritical bifurcations from noisy observations
papers.abstract: Early-warning methods can indicate that a system is approaching a loss of stability, but they do not usually reveal whether the approaching bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical. We investigate whether this distinction can be made from noisy pre-transition observations. For this investigation, we extend a regression-based stability method by including the leading cubic nonlinear term, whose sign is used to predict the bifurcation type. We test the method on a stochastic pitchfork model and a spatial stochastic Swift-Hohenberg equation. In both models, classification improves with longer observation horizons, closer proximity to the bifurcation, stronger noise, and larger nonlinear effects. However, these conditions are also linked to a higher risk of noise-induced tipping in the subcritical case. The useful early-warning window is therefore determined by a balance between obtaining enough information to identify the bifurcation type and doing so before noise-induced tipping becomes too likely. In spatially extended systems, we find that observing the full spatial field allows classification over shorter observation horizons, and performance improves when a broader range of spatial modes contributes to the observed dynamics. Altogether, we identify the conditions under which the method can reliably distinguish between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations.

papers.intro:
An important motivation for studying bifurcations is the understanding of tipping points in complex systems. A tipping point is a critical threshold at which a system undergoes a qualitative transition to a substantially different dynamical regime [21, 31, 16]. Such transitions occur in many natural and engineered systems, including climate dynamics, ecology, financial markets, infrastructure networks, and social systems [21, 1, 33]. Examples include shifts in ocean circulation [16], tipping of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets [17], abrupt shifts in arid ecosystems [22], cascading failures in power grids [1], financial market crashes [27], and abrupt changes in social conventions or the spreading of information through social systems [7, 33]. In many systems, the main question is therefore not only when a transition occurs, but also whether it develops gradually or through an abrupt shift between states.

Specifically, in the case that the system undergoes a pitchfork bifurcation with normal form (2.1), the distinction between gradual and abrupt transitions is closely related to whether the underlying bifurcation is supercritical or subcritical; the qualitative difference is illustrated in Figure 1, where u=u⁡(t)∈ℝu=u(t)\in\mathbb{R} denotes the unknown variable and μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R} is a parameter in the system that encodes the distance to the bifurcation point. In a supercritical bifurcation, stable finite-amplitude states emerge continuously when the critical threshold is crossed. In a subcritical bifurcation, unstable finite-amplitude states already exist before the bifurcation point [28, Sec. 3.4]. These states form a threshold that can be crossed by sufficiently large perturbations. Stochastic fluctuations can trigger such abrupt shifts before the deterministic bifurcation point is reached, a process known as noise-induced tipping [2]. The distinction between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations is therefore important both for the nature of the transition and for the sensitivity of the system to stochastic perturbations.

The distinction between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations also applies to spatially extended systems. In these systems, instabilities can give rise to spatial patterns, as in a Turing bifurcation [30, 8, 18]. The dynamics close to such an instability are determined by a universal amplitude equation, the (real) Ginzburg–Landau equation [8], whose structure closely resembles the normal form of the pitchfork bifurcation. The formal derivation and rigorous justification of these models in pattern-forming systems is by now a well-established theory; see, for example, [23] for the deterministic case, and [4] for the stochastic case. Therefore, as in the pitchfork case depicted in Figure 1, the pattern emerges continuously from the homogeneous state for a supercritical bifurcation, and it typically appears through an abrupt finite-amplitude transition for a subcritical bifurcation.

Traditional early-warning indicators, such as those based on the theory of critical slowing down, identify changes in the linearized dynamics near a stable equilibrium [21, 32, 35, 9]. These changes can signal a loss of stability and thereby provide an early warning of an approaching bifurcation. However, these indicators do not distinguish between supercritical and subcritical bifurcations because this distinction is determined by the nonlinear dynamics. In fact, leading nonlinear terms can already influence a system’s behavior and predictability before the bifurcation is crossed [19], suggesting that pre-transition observations may contain information beyond the linearized dynamics. This raises the question under which observational conditions these nonlinear contributions can be recovered reliably, thus enabling an early-warning indicator that is capable of distinguishing imminent supercritical bifurcations from subcritical bifurcations.

In this work, we investigate whether noisy observations of a system approaching a bifurcation can be used to determine its criticality. We extend the regression method introduced in [20], which estimated the linearized dynamics, by also estimating the leading cubic drift term from temporal and spatio-temporal data (Section 2). We consider synthetic data generated from a stochastic variant of the normal form for a pitchfork bifurcation (3.1), and a stochastic Swift–Hohenberg equation (4.1). The latter is a standard model for a pattern-forming system close to a Turing instability, and was first introduced as a model for temperature-driven convection in fluids [29]. For both models, we study how the prediction depends on the distance to the bifurcation and the observation horizon (Sections 3–4). For the Swift–Hohenberg equation, we additionally investigate how the strength of the spatial operator and the critical spatial scale affect the prediction of the bifurcation criticality (Section 4). Finally, in Section 5 we discuss the feasibility and limitations of applying the method to observational data from complex systems.

papers.title: EgoContact: Evaluating Physical Intelligence with Egocentric Video
papers.abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

papers.intro:
Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in controlled settings, yet reliable generalization to diverse, in-the-wild scenarios remains elusive. Such generalization calls for more than just passive semantic understanding of objects and available actions, requiring a model capable of translating high-level intent into concrete physical interactions in novel environments. Yet acquiring such physical grounding directly from robot experience is fundamentally difficult to scale, as real-world robot data remains costly and confined to narrow domains. By contrast, egocentric video offers a compelling source of scalable supervision. Everyday human activity captures a wide range of objects manipulated for diverse purposes in natural environments [1, 2]. Recent work therefore extracts pseudo-labeled interactions from egocentric video to pretrain dexterous and generalizable robotic policies [3, 4, 5]. While pseudo-labeled egocentric data has enabled scaling policy training, it offers no direct way to evaluate the physical knowledge these models actually acquire.

Evaluating such physical intelligence at scale, however, remains a fundamental challenge. Robot rollouts provide direct evidence, but are expensive, difficult to reproduce, and entangle physical understanding with perception, planning, embodiment, and control. Simulation is repeatable, but restricts the diversity of objects, interactions, and physical conditions and introduces a sim-to-real gap. Existing egocentric benchmarks retain real-world diversity, but primarily model the observed human through actions, narrations, objects, or motion [2, 1, 6, 7]. We instead ask whether human behavior can serve as a reproducible probe of the physical knowledge that makes that behavior possible.

We instead ask whether human behavior can serve as a reproducible probe of the physical knowledge that makes that behavior possible.

Each observed interaction ties a semantic intent to a concrete realization on an object surface. Knowing that a bottle is graspable, for example, does not specify where the fingers should make contact; recognizing that a drawer will be opened does not identify the handle through which opening can be realized. We therefore focus on a specific component of physical intelligence: the ability to ground an intended action in the object locations that physically support it. Predicting these locations before contact isolates an action-relevant decision without prescribing an embodiment-specific hand pose, trajectory, or controller. This leads to our central question: can current models robustly infer precise, action-conditioned contacts before interaction? Unfortunately, existing benchmarks cannot resolve this question, constrained either by limited spatial precision in their annotations [1] or by insufficient scale and diversity [8, 7, 9].

papers.title: A new sharp Sobolev inequality between the $Q$-curvature and the scalar curvature on Euclidean space
papers.abstract: We establish a sharp Sobolev-type inequality on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq 5$, that interpolates between the second-order energy and a weighted first-order term. Specifically, we determine the sharp constant $S_{4,2}$ in the inequality \begin{equation*} \int_{\mathbb R^n} (\Delta u)^2\,dx \ge S_{4,2} \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}|\nabla u|^{2}|u|^{\frac{4}{n-4}}\,dx\right)^{\frac{n-4}{n-2}}, \end{equation*} for any $u\in\dot H^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and we classify the cases of equality. This solves the problem of minimizing the total $Q$-curvature of among metrics on the sphere, conformal to the standard metric, with fixed total scalar curvature.

papers.title: Formalizing the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes by a Generalized Notion of Co-dimension
papers.abstract: In this work, we formalize the concept of intrinsic dimension of objective landscapes introduced in Li et al. (2018), which measures the structural complexity of learning problems by training along randomly generated subspaces. We define the intrinsic dimension of a set $\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^p$ as the minimal dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ such that a random plane of dimension $d_{\mathrm{int}}(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^p$ intersects $\Theta$ with probability one. We show that it is a generalized notion of co-dimension that depends on the global geometry of $\Theta$. We study mathematical properties of the intrinsic dimension and develop techniques to estimate the intrinsic dimension of sets $\Theta$ that arise in learning problems. More specifically, we derive upper and/or lower bounds where $\Theta$ is the set of optimal parameters in student-teacher settings with shallow and deep ReLU networks, including finite and infinite sample cases, and with and without regularization. We discuss how our theory leads to novel types of generalization bounds, thereby showing that the intrinsic dimension is a measure of learning complexity. Our results connect techniques from seemingly different areas of machine learning research such as classification of symmetries of ReLU networks and stochastic geometry.

Overparameterization plays an important role in both the optimization and generalization behaviour of neural networks, but it also makes the ambient parameter dimension only a coarse indicator of the complexity of a particular learning problem. In particular, the same architecture may be used to learn target functions of very different complexity while its number of parameters remains unchanged. To develop a theory that distinguishes learning problems beyond their ambient parameter count, it is therefore natural to seek complexity measures that depend on the particular task being solved. Existing measures of learning complexity such as the Vapnik–Chervonenkis (VC) dimension (Vapnik, 2013) and (empirical) Rademacher complexity (Koltchinskii, 2001) primarily quantify the richness of a hypothesis class, possibly relative to a given sample or data distribution. They do not, however, directly quantify the complexity of the particular target function within that class. This distinction is particularly transparent in a student–teacher setting: fixing the student architecture fixes architecture-level quantities such as its VC dimension, while varying the teacher can substantially change the structure and difficulty of the corresponding learning problem.

Although their study is empirical, the appeal of the approach lies in the fact that several components of the learning problem, including the target task, data distribution, hypothesis class, and optimization, jointly influence the resulting quantity.

papers.title: Implicit Bias of (Stochastic) Gradient Descent on Deep Linear Diagonal Networks
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models are often overparameterized, i.e., have more parameters than training data. This typically implies that the loss function admits multiple minimizers so that training methods (and their hyperparameter choices) have significant influence on the computed solution. We study this so-called implicit bias phenomenon in the context of training deep linear diagonal networks. Previous work has shown that the gradient flow for learning such networks converges to (almost) sparse solutions when initialized small. For an arbitrary number of layers, we extend this analysis to the practically more realistic (stochastic) gradient descent iterations. Our approach identifies (stochastic) gradient descent as a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent. This allows us to establish convergence and characterize the limiting solution, relating it to weighted $\ell_1$-minimization. Moreover, we provide sufficient conditions on the step sizes and quantify the influence of the step sizes on the implicit bias.

In recent years the size of machine learning models has increased dramatically. Typically, the amount of parameters is larger than the number of available training data so that many neural networks exist which interpolate the data exactly and therefore give zero loss – even for training data with random labels [zhang2017understanding]. It is surprising that nevertheless training often produces networks that generalize well to unseen data – in contrast to classical statistics which would predict overfitting and poor generalization.

In the situation of many global minimizers the optimization algorithm and its hyperparameter choices such as initialization have significant impact on the computed solution. Understanding such implicit bias (also called implicit regularization) and why it leads to good generalization property is key for understanding and further developing modern machine learning methods. One popular hypothesis is that training methods such as (stochastic) gradient descent and its variants promote neural network models of low complexity, e.g. in the form of sparsity and low rank, for suitable (small enough) initialization. Following Occam’s razor principle that reality prefers simple solutions, sparsity and other low complexity models should intuitively lead to models that generalize better than models of high complexity. (Of course, suitable notions of low complexity may depend on the precise machine learning task at hand.) In the context of signal processing, this idea has been exploited very successfully in the last decades in compressed sensing [DonohoCS06, 13].

Our approach consists in introducing a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent that accounts for the discrepancy between the discrete and continuous dynamics. Using this method, we prove convergence not only of the loss but also of the iterates themselves. In general, convergence of the loss does not imply convergence of the iterates and convergence of the iterates can be difficult to establish [1]. The implicit bias is then identified similarly as in the gradient flow case [11]. However, in comparison to the gradient flow case where the implicit bias is described by a parameterized minimization problem with parameter being the initialization, the parameter of the corresponding optimization problem in the (stochastic) gradient descent case is the initialization modified by a perturbation term that depends on the step size and the full trajectory of the iterates. We characterize the limit as a solution of this perturbed minimization problem and give a bound on the perturbation in terms of the step sizes – showing that the perturbation vanishes when the step sizes go to zero. Similarly as in [11], we relate this minimization problem to a weighted ℓ1\ell_{1}-minimization problem, where the weight depends on the perturbed initialization.

In Section 1.2 we give an overview of the regression problem setting and formally introduce our diagonal linear networks and start with a warm-up on gradient flows for one-layer diagonal networks (Section 2). Our main analysis is presented in Section 3, where we define a suitable perturbed mirror gradient descent. This enables us to establish convergence of the iterates under a suitable (but realistic) bound on the step size. In Section 3.1 we cover the case that all parameter coefficients are initialized positively (and then remain positive throughout training). In Section 3.2 we then extend this analysis to the setting where the linear network is parameterized as a difference of two factorizations. This allows also convergence to vectors with negative entries. Section 4 extends our analysis the deterministic gradient descent to stochastic gradient descent. In Section 5 we relate our characterization of the limit as minimizers of a certain Bregman divergence to a weighted ℓ1\ell_{1}-minimization problem. We conclude by illustrating our results with numerical experiments in Section 6.

papers.title: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) - System Design and Instrumentation
papers.abstract: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is designed to measure cosmic neutrinos in the EeV range through an array of radio antennas detecting nanosecond-long radio flashes. In this contribution, the RNO-G electronic system is outlined, illustrating how signals are measured from the antennas to the recorded pulses. We present new instrumentation developments, focusing on electric melters to install LPDA antennas into the Greenlandic ice sheet. The new system will simplify deployment and reduce positioning uncertainty to $\pm$2cm (x/y) and $\pm$1\deg (rotational). We report on field tests from the RNO-G site at Summit Station.

papers.title: Data-driven Random-feature Approximation of Koopman Generators of Nonlinear Continuous-time Systems
papers.abstract: Learning continuous-time dynamical systems from data is an active area of research. The Koopman formalism is often used here, because it is a flexible approach that is informative about the system's fundamental properties. The formalism represents dynamical systems through linear operators acting on a suitable function space. A practical difficulty arising in the numerical approximation of Koopman operators is the choice of a ``dictionary'', meaning an effective finite-dimensional representation of the function space. In this paper, we focus on learning dynamical systems in continuous-time, and so we consider numerical approximations of the Koopman generator instead of the Koopman operator. Our main contribution is a data-driven random-feature method to obtain a parsimonious and effective function representation for Galerkin approximation methods such as gEDMD. The representation we construct is data-informed, which allows us to improve upon data-agnostic methods. We empirically demonstrate the suitability of our method for forecasting tasks and system analysis. The numerical experiments show that our approach is accurate, and faster than iterative optimization. Further, we prove convergence of our approximation of the vector field and the resulting trajectories. In addition to the numerical results, we also make theoretical contributions, including a general convergence criterion for the semigroup generated by the gEDMD approximation and a counterexample showing that gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness. With our contribution, we advance the frontier of efficiently learning continuous-time dynamics from data, towards interpretable and mathematically robust modelling based on the Koopman framework.

papers.title: Ghosts in the nanomachine: dynamical slowing-down in the phase-space of nanomechanical strings
papers.abstract: The linear behavior of micro- and nanomechanical devices has been the topic of intense study over the past years. Their nonlinear behavior, on the other hand, continues to provide new and interesting dynamics. This work leverages a cavity opto-mechanical system whose very high sensitivity and low dissipation rate allows to capture the dynamics of fast transients that occur when strongly-driven nonlinear resonators relax to their equilibrium state. We experimentally study the ringdown dynamics of a nanomechanical Duffing resonator in both the time domain and in phase space. The resonator exhibits very different ringdown dynamics depending on whether it is subject to one or two tone driving. In the former case the ringdown follows a regular exponential decay, whereas the latter case shows exotic dynamics such as libration, slowing-down while scattering in phase-space, and ghost slowing-down. We demonstrate that this distinct difference can be attributed to the structure of the phase space itself. Surprisingly, we find that the energy in the resonator changes non-monotonously and that long delay between turning off the drive and the decay of the motion amplitude results in dynamical meta-states.

papers.title: Transport in spinful non-Hermitian gauge lattices
papers.abstract: We extend the generalized transfer-matrix method introduced in [H. Ghaemi-Dizicheh, Phys.\ Rev.\ B \textbf{107}, 125155 (2023)] to one-dimensional spinful non-Hermitian tight-binding lattices with matrix-valued Abelian and non-Abelian gauge couplings. We derive a minimal channel-resolved transfer matrix and identify its eigenvalues with the generalized Bloch factors. The same transfer matrix determines the periodic- and open-boundary spectra, generalized Brillouin zone, skin localization, and finite-sample scattering conditions. In the Abelian limit, the model separates into fixed spin sectors, yielding exact spectral results and closed finite-length transport expressions in terms of Chebyshev polynomials. These results reveal bipolar spin-dependent skin localization and distinguish the reciprocal hopping scale, which governs poles, zeros, and reflectionlessness, from the directed-amplification factor controlling transmission asymmetry, transparency, and invisibility. For non-Abelian gauge fields, noncommuting link matrices coherently mix the spin sectors, such that four transfer eigenmodes jointly determine the non-Bloch spectrum and transport eigenchannels. We show that this mixing produces spin-hybridized lasing and coherent-perfect-absorption channels, Zeeman-tunable lasing thresholds, and direction-dependent reflectionless transport accompanied by pronounced spin conversion. The resulting boundary-condition criteria describe lasing, coherent perfect absorption, reflectionlessness, transparency, and invisibility, while identifying spin polarization and conversion as experimentally accessible signatures that distinguish Abelian from non-Abelian non-Hermitian transport.

Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians provide effective descriptions of open and nonconservative systems that exchange probability, energy, or wave intensity with their surroundings [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. In quantum settings, they commonly arise after eliminating environmental degrees of freedom or conditioning the dynamics on selected measurement outcomes [10]. Classical-wave platforms provide particularly flexible realizations, with non-Hermiticity engineered through gain and loss, radiation, feedback, and nonreciprocal couplings in photonic, acoustic, mechanical, and electrical systems [11, 12]. These mechanisms produce complex spectra, exceptional points, nonorthogonal eigenstates, point-gap topology, and boundary sensitivity without direct Hermitian counterparts [13, 14].

A prominent manifestation of this boundary sensitivity is the non-Hermitian skin effect, in which an extensive number of bulk states accumulate exponentially near a boundary [15, 16, 17, 18]. The accompanying spectral rearrangement between periodic and open boundary conditions invalidates conventional Bloch theory in many nonreciprocal lattices. Non-Bloch band theory and the generalized Brillouin zone restore a bulk description by allowing the Bloch factor to acquire a nonunit modulus that accounts for spatial growth or decay [19, 20].

Internal degrees of freedom substantially enrich this connection. Spin, pseudospin, polarization, orbital, and sublattice structure turn scalar hopping amplitudes into matrices and permit synthetic gauge fields to rotate the internal state during propagation. Artificial Abelian and non-Abelian gauge potentials have been developed extensively in cold-atom and photonic settings, where they emulate magnetic fields, spin-orbit interactions, and matrix-valued parallel transport [31, 32, 33, 34, 35]. Commuting gauge links can be diagonalized in a common internal-state basis and reduce the propagation problem to independent channels. Noncommuting links instead mix these channels, so their propagation and scattering eigenstates need not coincide with any fixed spin quantization axis. The combination of matrix-valued gauge fields and non-Hermiticity has recently enabled spectral braiding, spin-selective skin localization, and tunable bipolar and unidirectional accumulation. This interplay is particularly evident in generalized Hatano–Nelson lattices, where synthetic non-Abelian gauge fields generate Hopf-link complex-energy braiding together with tunable bipolar skin modes [36, 37]. More recently, reciprocal non-Abelian couplings have also been shown to produce time-reversal-symmetry-protected ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} skin effects with pseudospin-resolved boundary localization and boundary-controlled conversion from bidirectional to unidirectional accumulation [38]. Spin-dependent Abelian and matrix-valued gauge couplings have produced spin-polarized skin effects, bipolar boundary localization, and magnetic control of the accumulation direction [39]. Recent electrical-circuit realizations have further demonstrated non-Abelian spectral braiding and spin-hybridized skin modes [40, 41]. Related proposals and mechanical implementations have explored time-reversal-protected skin effects and directly measurable non-Abelian gauge observables [38, 42].

papers.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026) has emerged as a promising paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), showing superiority over other post-training paradigms like Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) (e.g., GRPO (Guo et al., 2025)). In OPSD, the same model serves as both student and teacher. The student generates rollout responses, while the teacher provides supervision with access to privileged references, such as reference solutions. Compared with RLVR, OPSD provides dense token-level learning signals beyond sparse outcome rewards. Compared with SFT, it trains on trajectories sampled by the student itself, mitigating the exposure bias (Bengio et al., 2015).

However, these methods adapt at the response level. Although reference exposure may vary across responses, it remains fixed across tokens within each response. In other words, all tokens in a rollout are supervised by the same teacher.

As shown in Figure 2, we preserve a student-generated prefix, allow a candidate teacher to generate a short continuation at a selected token position, and then return control to the student to complete the response. The accuracy gain from this “student-teacher-student” relay over pure student generation serves as a proxy for the teacher preference at that token position. A large gain implies a compatible teacher for that position, while a small gain suggests the opposite. Interestingly, the results are simple, yet clear and compelling. First, teacher preferences differ across tokens, even within the same response. Second, at the token level, majority voting yields a subset of reliable teachers, and the preferred teacher always exhibits a large student-teacher KL distance. The first finding validates our claim, and the second finding motivates a practical rule for token-level teacher selection.

papers.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
papers.abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

papers.title: Seeing Unseen Gravitational Wave Inspirals at the Galactic Center
papers.abstract: The Galactic Center is expected to host a population of extremely large mass-ratio inspirals (X-MRIs) migrating toward the supermassive black hole. We propose an observational approach utilizing the secular gravitational torque exerted by X-MRIs on the highly eccentric S-star S301. This approach is intrinsically limited by the stochastic nature of the surrounding stellar-mass black hole cusp. As S301 propagates through this granular medium, it experiences discrete gravitational encounters. Standard orbital fitting procedures inherently assume a smooth background potential; applying them to stochastic trajectories averages these discrete velocity discontinuities into a continuous secular drift. This introduces a systematic bias that mimics the X-MRI precession signal, invalidating traditional mass estimation techniques. To resolve this degeneracy, we implement a methodology based on the Wavelet Transform Modulus Maxima method to characterize the local H\"older regularity of the orbital motion. This model isolates the singular discontinuities induced by stellar-mass black hole encounters from the continuous torque of the X-MRI distribution, allowing for detection even when instantaneous accelerations are below the instrumental noise threshold. We demonstrate analytically that S301 is highly sensitive to the interior X-MRI population while remaining dynamically decoupled from the secular influence of the exterior cusp. Combining precision astrometry and radial velocity projections, we establish that a minimal population of two X-MRIs is detectable within a five to nine-year timeframe, allowing us to constrain the presence of an unseen orbiter population prior to the launch of space-based gravitational wave detectors.

The center of our galaxy is a dense environment where stars and stellar remnants orbit a supermassive black hole (SMBH), Sgr A*. High-precision monitoring of these stars has already confirmed predictions of General Relativity, such as the Schwarzschild precession of S2 [16, 17]. The highly eccentric S-star S301 [11] is particularly well suited as a probe for this environment. This region is expected to host hidden populations of compact objects. Deep in the gravitational potential, there may be a population of brown dwarfs (BDs) and very low-mass red dwarfs (M-dwarfs near the hydrogen-burning limit) inspiralling toward the SMBH, known as extremely large mass-ratio inspirals [2, 34, 32, 8, 5, 35, 12, 33, X-MRIs,]. Further out, a cusp of stellar-mass black holes (SBHs) is predicted to exist, some in the early phases of inspiral [4, 5, early-stage extreme mass-ratio inspirals, or E-EMRIs,].

papers.title: Thinner Disks Struggle to Launch Jets: GRMHD Simulations of Magnetic Field Generation and Transport
papers.abstract: Relativistic jets are observed in some accreting black-hole systems but not others. In X-ray binaries, jet production is closely associated with geometrically thicker accretion states, suggesting that disk thickness may influence the conditions for jet launching. We investigate this connection using three-dimensional GRMHD simulations of disks with $h/r=0.1$--$0.3$, initialized with a toroidal magnetic field with plasma $\beta=5$. We find that the magnetorotational instability (MRI) generates large-scale poloidal fields through non-axisymmetric shearing waves, with an additional contribution from axisymmetric induction through stretching by channel-like modes. The resulting mean fields become progressively weaker as the disk becomes thinner. Because these fields regulate MRI turbulence, thinner disks exhibit weaker angular-momentum transport and accrete more slowly than the standard $v_{\rm acc}\propto(h/r)^2$ thin-disk scaling would predict. The magnetic-flux transport velocity remains comparable to the accretion velocity, so weaker field generation and slower transport combine to strongly suppress black-hole flux accumulation at smaller $h/r$. Correspondingly, the thinnest disk ($h/r=0.1$) produces an electromagnetic jet efficiency of only $\eta_{\rm{EM}}\sim1\%$, while the thickest disk reaches the magnetically arrested disk (MAD) state and attains $\eta_{\rm{EM}}\geq100\%$. Using the measured large-scale magnetic flux distribution and transport velocities, we estimate the time required to accumulate MAD-level magnetic flux. Only the $h/r\sim0.3$ disk reaches MAD in the duration of our simulations, at $t\simeq2\times10^4\,r_g/c$, whereas for $h/r=0.1$ we estimate a timescale of $\sim10^8\,r_g/c$. These results link disk geometry to magnetic-flux accumulation and jet launching, with direct implications for the timescales over which jets can emerge in transient accreting systems.

papers.intro:
Relativistic jets provide a powerful channel through which accreting black holes release energy and angular momentum, from stellar-mass black holes to supermassive black holes (SMBHs). They accompany some of the most luminous transient events, including gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), whose central engines can arise from compact-object mergers or the collapse of massive stars (Woosley, 1993; Metzger, 2020; Rastinejad et al., 2022). A subset of tidal disruption events (TDEs) also produces powerful relativistic jets (Zauderer et al., 2011; Burrows et al., 2011; Cenko et al., 2012; Pasham et al., 2023), while jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can inject substantial energy into their host galaxies and larger-scale environments (Blandford et al., 2019; Hardcastle and Croston, 2020). Relativistic jets can extract rotational energy from the black hole and drive its spin evolution toward lower values (Lowell et al., 2024; Lowell et al., 2025). Understanding why some accreting black holes launch powerful jets while others do not is therefore a fundamental problem across a wide range of astrophysical systems.

Observations demonstrate that jet production is intimately connected to the state of the accretion flow, but that accretion power alone does not determine whether a jet is present. In X-ray binaries (XRBs), persistent compact jets are associated with the hard state, in which the inner flow is hot and geometrically thick, whereas jets are strongly quenched when the system transitions to the soft, thin-disk state (Done et al., 2007; Fender et al., 2004). Powerful transient ejecta can also accompany these state transitions (Fender et al., 2004). A similar connection between accretion geometry and jet production may extend to AGN, where radio-loud systems are preferentially associated with radiatively inefficient, geometrically thick accretion flows (Narayan and Yi, 1994; Meier, 2001), although only a fraction of AGN are strongly jetted (Padovani, 2011). The connection between inflow and outflow is also reflected in the observed radio–X-ray correlation in hard-state XRBs (Corbel et al., 2003; Gallo et al., 2003; Corbel et al., 2013b) and, after accounting for black-hole mass, in the fundamental plane extending from stellar-mass black holes to AGN (Merloni et al., 2003; Zamaninasab et al., 2014).

Their accretion flows are expected to evolve from initially super-Eddington, geometrically thick configurations toward thinner disks as the fallback and accretion rates decline (Strubbe and Quataert, 2009; Dai et al., 2018). While only a small subset are observed to produce prompt relativistic jets (Zauderer et al., 2011; Burrows et al., 2011; Tchekhovskoy et al., 2014; Pasham et al., 2023), late-time radio observations have revealed outflows launched hundreds to thousands of days after disruption in a broader population of TDEs (Cendes et al., 2022; Cendes et al., 2024). Together, these observations suggest that the structure and geometry of the accretion flow may play a fundamental role in regulating both the formation and timing of relativistic outflows.

Large-scale magnetic flux threading the inner accretion flow and black-hole horizon is required to efficiently extract energy and angular momentum and power a relativistic jet (Blandford and Znajek, 1977; Blandford and Payne, 1982). At the same time, magnetic fields are essential for accretion itself, either by driving turbulence through the magnetorotational instability (MRI) (Balbus and Hawley, 1991; Balbus and Hawley, 1998) or by exerting large-scale magnetic torques on the accretion disk (Blandford and Payne, 1982; Ferreira and Pelletier, 1995).

Thus, if jet launching requires a large-scale organized magnetic field, the accretion flow must not only release gravitational energy but also generate, organize, and transport magnetic flux toward the black hole. The key question is therefore whether the field can form coherent large-scale structures and be advected inward against turbulent diffusion (Lubow et al., 1994; Guilet and Ogilvie, 2012; Begelman, 2024). This question might be related to why systems with similar accretion luminosities can produce very different jet powers, and why individual systems can transition between jetted and unjetted states.

This problem is particularly important because accretion flows do not naturally begin with the coherent vertical magnetic flux required for jet launching, which is commonly imposed in numerical simulations. In dynamically assembled disks, strong shear preferentially amplifies azimuthal magnetic fields, as expected in tidal disruption events and black-hole–neutron-star (BHNS) and binary-neutron-star (BNS) mergers (Bonnerot et al., 2017; Most et al., 2021; Aguilera-Miret et al., 2023). A similar situation arises during AGN disk formation, where the accretion of magnetized intergalactic or interstellar plasma is expected to produce predominantly azimuthal fields rather than coherent vertical flux (Gaburov et al., 2012; Hopkins et al., 2024; Squire et al., 2025; Kaaz et al., 2025). Finally, collapsar events also show an initial toroidal field present after the accretion disk is formed (Chan et al., 2026). Moreover, the progenitors of TDEs and compact-object mergers are not generally expected to supply enough coherent large-scale magnetic flux to account directly for the most powerful observed jets, such as that of Swift J1644+57 (Tchekhovskoy et al., 2014). These systems therefore point toward a common requirement: a mechanism must generate and organize large-scale poloidal magnetic flux from fields that are initially predominantly small-scale and toroidal.

papers.title: Spokes, not a Ring: Revisiting the Weekday Manifold in Language Models
papers.abstract: Recent work has hypothesised that large language models may represent some concepts as multi-dimensional manifolds instead of single directions. Using these manifolds to interpret or steer representations often assumes that moving along them corresponds to a continuous change in the represented concept. In this work, we test this continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday manifold. Despite its striking circular geometry, we find that the weekday representations behave more like seven discrete states arranged in a circle than a continuous ring. First, we show that local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping between representation and behaviour under on-manifold steering. Second, we test whether any concepts are represented along the manifold outside the seven discrete states, and find neither time of day, uncertainty, nor natural text populate the intermediate space. Together, these results challenge the continuous interpretation of the weekday manifold and motivate testing whether movement along other representation manifolds correspond to meaningful changes in model representations and behaviour.
papers.intro:
A growing body of work proposes that some concepts are represented by language models not as single directions in activation space but as low-dimensional geometric structures or manifolds. The canonical example is the days-of-the-week ring: activations for the seven days lie in a low-dimensional subspace and are arranged in calendar order around a circle (Engels et al., 2025; Modell et al., 2025; Wurgaft et al., 2026). Similar geometric structures have been reported for spatio-temporal (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024), numerical (Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025), belief-like (Shai et al., 2024; Sarfati et al., 2026), and many others concepts (Tiblias et al., 2026; Bhalla et al., 2026). The manifold view is appealing because geometry in activation space can reflect semantic relationships between the underlying concept values. For example, real-world relationships between places and times can be recovered from the activation space of language models (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024; Tiblias et al., 2026; Modell et al., 2025).

The canonical example is the days-of-the-week ring: activations for the seven days lie in a low-dimensional subspace and are arranged in calendar order around a circle (Engels et al., 2025; Modell et al., 2025; Wurgaft et al., 2026). Similar geometric structures have been reported for spatio-temporal (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024), numerical (Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025), belief-like (Shai et al., 2024; Sarfati et al., 2026), and many others concepts (Tiblias et al., 2026; Bhalla et al., 2026). The manifold view is appealing because geometry in activation space can reflect semantic relationships between the underlying concept values. For example, real-world relationships between places and times can be recovered from the activation space of language models (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024; Tiblias et al., 2026; Modell et al., 2025).

In practice, however, these geometric structures are inferred from a finite set of observed representations. A continuous manifold is then fit through those points, so the regions between them are determined by interpolation. The interpolated regions may correspond to representations of intermediate concept values, such that semantic structure extends continuously across the manifold. Alternatively, they may simply connect discrete representational states, causing steering along the fitted manifold to pass through activation regions that are geometrically well defined but have no meaningful semantic interpretation. We refer to the assumption that points throughout the manifold correspond to meaningful values of the represented concept as the continuous manifold assumption.

papers.title: 3Dtrees.earth: community research infrastructure for tree and forest analysis using close-range LiDAR data
papers.abstract: From individual trees to forest stands, three-dimensional structure shapes carbon, water, and energy flows, habitat conditions, and resource availability. Yet tree and forest structural attributes remain difficult to assess consistently across space and time. Close-range LiDAR (light detection and ranging) records detailed 3D structure from branches and trees to forest plots, including trees outside forests. However, broader reuse is constrained when data, acquisition context, processing, computation, and access conditions are maintained separately. We present 3Dtrees.earth, an operational community research infrastructure that brings close-range LiDAR datasets, analysis tools, and computing resources together while linking original observations to their metadata and processing outputs. As of 23 October 2026, the platform comprised 2,760 datasets, including 2,481 publicly visible datasets. These point cloud datasets span 46 countries on all six inhabited continents and include terrestrial, mobile, and uncrewed aerial laser scanning. Users can contribute and discover datasets, run standardized processing workflows on shared computing infrastructure, inspect point clouds and model predictions in the browser, and access data and processing outputs together with citation information. Workflows combine rule-based and machine-learning methods, with tools updated as methods advance. Outputs include raster products, individual-tree and semantic segmentation, and tree- and stand-level metrics. Original point clouds and processing records are retained, enabling reprocessing with improved tools while preserving provenance. With broader coverage, curation, and validation, this shared resource could extend individual surveys into a basis for model evaluation and benchmarking, cross-site synthesis, calibration and validation of larger-scale Earth observation products, and macroecological analysis.

papers.intro:
Trees form complex three-dimensional structures in forests, savannas, agricultural landscapes, and urban areas. Forests alone cover roughly a third of the Earth’s land surface, regulate global carbon, water, and energy cycles, and sustain a large share of terrestrial biodiversity (Krieger, 2001; Groombridge and Jenkins, 2002; Pan et al., 2013; Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2020; Santoro et al., 2021). Ecosystem processes in tree-dominated ecosystems are inherently three-dimensional, with structural complexity shaping habitat availability, microclimate, biodiversity, ecosystem fluxes, and resilience to climate change (Ehbrecht et al., 2021; Lines et al., 2022b; Atkins et al., 2023; Schnabel et al., 2025). At the same time, tree mortality, forest degradation, and forest management are altering ecosystem structure (IPBES, 2019; McDowell et al., 2020; Schiefer et al., 2025). Furthermore, climate-driven disturbance regimes are intensifying (Seidl et al., 2017; Mahecha et al., 2024), creating an urgent need to quantify dynamics in tree and forest structure consistently across large areas (International Tree Mortality Network, 2025). However, obtaining comparable structural observations across sites and through time remains challenging (Fassnacht et al., 2024).

Furthermore, climate-driven disturbance regimes are intensifying (Seidl et al., 2017; Mahecha et al., 2024), creating an urgent need to quantify dynamics in tree and forest structure consistently across large areas (International Tree Mortality Network, 2025). However, obtaining comparable structural observations across sites and through time remains challenging (Fassnacht et al., 2024).

Traditional field methods capture that geometry only to a limited extent. Forest inventories provide reference measurements for many forest attributes, but collecting them is labor-intensive, limiting the number of sites that can be surveyed and how frequently measurements can be repeated (Tomppo et al., 2008; Avery and Burkhart, 2015). National forest inventories use country-specific sampling designs, with differing plot sizes, sampling densities, and revisit intervals (Vidal et al., 2016). These designs support inference at broad reporting scales but provide limited resolution in terms of fine-grained spatial variation and short-term structural change (Kandler, 2009; Nesha et al., 2021). Access to exact national forest inventory plot locations is often restricted, which can complicate integration with remote sensing observations (Gessler et al., 2024; Schumacher et al., 2026). Plot locations are also often poorly georeferenced because dense canopies weaken satellite-positioning signals (Maack et al., 2016). Field assessments that rely on expert judgment rather than direct measurement can also be subject to observer bias (Innes, 1988; Bacaro et al., 2026). Therefore, field-based monitoring is limited by the range of structural metrics it can quantify and the sampling error caused by restricted spatial and temporal coverage (McDowell et al., 2020; International Tree Mortality Network, 2025).

Close-range LiDAR (light detection and ranging) fundamentally changes this measurement paradigm: rather than inferring tree structure from a limited set of plot-level measurements, it resolves tree geometry directly in three dimensions. Terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), mobile laser scanning (MLS), and uncrewed aerial laser scanning (ULS) systems detect reflected laser pulses and record up to millions of three-dimensional point coordinates per second. The resulting point clouds reconstruct the explicit three-dimensional geometry of trees and forest stands (Liang et al., 2016; Calders et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2022; Coops et al., 2025), and repeated acquisitions can document structural change over time (Sheppard et al., 2017; Gassilloud et al., 2026). Three-dimensional observations enable detailed estimates of tree dimensions and crown structure (Owen and Lines, 2024), as well as foliage density and biomass (Calders et al., 2015; Béland and Kobayashi, 2021). Close-range LiDAR therefore provides structural variables that are difficult to obtain from conventional surveys (Calders et al., 2015; Béland and Kobayashi, 2021; Puliti et al., 2024; Feigl et al., 2025). These observations complement established forest inventories rather than replace their long-term measurements and sampling frameworks (Fassnacht et al., 2024).

A growing set of methods offers opportunities to translate LiDAR data into quantitative, tree- and stand-level assessments of forest structure and function, as illustrated by a dataset in footnote 1. Separation of leaf and wood points supports estimates of leaf distribution and leaf area index (Brown et al., 2025), while instance segmentation of individual trees (Wielgosz et al., 2024; Xiang et al., 2025) supports forest inventories and the estimation of structural attributes (Puliti et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2024). On delineated instances, species recognition and biomass estimation support biodiversity monitoring and carbon accounting (Calders et al., 2015; Schindler et al., 2023; Puliti et al., 2025; Coops et al., 2025; International Tree Mortality Network, 2025). Reconstructed 3D structure informs radiative-transfer simulations (Frey et al., 2025) and the study of competition for light (Kröner et al., 2026). It also supports microclimate modeling (Schnabel et al., 2025) and the estimation of finer-grained attributes such as tree age (Puliti et al., 2026) and habitat quality (Holland et al., 2024). Within surveyed areas, these methods can enable highly detailed, spatially explicit characterization of individual trees and stands, thereby extending the range of structural attributes accessible through conventional field inventories.

papers.title: The scale of homogeneity in DESI Data Release 1
papers.abstract: We present measurements of the scale of cosmic homogeneity using the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the largest publicly available spectroscopic extragalactic survey to date. Using a counts-in-spheres estimator applied to nearly 5 million galaxies and quasars across six independent redshift bins spanning $0.1 < z < 2.1$, we measure the correlation dimension $D_2(r)$ and define the homogeneity scale $R_H$ as the point at which the galaxy distribution reaches within 1\% of the homogeneous asymptotic value. We find that all tracers clearly transition to homogeneity, with the galaxy homogeneity scale ranging from $93.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}$ to $142.6^{+1.4}_{-1.4}$ $h^{-1}$Mpc depending on the tracer redshift, galaxy bias, and modelling used to extract the scale. Using a cosmology-dependent model, we reconstruct the underlying matter homogeneity scale, finding it decreases monotonically with redshift in excellent agreement with $\Lambda$CDM predictions. We identify a systematic offset of up to $\sim 10\%$ between measurements in the North and South Galactic Caps, largely due to fiber assignment effects reproduced in our simulations. Accounting for this, and with a complementary demonstration using toy models that our methodology correctly identifies inhomogeneous universes in all but rather finely-tuned observer configurations, this hence provides strong evidence in favour of the cosmological principle across our full redshift range. For these reasons, several methods and techniques have been developed to measure the transition to homogeneity, as reflected by the large literature on the subject. Constraints on the anisotropy of the early Universe from CMB, X-ray and radio observations, combined with the Copernican principle (the assumption that we do not live in a special place in the Universe), can be used to infer the homogeneity scale (e.g. Scharf et al. 2000; Blake and Wall 2002; Camacho-Quevedo and Gaztañaga 2022; Shao et al. 2025b). papers.title: Emergent higher-order optical nonlinearity in self-assembled polar supertextures
papers.abstract: Giant optical nonlinearities enable advanced materials control and bridge exotic light-matter phenomena to next-generation photonics. However, materials exhibiting strong higher-order optical nonlinearity beyond the second order are typically rare. Here, we report the discovery of a giant and ultrafast second-harmonic generation (SHG) in self-assembled polar skyrmions under mid-infrared excitations. The transient SHG intensity exhibits a distinctive power dependence originating from higher-order nonlinearity. More generally, we show that large higher-order nonlinearity emerges across diverse domain structures in polar superlattices. Phase-field simulations demonstrate a strong and periodic local permittivity variation within each polar texture at equilibrium, and further confirm the fast polarization oscillation in polar skyrmions with mid-infrared excitations. This intense local permittivity modulation can satisfy epsilon-near-zero conditions, unlocking dramatically enhanced nonlinear optical responses without photonic engineering. Consequently, the self-assembled polar topologies with strong inherent optical nonlinearity could establish a platform for quantum information processing and high-speed optical communications.
