Optical nonlinearityShen (2002); Boyd (2008) has revolutionized material control since the advent of lasers. Materials with strong optical nonlinearities, such as non-centrosymmetric crystals, plasmonic nanostructures, and engineered metamaterials are critical for nonlinear optical applicationsFiebig et al. (2005); Denev et al. (2011); Kauranen and Zayats (2012); Pettine et al. (2024). Second-order nonlinear effects drive frequency doublingFranken et al. (1961); Guyot-Sionnest et al. (1987); Manzoni and Cerullo (2016). Third-order effects enable four-wave mixing including third harmonic generationNew and Ward (1967); Hendry et al. (2010); Yue et al. (2024). Higher-order nonlinear optical phenomena (third order and above) in conventional materials are typically weakShkurinov et al. (1993); Hafez et al. (2018), limiting their utility in integrated photonics. Materials exhibiting strong higher-order optical nonlinearities with short response times are highly desirable for optoelectronic devices that leverage multiphoton interactions and non-degenerate wave mixing processesYue et al. (2024). Such devices, including photonic switches and frequency converters, are critical for applications in quantum information processing, optical remote sensing, and high-speed optical communicationsDutt et al. (2024). However, achieving these properties often requires complex and intricate material engineering. In artificially structured metamaterials and photonic crystals, the strong spatial variation of permittivity from periodically arranged materials enables the epsilon-near-zero condition, thereby greatly enhancing nonlinear optical responseLiberal and Engheta (2017). Alternatively, nanoscale self-assembled polar textures with large optical nonlinearity offer a new route for nanophotonics designSun et al. (2025).

Ferroelectric superlattices have emerged as engineered quantum materials wherein layers of ferroelectric and dielectric materials are stacked periodically at the nanoscale. In superlattices, mechanical constraints, particularly epitaxial strain from lattice mismatch, couple with electrostatic effects arising from polarization discontinuities at ferroelectric-dielectric interfaces. The coupled effects of mechanical and electrostatic boundary conditions modify the local symmetry of ferroelectric unit cells, generating stable self-organized and topologically nontrivial texturesJunquera et al. (2023), including polar skyrmionsDas et al. (2019), polar meronsWang et al. (2020), and polar vorticesYadav et al. (2016). These emergent polar textures host spatially varying unconventional dielectric propertiesZubko et al. (2016); Yadav et al. (2019); Das et al. (2021), and exhibit strong light-matter interactionsStoica et al. (2019); Gao et al. (2024) including sub-terahertz collective modesLi et al. (2021); Wang et al. (2025). The topologically nontrivial polar textures are also highly susceptible to electric fieldsHong and Chen (2018); Nahas et al. (2020); Das et al. (2021); Han et al. (2022); Zhu et al. (2022); Behera et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2024). Under a moderate out-of-plane electric field, the polar skyrmions can be fully polarized to a single cc-domain stateDas et al. (2021); Zhu et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2024), with tens of nanoseconds recovery timeDas et al. (2021). Despite extensive interest in these systems, little is known about their nonlinear light-matter interaction at ultrafast time scales. Potential large optical nonlinearities in polar textures remain a frontier awaiting exploration.

papers.title: Can LLMs Faithfully Solve Ontology Engineering Tasks? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study
papers.abstract: Ontological knowledge underpins large language model (LLM) performance on knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing evaluations of LLMs' ontological understanding largely rely on behavioral correctness, leaving the underlying mechanisms unexplained. Existing mechanistic interpretability work has largely focused on instance-level factual knowledge, leaving ontological knowledge under-explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MIOE, a causal-abstraction benchmark that evaluates interchange interventions for two ontology engineering tasks: entity typing and subsumption prediction. MIOE tests whether learned internal intervention targets can change an ontology-level target answer while preserving class-specific auxiliary information. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, we evaluate SAE-, DBM-, and DAS-based methods, including multi-task and multi-layer variants. Distributed subspace methods give the strongest results and generalize across prompt settings, but the induced changes remain only partially separated from auxiliary class-specific information. Multi-task objectives and contiguous layer-window interventions improve this balance, while class-level analyses reveal substantial variation across ontology classes. These results suggest that ontological predictions are mechanistically accessible in LLMs, although current methods do not yet isolate a cleanly disentangled causal mechanism for ontological knowledge.

Formal ontologies provide schema-level knowledge for many knowledge-intensive tasks in the AI era. They define classes, relations, constraints, and hierarchies that support structured knowledge representation, semantic reasoning, and data integration (Pan et al. 2023). As LLMs become increasingly capable of generating, validating, and revising knowledge, they are also being explored as assistants for ontology engineering tasks, including ontology construction, completion, alignment, and evaluation (Babaei Giglou et al. 2023; Lo et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2025a; Zhang et al. 2025b).

As LLMs become increasingly capable of generating, validating, and revising knowledge, they are also being explored as assistants for ontology engineering tasks, including ontology construction, completion, alignment, and evaluation (Babaei Giglou et al. 2023; Lo et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2025a; Zhang et al. 2025b).

Despite this promise, recent empirical evidence suggests that LLMs still face substantial limitations in ontology engineering. While they can perform well on basic ontology-related tasks (He et al. 2023; Babaei Giglou et al. 2023), their performance remains suboptimal and often unpredictable on more advanced tasks, such as ontology evaluation (Tsaneva et al. 2025). This leaves open a critical question: whether correct ontology-oriented outputs are supported by internal computations that track the relevant ontological relation, and how these computations interact with broader subject information. This raises a concern about faithfulness, defined as the degree to which a model’s output reflects the internal process that produced it (Wiegreffe and Pinter 2019; Jacovi and Goldberg 2020). However, most existing evaluations of LLMs for ontology-related tasks remain behavioral, asking whether the model outputs the correct label, axiom, or judgment under a given prompt. Such evaluations are necessary, but they do not reveal the mechanism by which the answer is produced.

Mechanistic interpretability offers a way to study this problem by connecting high-level variables to causal mechanisms inside the model. Interchange interventions provide a causal abstraction test: they replace internal representations across inputs and examine whether the model’s behavior changes according to the corresponding high-level variable (Geiger et al. 2021; Geiger et al. 2022). Prior work has applied mechanistic interpretability to factual knowledge in LLMs, including the localization, editing, causal role of factual associations, and feature disentanglement (Geva et al. 2022; Dai et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2022; Huang et al. 2024). However, ontological knowledge plays a different role from ordinary factual or attribute-level knowledge. While factual attributes capture local properties of a subject, ontology-level relations determine its type, taxonomic position, and the constraints or properties that are applicable to it. This makes ontological knowledge a distinctive target for mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Neural Explicit Shape Representation
papers.abstract: Existing neural 3D representations separately address continuous surface modeling, efficient image synthesis, or object-specific compression. They do not jointly provide the explicit surface queries required by ray tracing and a structured output space that can be predicted across objects. We introduce NeuOctree, a neural explicit representation that directly predicts whether and where a ray intersects a surface, together with its normal and albedo. NeuOctree stores shared features at the corners of sparse octree voxels and interpolates them into a continuous local field. A lightweight decoder with recurrent intersection-guided sampling refines each query near the predicted surface, enabling direct surface rendering without mesh extraction or texture baking and accommodating open, non-watertight geometry. The same octree structure supports both compact per-object optimization and a shared octree CNN that constructs renderable assets from colored point clouds without per-object fitting. Across seven meshes and four storage budgets, NeuOctree achieves the lowest positional error in 24 of 28 comparisons while retaining competitive normal accuracy, and substantially improves joint geometry--appearance reconstruction over N-BVH and VQAD. The feedforward model constructs a representation in 0.05 seconds and transfers from Objaverse to ShapeNet without retraining. We further demonstrate ray-traced rendering and image-conditioned generation, showing that NeuOctree provides a common output space for neural inference and direct surface rendering. Code is available at https://github.com/octree-nn/neural-octree.

Existing representations address different parts of this problem. Signed distance fields (Park et al., 2019; Chabra et al., 2020) and occupancy fields (Mescheder et al., 2019) encode surfaces as level sets of learned scalar functions. NeRF (Mildenhall et al., 2020) jointly models density and radiance, with hash encodings (Müller et al., 2022) and sparse voxel structures (Yu et al., 2021; Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2020b) reducing the cost of field evaluation and rendering. These advances illustrate the value of compact, spatially organized representations. However, density or occupancy values do not directly specify the intersection and material attributes required by a surface ray tracer: these quantities must be recovered through additional surface localization or geometry extraction.

Features sampled only at a voxel’s boundary may be far from the surface, and rays observing the same surface point can enter the voxel at different locations. We therefore introduce a recurrent sampling strategy that uses predicted intersections to guide subsequent feature queries. This refinement brings queries closer to the surface and encourages rays from different views to access features near the same location. The ablation shows improved intersection and normal accuracy over endpoint-only and uniform sampling.

papers.title: DES-JEPA: Learning a Shared Vocabulary for High-Dimensional Discrete Event Sequences
papers.abstract: Temporal foundation models such as Chronos and TimesFM generalize across domains through a shared numerical observation space. In contrast, discrete event sequences (DESs), including operational event logs or patient clinical-event trajectories, have domain-specific event vocabularies whose labels lack a consistent correspondence across domains. Beyond this lack of consistency, the number of distinct events in real-world settings is high enough to challenge both classical temporal point process modeling and current in-context foundation inference models such as FIM-PP. Critically, current foundation models for DESs are limited to a small, fixed number of event types, restricting their applicability to realistic, high-dimensional event streams. To address this, we propose two complementary modules: (i) DES-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that learns a shared discrete vocabulary from synthetic stochastic processes with unaligned event vocabularies; and (ii) DES-PFN, a discrete event sequence prior-fitted network that reuses the learned vocabulary for in-context next-event prediction. Without task-specific fine-tuning, this framework achieves competitive zero-shot performance on eight unseen real-world datasets and scales up to 700 distinct event types.

papers.title: Simultaneous Gradient Learning in First-Price Auctions
papers.abstract:
We study equilibrium learning in discretized Bayesian games, focusing on first-price auctions as a testbed for gradient-based learning dynamics under private information. While the symmetric independent private values model admits a unique Bayesian correlated equilibrium (BCE) in the continuous limit, standard convergence guarantees for gradient-based learners do not apply: classical no-regret theory predicts convergence only to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), which can remain large and far from the competitive equilibrium even under fine discretizations.
  To bridge this gap, we introduce the notion of Bayesian semicoarse correlated equilibrium (BSCCE), an equilibrium concept that refines BCCE by restricting deviations to probability-preserving transformations consistent with projected gradient dynamics. We provide a linear programming characterization of BSCCE with polynomially many variables and constraints and establish the inclusion hierarchy $BCE \subseteq BSCCE \subseteq BCCE$.
  Our main finding is that the BSCCE set contracts in many cases as the discretization of the Bayesian game is refined. Even with priors for which BCCE fails to concentrate, the diameter of the BSCCE polytope shrinks toward zero, indicating convergence to the unique continuous-game Bayes-Nash equilibrium.
  These results provide a principled explanation for the observed robustness of gradient-based learning in discretized Bayesian games, showing that these dynamics select a smaller equilibrium set than standard no-regret theory predicts.

Learning in multi-agent systems fundamentally differs from single-agent learning: strategy updates are shaped by the adaptation of other agents. As a result, learning dynamics in games need not converge, may cycle, exhibit chaotic behavior, or converge to different outcomes depending on initial conditions. Understanding the subset of games where commonly used learning algorithms converge to meaningful equilibrium predictions remains a central challenge at the intersection of machine learning, optimization, and game theory.

As a result, learning dynamics in games need not converge, may cycle, exhibit chaotic behavior, or converge to different outcomes depending on initial conditions. Understanding the subset of games where commonly used learning algorithms converge to meaningful equilibrium predictions remains a central challenge at the intersection of machine learning, optimization, and game theory.

Somewhat surprisingly, recent papers observe convergence close to the Bayes-Nash equilibria (BNE) in economically relevant Bayesian games (Bichler et al., 2023; Bichler et al., 2021). These methods build on gradient learning, and we will focus on its simplest variant, projected gradient ascent, in this paper.

We will deliberately restrict our attention to first-price single-item auctions. This game is a canonical example used in large-scale applications such as display advertisements. However, despite the uniqueness of the BNE, the empirical convergence of gradient-based algorithms has not yet been fully theoretically justified. Here, we aim to provide an explanation for the convergence of projected gradient ascent in first-price auctions under increasingly finer discretizations. The BSCCE, however, is a broader concept and can be applied to all games with private information.

While it is known that Nash equilibria are equilibria of the resulting dynamical system, strong assumptions, including strict monotonicity, are usually needed to guarantee uniqueness and the convergence of the dynamics to such an equilibrium in last-iterate, independent of initial conditions (Mertikopoulos and Zhou, 2018; Zhang and Nagurney, 1995). Similarly, Lyapunov-function-based arguments can be used to show stability (Mertikopoulos and Sandholm, 2016). In general, the dynamics of a game may also cycle, prohibiting last-iterate convergence statements in general.

Formally, BSCCE extends the notion of Semicoarse Correlated Equilibrium (SCCE), originally developed for complete-information games (Ahunbay and Bichler, 2025), to Bayesian settings. However, this extension must be handled carefully, as the strategic normal form of a Bayesian game is exponential in the number of types. Thus, applying the SCCE to the strategic normal form is computationally infeasible. In contrast, our approach is based on the partial Bayesian approach Forges (1993), which allows a polynomial characterization of BSCCE in terms of the game size and thus makes BSCCE tractable in discretized games.

papers.title: The Alpha--Omega Problem in the Assessments of Atmospheric Power
papers.abstract: Atmospheric power is commonly assessed with two Lorenz-cycle formulations treated as equivalent: the $\alpha\omega$ formulation, yielding gas expansion power $W_\omega$, and the $\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla z$ formulation, yielding kinetic-energy generation by horizontal pressure gradients, $W_K$. We show that, for a statistically stationary global moist atmosphere, $W_\omega=W_K+W_P+W_{\rm nh}$, where $W_P$ is the power of lifting precipitating water and $W_{\rm nh}$ is power associated with departures from gas-phase hydrostatic balance. Since $W_P\simeq1$ W m$^{-2}$ globally, equality would require $W_{\rm nh}\simeq-W_P<0$, so the associated vertical force imbalance would have to do negative work globally. Using six-hourly ERA5, JRA-3Q, and MERRA-2 fields for 2025, we find that resolved $W_\omega$ varies by a factor of 1.7 (1.9--3.2 W m$^{-2}$), versus 1.2 for $W_K$ (2.4--2.8 W m$^{-2}$). Zonal-mean $\alpha\omega$ profiles have area-weighted contributions near $\pm50$ W m$^{-2}$, making global $W_\omega$ a cancellation residual, whereas $\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla z$ profiles vary much less with latitude. The difference $W_\omega-W_K$ ranges from $-0.61$ to $+0.87$ W m$^{-2}$. Thus reanalysis-derived $W_\omega$ cannot provide an independent constraint on atmospheric power. Two treatments of the omitted surface layer give cross-reanalysis mean $W_K$ of 2.8 and 3.1 W m$^{-2}$, with corrected values spanning 2.6--3.5 W m$^{-2}$. Both exceed the observation-based Lorenz available-potential-energy generation estimate of 1.2 W m$^{-2}$. Assuming $W_{\rm nh}\geq0$, adding $W_P\simeq1$ W m$^{-2}$ gives total atmospheric power of about 3.8--4.1 W m$^{-2}$, motivating investigation of additional power-generation mechanisms.

papers.title: GRAVITY-RESOLVE: A comprehensive image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations with GRAVITY
papers.abstract: We aim to improve and extend the imaging capabilities of the GRAVITY beam combiner instrument of ESOs VLTI with respect to reconstruction software in the Galactic Center. We revise and develop the image reconstruction code GRAVITY-RESOLVE $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, which has been specifically developed to reconstruct stars in the Galactic Center with GRAVITY. The main objectives are to increase the limiting magnitude in GRAVITY images, reduce its computational runtime, and allow for a joint reconstruction of multiple, spatially separate datasets/pointings on sky. We apply $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ to recent GRAVITY data, featuring the implemented GRAVITY-faint mode as part of GRAVITY+, the upgrade of GRAVITY. We reconstruct visibility phases and amplitudes and present the first GRAVITY image reconstructed with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ from these quantities. We demonstrate NIR mosaicking with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ by jointly reconstructing nine separately acquired datasets of 2025 into a single image on a scale of $\simeq 3390\ \text{AU}\times 3390\ \text{AU}$, corresponding to $409.6\ \text{mas}\times 409.6\ \text{mas}$. With dedicated injection tests of point sources into GRAVITY data, we estimate the limiting magnitude to be $m_{\text{K}}\ \simeq\ 20.0$ within a radius of $25\ \text{mas}$ around the field center when reconstructing from closure phases and visibility amplitudes. We report on the discovery of two new faint stars in the Galactic Center: S303 and S304. Finally, we find a decrease in computational runtime by a factor of at least $\sim10$. With $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, we demonstrate GRAVITYs capabilities for NIR imaging. We show that $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ is a fast, precise, and deep image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations, enabling the discovery of even more faint stars.

papers.intro:
The Galactic Center (GC) is a unique environment to test general relativity in the gravitational potential of a supermassive black hole (SMBH) due to its proximity compared to other galactic nuclei (Genzel et al., 2010). The GC’s SMBH SgrA* is enshrouded in an isotropic cluster of S-stars on eccentric orbits (Gillessen et al., 2017). Astrometry and radial velocity measurements of the orbits of the S-stars yielded a precise measurement of the distance and mass to/of SgrA* (GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2024; Abuter et al., 2022; Abuter et al., 2019; Do et al., 2019; Gillessen et al., 2017; Boehle et al., 2016) and have delivered an upper bound of the enclosed mass of down to ∼1200​M⊙{\sim}1200\ M_{\odot} within the orbit of S2 at 1​σ1\sigma confidence (GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2024; Abuter et al., 2022). Moreover, the S-stars can also serve as test particles to probe effects beyond Newtonian gravity (Zucker et al., 2006; Weinberg et al., 2005; Rubilar and Eckart, 2001; Jaroszynski, 1998). One of the brightest members of this cluster, S2, is particularly prone to effects of General Relativity due to its comparably eccentric orbit and short semi-major axis (Grould et al., 2017). With S2, two post-Newtonian (PN) effects have been detected with the interferometric beam combiner instrument GRAVITY (Abuter et al., 2017) of ESO’s VLTI (Schöller, 2007). By closely monitoring the proper motion of S2 during its pericenter passage with GRAVITY’s unmatched astrometric precision (Abuter et al., 2017), the Schwarzschild precession in the orbit of S2 (Abuter et al., 2022; Abuter et al., 2020b), the gravitational redshift along with the relativistic transverse Doppler effect (GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2018), have been detected with high significance. S2 also delivered the first test of Einstein’s equivalence principle in the gravitational field of a SMBH (GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2019). According to the no-hair theorem, a stationary black hole (BH) is characterized by its mass, spin, and electric charge (Israel, 1967, e.g.). Since the mass of SgrA* has been constrained across the past three decades with ever-increasing accuracy and precision (Haller et al., 1996; Eckart and Genzel, 1996; Genzel et al., 1996; Eckart and Genzel, 1997; Genzel et al., 1997; Ghez et al., 1998; Schödel et al., 2002; Schödel et al., 2003; Ghez et al., 2003; Ghez et al., 2005; Eisenhauer et al., 2005; Ghez et al., 2008; Gillessen et al., 2009b; Gillessen et al., 2009a; Boehle et al., 2016; Gillessen et al., 2017; Do et al., 2019; Abuter et al., 2019; Abuter et al., 2022), the next step is to constrain the BH’s spin. The "Eigenrotation" of a BH induces 1.5 PN order corrections to the PN expansion of the equations of motion and effectively shifts both the orbit as well as the orbital plane of circling bodies, resulting in a precession, known as Lense-Thirring precession (Alexander, 2005; Lense and Thirring, 1918) (hereafter LT-precession). The star S2 is, in theory, susceptible to this effect, but its minute LT-precession is out of reach of current facilities or would only be detectable in long-term observing campaigns after multiple revolutions of its orbit (Grould et al., 2017). Additionally, stars and stellar remnants could imitate this precession by means of vector resonant relaxation (Merritt et al., 2010; Rauch and Tremaine, 1996). Moreover, the LT-precession drops as ∝r−3\propto r^{-3} with distance rr to the central massive object (Will, 2008). To measure the spin, hence, requires the discovery of stars that are orbiting closer to SgrA*. To find new, yet undiscovered, faint stars in the GC, which offer potentially closer pericenter distances, image reconstruction of interferometric data is the tool of choice. Interferometric imaging, in both radio and near-infrared (NIR) wavelength regimes, is a powerful approach as the limitations of single-aperture imaging are overcome. The size of a synthesized aperture array is only limited by its infrastructure, allowing to achieve almost arbitrarily high spatial resolutions. The multitude of science cases to which interferometric imaging can be applied led to an entire plethora of image reconstruction methods that have emerged over the past decades. Pioneered by developments in radio interferometry (Abuter et al., 2021b; Greisen, 2003; Högbom, 1974) and fostered by an imaging contest (Lawson et al., 2004, e.g.), a number of reconstruction codes in NIR interferometry have been introduced. Most of optical/NIR interferometry reconstruction software is general purpose, i.e. can be applied to a wide variety of objects and comprise ORGANIC (Claes et al., 2020), IRBis (Hofmann et al., 2014), SQUEEZE (Baron et al., 2010), MIRA (Thiébaut, 2008), MACIM (Ireland et al., 2006), WISARD (Le Besnerais et al., 2008), and BSMEM (Buscher, 1994), while other tools like SPARCO (Kluska et al., 2014), and ROTIR (Martinez et al., 2021), SURFING (Roettenbacher et al., 2016), are focused on reconstructing Young Stellar Objects and stellar surfaces, respectively. In this work, we present a comprehensive revision, update, and extension of the image reconstruction method GRAVITY-RESOLVE11 1 GRAVITY-RESOLVE is available at: https://gitlab.mpcdf.mpg.de/mpe/ir/gravity-resolveGR\text{G}^{\text{R}} (GRAVITY Collaboration et al., 2022) and give a new upper limit of the limiting magnitude of GRAVITY in the Galactic Center. In Section 2 we outline the revised model of the Galactic Center implemented in GR\text{G}^{\text{R}}. Furthermore, we describe a method for reconstructing a mosaic of spatially separated datasets. In Section 3, we give an overview of the GRAVITY data, which is used for reconstructing complex visibilities, the demonstration of the mosaicking approach, and a performance test of GR\text{G}^{\text{R}} in Section 4. Finally, in Section 5 we discuss the results and give concluding remarks in Section 6.

papers.title: Episodic Plasma Flows and Coronal Brightenings in an Arch Filament System Observed with SUNRISE III
papers.abstract: Emerging flux regions (EFRs) transport magnetic flux and release energy in the solar atmosphere, often hosting arch filament systems (AFSs). We present high-resolution observations of an EFR obtained with Sunrise III, combining the Tunable Magnetograph (TuMag), the Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared Spectro-Polarimeter (SCIP), and the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The dataset follows an AFS continuously for nearly four hours. Line-of-sight (LOS) velocities derived from the Mg I b$_2$ line reveal three episodic plasma-flow events, with downflows reaching approximately 17 km s$^{-1}$ at the footpoints and enhanced upflows near the loop tops. Although this pattern agrees with the classical emergence and draining scenario, the strongest upflows and downflows occur nearly simultaneously. Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) observations at 304 and 171 Angstrom reveal transient extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) brightenings in the surrounding emerging system. Some occur during enhanced-flow episodes, while others do not, indicating that the temporal correspondence is not systematic. Multiline spectropolarimetric inversions reveal temperatures between approximately 4000 and 10,000 K and a smooth variation of magnetic field inclination along a representative AFS loop. Non-force-free-field extrapolations provide the large-scale magnetic context of the low-lying AFS loops and surrounding coronal structures. Together, the observations reveal a spatially and temporally complex evolution without establishing a direct causal connection between local plasma-flow enhancements and EUV brightenings.

papers.intro:
Emerging flux regions (EFRs) are the main manifestation of the process by which magnetic fields rise from the solar interior into the solar atmosphere, leading to the formation of active regions and driving a wide range of dynamic phenomena [42, 64, 11, 10]. As magnetic flux emerges in the form of rising Ω\Omega-loops, it leads to the formation of structured magnetic configurations and associated plasma flows in the overlying atmosphere [37]. In the chromosphere, this process is commonly observed as arch filament systems (AFSs), consisting of bundles of dark fibrils connecting opposite magnetic polarities and tracing the evolution of newly emerging loops [7, 8, 18, 20]. These structures are highly dynamic, exhibiting upflows at loop tops and strong, often supersonic, downflows at their footpoints, which reflect plasma drainage along magnetic field lines [55, 32, 33, 61, 19, 58]. This basic dynamical picture was already established by classical observations of AFSs. In particular, Chou and Zirin [12] showed that individual arch filaments are short-lived structures that rise while plasma drains toward their footpoints, and derived characteristic velocities and thermodynamic properties of the cool material. Later, the comprehensive multiwavelength study of Malherbe et al. [36] combined high-resolution Hα\alpha spectroscopy, photospheric magnetic measurements, magnetic-field extrapolations, and Yohkoh X-ray observations, showing that short-lived chromospheric arches continuously reform within a longer-lived AFS and coexist with hotter coronal loops. Their analysis also emphasized the complex magnetic connectivity of emerging systems and the still unresolved relation between flux emergence and heating of the overlying atmosphere.

High-resolution observations have further demonstrated that magnetic flux emergence is considerably more complex than the smooth rise of a single large-scale Ω\Omega-loop. The Flare Genesis Experiment provided an important step in this direction. Bernasconi et al. [4] identified moving dipolar features embedded in nearly horizontal emerging fields and interpreted them as U-shaped portions of flux ropes that remained anchored in the photosphere by dense plasma. Building on these observations, Pariat et al. [41] showed that emerging magnetic structures can develop a serpentine topology composed of successive Ω\Omega- and U-shaped segments. In their scenario, the upper portions of undulatory flux tubes emerge through magnetic buoyancy, while reconnection at bald patches and their associated separatrices allows dipped portions of the field to progressively emerge. This picture suggests that AFSs and the overlying coronal loops may develop through the progressive emergence and reconnection of such undulatory magnetic structures rather than through the rise of a single coherent loop system.

Although the basic plasma-flow pattern of AFSs and the complex, fragmented nature of magnetic flux emergence are therefore well established, the temporal connection between individual episodes of enhanced plasma motion within an AFS and transient energy release in the overlying atmosphere remains much less constrained. Previous observations have demonstrated that cool AFS structures can coexist with hotter coronal loops [36, e.g.,], but establishing how short-lived changes in the chromospheric plasma dynamics are related to brightenings at transition-region and coronal temperatures requires sufficiently long and continuous observations. The employed data combine spectropolarimetric measurements from the photosphere to the chromosphere with complementary extreme ultraviolet (EUV) observations from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly [34, AIA;] onboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory [43, SDO;]. The combination of high spatial resolution, multiline diagnostics, and continuous temporal coverage over nearly four hours allows us to follow the evolution of the AFS over a time interval substantially longer than the lifetime of an individual arch filament and to identify recurrent episodes of enhanced plasma activity.

These observations enable us to simultaneously investigate the evolution of the magnetic and thermodynamic properties inferred from spectropolarimetric inversions, together with the plasma motions derived from Doppler measurements. In particular, we use the long Mg I b2 time series to follow the LOS velocities in representative loop-top and footpoint regions of the part of the AFS where the strongest dynamical episodes occur. The nearly four-hour sequence reveals three distinct episodes of enhanced plasma flows, while contemporaneous AIA observations provide the higher-atmospheric context of the emerging system and reveal transient EUV brightenings during its evolution. Our aim is therefore not to revisit the well-established presence of upflows at AFS loop tops and downflows at their footpoints, but to characterize the episodic temporal behavior of these flows within the broader multilayer evolution of the emerging region.

papers.title: Shock detection in meshless finite mass hydrodynamic schemes
papers.abstract: Shocks are prevalent in a multitude of astrophysical plasmas. They are essential in the dissipation of gravitational potential energy during structure formation, where they channel it into heat, turbulence, magnetic fields, and particle acceleration. Accurately capturing shocks in simulations of cosmological structure formation is a considerable challenge, due to the complexity of overlapping and colliding shocks, embedded in a medium experiencing complex shear flows. Fully Lagrangian hydrodynamical methods have historically been inferior in this regard compared to Eulerian or pseudo-Lagrangian methods. This work aims to remedy this discrepancy. We present the first efforts to implement a shockfinder algorithm with shock surface reconstruction for meshless finite mass (MFM) hydrodynamic schemes. We show its accuracy compared to analytic predictions and a legacy smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH)- based shock-finding method. We apply this new shock-finding method to simulations of cosmic structure formation to obtain improved predictions for shock energy dissipation and cosmic ray (CR) acceleration.

papers.intro:
Shocks are the primary energy dissipation channel in most astrophysical systems. In cosmic structure formation, they dissipate the potential gravitational energy which is freed in the process of hierarchical merging of substructures [e.g. 22, for a review]. This heats the intracluster medium (ICM) to temperatures of kB​T≈keVk_{B}T\approx\mathrm{keV} [e.g. 11, 53, for reviews], injects turbulent energy into the system, which leads to the amplification of magnetic fields [e.g. 18, for a review], and accelerates electrons (and likely protons) to relativistic energies [e.g. 19, for a review]. On smaller scales, within the interstellar medium (ISM), shocks are driven by supernova (SN) explosions, which leads to local heating of the ISM, contributing to its multi-phase nature [60, 47, 57, 37, 51, e.g.], the (re-) distribution of metals [58, 91, 50, 52, 86, e.g.], and to the injection of turbulence [e.g. 59, 33, for reviews], magnetic field amplification [5, 38, 70, 35, e.g.] and the acceleration of cosmic rays [CRs, e.g. 9, 10, 71, for reviews].

Within (magneto-) hydrodynamic simulations of cosmic structure formation, accurate shock capturing is one of the key proving grounds of any hydro solver [87, 81, 82, 21, 77, 30, e.g.]. On top of the accurate capture of the shock physics within the chosen hydro scheme, an additional complexity arises when trying to identify the location of shocks within the simulation. This is especially relevant in the highly complex simulations of cosmic structure formation, where the continuous merging of structures, active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity, or SNe drive complex, often overlapping shock waves [15, 56].

Various astrophysical codes have found solutions to this problem, each tailored to the underlying hydro scheme, but sharing common design choices and yielding similar results [see 90, for a comparison]. Most commonly, the shock capturing follows three fundamental steps: • Identify a local pressure, temperature, or density gradient, and use it to construct a potential shock normal. • Calculate the local up- and downstream properties along the shock normal and evaluate the Rankine-Hugoniot (RH) conditions. • Filter out spurious detections by applying a number of filters on the selected shock candidates.

This was first used for the detection of shocks in post-processing of simulation snapshots by Keshet et al. [49] and Hoeft et al. [43].

The first implementation for on-the-fly shock detection using this method was presented by Pfrommer et al. [67]. They derived an analytic description (supported by empirical modeling on shock tubes) for the entropy jump a SPH particle can experience per timestep as it passes through a numerically broadened shock. This results in an equation that can be solved via root-finding methods. To circumvent the numerical broadening, they define a decay time and record the maximum Mach number that is captured during this time interval as the sonic Mach number of the shock.

An alternative shock-finding scheme for SPH was introduced by Beck et al. [6], who used an SPH kernel-based approach to compute the up- and downstream quantities fed into the RH conditions. In this method, a pressure gradient within the kernel of a particle is constructed and identified as a potential shock normal. Neighboring particles are then projected onto this shock normal, sorted into up- and downstream according to their projected position, and weighted according to the inverted kernel of the central particle. Subsequent projection of the particles onto two axes perpendicular to the shock normal and standard kernel weighting shapes the evaluation weight into what can be imagined as a top- and bottom-heavy cylinder. The up- and downstream weighted quantities are then used to compute a shock speed from the RH jump conditions (if the temperature and density jumps clear high-pass filters), which together with the upstream sound speed estimate gives a value for the sonic Mach number of the shock. However, all these SPH schemes are susceptible to numerical broadening across the SPH kernel and reliant on accurate capturing of SPH gradients [46, 7].

papers.title: Guidance List for repOrting Bibliometric AnaLyses (GLOBAL): A Reporting Guideline Informed by a Two-Round Modified Delphi Study
papers.abstract: Background: Despite the growth of bibliometric analyses, few studies offer guidance on how to report them, resulting in a lack of research transparency and completeness. To address this gap, we developed the Guidance List for the repOrting of Bibliometric AnaLyses (GLOBAL). Methods: An initial list of items for the GLOBAL was generated through a scoping review and refined through a modified two-round Delphi, as recommended by the EQUATOR Network. The guideline was finalized through a pilot test, where participants assessed their manuscripts using the checklist and Elaboration and Explanation (E&E) document, which outlines item expectations and provides examples. Results: The scoping review resulted in 32 items. In Round 1, 24 items reached consensus and thematic content analysis resulted in one additional item. This item, along with the eight items that did not reach consensus, were discussed in detail in Round 2. During the in-person meeting, one item was split into two, totalling ten voting items. Eight out of ten items reached consensus, five for inclusion and three for exclusion. Conclusions: The finalized 28-item GLOBAL (and its accompanying E&E document) provides users with a framework to report bibliometric analyses, aimed at promoting high-quality reporting of bibliometric analyses in scholarly literature.

papers.title: A 211K Parameter Foundation Model: Genetic Prompting in Neural Cellular Automata
papers.abstract: The scale of modern foundation models enables broad task generalization. In medical imaging, where segmentation demands vary widely across clinical contexts, such flexibility is invaluable. But current models, such as SAM trade adaptability for scale, locking their utility behind high-end infrastructure and leaving behind the low-resource environments most in need of diagnostic support. To bridge this gap, we introduce Foundational-NCA, a lightweight foundation model capable of adapting to a wide range of medical segmentation tasks without retraining. Built on Neural Cellular Automata (NCA), Foundational-NCA incorporates gradient-based learning with genetic optimization over a latent task space, using a compact task vector to guide predictions. This enables dynamic adaptation via a genetic prompt mechanism, allowing the model to generalize across tasks while keeping the parameter count magnitudes lower at just 211 thousand, compared to SAM-based models with 38.9 to 636 million parameters. We evaluate Foundational-NCA on 15 trained and 6 entirely unseen segmentation tasks from the TotalSegmentator dataset, achieving an average Dice score of 84.5% on known tasks and 60.4% on unseen ones. These results demonstrate that task generalization is possible in ultra-compact models, laying the groundwork for resource-efficient, deployable foundation models in clinical environments where infrastructure is limited. By reducing model size by over 180 times, Foundational-NCA takes a step toward a more equitable future for medical AI, one where powerful tools are within reach of every healthcare setting.

papers.intro:
The rise of foundation models has marked a shift from task-specific tools to scalable, unified systems capable of broad generalization. In medical imaging, this versatility promises transformative improvements in diagnostics and patient care [29], enabling accurate, scalable segmentation across clinical contexts. Yet, the immense computational scale of these systems, typically involving hundreds of millions of parameters, restricts their deployment to high-resource environments [1]. Consequently, their substantial benefits remain inaccessible precisely in regions where advanced AI could make the greatest difference: low-resource healthcare settings, such as low and middle-income countries with critical shortages of medical personnel [4, 7, 16, 18, 21].

In this work, we introduce Foundational-NCA, the first NCA-based foundation model capable of adapting dynamically across multiple segmentation tasks via prompt-based conditioning. Central to our approach is a compact, continuous task vector, optimized using genetic algorithms (GA) [27] to encode specific segmentation objectives. This task vector modulates the NCA’s update dynamics at each step, allowing a single fixed model to perform diverse segmentation tasks without any weight modifications (Figure 1). By integrating genetic optimization for task conditioning with gradient-based training of model parameters, Foundational-NCA generalizes effectively across 15 trained anatomical targets and demonstrates promising adaptability to 6 entirely unseen segmentation tasks, delivering foundation-level versatility with only 211K parameters.

papers.title: OneScene-Bench: Do Vision-Language Models Integrate Evidence Across Views?
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly process multiple views of the same scene, but it remains unclear whether they integrate these observations into a coherent scene-level representation. Existing multi-image evaluations do not isolate this capability, as tasks may admit correct solutions through independent per-view processing without requiring cross-view correspondence. We introduce OneScene-Bench, a controlled benchmark designed to explicitly distinguish when cross-view integration is necessary. Our benchmark evaluates three complementary capabilities on real-world multi-view scenes: unique object counting, cross-view consistency, and spatial reasoning. For counting, we control object overlap across views to separate cases solvable by simple per-view aggregation from those requiring instance-level correspondence. For consistency, we introduce localized edits in shared and view-specific regions, testing whether models distinguish genuine scene contradictions from differences caused by viewpoint and visibility. For spatial reasoning, we construct object relations that require combining spatial evidence across viewpoints to compare physical proximity. We evaluate twelve state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary VLMs and find that counting accuracy drops substantially on complementary views, ranging from 4.5-50.0%, compared with 45.5-81.5% on complete-overlap examples. Moreover, cross-view consistency remains around 50% across models, including recent proprietary VLMs, despite substantially stronger performance on spatial reasoning. Our results reveal a substantial gap between processing multiple images and integrating evidence across them, highlighting the need for evaluations that explicitly test scene-level multi-view understanding. Code and data are available at https://github.com/swathisuhas/OneScene-Bench.

papers.intro:
Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly support multiple images as input, enabling them to reason over different observations of the same physical scene. Unlike generic multi-image understanding, multi-view scene understanding requires models to recognize repeated objects across viewpoints, account for viewpoint-dependent visibility, and combine complementary observations into a coherent representation of the scene. These capabilities are particularly important in embodied settings such as robotics and autonomous systems, where an agent observes the same environment from multiple viewpoints but must reason about it as a single scene.

These capabilities are particularly important in embodied settings such as robotics and autonomous systems, where an agent observes the same environment from multiple viewpoints but must reason about it as a single scene.

However, multi-view input does not necessarily imply multi-view reasoning. Consider counting unique objects across two views. A model should recognize repeated instances across viewpoints and count each physical object only once. Yet when both views contain the same objects, or one contains only a subset of the other, taking the larger per-view count gives the correct answer. When each view contains instances not visible in the other, the model must instead determine which objects are shared to recover the total. A model with scene-level understanding should correctly integrate information across different configurations, regardless of how objects are distributed across the views. This reveals a fundamental ambiguity in multi-view evaluation: a correct answer does not necessarily show cross-view integration. Recent benchmarks evaluate reasoning across multiple images and viewpoints in diverse environments [8, 18, 37, 42]. However, these evaluations do not explicitly distinguish between predictions that require cross-view integration and those that can be solved through independent per-view processing. As a result, strong benchmark performance does not necessarily mean that a model has integrated and correctly linked information across views. A reliable evaluation must therefore control whether cross-view integration is actually necessary to obtain the correct answer.

papers.title: IMPACT: Constraint-Aware Search for Imperfectly Factorized Accelerator Mappings
papers.abstract: The efficiency of Deep Neural Network (DNN) accelerators depends on how each tensor operation is mapped onto the hardware. A mapping specifies how the computation is tiled across the memory hierarchy, ordered, and parallelized across the processing elements. These choices form a combinatorially large search space, where efficient mappings are hard to find. Most violate hardware constraints, and most remaining mappings underutilize the hardware. Existing mappers either search only part of this space to keep the search tractable, excluding the most efficient mappings, or sample the full space randomly, so most mappings they evaluate are infeasible. We present IMPACT, a mapper that searches the full space. IMPACT pairs a genetic algorithm with a constraint-aware repair operator that converts each infeasible mapping into a feasible one instead of discarding it. On a flexible accelerator, IMPACT outperforms state-of-the-art mappers in EDP, latency, and energy on every DeepBench workload. On a compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerator, whose constraints leave few mappings feasible, it reduces EDP by 66%, latency by 47%, and energy by 18% over the strongest prior mapper across five networks, and rivals hand-crafted expert mappings. Across flexible and highly constrained accelerators, IMPACT finds efficient mappings automatically. IMPACT will be released as open source.

papers.intro:
DNN workloads are dominated by tensor operations, such as convolutions and matrix multiplications, that demand extreme compute throughput and memory bandwidth (Sze et al., 2017; Sevilla et al., 2022). DNN accelerators meet these demands with arrays of processing elements (PEs) that compute in parallel, and a hierarchy of memory buffers that keep data close to the PEs to maximize reuse (Jouppi et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2016). These buffers, however, hold only a small fraction of data at a time, so the computation must be split into tiles that fit each memory level and distributed across the PEs. Executing an operation therefore requires assigning the computation to the hardware: how large a tile each level holds for each dimension of the operation (tiling factors), how many PEs process each dimension in parallel (spatial unrolling), the order each level steps through its tiles (loop order), and which tensors each level retains (keep/bypass). This assignment is called a mapping. Once the hardware is fixed, the mapping determines how effectively its resources are used. Two mappings of the same operation can produce very different memory traffic and PE utilization, and thus may differ by orders of magnitude in latency and energy(Parashar et al., 2019; Horeni et al., 2022).

Selecting the best mapping is a combinatorial optimization problem. Because every choice is made per dimension and memory level, the number of possible mappings grows exponentially with both; for a single convolution on a realistic accelerator, the search space contains at least 102010^{20} candidates (Parashar et al., 2019). Most of these candidates are infeasible, because every choice must simultaneously satisfy every hardware constraint, such as buffer capacities and PE array dimensions. The feasible mappings, therefore, are only a small part of this larger space, yet too large to enumerate, and they are not equally efficient. A spatial unrolling that occupies only part of the PE array leaves the remaining PEs idle, and tiling factors that capture little reuse force the same data to be re-fetched, inflating latency and energy (Chen et al., 2017; Horowitz, 2014). Efficient mappings are therefore a small fraction of the already small feasible subspace. As a result, an effective mapper must satisfy three requirements. It must search the entire space, isolate the feasible subspace, and identify the most efficient mappings within it.

It must search the entire space, isolate the feasible subspace, and identify the most efficient mappings within it.

Existing mappers meet these requirements only in part. Timeloop (Parashar et al., 2019) and ZigZag (Mei et al., 2021) restrict the space to tiling factors and spatial unrollings that perfectly divide the tensor dimensions, and randomly sample the reduced search space. SALSA (Jung et al., 2023) restricts it further, fixing the spatial unrolling as input and annealing over loop orderings and tiling factors. This reduced space, however, excludes the most efficient mappings: when the tensor dimensions and the PE array are misaligned, the mappings that fill the array are exactly those excluded, and they remain out of reach however long the reduced space is searched. GAMMA (Kao and Krishna, 2020) searches the same reduced space with a genetic algorithm, but its operators recombine mappings without regard for hardware constraints, so it spends most evaluations on infeasible offspring. Ruby (Horeni et al., 2022) expands the space, extending Timeloop’s model with tiles and spatial unrollings that need not divide the tensor dimensions, recovering utilization the other mappers sacrifice. However, Ruby samples the expanded space randomly, with no mechanism to only search within the feasible subspace, so nearly all its evaluations are spent on mappings that are infeasible. In short, the most efficient mappings are either excluded to keep the search tractable, or admitted into a space that no existing search can navigate. papers.title: Weighted Tur\'an densities for hypergraphs
papers.abstract:
Bondy and Tuza generalized the Tur\'an problem for graphs to weighted graphs. Subsequently, F\"uredi and K\"undgen gave a solution in the case of cliques. We consider the weighted Tur\'an problem on hypergraphs and prove the first tight asymptotic result for 3-uniform hypergraphs. Specifically, we determine the weighted Tur\'an density of the generalized triangle $F_5 = \{abc, abd, cde\}$. We also prove weighted stability results and exact results.
  Many intriguing open problems remain, the most tantalizing of which is to determine the weighted Tur\'an density of the tetrahedron. Bounds for this density using flag algebras are presented.

A central problem in extremal combinatorics is to determine the maximum number of edges in an FF-free graph on nn vertices. This is called the Turán number of FF, and it is denoted by ex⁡(n,F)\ex(n,F). The asymptotic behavior is given by the Turán density, denoted π⁡(F)=limn→∞ex⁡(n,F)/(n2)\pi(F)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\ex(n,F)/\binom{n}{2}. Much is known in the graph setting. For example, the Turán numbers of complete graphs are determined by Turán’s Theorem [11]. Furthermore, for all non-bipartite graphs FF, the Turán densities are given by the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits Theorem [2, 3].

papers.title: On the well-posedness of a certain model with mixed diffusion appearing in the mathematical biology
papers.abstract: The work deals with establishing the global well-posedness in the space $W^{(1,2),2}(R^{2}\times R^{+})$ of the integro-differential equation in the space of two dimensions in the situation when the diffusion term involves the standard Laplace operator in one direction and the fractional Laplacian in another direction in the presence of the drift term. Such model is relevant to the cell population dynamics in the Mathematical Biology. The proof is based on a fixed point technique.

papers.title: A universal relation predicts the observed reversal of a supernova chirp
papers.abstract: Superluminous supernovae, among the brightest stellar explosions, are thought to be powered by newborn magnetars. One such event, SN 2024afav, ``chirped'', displaying sinusoidal, increasing-frequency ($P(99\textrm{ d})\sim39\pm8$ d to $P(166\textrm{ d})\sim17\pm5$ d) light-curve modulations. The model explaining this chirp, a precessing disk falling onto the dimming magnetar, generalizes to a normalization-independent universal relation between the period derivative and the dimming rate of the light curve. Applied to the published chirp alone, with the spin-down time measured from the unmodulated light curve, the relation predicts that the chirp must halt near $t \approx 150$ d and reverse. With continued follow-up of SN 2024afav, we report the discovery of five new modulations in which the chirp reverses ($P(177\textrm{ d})\sim24\pm4$ d to $P(208\textrm{ d})\sim38\pm2$ d) at $t=147\pm3$ d, as predicted. Applied to chirping events from upcoming surveys, the relation could identify the precession mechanism and disk physics of each engine.

papers.title: MRC-MMAgent: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Role Collaboration in Multimodal Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal tool-using agents augment vision-language models with access to external information and capabilities, enabling them to solve knowledge-intensive and visually complex tasks that cannot be addressed using visual context alone. However, existing reinforcement learning pipelines largely train single-role agents to search and answer using terminal rewards, overlooking how humans inspect retrieved evidence, reformulate queries, and revise conclusions during search. Consequently, they fail to optimize this self-corrective process over complete interaction trajectories. We propose MRC-MMAgent, a multi-role collaborative reinforcement learning framework that incorporates trajectory assessment and continuation directly into the executable agent loop. First, the framework establishes a multi-role collaborative loop that integrates solving, inspection, and continuation, enabling the agent to acquire evidence through tools, evaluate the preceding trajectory, and resume problem solving when the current answer is insufficiently supported. Second, we introduce a role-coupled learning objective that combines task success, interaction validity, and successful correction with full-trajectory policy optimization across the decisions generated by all roles. Extensive experiments show that, using only the original baseline training set without constructing additional datasets, our method consistently outperforms the corresponding base models and achieves leading or highly competitive performance across benchmarks.
papers.intro:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Liu et al. 2024; Chen et al. 2024b; Liu et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2024a) have rapidly improved on perception, recognition, and visual question answering, yet many user questions cannot be answered from images alone. Multimodal agents address this limitation by coupling a foundation model with tools such as reverse image search, text search, region zooming, and retrieval (Chen et al. 2022; Chen et al. 2024a; Yu et al. 2024; Hu et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2024b). Systems such as MMSearch-R1, WebWatcher, DeepEyes2 optimize tool-augmented policies for multimodal search and visual question answering (Wu et al. 2025; Geng et al. 2025; Hong et al. 2025). SenseNova-MARS (Chng et al. 2025) further constructs high-resolution multimodal agent data and proposes BN-GSPO for training autonomous tool-using VLMs. These methods establish Reinforcement Learning (RL) as a foundation for developing agents’ core tool-use capabilities.

However, prevailing RL formulations train multimodal tool agents as single-role solvers under terminal-answer supervision, leaving a critical control process weakly supervised. This formulation has two limitations: its single-role design lacks a dedicated mechanism for evidence assessment and continuation control, while terminal-only rewards fail to jointly optimize assessment, control, and revision across the full trajectory. First, as illustrated in Figure 3, a single agent loop may retrieve relevant snippets and still answer based on the wrong comparison basis, they lack an explicit, trainable mechanism that connects evidence assessment with trajectory control, making it difficult to identify under-supported answers and initiate targeted continuation. Second, as shown in the "reflection" part of Figure 3, where we insert the inspection stage into the solver’s loop, the reflection merely repeats or rationalizes the initial reasoning. Mirroring human information seeking, the agent assesses the preceding solution trajectory, finalizes the answer when it is sufficiently supported, and otherwise resumes tool use to refine its reasoning and revise the answer. This conditional assessment-and-continuation process closes the loop over the entire interaction, highlighting the importance of full-trajectory optimization for reliable reasoning.

Mirroring human information seeking, the agent assesses the preceding solution trajectory, finalizes the answer when it is sufficiently supported, and otherwise resumes tool use to refine its reasoning and revise the answer. This conditional assessment-and-continuation process closes the loop over the entire interaction, highlighting the importance of full-trajectory optimization for reliable reasoning.

To address these limitations, we propose a multi-role collaborative reinforcement learning framework for multimodal tool agents. First, we organize solving, inspection, and continuation as role-specific behaviors within a unified executable loop. The solver gathers external evidence and proposes a candidate answer, while the inspector assesses whether the accumulated visual–textual observations support it. If the evidence is sufficient, the rollout terminates; otherwise, the Inspector returns control to the solver for targeted tool use and revision. This design turns evidence assessment into a trainable control decision and enables all roles to co-adapt within a shared policy. Second, we formulate a role-coupled learning objective. We define behavioral rewards tailored to solving, inspection, and continuation, and aggregate them into a trajectory-level reward. Full-trajectory GRPO applies the aggregated reward signal to all role decisions rather than confining each role-specific signal to its corresponding role, thereby coupling optimization across the complete trajectory. Theoretical analysis and controlled ablations validate both the reward and optimization designs. Using only the MMSearch-R1 training set, with no additional supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trajectories or RL data, our method improves upon the base model by 11.1 points. Extensive experiments show that, without constructing any extra datasets, our method consistently outperforms the corresponding base models and achieves leading or highly competitive performance across search-intensive and visually complex benchmarks. Our contributions are: • We propose a multi-role collaborative reinforcement learning framework that organizes solving, trajectory inspection, and continuation within a unified executable loop, enabling evidence-conditioned finalization and targeted recovery in multimodal tool use. • We formulate a role-coupled learning objective that combines a trajectory reward for task success, interaction validity, calibrated finalization, and effective correction with full-trajectory over all generated role decisions. • Across diverse multimodal benchmarks, our method delivers consistent gains over its base models and leading or competitive results among same-scale systems, without auxiliary SFT trajectories or additional training data.

papers.title: The Disk Awakens: IXPE's Sequel Observation of GS 1354-64 Suggests Changing-Look Behavior in the Steep-Power-Law State
papers.abstract: After decades of only failed transitions, the black hole X-ray binary GS 1354-64 has undergone a complete outburst again. We present its first X-ray polarimetric investigation in the fading steep-power-law (SPL) state, following an earlier intermediate-state IXPE campaign during the same outburst. The 2-8 keV emission has a polarization degree (PD) of 2.3 +/- 0.2% and polarization angle (PA) of 5 +/- 3 degrees. Compared with the intermediate state, where PD=3.9 +0.3/-0.2% and PA=-2 +/-2 degrees, the broadband PD is lower while the PA remains consistent. The intermediate-state type-C quasi-periodic oscillation state has also disappeared, marking a major reconfiguration of the accretion flow. Assuming a distance of 7 kpc, the observed the intensity drop from 2.5% to 1.6% of the Eddington luminosity over 10.2 days is punctuated by several broad hour-to-day-scale troughs, tracing two distinct tracks in hardness-intensity space. Simultaneous spectroscopy shows the troughs' spectra contains a cooler disk with smaller apparent normalization, while no change in the Compton component's photon index or normalization is required between tracks. The model-independent analysis identifies a steeper increase in PD with energy outside the troughs, yielding G_E=1.5 +/- 0.2%/keV, compared with G_E=0.7 +0.3/-0.5%/keV during the troughs. Their duration and spectropolarimetric morphology distinguish the troughs from traditional short absorption dips seen in X-ray binaries, providing a possible stellar-mass analog of the recurrent accretion changes that drive "changing-look" behavior in supermassive black hole systems.

papers.intro:
Black hole X-ray binaries (BHXBs) serve as dynamic laboratories of accretion, changing their luminosity, spectral shape, and rapid variability as they traverse a sequence of characteristic X-ray states [71, 17]. During a canonical outburst, a source generally rises into a luminous hard state dominated by Comptonized emission from a hot inner flow or corona, passes through one or more intermediate states, and enters into a thermal-dominant soft state or a steep power-law (SPL; historically, very-high) state [53, 71, 17]. The SPL state is characterized by the coexistence of substantial thermal-disk emission and a steep Comptonized tail (commonly with photon index Γ≳2.4\Gamma\gtrsim 2.4) together with substantially weaker broadband variability than in the hard and hard-intermediate states. The SPL state can exhibit QPOs and moderate rapid variability, but its timing properties span a broader range than those of the thermal-dominant state [53, 71].

During a canonical outburst, a source generally rises into a luminous hard state dominated by Comptonized emission from a hot inner flow or corona, passes through one or more intermediate states, and enters into a thermal-dominant soft state or a steep power-law (SPL; historically, very-high) state [53, 71, 17]. The SPL state is characterized by the coexistence of substantial thermal-disk emission and a steep Comptonized tail (commonly with photon index Γ≳2.4\Gamma\gtrsim 2.4) together with substantially weaker broadband variability than in the hard and hard-intermediate states. The SPL state can exhibit QPOs and moderate rapid variability, but its timing properties span a broader range than those of the thermal-dominant state [53, 71].

The hard-to-soft transition may be accompanied by transient relativistic ejections, and once the source is in a disk-bright state, broadband X-ray variability is generally reduced and the compact, steady radio jet is quenched. Changes in the geometry of the accretion disk and corona are also inferred [24, 28, 71, 17]. Although this broad phenomenology is well established, how the inner disk and corona reconfigure during state transitions and what drives substantial variability within nominally stable states remain uncertain.

The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) [79, 93] provides a new view of this evolution by measuring the linear polarization of X-rays in the 2–8 keV band. The polarization degree (PD) and polarization angle (PA) depend on the geometry and orientation of the emitting and scattering regions, providing complementary diagnostics to X-ray spectroscopy and timing. In hard and intermediate states, the IXPE band is often dominated by Comptonized emission whose polarization can constrain the shape and orientation of the corona [39, 89, 30, 23].

In SPL states, IXPE probes radiation emerging from the optically thick accretion disk alongside a substantial steep Comptonized component, making the observed polarization signal sensitive both to the intrinsic disk signal and its dilution or modification by coronal scattering. Classical models of thermal disk polarization assume a plane-parallel, pure electron-scattering atmosphere with photon sources at its base [14, 78, 70]. In this case, the PD depends primarily on inclination. However, absorption in partially ionized plasma and distributed photon sources can significantly alter this picture [42, 46, 87]. General and special relativistic effects modify the local polarization signatures by rotation of PA, resulting in PD reduction [81, 15, 18]. Because higher-energy disk photons preferentially originate at smaller radii, these effects are expected to produce energy-dependent polarization signatures that encode the structure of the innermost disk. Black hole spin influences this signal by setting the location of the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) and therefore dictating the magnitude of the PD reduction and PA rotation effects, as well as controlling the strength of returning radiation—photons that are bent back onto the disk and scatter before reaching the observer [76, 77]. X-ray polarimetry in disk-bright soft and SPL states can therefore complement continuum-fitting and reflection measurements of black-hole spin while testing assumptions about disk thickness, atmospheric scattering, coronal geometry, and alignment of the innermost disk [52, 72, 54].

The growing sample of disk-bright BHXBs observed by IXPE reveals remarkable diversity. In 4U 1957++115, a soft-state polarization signal at the few-percent level has been interpreted in the context of relativistic disk models as evidence for a rapidly spinning black hole under the assumed system geometry [49]. The soft-state transient 4U 1630−-47 exhibited a much larger PD, approaching ∼8%\sim 8\%, together with a pronounced increase with energy, motivating interpretations involving a highly inclined disk, an extended scattering atmosphere, potential departures from a standard geometrically thin disk, and considerable disk-wind contributions to the observed polarimetric properties [66]. A subsequent IXPE observation of 4U 1630−-47 in the SPL state likewise measured a large PD that increased strongly with energy while the PA remained approximately constant, demonstrating that pronounced energy-dependent polarization can persist when substantial thermal-disk emission coexists with a steep Comptonized component [75]. The low-inclination LMC X-1 produced an upper limit of 1%1\% PD when observed by IXPE, while the higher-inclination LMC X-3 showed a low, few-percent PD consistent with an energy-independent PA, and consistent with relativistic disk calculations for its low spin [86]. These observations demonstrate how the range of polarimetric morphology present among disk-bright sources can reflect differences in inclination, disk structure, returning radiation, and geometry of the residual Comptonized component.

Multi-epoch IXPE observations have also begun to trace how polarization evolves across accretion-state transitions. In the persistent BHXB Cygnus X-1, the hard state shows a PD of approximately 4%4\% with a PA aligned with the radio jet, favoring a corona extended in the plane of the disk [39]. In the soft state, the PD decreases while the PA remains broadly stable, consistent with an increasing contribution from thermal disk emission [83, 38]. Similarly, during the 2023–2024 outburst of Swift J1727.8−-1613, IXPE followed the source from the hard and intermediate states into the soft state and subsequently toward the returning hard state [89, 85, 30, 63]. Its PD fell from ∼3\sim 3–4%4\% in the hard state to below ∼1%\sim 1\% as the thermal disk came to dominate, before the hard-state PD returned during the soft-to-hard transition. IXPE additionally observed GX 339−-4 during the soft-intermediate and soft states of its 2023–2024 outburst, detecting polarization during the soft-intermediate observation but obtaining only an upper limit in the soft state [50]. These campaigns establish that PD responds sensitively to state evolution, but often lack insight into the PA evolution across state transition, as significant disk-bright polarization has not previously been reported for a transient BHXB that was also observed polarimetrically in a harder state of the same outburst.

papers.title: SymKL: A Unified Representation-Space Measure of Signal Degradation
papers.abstract: Quantifying degradation between a pristine signal and its degraded observation is fundamental to signal processing, yet existing full-reference measures are inherently modality-specific. We introduce SymKL, a unified full-reference degradation measure based on implicit neural representations (INRs). An INR is fitted once to the pristine reference and characterized by its diagonal Fisher information, which captures the local information geometry of the learned representation. Evaluating the Fisher information with the pristine reference and a degraded observation yields two parameter-sensitivity profiles whose symmetric KL divergence defines the degradation score. The proposed formulation requires only the reference and degraded observation, without knowledge of the corruption process or degradation severity, making it applicable across images, audio, and 3D data. We further derive an exact closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher of SIREN, enabling efficient computation. Experiments on image, speech, and volumetric 3D benchmarks demonstrate that SymKL accurately tracks degradation severity, remains monotonic where conventional metrics saturate or fail, and provides a unified modality-agnostic measure of signal degradation. Code will be made publicly available after the review process.
papers.intro:
Signal degradation is an inevitable consequence of acquisition, transmission, compression, and reconstruction processes, making its accurate quantification a fundamental problem in signal processing. Reliable measures of reconstruction fidelity are indispensable for developing restoration algorithms, benchmarking competing methods, and evaluating reconstruction quality across a wide range of applications. Consequently, numerous degradation measures have been developed for different signal modalities. Images are commonly evaluated using pixel-fidelity measures such as PSNR (Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari 2008), structural similarity measures including SSIM (Nilsson and Akenine-Möller 2020) and MS-SSIM (Rouse and Hemami 2008), and learned perceptual measures such as LPIPS (Zhang et al. 2018b) and DreamSim (Fu et al. 2023). Audio quality is typically assessed using signal-fidelity measures including SNR (Johnson 2006) and SI-SDR (Le Roux et al. 2019), together with perceptual measures such as PESQ (Rix et al. 2001) and STOI (Zhang et al. 2018a), while 3D representations are commonly evaluated using geometric measures such as Chamfer Distance (Wu et al. 2021), Intersection-over-Union (IoU) (Zhou et al. 2019), and the F-score (Tatarchenko et al. 2019). Collectively, these measures have become the standard tools for evaluating reconstruction quality within their respective domains.

Despite their success, these methods have largely evolved independently for different signal modalities and are built upon fundamentally different representations and similarity criteria. Image domain measures compare pixels, structural statistics, or learned visual features, audio measures evaluate waveform fidelity or perceptual intelligibility, while geometric measures assess spatial correspondence between shapes. Consequently, different modalities require fundamentally different degradation algorithms, each tailored to the characteristics of its underlying representation. Moreover, even within a single modality, the response of existing measures may become progressively less informative over parts of the degradation spectrum. For example, on the non-eccentricity distortion of KADID-10k (Lin et al. 2019), increasing the number of displaced image patches by a factor of five changes CLIP (Radford et al. 2021) similarity by less than 1%1\% (from 0.9980.998 to 0.9900.990), while the visual distortion increases substantially. A similar phenomenon can be observed in 3D geometry, where the mesh F-score collapses to zero once the surface displacement exceeds its matching tolerance, despite geometric differences continuing to increase thereafter (See Supplementary). These observations motivate a fundamental question, is there a unified representation in which signal degradation can be characterized consistently across different modalities while preserving sensitivity to distortion severity?

Implicit neural representations (INRs) provide a promising foundation for addressing this question. Rather than representing signals as pixels, waveform samples, or geometric primitives, INRs learn continuous functions from discrete observations using a common coordinate-based neural network formulation. The same representation has been successfully applied to images, audio, videos, occupancy fields, signed-distance fields, neural radiance fields, and many other signal modalities. Unlike conventional degradation measures, which require different algorithms for different data types, INRs provide a unified representation capable of modeling a broad range of signals (Essakine et al. 2024; Jayasundara and Patel 2026). This naturally leads to the central question of this work, how is signal degradation encoded within this shared neural representation?

Directly comparing INR parameters is uninformative because different parameters contribute unequally to representing the signal. Instead, SymKL compares their functional importance, quantified by the Fisher information (Ly et al. 2017), which measures the sensitivity of the reconstruction objective to parameter perturbations. A reference INR is fitted once to the pristine signal and then frozen. Evaluating its Fisher information using the pristine and degraded observations yields two parameter-sensitivity profiles whose discrepancy defines a modality-agnostic representation-space measure of degradation (see Figure 1).This naturally raises the question of why we characterize the representation using the Fisher information rather than gradients or the Hessian. The mean gradient vanishes near a fitted solution and therefore provides little information about the learned representation, while the Hessian, although capturing second-order curvature, can be computationally prohibitive for large INRs. The Fisher information retains the required second-order information while for SIREN networks, admits the exact closed-form expression.
