Making the SymKL framework practical requires overcoming two computational challenges. Computing Fisher information through conventional automatic differentiation can be prohibitively expensive for large INRs. We therefore derive an exact closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher information of SIREN networks (Sitzmann et al. 2020), reducing the computation to efficient matrix operations while preserving exactness. In addition, fitting a high-quality INR independently for every reference signal is computationally demanding. To address this limitation, we develop an amortized fitting framework based on a hypernetwork (Chauhan et al. 2024) with first-order MAML (Nichol et al. 2018) adaptation that rapidly produces accurate reference representations using only a small number of optimization steps. Finally, we introduce a physically grounded evaluation protocol that compares heterogeneous degradation measures according to their responsiveness to continuously varying physical distortion severity. Extensive experiments on natural images, audio, occupancy fields, and medical imaging demonstrate that the SymKL consistently tracks degradation severity, remains discriminative in regimes where conventional degradation measures become less informative, and substantially outperforms alternative weight-space characterizations.

papers.title: Non-Asymptotic Confidence Regions for Separable Nonlinear Models
papers.abstract: This paper studies robust uncertainty quantification for separable nonlinear least squares (SNLLS) problems. We propose two identification methods, (i) Residual-Perturbed Gradient (RPG) and (ii) Global-Fit-Gap (GFG), to construct joint distribution-free confidence regions for both the linear and nonlinear parameters. By exploiting assumed group invariance of the noise (such as symmetry or exchangeability), we apply random perturbations (such as sign-changes or permutations) to build the regions based on resampling and ranking. We prove that both methods guarantee non-asymptotically exact coverage (type I error). Finally, we illustrate the constructions through two numerical experiments: (i) identifying generalized finite impulse response (GFIR) systems using Laguerre polynomials with an adjustable decay rate and (ii) fitting Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) models with variable knots and widths.

Many inverse problems arising in machine learning, system identification, and signal and image processing can be formulated as separable nonlinear least-squares (SNLLS) problems [1]. In these models, the parameters can be naturally partitioned into a nonlinear component and a linear component. Typically, the nonlinear parameters form a relatively small set with direct physical interpretation, such as absorption coefficients, dominant frequencies, or phases, while the linear parameters correspond to coefficients associated with basis functions or system responses.

Typically, the nonlinear parameters form a relatively small set with direct physical interpretation, such as absorption coefficients, dominant frequencies, or phases, while the linear parameters correspond to coefficients associated with basis functions or system responses.

A widely used approach for solving SNLLS problems is the variable projection (VP) method [2], which reduces the dimensionality of the search space and transforms the original problem into a lower-dimensional nonlinear optimization problem that is often easier to solve and numerically more stable. VP methods are particularly attractive for a wide range of inverse problems [3], including time-series prediction using RBF-ARX models [4], frequency identification [5], blind image deconvolution, and image denoising [1]. Non-smooth [6, 7] and large-scale [8] extensions have only recently been considered, further highlighting the potential of the SNLLS framework and the VP approach.

Golub and Pereyra showed that the gradient of the VP objective functional can be computed explicitly [2], which has attracted considerable attention from the machine learning community. In particular, the VP algorithm can be used to train feedforward neural networks [9]. Recently, this approach has been generalized to non-quadratic objectives, allowing VP-based training of neural networks for tasks including segmentation and classification [10]. The VP operator has also been used as an activation mechanism that integrates domain knowledge into network architectures through a layer-wise SNLLS formulation of the target problem [11].

Despite its critical importance, there are very few methods that address the issue of constructing confidence regions around VP estimates. Currently, the prevailing general solution relies on the asymptotic distribution of the scaled estimation error [12, 13]. However, ensuring the existence of the limiting distribution is nontrivial for complex nonlinear structures [14]. The Residual-Perturbed Gradient (RPG) method is computationally efficient, but it might capture artifacts. papers.title: Evaluation of attenuation-based simulated X-ray images for image-guided radiotherapy
papers.abstract: In image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT), in-room X-rays are often used for patient positioning and monitoring, however, usually default imaging settings are utilized for each indication. Obtaining patient-specific imaging settings before treatment is achievable using simulated X-rays, which can facilitate IGRT workflow optimization. This study evaluated the image quality of simulated X-rays for thoracic, cranial and pelvic regions. Simulated X-rays were created from computed tomography (CT) scans with indication-specific default settings using a pre-release pilot software, which mimics the geometry of the room-mounted ExacTrac Dynamic (ETD) system (Brainlab SE, Germany). The basis of this algorithm was the Beer-Lambert law. Linear attenuation coefficients were approximated from the CT hounsfield units, while incident intensities were defined by flood images. CT scans were included from three anthropomorphic phantoms and 57 patients (13 lung, 20 glioblastoma, 24 prostate). For evaluation, real X-rays were used as ground truth. Three image quality metrics - Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC), Normalized Mean Absolute Error (NMAE) - complemented by histogram and intensity profile comparisons were used for evaluation. SSIMs for phantom and patient average were 0.87 and 0.80 for the thoracic, 0.94 and 0.88 for the cranial and 0.85 and 0.79 for the pelvic region. Corresponding NCCs yielded values of 0.99 and 0.89, 0.99 and 0.99 and 0.99 and 0.60. NMAEs were 4.1% and 10.7% (lung), 2.6% and 3.2% (brain) and 2.6% and 4.0% (pelvis). Histograms of real X-rays and simulated X-rays (sX-rays) were slightly shifted and showed differences at the background pixel value. Intensity profiles exhibited similar trends with some differences in absolute values. The investigated simulated X-rays demonstrated promising quality for individualized IGRT treatment preparation.

papers.intro:
In image-guided radiation therapy (IGRT), in-room X-rays are frequently utilized for daily patient positioning and monitoring, to ensure target coverage during treatment.1 Typically, indication-specific default imaging settings are used for X-ray acquisition regardless of the patient dimensions and classical digitally reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) serve as reference images for daily positioning.2 Classical DRRs are calculated as the exponential of the line integral of the linear attenuation coefficients along each CT projection ray, but are not calibrated to the imaging energy of the simulated X‑ray system.3 This limits their usability for direct comparison to clinical X-rays acquired during treatment as well as pre-treatment imaging setting optimization.

In X-ray imaging varying patient dimensions require different imaging settings for optimal visualization of the anatomy.4, 5 Patient-specific imaging optimization can therefore lead to an improvement of the IGRT workflow by increasing the information content of the intra-treatment X-rays, while reducing the imaging dose in accordance with the As Low As Reasonably Achievable (ALARA) principle. This is especially relevant for patients receiving multi-fraction treatment courses or intra-fractional imaging.6, 7 By accurately simulating the imaging system, optimized settings could be established during treatment preparation via simulated X-rays (sX-rays). Such sX-rays provide closer resemblance to the acquired X-rays than classical DRRs and have therefore the potential to improve both X-ray-based patient positioning and monitoring.

papers.title: Detection of HNCOH+ in the interstellar medium
papers.abstract: Only five out of the $\sim$350 molecules detected in the interstellar medium (ISM) carry the isocyanate functional group (NCO), the essential substructure of peptide bonds in proteins. Among them are isocyanic acid (HNCO) and its most stable N-protonated isomer H$_2$NCO$^+$. Previous studies have predicted that the O-protonated isomer HNCOH$^+$ should be present in the ISM; yet this species has remained elusive. We search for the metastable HNCOH$^+$ towards the Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027, where H$_2$NCO$^+$ has already been detected. We use an ultra-deep broadband spectral survey carried out towards G+0.693-0.027 with the Yebes 40-m, IRAM 30-m and APEX telescopes covering nearly 150 GHz of bandwidth between 31 and 275 GHz. We report the first detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM with a column density of $N$ = (9.9 $\pm$ 0.5)$\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, which corresponds to a molecular abundance relative to H$_2$ of (7.3$^{+1.3} _{-1.0}$)$\times$10$^{-11}$. With the measured H$_2$NCO$^+$ column density of $N$ = (2.6 $\pm$ 0.3) $\times 10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, this yields a HNCOH$^+$/H$_2$NCO$^+$ ratio of 3.8$^{+0.5} _{-0.4}$. This result is consistent with recent kinetic calculations that favour the formation of HNCOH$^+$ over H$_2$NCO$^+$. The detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM broadens the inventory of molecules known to contain the isocyanate functional group and reinforces recent works showing that isomer abundances in the ISM do not necessarily correlate with thermodynamic stability.

papers.intro:
A substantial number of molecules detected in space can be assembled from only the four elements H, C, N, and O. These elements constitute the fundamental building blocks of organic and prebiotic chemistry and, when arranged appropriately, give rise to key functional groups such as carboxyl (-COOH) and amino (-NH2), present in biologically relevant molecules such as amino acids. Alternatively, they can link together forming a peptide bond –C(=O)–N(–H)–, enabling the formation of large proteins (Marcelino et al., 2018). The detection of simple molecules containing the isocyanate group (-N=C=O) in the interstellar medium (ISM) is particularly significant, as they may offer insight into the earliest chemical steps leading to peptide synthesis.

HNCO exhibits several metastable isomers in the singlet ground electronic state: HOCN, HCNO, and HONC, which lie at 24.7, 70.7, and 84.1 kcal mol-1 (12430, 35578, and 42321 K) above HNCO, respectively (Schuurman et al., 2004). These species can be formed through a variety of chemical pathways. In the gas phase, the protonation and subsequent hydrogenation of the radicals NCO and CNO yield the protonated [C,H,N,O] ions, including H2NCO+, HNCOH+, HCNOH+, H2OCN+, and H2CNO+ (Marcelino et al., 2010; Quan et al., 2010; Quénard et al., 2018; Hochlaf et al., 2026). By dissociative recombination (DR) reactions, these ions produce all the [C,H,N,O] isomers, among them HONC, the highest-energy isomer, which has not yet been detected in space (Marcelino et al., 2018).

Quantum-chemical calculations reveal that the N-protonated variant of isocyanic acid, H2NCO+, is the global minimum, followed by the O-protonated variant HNCOH+ (Lattanzi et al., 2012; Hochlaf et al., 2026, 18 kcal mol-1, ∼\sim9060 K;). Furthermore, Murakami et al. (2024) investigated the thermal rate coefficients and branching ratios for the gas-phase reactions H+3{}_{3}^{+} + HNCO →\rightarrow H2 + HNCOH+/H2NCO+ which is expected to be one of the main pathways for forming these species, since protonation by H+3{}_{3}^{+} in the ISM has been shown to be one of the most efficient mechanisms (Oka, 2006). Their calculations showed that the channel leading to HNCOH+ is favoured over the formation of H2NCO+, with branching ratios of ∼\sim80% and ∼\sim20%, respectively. These results are consistent with laboratory rotational spectroscopy measurements, which reveal that the abundance of HNCOH+ in the original Fourier-transform microwave spectroscopy (FTMW) study is twice that of H2NCO+ (Lattanzi et al., 2012). Moreover, the proton-affinity-induced isomerisation from the meta-stable HNCOH+ to the stable H2NCO+ is unlikely to occur due to the substantial high barrier (Ijjaali et al., 2001, 100 kcal mol-1, ∼\sim50320 K;) between them. Despite this, only H2NCO+ has been detected in the ISM (Marcelino et al., 2018; Rodríguez-Almeida et al., 2021). Therefore, the detection of HNCOH+ yields a key step that had been missing in our understanding of the interstellar chemistry of HNCO and its protonated isomers.

These results are consistent with laboratory rotational spectroscopy measurements, which reveal that the abundance of HNCOH+ in the original Fourier-transform microwave spectroscopy (FTMW) study is twice that of H2NCO+ (Lattanzi et al., 2012). Moreover, the proton-affinity-induced isomerisation from the meta-stable HNCOH+ to the stable H2NCO+ is unlikely to occur due to the substantial high barrier (Ijjaali et al., 2001, 100 kcal mol-1, ∼\sim50320 K;) between them. Therefore, the detection of HNCOH+ yields a key step that had been missing in our understanding of the interstellar chemistry of HNCO and its protonated isomers.

In this Letter, we report the first detection of HNCOH+ in the ISM towards the Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027 (hereafter, G+0.693), a source known for its exceptionally rich chemistry driven by large-scale shocks, likely induced by a cloud–cloud collision (Zeng et al., 2020). These shocks efficiently sputter material from both the icy mantles and refractory cores of dust grains, injecting large amounts of molecular material into the gas phase. As a result, G+0.693 stands out as one of the most prolific astronomical environments for identifying new interstellar molecules.

papers.title: Practical Assessment of Agentic Systems in Acoustics
papers.abstract: In engineering, applications of artificial intelligence have so far been largely limited to surrogate models and optimization tasks. Large language models changed this, as they can write software from a task given in words. Placed inside a harness, a system of components that lets it search for information and execute software, such a model becomes an agent that can take over recurring engineering tasks. This work measures how the model and the elements of the harness shape the performance and behavior of the agent in two common acoustic applications. In the first, the agent detects and locates faults in audio recordings from a vehicle interior with near-perfect accuracy. A benchmark on this task shows that a weak model sets a limit that no harness design can overcome, and that design choices take effect only once the model is capable enough to use them. In the second, a case study on the design of a metamaterial unit cell, the agent reliably finds designs that achieve a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range. The results aim to help the reader understand what each element of an agent contributes and how to design an agent for acoustic tasks.

When applied like this they are often referred to as machine learning and are well established in acoustics (Cunha et al., 2023; Schmid et al., 2024; Bianco et al., 2019). Recent developments in the field of large language models (LLM) allow artificial intelligence to interpret complex texts and to write pieces of software independently. Given a task, the model relies on the user for additional information and it is not able to take actions with the information that is generated by it. An agent can therefore write and execute software on its own, and by this take over or support recurring engineering tasks. Ready-made pieces of software that the agent can invoke are referred to as skills.

papers.title: Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract:
Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations.
  Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.

papers.intro:
Emerging in-memory and neuromorphic computing systems, particularly those based on memristive crossbar arrays, are becoming a key paradigm for energy-efficient edge intelligence (Ielmini and Wong, 2018; Seekings et al., 2025). By co-locating computation and memory, and leveraging event-driven spiking dynamics, these systems significantly reduce data movement and energy consumption and can achieve orders-of-magnitude improvements in energy efficiency compared to conventional von Neumann architectures (Ielmini and Ambrogio, 2020; Peng et al., 2024) when implementing data-intensive applications.

However, the same physical properties that enable high energy efficiency and parallel computation also introduce new security and reliability challenges (Sorrentino et al., 2026; Nazari et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b). Memristive hardware inherently exhibits non-deterministic behavior due to device variability, analog noise, conductance drift, and temporal dynamics (Le Gallo et al., 2023; Lammie et al., 2025). These effects complicate whether functional behavior and privacy exposure characterized at the model level remain representative after deployment onto the analog substrate. Consequently, as these systems move toward real-world deployment, their privacy implications remain insufficiently understood, particularly when hardware behavior may differ from that of the software SNN.

In memristive neuromorphic systems, synaptic weights learned during training are directly mapped to device conductance states (Ielmini and Wong, 2018). As a result, the trained SNN becomes tightly coupled to its physical implementation. Device variability, temporal drift, peripheral quantization, and other implementation effects can therefore alter the effective computation performed during inference (Ielmini and Ambrogio, 2020). Prior work has further shown that neuromorphic and in-memory computing systems expose hardware-dependent security surfaces, including side-channel and fault-related behaviors (Wang et al., 2024a; Inglese et al., 2023; Sapui and Tahoori, 2024; Ensan et al., 2021). These observations motivate privacy analysis that treats the hardware state as part of the deployed system rather than assuming that the software SNN fully describes inference behavior.

papers.title: Adaptive Federated Optimization Across Smooth and Nonsmooth Regimes
papers.abstract: AdaGrad-style methods can simultaneously adapt to both the order and constants of smoothness in centralized optimization. However, existing extensions to federated optimization with heterogeneous client objectives and multiple local steps require the smoothness order to be specified in advance. We address this limitation with AdaFed, a federated method that adapts across several regimes under a single choice of parameters. In the deterministic setting, AdaFed achieves an $O(1/T)$ convergence rate for both smooth nonconvex and smooth convex objectives, and an $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rate for Lipschitz nonsmooth convex objectives up to logarithmic factors. Under a light-tailed stochastic-gradient noise assumption, these guarantees extend to the stochastic setting with additional logarithmic factors and noise-dependent terms. Experiments across the three problem classes further support our theoretical findings.

papers.title: WorldProbe: When Video World Models Fall Apart under Long-Horizon Spatial Exploration
papers.abstract: Video world models generate future visual observations from camera or action inputs, with the goal of synthesizing persistent 3D worlds that can be explored across time and space. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate short interactions or rely on camera trajectories fixed before generation. The performance of video world models under long-horizon exploration with extensive camera motion remains under-explored. We introduce WorldProbe, a diagnostic benchmark that uses a goal-conditioned multimodal agent to adapt camera actions online during generation. WorldProbe comprises 164 test cases across four probing families. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, we generate more than 1,600 rollouts totaling approximately 800 minutes, with horizons up to 180 seconds. Our evaluation across four dimensions reveals both the degradation of local measures and the emergence of long-range inconsistencies. We find that recent models sustain visual and content quality for longer, while long-range memory and evolution remain weak. These results expose a gap between locally stable generation and persistent world consistency that is largely missed by existing benchmarks. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/Untitled-W/WorldProbe.

Video generation is moving from fixed-sequence synthesis toward interactive world simulation (OpenAI, 2024; Bruce et al., 2024; Parker-Holder et al., 2024; Parker-Holder and Fruchter, 2025). Instead of passively viewing a predetermined video, users can steer the camera to dynamically shape subsequent rollouts (Zhang et al., 2025). Beyond visual quality improvements, recent advances in autoregressive architectures and long-context modeling enable such interactions to unfold over extended horizons and flexible spatial trajectories (Wang et al., 2026c; Robbyant Team et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2026).

Yet a world model should not merely render plausible frame sequences. It should instead sustain a persistent, evolving world. The scene should remain consistent upon revisitation, expand coherently into unseen regions, and follow camera commands without semantic drift (Sun et al., 2026; Ren and others, 2025; HunyuanWorld Team et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a). However, current benchmarks provide limited evidence in this regime (Li et al., 2025a; Duan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026b; Ying et al., 2026; Lian et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2026). This stems from three limitations. First, models are usually evaluated on short rollouts with limited camera motion. Failures in memory, consistency, and scene evolution often emerge only under long-horizon exploration with substantial camera motion. Second, current benchmarks rely on camera trajectories fixed before generation. Such trajectories cannot adapt to newly revealed geometry or redirect exploration toward newly selected targets, limiting the complexity of probing tasks. Third, existing metrics primarily assess local cues and are typically computed over neighboring frames or views with geometric priors or learned scorers for control and image quality (Huang et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026a). Existing memory tests extend the temporal gap, but still rely on pairwise matching at identical camera poses (Xu et al., 2026b; Lian et al., 2025). As a result, these metrics do not naturally capture the long-range failures that emerge over extended rollouts. Each probe starts from an initial frame and a spatial objective designed to elicit diagnostic camera motion. papers.title: On the Stability Analysis of Infinite-Dimensional Port-Hamiltonian Systems Within the Variational Framework
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the stability analysis of a class of linear infinite-dimensional port-Hamiltonian systems formulated within the variational framework. We derive verifiable conditions for the equivalence of the Hamiltonian-induced energy norm and the natural state-space norm, as well as for the generation of a contraction semigroup by the associated system operator. The semigroup generation result is obtained by establishing dissipativity and verifying the required range condition. The proposed conditions simplify the functional-analytic stability analysis of this class of systems in a manner similar to established results for the Stokes-Dirac setting.

papers.intro:
The physically-motivated modelling of ordinary differential equations as port-Hamiltonian systems provides a well-established framework for energy-based controller and observer design, see e.g. Ortega et al. (2001). Several formulations have been proposed to extend the port-Hamiltonian framework to infinite-dimensional systems, among which the Stokes–Dirac approach as in van der Schaft and Maschke (2002), Le Gorrec et al. (2005) and the variational framework as in Schöberl and Siuka (2014), Schöberl and Siuka (2012) are two prominent examples. Both approaches have been successfully applied to the design of in-domain and boundary controllers for a variety of systems of partial differential equations (PDEs) with one dimensional spatial domains, see e.g. Macchelli et al. (2004), Malzer et al. (2020), Rams et al. (2018).

The main difference between the Stokes–Dirac and variational formulations lies in their underlying geometric structures. While the Stokes–Dirac formulation is based on Stokes–Dirac structures, the variational framework is closely related to the calculus of variations and relies on jet-bundle structures. As a consequence, the choice of state variables and the resulting structure of the PDEs differ between the two formulations. In the Stokes–Dirac setting, the state variables are typically chosen such that the energy density can be expressed as a quadratic function of the states. In contrast, within the variational framework, the energy density may depend on both the states and their spatial derivatives. For mechanical systems, the Stokes–Dirac approach commonly uses strains, curvatures, and momenta as state variables, whereas the variational framework allows the direct use of displacements and the corresponding momenta. This can be advantageous for position-based control schemes such as those considered in Malzer et al. (2020), Rams et al. (2018). However, due to the different PDE structures arising from the two formulations, the corresponding stability analysis also differs.

The goal of this paper is to reduce the complex stability analysis of a general class of ipH-V systems to a set of simply verifiable conditions, thereby greatly reducing the required functional-analytic effort. For linear ipH-V systems, the proof of stability requires showing that the associated system operator generates a contraction semigroup, which can be established by the application of the Lumer-Phillips theorem see e.g. Jacob and Zwart (2012). In order to do so, we make use of an energy norm induced by the Hamiltonian of the system, where we have to show that it constitutes a norm of the underlying state space. We show how under certain assumptions, which naturally occur for physical systems, these steps can be reduced to an examination of the boundary conditions.

papers.title: Data-Driven or Model-Constrained? Comparing Airflow Estimation Methods under Sparse Sensing
papers.abstract: Airflow-driven advection is the primary mechanism for gas and aerosol dispersion in real-world scenarios, making accurate airflow estimation essential for ventilation monitoring, gas source localization, and contaminant spread analysis. Since obtaining airflow maps via high-resolution spatial sensing is usually infeasible in practice, flow field estimation methods must cope with sparse measurements by introducing statistical or physical priors to compensate for limited data. Existing approaches mainly differ in how they incorporate fluid-flow constraints and environmental geometry. However, due to the lack of systematic comparisons across this spectrum of methods, the potential benefits of physics-based priors for airflow estimation under sparse sensing remain underexplored. To address this question, we quantitatively evaluate four airflow estimators across three simulated 2D scenarios under steady-state conditions and varying sampling densities. The methods range from Gaussian Process Regression and graph-based Gaussian Markov Random Fields to two Navier-Stokes-based approaches, including a novel strong-form residual minimization variant. Our results show that physical priors provide the greatest benefit at low sampling densities by compensating for missing spatial information. Although data-driven Gaussian Process Regression becomes increasingly competitive as sensor coverage increases, model-based estimators retain an accuracy advantage across the evaluated scenarios.

papers.title: Arbitrary Dirichlet Eigenvalue Multiplicities on Smooth Star-Shaped Euclidean Domains
papers.abstract: In every fixed dimension \(N\ge3\), for any finite list of positive integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_\ell\), we construct smooth strictly star-shaped Euclidean domains whose first \(\ell+1\) distinct Dirichlet eigenvalues can have multiplicities \(1,m_1,\ldots,m_\ell\) respectively. The condition "star-shaped" is almost optimal in the sense that this statement can not hold for bounded convex domains. In fact, we show that the second Dirichlet eigenvalue of any bounded convex domain has multiplicity at most $N$, and this bound is sharp.

papers.title: On convex envelopes of bilinear terms over polygonal domains
papers.abstract: We develop an algorithm for computing the convex envelope of the bilinear function $f(x,y)=xy$ over possibly nonconvex polygonal domains. Building on existing methods for convex polytopes, our approach uses the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions and an analysis of the contact points between affine underestimators and the graph of $f$. Nonconvex domains admit additional contact configurations that prevent several simplifications available in the convex case. We resolve these configurations explicitly and show that the envelope admits a finite polyhedral subdivision with affine, quadratic, or rational expressions on its cells. For orthogonal polygons, whose edges are horizontal or vertical, we establish substantial reductions in the generator sets needed to compute the envelope. We also present methods for constructing such domains as relaxations of two-dimensional projections of nonlinear optimization problems. An illustrative example quantifies the loss in relaxation strength caused by convexifying the domain before computing the envelope. Computational experiments on MINLPLib instances show that cuts derived from orthogonal polygons strengthen root relaxations and reduce branch-and-bound nodes in aggregate.

papers.title: SHPRR: An Algorithm for Pure Exploration under Constrained Regret
papers.abstract: Best Arm Identification (BAI) conventionally measures the cost of experimentation by the number of samples collected. In many operational settings, however, the cost of exploration relative to a trusted baseline already in place is equally important. We study BAI under both a fixed sampling horizon and a regret budget. Unlike generic resources considered in constrained pure exploration, regret has a distinctive structure: sampling better arms is less costly relative to the baseline. We theoretically show that the regret cost of exploration decreases across the phases of Sequential Halving, a widely used pure-exploration algorithm. This observation yields improved guarantees on the probability of identifying the best arm and motivates a more effective allocation of the regret budget. We propose Sequential Halving with Proportional Regret Rationing (SHPRR), which front-loads the regret budget to allow more exploration when many arms remain. Experiments on synthetic and real-world instances show that SHPRR improves best-arm identification performance over uniform regret allocation and existing baselines.

In classical settings—such as offline algorithm selection or clinical pre-screening—the cost of learning is measured naturally in sample complexity: every pull incurs an identical, uniform cost, and the goal is to identify the optimal arm using as few observations as possible.

papers.title: Exploring the Potential of Symbolic Regression in Precision Livestock Farming
papers.abstract: The ability to predict farrowing time in pigs is crucial for optimal farm management and ensuring piglet survival. This study investigates the potential of explainable artificial intelligence for precision livestock farming, focusing on acceleration sensor data from sows around the time of farrowing. Accurately predicting farrowing allows farmers to balance both, piglet safety by avoiding piglet crushing events and the mother sow's welfare, by avoiding early crating. Traditional machine learning models often lack interpretability (``closed-box'' problem). Explainable artificial intelligence offers a solution by revealing the decision-making processes within the models. This work is split into two stages. First the detection of nest building behaviour and second the prediction of the remaining time to farrowing. The nest building detection was possible for 166 out of 180 sows and successful within 48 hours before farrowing for 149 sows. The nest building detection is purely based on the change of a sow's activity level and uses no machine learning techniques. Further, this study utilizes symbolic regression, an open-box modelling technique that generates interpretable mathematical formulas, to predict the remaining time until the onset of farrowing. The results are compared with closed-box models, like support vector regression and artificial neural networks, for both explainability and performance. Notably, symbolic regression achieved a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours for the time-to-farrowing prediction, outperforming the closed-box models in terms of performance and interpretability. This research demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence, specifically symbolic regression, can offer both interpretable results and competitive performance in precision livestock farming.

papers.intro:
Sows are routinely confined in crates a few days before giving birth (farrowing) mainly to prevent piglets from being crushed. While this practice protects piglets (King et al., 2019), it comes at the cost of increased stress and restricted natural behaviours for the mother sow (Hansen et al., 2017; Heidinger et al., 2022; Jarvis et al., 2006). To balance piglet safety and sow wellbeing, modern farms have started to use temporary crating, delaying confinement previous to nest building and ideally at least 24 hours before farrowing (Cheon et al., 2022). However, pinpointing the optimal time for crating to maximize welfare for both sows and piglets remains a challenge (Oczak et al., 2019). This study proposes a two-step alarm system using explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to address this challenge. The system will first detect the onset of nest building behaviour and then predict the time remaining until birth. We focus on symbolic regression (SR), an open-box machine learning (ML) technique within XAI. Unlike traditional “closed-box” models like artificial neural networks (ANNs) (Wang, 2003), SR generates interpretable mathematical formulas, leveraging genetic programming (Affenzeller et al., 2009). These formulas reveal the relationships between sensor data and the predicted time to farrowing, providing valuable insights for precision livestock farming (PLF) (Hoxhallari et al., 2022; Najjar et al., 2023). Genetic Programming has already been tested in other areas of PLF, such as beef cattle management (Abbona et al., 2020). Building upon previous farrowing prediction research (Oczak et al., 2019), this work aims to improve prediction accuracy by leveraging XAI with data from sow ear tag accelerometers. This approach differentiates itself from recent studies that rely on computer vision (CV) for farrowing prediction (Chen et al., 2023; Oczak et al., 2023).

papers.title: From Trees to Binary Trees: Approximation Algorithms and a PTAS
papers.abstract: Kellerhals, Krebs, Nichterlein, and Schmid introduced the optimization problem Tree in Binary Tree (TBT), where, given a tree $T$, the task is to find a binary tree $S^*$ with $V(T)=V(S^*)$ that minimizes $\sum_{uv\in E(T)} \operatorname{dist}_{S^*}(u,v)$. They also introduced the variant Tree in Binary Tree With Steiner Nodes (TBT-SN), where the condition $V(T)=V(S^*)$ is relaxed to $V(T)\subseteq V(S^*)$. We give a simple linear-time $\frac{8}{3}$-approximation algorithm for TBT and a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for TBT-SN. Our main building idea in both algorithms is to iteratively consider subtrees of the tree $T$ which contain all vertices below some vertex $v$ and construct a solution where $v$ has degree 1. For the PTAS, we cut $T$ into smaller trees, solve these instances, modify the obtained solutions, and combine them to achieve a solution for the original instance.

We focus on this step from general trees to trees of bounded degree, more specifically, binary trees. papers.title: Compressed Orientation Reachability Maps for Sub-Second Robotic Needle Entry Point Planning
papers.abstract: In the context of multi-stage trajectory planning for robotic percutaneous liver interventions, identifying a kinematically feasible entry point remains a critical computational bottleneck. Existing methods rely on exhaustive inverse kinematics or randomized searches, incurring delays of 13 to 27 seconds per target and limiting real-time intraoperative adaptation. This paper introduces an Orientation-Based Reachability Map (ORM) that precomputes the kinematic feasibility of a 6 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) serial manipulator across 188,873 workspace positions and encodes orientation feasibility into a compact, indexed 83 MB map. A Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled runtime pipeline replaces live optimization with near-instantaneous array lookups. Experimental evaluation demonstrates a reduction in planning latency from 13.5-26.9 s to 0.289-0.349 s per target while maintaining high geometric fidelity, achieving a mean convex hull volume overlap ratio of 0.933 and a mean alpha-shape volume ratio of 0.976 relative to the baseline reachable point cloud. The proposed ORM framework enables sub-second entry point planning and provides an efficient computational framework for robotic needle insertion in percutaneous liver ablation.

papers.intro:
Liver cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with approximately 865,000 new cases and 757,948 deaths reported in 2022 [1], and a 5-year survival rate of only 22% [2]. For patients with underlying liver disease who are not eligible for surgical resection, percutaneous thermal ablation techniques such as radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and microwave ablation (MWA) are established first-line therapies for small hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and selected liver metastases [3, 4, 5]. These minimally invasive procedures offer reduced morbidity, shorter hospital stays, and tissue preservation, but their effectiveness depends critically on accurate needle placement to ensure complete tumor coverage with an adequate safety margin (typically 5–10 mm) while avoiding major vessels and bile ducts [5, 6, 7, 8].

These minimally invasive procedures offer reduced morbidity, shorter hospital stays, and tissue preservation, but their effectiveness depends critically on accurate needle placement to ensure complete tumor coverage with an adequate safety margin (typically 5–10 mm) while avoiding major vessels and bile ducts [5, 6, 7, 8].

papers.title: Electronic liquid crystals and superconductivity from doping a moir\'e Mott insulator
papers.abstract: Electronic liquid crystals, such as stripe phases and nematics, are self-organized states of matter with spontaneously broken rotational symmetry. They are expected to emerge in a doped Mott insulator as a compromise between short- and long-range Coulomb interactions, and are believed to be intimately connected to the emergence of high temperature superconductivity either as a competing order or an intertwined order. Moir\'e semiconductors provide a controllable platform to explore the relationship between stripe phases and superconductivity near a Mott insulator. Here we report the generic appearance of stripe phases in a doped moir\'e Mott insulator and the observation of a stripe to-superconductor quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer WSe2. The stripe phases were revealed by electrical transport studies as a thermodynamic phase transition from a high temperature isotropic phase to a low-temperature anisotropic phase accompanied by a Fermi surface reconstruction. Near the stripe-to-superconductor transition, we also observed an additional thermodynamic phase transition from metallic stripes to pinned insulating stripes. The stripe-to-superconductor transition further exhibits an intriguing self-similarity that highlights the intimate relationship between the two orders. Our results pave the path for studying intertwined orders in moir\'e materials.

papers.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information
papers.abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts with a learned world model. We obtain that, when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, which floors its TD target and attributes this floor to the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. A pilot retrieval system, to be trained and improved with this signal, solves a memory task with reduced context.

papers.intro:
Consider a robot replacing a control board inside an unfamiliar appliance. Mechanically identical connectors attach behind the service panel frame, so before unplugging them the robot has to move its camera to look, and once the board is out that arrangement cannot be observed again. Hundreds of steps later each cable has to go back to the right socket, and each decision rests on one frame among thousands. Attending over all stored frames at every step to find it is what makes memory expensive on a robot. Harder still is learning which observations to make in the first place: Transformer agents fail on long-horizon tasks when they must first act to observe a cue [1]; we call this the observation credit assignment problem (O-CAP). Both problems require knowing which information matters at which decision before retrieving it: its information value, following Howard [2].

papers.title: Data-driven Regularization for Inverse Problems
papers.abstract:
In many applications, we are interested in studying an object of interest $x$. However, its properties are often not directly measurable. Instead, we only observe $y = F(x)$, where the (known) function $F$ is referred to as the forward mapping. To infer about $x$ from the observation $y$, we seek an (approximate) inverse mapping $x \approx F^{-1}(y)$. This process is known as solving the inverse problem.
  In practice, the inverse mapping $F^{-1}$ may be ill-defined or discontinuous, which forces us to choose a certain solution from many possible ones based on prior assumptions on $x$. Such assumptions about $x$ are typically incorporated into the inversion process through regularization. Therefore, the first part of this course focuses on the classical regularization theory of inverse problems.
  In the second part, we transition to algorithmic approaches for solving inverse problems. The foundation for this lies in the variational formulation of inverse problems, where reconstructions are obtained by minimizing specific functionals. Here, we will explore key optimization principles, discuss their practical implementation, and examine how they contribute to robust reconstructions.
  Today, classical methods are often modified to incorporate data-driven machine learning techniques, which improve the empirical performance. However, this often comes at the cost of explainability or convergence guarantees. Such properties are critical, for example, in medical applications, where one wants to be confident that reconstructed abnormalities are of physical nature and not phantoms resulting from the method.
  For these reasons, we discuss a number of machine learning methods for inverse problems, such as unrolling techniques, learned regularizers and plug-and-play methods, and explore their performance guarantees.

papers.title: Apple Vision Pro: The good, the bad, the ugly
papers.abstract: Apple Vision Pro (AVP), the headset Apple introduced as its first ``spatial computer,'' built by a single, vertically integrated vendor, entered the market in February 2024 and has since accumulated a fast-growing body of primary research spanning surgery, education, accessibility, design, and human-computer interaction. In this paper, we adopt the tripartite structure of Leone's 1966 film to organize a systematic review of this literature: we cataloged the validated, working applications of AVP (the good), the persistent technical and ergonomic limitations of a still-early-generation headset (the bad), and the ethical concerns and structural harms that follow from deliberate design, marketing, and deployment choices (the ugly). The review is built from a Scopus export of 218 records mentioning AVP, which we narrowed to 104 papers (2024--2026) with a primary focus on AVP, using explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria that we report in full, alongside a PRISMA-informed flow diagram of the screening process. We find the corpus heavily skewed toward validating benefits (medicine and surgery, education, and software tooling account for over half of the included papers) and comparatively thin on documented risks or misuse, a pattern we treat as a finding in its own right rather than a limitation to be explained away. We further show that several recurring issues, namely price, simulated social presence, and the gaze-tracking privacy architecture, resist a clean separation into ``bad'' or ``ugly'' using the published evidence alone, since both readings remain compatible with the same data. We close by identifying where the evidence base most needs to grow: independent risk and ethics research, bystander- and equity-focused study designs, and disclosure that would let researchers distinguish an engineering backlog from a structural choice.

papers.title: VideoMemBench: How Well Do MLLMs Remember in Video Conversations?
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can now process hour-long videos, making extended multi-turn dialogue over a single video a natural mode of use. Sustaining such a dialogue requires more than answering each question in isolation: the model must retrieve and reuse information established earlier in the conversation, both what it has seen and what it has said, an ability we term in-context video memory. Existing video QA benchmarks leave this ability unmeasured: their questions are mutually independent, never reference one another, and each is answerable from the video alone, so nothing ever requires carrying information across turns. We introduce VideoMemBench, in which each sample pairs a single video with a long multi-turn dialogue, whose turns are connected by typed cross-turn dependencies: an Episodic Dependency refers back to a visual episode described in an earlier turn, probing memory of what the model has seen, while an Answer Dependency builds on the model's own earlier answer, probing memory of what the model has said. Every dependency is verified considering two properties: 1) necessity, meaning the question cannot be answered without its earlier turns, and 2) non-leakage, meaning the question does not restate the information from its earlier turns. To enforce these properties, we design a construction pipeline with three LLM roles: a planner, a generator, and a judger, with each dialogue reviewed by human experts. VideoMemBench comprises 326 videos with 2,476 turns, of which 1,387 depend on earlier turns, including multi-parent dependencies and long-range call-back. Among over 20 evaluated open- and closed-source MLLMs, Claude Opus 5 performs the best with an overall score of only 45.7\%, highlighting the challenge of in-context video memory. Our dataset and evaluation are released.

papers.title: A compact NH$_2$D source without NH$_3$ counterpart in the S187 high-mass star-forming region
papers.abstract: Our goal is to investigate a so far only tentatively detected compact NH$_2$D source devoid of a notable NH$_3$ counterpart, located rather close to the luminous IRAS 01202+6133 source (the projected distance is $\lesssim$0.3 pc) in the S187 high-mass star-forming region. A high ammonia deuteration in such an environment is unusual. We performed observations of this area with the 20-m OSO radio telescope in several frequency ranges from $\sim$72 to $\sim$112 GHz. The area was mapped at the lower frequencies while at the higher frequencies only the position of the NH$_2$D emission peak was observed. The data were analyzed using non-LTE modeling. The data confirm a compact NH$_2$D source with a size of $\lesssim$0.2 pc. In addition, emission from about 20 molecules was detected, but only the DCO$^+$(1-0) peak coincides with the NH$_2$D clump. The clump is not associated with any known astronomical source or an NH$_3$ emission peak but the dust continuum map shows an enhancement at approximately the same position. The gas kinetic temperature derived from various indicators is $\sim$20-30 K, which possibly characterizes the surrounding material. The intrinsic NH$_2$D line width ($\sim$0.4 km/s) implies a clump with subsonic or transonic turbulence. The ortho/para NH$_2$D line intensity ratio is consistent with an abundance ratio of 3, expected from the spin statistics. The NH$_2$D/NH$_3$ abundance ratio may be $\sim$1. In general, the data hint at a compact cold gravitationally stable dense core within the warm environment, which may represent pristine material. However this picture still needs a verification with observations at a higher angular resolution.

papers.intro:
High mass star-forming (HMSF) regions are not only composed of hot freshly ionized gas forming H ii regions and an active warm molecular environment, but there may also still remain cool pockets of dense molecular gas well enough shielded to exhibit chemical properties, which strongly differ from those of the environment. This component, potentially representing pre-collapse gas (Minh et al., 2018, e.g.), deserves particular attention. The recent ASHES (ALMA Survey of 70 μ\mum-dark High-mass clumps in Early Stages) and QUARKS (Querying Underlying mechanisms of massive star formation with ALMA-Resolved gas Kinematics and Structures) surveys (Sanhueza et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2026) provide the first systematic, large-sample comparison of starless core properties across distinct evolutionary stages of high-mass star formation. The combined sample comprises 324 candidate starless cores: 197 from early-phase infrared-dark clouds (IRDCs; ASHES) and 127 from evolved-phase infrared-bright clouds (IRBCs; QUARKS). Both datasets utilize matched-resolution (approximately 0.5–0.6 arcseconds) ALMA Band 6 continuum and line data at 1.3 mm. In summary, observations from ASHES and QUARKS favor competitive-like dynamical accretion scenarios for high-mass star formation.

Good tracers of cold gas are deuterated molecules (Fontani et al., 2011; Gerner et al., 2015, e.g.,). In 2017–2018, we performed a survey of a large sample of high-mass star-forming regions with the 20-m Onsala radio telescope in the lines of several deuterated molecules and their hydrogenated isotopologues (Trofimova et al., 2020; Trofimova et al., 2024b). During this survey we tentatively detected a compact peak of the ortho-NH2D emission in the S187 HMSF region far away from the NH3 peak but rather close to the luminous IR source IRAS 01202+6133 (the projected distance is ≲\la0.3 pc). The peak is not associated with any known astronomical object. Later this peak was covered with the IRAM-30m radio telescope observations (Pazukhin et al., 2023). However, it was located at the very edge of the map. With the 100-m Effelsberg radio telescope, weak NH3(1,1) emission was detected without a clear peak at this position. The intensity of the NH3(1,1) line was lower than or comparable to the intensity of the ortho-NH2D line, which implied a very high degree of ammonia deuteration.

The S187 (also known as Sh2-187, KR120, LBN 126.7-00.80) HMSF region at a distance of ∼\sim1 kpc is well studied from optical to radio wavelenghts (Zemlyanukha et al., 2022, a detailed description is presented in). It contains ionized gas, molecular clumps at different stages of evolution and a fragmented atomic shell around its H ii region. Arvidsson & Kerton (2011) found it to be a likely site for triggered star formation. A couple of outflows were reported in the area discussed here (Salas et al., 1998; Jiang et al., 2001). IRAS 01202+6133 (M∼21M\sim 21 M⊙) with a luminosity of L∼5600L\sim 5600 L⊙ is embedded in the envelope of the S187 H ii region. Surroundings of such objects are usually rather warm. Chemical models predict a rapid drop of the ammonia deuteration with increasing temperature at T≳20T\ga 20 K (Roueff et al., 2007, e.g.,), which is confirmed by observations (Pazukhin et al., 2023). Therefore, a high ammonia deuteration in this area is unexpected.

Pillai et al. (2007) derived NH2D/NH3 ratios in the range 0.004–0.67 for a sample of pre/protocluster clumps found in 32 HMSF regions. Targeted case studies, such as G35.20-0.74, revealed extreme ammonia deuteration in its coldest subcores (kinetic temperatures ∼15\sim 15 K), with NH2D/NH3 ratios reaching levels of order unity after opacity corrections (Busquet et al., 2010). papers.title: Judged in Company: In-Context Batching Makes LLM Verdicts Depend on Other Items
papers.abstract: To save cost, practitioners often ask a language model to grade many independent items in one prompt. This assumes that verdicts are separable: that the verdict on an item does not depend on the other items in the prompt or on its position among them. Across three judgement tasks (harm in social-media comments, short-answer grading and review star ratings) and five open-weight models with 4-9B parameters, assigning the same 2,000 items to different random batches of 25 changes 11-22% of decisions on harm and grading, 6.5-13.3 points more than renaming the item keys or rewording the instruction, while AUROC against human labels differs from single-item grading only by -0.033 to +0.010; for four models with 14-32B parameters, 6-15% of decisions change, 4.2-9.1 points more. We show that flip rates decompose exactly into components of order, slot and membership, and that under a threshold model they grow with the square root of the variance that the context contributes, so that effects that are small for scores are large for decisions. Most of the latent dissimilarity between partitions comes from the order of the neighbours and the slot. The main effect of which items share the prompt, the part that voting over permutations of a batch cannot remove, accounts for 0.11-0.22 of it, and majority votes over nine permutations still leave 52-60% of the flips. Batched verdicts also differ systematically from single-item verdicts: even the majority of fifteen random batches disagrees with them on 8.4-17.8% of decisions. Editing a single generation shows that both the model's own earlier verdicts and the neighbours' texts carry the effect. On the easy task, star ratings, only 2.9-3.9% of decisions change. We recommend grading ambiguous items one per prompt, recovering most of the cost with a cached prefix, and reporting agreement with single-item grading whenever items are batched.

papers.intro:
Language models are now routinely used to label, grade and moderate text at scale. Because every request repeats the same instructions, a common way to cut cost is in-context batching: many items are placed in one prompt and the model returns one verdict per item, for example as a JSON object (Cheng et al., 2023). Vendors recommend it for moderation that need not happen in real time (Anthropic, 2026a), and a recent study of social-science annotation finds batches of 25 to 100 items, with up to ten coded variables per prompt, safe for most current models: they save more than 80% of token costs and lose less than 2 points of accuracy (Pipal et al., 2026).

Batching rests on an assumption that is rarely stated: that the verdict for an item depends only on that item and not on its company (the other items in the prompt) or on its position among them. Nothing in a decoder-only model enforces this. When the model writes the verdict for the twelfth item, it has read the other 24 items and the eleven verdicts it has already written. Accuracy is also a poor test of the assumption, because shifts that push some items up and others down can leave aggregate scores almost unchanged.

papers.title: Confidence-Aware Speed-over-Ground Estimation from Doppler Spectra via Reconstruction-Based Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation from ground-facing Doppler spectra is essential for mobile platforms such as railway systems. Classical signal-processing approaches can provide accurate estimates under favorable conditions, but often degrade in challenging conditions. We propose confidence-aware speed-over-ground estimation trained on rail-domain data that estimates speed over ground and frame-level confidence from Doppler spectra with several novel contributions: First, we transfer the idea of exploiting a reconstruction task by an autoencoder for performance estimation from previous work to Doppler RaDAR. Second, we append a speed-over-ground estimation head operating on the autoencoder's latent space features. Third, we omit the reconstruction decoder during inference but add a low-cost dedicated confidence head for frame-wise error-bound estimation. Fourth, we reveal how noise augmentation training can provide high robustness to the method. Experiments show that our approach improves speed estimation accuracy over classical baselines while providing informative confidence estimates that indicate the reliability of individual predictions, even under adverse signal conditions.
papers.intro:
Ego-velocity estimation is essential in both automotive and railway applications, particularly for automated driving, where highly precise velocity information is required. While automotive systems predominantly rely on inertial measurement units and wheel-speed sensors for ego-velocity estimation [15], RaDAR-based approaches have also been investigated in the automotive domain [19]. In railway applications, sensor configurations include ground-facing Doppler RaDAR, which estimates the train velocity from the Doppler frequency shift in the reflected RaDAR waves from the track bed [16]; this task is commonly referred to as speed-over-ground estimation. Reflected RaDAR waves from the train bed can, however, be affected by surface conditions, weather, contamination, or other environmental influences [17].

Although related in terminology, ego-motion and position estimation in robotics constitute a different problem setting and should not be confused with the speed-over-ground estimation considered in this work. Such approaches typically rely on 3D RaDAR data and exploit spatial information such as range, azimuth, and elevation. In contrast, speed-over-ground estimation is based solely on the Doppler spectrum and therefore lacks the explicit 3D spatial information required by these methods [9, 23, 22, 12, 1], making them not directly applicable to our setting.

papers.title: A Candidate Binary Microlensing Event in the 2018 Gamma-Ray Flare of 3C 279
papers.abstract: The April 2018 gamma-ray flare of the flat-spectrum radio quasar 3C~279 exhibited sharp peaks within a broader outburst. Its rapid substructure was previously attributed to magnetic reconnection. Motivated by its distinctive temporal profile within our comparison sample of bright blazar flares and its resemblance to caustic-crossing features in optical microlensing events, we investigate a finite-source binary-microlensing interpretation. A jointly fitted model of binary-lens magnification, a smooth intrinsic flare, and Gaussian-process variability reproduces the principal double-peaked structure of the GeV light curve. The adopted local solution has a binary mass ratio of $q\simeq0.098$ and an Einstein timescale of $t_{\rm E}\simeq0.327$~d. The absolute lens mass and projected source radius depend on the lens distance and relative proper motion. The fitted geometry can correspond to a Galactic planetary-mass binary or an intervening stellar or substellar system, with different physical source sizes in each case. We present binary microlensing as a testable interpretation of this event, with the finite-source structure offering a potential probe of the compact GeV-emitting region.

Rapid gamma-ray variability in blazars probes compact emitting regions within relativistic jets, but their angular sizes remain far below the resolution of gamma-ray telescopes [3]. Gravitational microlensing offers a complementary probe: near a caustic, the magnification depends on the source size and surface-brightness distribution [15, 23, 20]. In the strongly lensed blazar B0218+357, the gamma-ray flux ratio between the lensed images differs from the radio ratio and varies with time. These properties have been interpreted as additional microlensing by stars in the lensing galaxy, yielding constraints on the size of the gamma-ray emitting region [21]. For a binary lens, the caustic geometry allows multiple magnification peaks along a single source trajectory [22].

papers.title: Manual binding and semi-automated interface generation for efficient simulation backends with user-friendly frontends: A~demonstration for epidemic use cases
papers.abstract:
Challenges and chances of mathematical software are directly entangled with the programming language used. Depending on the background of developers and users, conflicts between different goals may arise. While several, e.g., scripting languages allow a low barrier and user-friendly entry to mathematical modeling and simulation, corresponding implementations will most likely not allow timely outcomes for detailed simulations.
  In infectious disease modeling, while several large-scale software frameworks rely on C or C++ implementations, most models are implemented in Python or R. While the latter allow for fast prototyping and more interactive development, it has been shown for several applications that C or C++ implementations outperform plain Python or R implementations by factors between one and three orders of magnitude. In particular, in times of pandemics, the urgent need for swift estimation of the system's dynamics makes the use of large-scale models in these noncompiled languages prohibitive.
  In order to create synergies and close the gap between scientists from the application and the computational domain, binding libraries allow to execute entire, compiled software frameworks from languages such as Python. However, with iterative model development, extension, or addition of new models, implementing bindings can represent another relevant barrier to developers of the C or C++ backends. In this paper, we show how a large-scale software framework with a multitude of infectious disease models can be efficiently exposed to Python. In addition, we suggest a semi-automated way to generate interface code by analyzing generic C++ code through abstract syntax trees, enabling a modularized approach working with intermediate representations.

papers.intro:
With individual programming languages serving different purposes, different challenges and opportunities arise. In particular, developers and users need to gain substantially different levels of computational expertise for implementing and using mathematical methods. In epidemiological modeling, languages such as R and Python are most widely spread (Bicker et al., 2026), as they offer a low-barrier access to mathematical-epidemiological modeling. However, it has been shown for different applications (Pereira et al., 2017; Portegies Zwart, 2020) that compiled languages such as C or C++ outperform Python with respect to time to solution by factors around 50, 100, or more. This well-known fact has led to the development of C, C++, or Fortran compiled packages to, e.g., solve ordinary differential equation-based (ODEs) models in R or Python (Karline Soetaert et al., 2010; Virtanen et al., 2020) and for the well known pytorch library, it was recently stated, how non-Python environments such as C++ help to bridge the gap between research prototypes and production deployment (Stryker, 2023). However, addressing individual software components such as numerical ODE solvers for ODE-based problems might not be enough if other costly tasks are conducted in a scripting approach. In (Bicker et al., 2026), it has recently been shown that ODE-based problem formulations with a modest number of spatially distributed subpopulations are simulated 1-2 orders of magnitude faster in fully-bound C++ than when only seeking Fortran or C compiled routines to solve the ODE system. With computation times at the order of seconds, individual simulations will rarely present a bottleneck. Nevertheless, with iterative model development or thousands of simulations necessary for parameter exploration and model calibration, execution will become incompatible with the high timely pressure that is imposed by unfolding or ongoing epidemics. In that direction, efficiently implemented models contribute substantially to timely outputs – an important use factor that increases modeling relevance for policy (Roebl et al., 2026).

While several large-scale software models for infectious disease modeling like OpenABM (Hinch et al., 2021), EpiHiper (Chen et al., 2025), FRED (Grefenstette et al., 2013) are implemented in C and C++, primarily targeting users with background knowledge in these languages, others like Covasim (Kerr et al., 2021) or MatSim-episim (Müller et al., 2021) provide optimized Python or Java implementations to increase the developer and user base. However, eventually, these optimized versions will stay behind the potential of software written in compiled languages. Even other frameworks such as Repast (Collier and North, 2013; Collier and Ozik, 2022) provide separated repositories with models implemented in either C++ or Python. BoostPython (Abrahams and Seefeld, 2015), pybind11 (Jakob, 2016), and nanobind (Jakob, 2022) are well established methods to provide Python bindings to C++ implementations. More recent developments based on the Cling C++ interpreter promise better Python binding performance than established solutions with pybind11 but are also less popularized yet (Kundu et al., 2023). The software frameworks EMOD (Bershteyn et al., 2018), EpiABM (Gallagher et al., 2022), and MEmilio (Bicker et al., 2026) provide Python frontends to their C/C++ backends where the latter both use pybind11. Through this approach, EMOD, EpiABM, and MEmilio are capable to offer low-barrier interfaces tailored to domain-specific users. In these, additional difficulties arise as developers need to understand the particularities of different programming languages using objects through, e.g., pointers, references, or different types of copies. On the other hand, binding large code bases yields a lot of opportunities and, compared to fully new implementations, comes at substantially reduced cost.

To avoid or reduce the cost of manual binding implementations, (semi-)automated approaches have been proposed. AutoWIG (Fernique and Pradal, 2017) or CppInterOp (Jomy et al., 2025) are two approaches that have been suggested for the automated binding generation of C++ libraries. For our application, we distinguish two complementary use cases where automation can come into play. In cases where a clearly separated software module (e.g., a new disease model) is added to the software, bindings can be directly generated with the backend code. Here, a unified description as in MEmilio (Bicker et al., 2026) or a domain-specific language (DSL) as in EMULSION (Picault et al., 2019) is needed. A popular example of a DSL in biological applications is the Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) standard (Hucka et al., 2003) which facilitates the task of generating model backend and interface simultaneously from a description in xml or yaml formats. DSLs are also used in other domains, e.g., to generate stencil-based code for high-performance computing applications (Schmitt et al., 2014; Bauer et al., 2021; Alhaddad et al., 2022). In cases where the backend code is already available in the compiled language, an analysis of the abstract syntax tree (AST) can enable the semi-automated generation of binding code. For our application, we furthermore distinguish the second use case by the settings where an existing but entire module might need a binding interface or where bindings should only be generated for small entities such as individual functions.

papers.title: Combining heavy-tailed keystroke dynamics with eye tracking reveals temporal flexibility in human problem solving
papers.abstract: Human problem solving unfolds through complex temporal dynamics that reflect the coordination of perception, cognition, and action. The fine structure of this process is still not very well understood. We use high resolution keystroke logging combined with synchronized eye tracking to examine the micro-temporal structure of human problem solving during written solution construction. Looking at 131,718 inter-keystroke intervals, we find heavy-tailed timing patterns spanning multiple orders of magnitude within the observed range. A three-component Gaussian mixture summarizes overlapping short, intermediate, and long pause ranges. Triangulation with gaze data reveals a systematic shift of attention toward external representations with increasing pause duration. Associations between tail exponents and performance differ across tasks. A larger across-task range of tail exponents ($\alpha_{\mathrm{range}}$) is positively associated with overall performance after adjusting for prior knowledge and measured process covariates ($\beta = 0.351$, $p_{\mathrm{HC3}} = 0.0165$), accounting for an additional 11.3 percentage points of explained variance in this sample. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that successful reasoning involves adaptive reconfiguration of temporal organization across task demands. The heavy-tailed timing dynamics represent a signature of task dependent cognitive organisation and highlight the potential of keystroke data as an unobtrusive and scalable window into the process of problem solving.

papers.intro:
Complex cognitive tasks (e.g. explaining a scientific concept in writing, solving a multi-step problem, writing code) don’t proceed as a continuous stream of activity but as temporally structured episodes of production and pause [1, 2]. They are typically characterised by periods of rapid production interspersed with pauses that can range from a few tens of milliseconds to many seconds. This intermittency is not just noise: across cognition and behaviour there is a tendency for temporal patterns to be heavy-tailed and self-similar, with 1/f1/f-like fluctuations and bursty inter-event times [3, 4, 5]. Work on human activity records further show bursty temporal organization and heavy-tailed inter-event time distributions [6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. The distribution of interval durations and dependencies in their temporal ordering are distinct properties. These findings motivate a distributional analysis of pause timing, but do not by themselves establish an exact power-law mechanism [11, 12]. A related measurement challenge is that most studies of complex reasoning still rely on static outcomes (final answers) or coarse timing measures (total time-on-task). These summaries collapse the within-task dynamics that likely matter for success: planning and monitoring, updating partial solutions, switching strategies, and integrating external information [13, 14, 15]. In other words, what distinguishes successful from unsuccessful solvers may not be a single “speed” parameter, but how flexibly they reconfigure processing modes as task demands change.

Process-tracing methods offer a way to study these dynamics directly. In writing research, keystroke logging has long been used to capture fine-grained production traces and to operationalize pauses and bursts as windows into ongoing cognitive processes [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. Pauses are commonly interpreted as reflecting transitions between nested subprocesses—motor execution, lexical/formulation processes, and higher-level planning or revision—yet pause distributions are typically skewed and heterogeneous, making threshold-based analyses and mean-based summaries fragile [20, 22]. Recent work therefore emphasizes distributional approaches and mixture perspectives to describe multiple, potentially overlapping time scales in the same observable trace [22, 23, 24]. Keystroke time-series studies have also linked fractal scaling to essay quality beyond essay length [25]. These time-series measures are distinct from the tail exponents of interval distributions studied here. Timing data alone, however, are often underspecified: the same pause duration can correspond to qualitatively different cognitive states. A principled way to increase interpretability is to triangulate production traces with measures of information uptake. Eye tracking provides a complementary view by indexing how attention is allocated across text, diagrams, and other external representations, and by revealing gaze patterns related to information uptake and comprehension [26, 27, 28, 29].

Beyond the interpretation of individual pauses there is a second question to be asked, namely whether the temporal organisation of activity changes as a function of task demands. In this context, adaptive expertise distinguishes efficient execution of familiar procedures from the capacity to reorganize processing when routine procedures are insufficient [33, 34]. This does not necessarily mean that the successful solver is always going to be the faster one. Rather, it motivates the expectation that the balance between fluent production and extended episodes of information search, monitoring, or reformulation may vary across tasks. Work on external representations has also demonstrated that adaptation can involve an initial investment of time in reorganising information for future use [35]. Crucially, adaptive strategy use is about the match between behaviour and the task, the person and the context rather than simply the amount of variation [36, 37]. People can differ in their degree of adjustment of strategy use as a function of changing rates of success and this can in turn be relevant to performance [38]. We therefore make a distinction between task-specific associations between timing and performance and the amount of temporal variation across tasks in the same individual. The latter may be consistent with temporal flexibility but does not establish that the variation is appropriate to each task. We use this framework to motivate tests of task-contingent temporal organization rather than to operationalize adaptive expertise directly.

papers.title: A Unified Benchmark for Aerial-Enhanced Autonomous Driving: The KITScenes Aerial Dataset
papers.abstract: Aerial imagery provides complementary spatial context for autonomous driving by exposing road structure beyond the immediate perception range of onboard sensors. Yet map construction from aerial imagery, aerial-assisted online HD mapping, and cross-view localization are typically studied on separate data and benchmarks. We introduce KITScenes Aerial, an extension of the KITScenes Multimodal dataset that augments synchronized onboard sensor data, vehicle poses, and rich Lanelet2 map annotations with spatially associated aerial imagery and higher-resolution neural representations, providing a common basis for a variety of research tasks. Our mapping evaluation focuses on all 53 KITScenes map classes across different model designs, spatial ranges, and aerial resolutions, while retaining compatibility with the widely used three-class setting. Representative baselines show that aerial context is particularly beneficial for fine-grained and extended-range mapping, more than doubling 53-class mAP at the larger mapping extent. Higher-resolution aerial imagery yields a further 4.3 mAP (+24 %) improvement, with gains extending to challenging map elements such as traffic lights. We additionally evaluate cross-view localization under geographically disjoint conditions, where an adapted fine-grained feature-matching baseline achieves a mean translation error of 5.13 m. KITScenes Aerial thus enables unified study of aerial and ground-level information across complementary mapping and localization tasks. Project page: https://kitscenes.com/aerial
