papers.intro:
Onboard sensors of autonomous vehicles are limited by occlusions, field of view, and perception range. Aerial imagery provides a complementary view of road environments and has become relevant across three closely related research directions: (i) aerial-only map construction, where high-definition (HD) maps are constructed directly from aerial observations [44, 2]; (ii) aerial-assisted online map construction, where aerial context complements onboard sensors [8, 19, 20]; and (iii) cross-view localization, where ground-level observations are related to geo-referenced aerial imagery for vehicle pose estimation [7, 41]. Although these directions pursue different objectives, they rely on overlapping combinations of aerial imagery, ground-level sensor data, vehicle poses, and map annotations.

Although these directions pursue different objectives, they rely on overlapping combinations of aerial imagery, ground-level sensor data, vehicle poses, and map annotations.

Early datasets including aerial imagery were typically designed around individual research settings, such as aerial-to-map reconstruction [11, 2] or ground-to-aerial localization [40, 26]. More recent datasets increasingly connect these previously separate domains by associating aerial imagery with autonomous vehicle (AV) recordings [44, 8, 18] or jointly providing ground-level and aerial modalities [5]. However, these extensions remain constrained by the properties of their underlying data, including map representation, geographic coverage, and the accuracy of the ground–aerial association. Previous work further reports pose-to-aerial misalignment and scene changes caused by temporal differences between ground and aerial acquisitions [35, 38, 7, 18, 31] as challenges for the field.

The mapping experiments cover two settings: all 53 KITScenes map element classes derived from its Lanelet2 annotations and the widely used three-class HD map construction setting [27, 23, 43], both evaluated across different spatial ranges and aerial imagery resolutions.

papers.title: LucidLyra: Feed-Forward Generative 3D Scene Reconstruction and Joint Understanding via Multi-Task Distillation
papers.abstract: We present LucidLyra, a framework that makes generatively reconstructed 3D scenes directly queryable for semantics and instances in a feed-forward manner from video latents. While generative 3D reconstruction can synthesize virtual environments from a single image, downstream applications in robotics and physical AI require not only visual realism but also access to scene semantics and object identities. Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

papers.intro:
Recent generative reconstruction methods can turn a single image into a renderable 3D environment. Building upon learned generative models, they can imagine content beyond the observed field of view and consolidate it into a scene that can be viewed from new perspectives [14, 72, 52, 85, 76, 2]. Generated 3D environments are promising for scalable content generation in interactive media, physical AI simulation, and industrial applications in engineering and manufacturing [16]. However, existing generated scene representations primarily capture geometry and appearance, while lacking an explicit understanding of their content. Downstream applications in embodied AI and physical simulation cannot interact with an collection of colored primitives; they require structured scene elements with semantic roles and discrete instance boundaries to support collision reasoning, physical manipulation, and interactive scene editing.

A natural solution might seem to generate an appearance-only scene first and recover semantic and instance representations post-hoc. However, this two-stage route breaks down in the single-view generative setting. Existing post-hoc methods either attach 2D foundation-model predictions to an existing reconstruction through per-scene optimization [67, 105, 87, 100], or jointly infer geometry and understanding from multiple captured views [117, 26, 88]. The former requires expensive scene-specific foundation model preprocessing and optimization. The latter relies on captured multi-view inputs and is constrained by the limited scale and domain diversity of multi-view training data. Neither route directly yields a structured 3D scene that has been generated from a single image.

Generated regions lack paired ground-truth supervision, so estimated geometry, semantics, and object boundaries can drift and disagree across views. Predictions from 2D vision models compound this, as their semantics and masks are not guaranteed to be view-consistent. The central challenge is to turn complementary but imperfect generative and perceptual signals into a consistent 3D representation while balancing geometry, appearance, semantics, and instances without compromising generation quality. An integrated model should let semantic priors and geometry reinforce each other, rather than tagging an isolated reconstruction with semantic or object information.

We introduce LucidLyra, a framework that unifies feed-forward generative 3D reconstruction and scene understanding in an explicit Gaussian representation (Fig. 1). Our central insight is that a video generator provides a unified foundation for structured 3D scene generation, serving both as the shared backbone and as the source of training data. Building on Lyra’s latent-to-Gaussian formulation [2], LucidLyra learns a 3D scene representation from camera-controlled video latents through multi-task distillation. Given a single input image, we denoise the corresponding video latents across camera trajectories, and process them through two parallel branches. The teacher branch decodes the latent into an RGB video and applies frozen vision-language, segmentation, and tracking foundation models to obtain semantic and instance supervision. The student branch incorporates vision cues of the input view into the video latents and directly maps the shared latent into a 3D Gaussian scene. We consolidate the teacher predictions across the generated views and distill them into persistent semantic and instance fields on the Gaussian primitives, jointly with geometry and appearance. A single shared representation can therefore support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping. As an initial exploration toward generative 4D scene understanding, we also extend the formulation to monocular video inputs and predict semantics- and instance-aware dynamic 3D scenes. For this novel task, we introduce an evaluation protocol with benchmarks covering static scenes, real-image domain transfer, and dynamic scenes.

papers.title: The IRAC Distant Cluster Survey
papers.abstract: We present the Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) Distant Cluster Survey (IDCS), a catalog of 825 galaxy cluster and group candidates identified in the Bo\"otes field using the PZWav detection code. Candidates are selected using photometric redshift probability distributions derived from twelve-band optical and infrared imaging. The catalog spans $0.08 < z < 2.0$ (median $z = 0.93$) and includes 147 systems at $z \geq 1.5$. For $z < 1.5$, simulations indicate a purity of $93\%$ at the adopted S/N $\geq 4$ threshold and $50\%$ completeness at $\log(M_{200c}/M_\odot) = 13.74 \pm 0.01$. We validate the cluster photometric redshifts through comparison with spectroscopic data, finding $\sigma_z/(1+z)=0.017$. Including 18 previously published IRAC Shallow Cluster Survey (ISCS) systems, a total of 80 IDCS cluster candidates are now confirmed through spectroscopy and/or X-ray observations. DESI DR1 spectroscopy provides redshifts for 38 systems, including 23 newly confirmed clusters. These DESI-confirmed systems span $0.12 < z < 0.93$ and have at least 10 spectroscopic members each, from which we measure a median velocity dispersion of $\sim 490$ km s$^{-1}$, corresponding to a median halo mass of $1.1 \times 10^{14} M_\odot$. A positional comparison with 39 independently confirmed literature clusters yields a median centroid offset of 211 kpc. The IDCS catalog provides a cluster sample spanning a wide redshift range, with a selection function characterized through simulations and is a valuable resource for studies of large-scale structure, galaxy evolution in dense environments, and the calibration of cluster detection techniques for current and upcoming wide-field surveys, including LSST, Roman, and Euclid.

We are entering an era where wide-area surveys are capable of discovering large samples of galaxy clusters extending from the local universe out to the epoch of cluster assembly at z∼2z\sim 2. Facilities including the Rubin Observatory [50], the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [79] and Euclid [1] expect to discover hundreds of thousands to millions of clusters spanning this redshift range. Meanwhile, cosmic microwave background (CMB) surveys with facilities such as the Atacama Cosmology Telescope [65, 48, ACT,], the South Pole Telescope [78, 56, 14, SPT-3G,], the Simons Observatory [39], the CMB-S4 experiment [3], and deep XMM surveys such as FornaX [76] have started surveying the intracluster medium (ICM) extending over this redshift range.

The Infrared Array Camera (IRAC) Shallow Cluster Survey [32, ISCS,] was among the first large tomographic surveys to identify galaxy clusters out to high redshift, using photometric redshifts to detect overdensities in redshift slices. Recent advances in photometric surveys and cluster identification techniques have greatly expanded the detection and characterization of galaxy clusters, particularly through large-area, multi-wavelength data sets. For example, the series of cluster catalogs by Wen et al. [90], Wen et al. [91] and Wen and Han [92], Wen and Han [93] identified a total of 110,621 clusters across several wide-area optical surveys. This growth has accelerated with surveys based on the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) and the Dark Energy Camera (DECam). The second release of the Massive and Distant Clusters of WISE Survey [83, 84, MaDCoWS2;] reported 133,036133{,}036 candidates at 0.08<z<20.08<z<2 over 64006400 deg2, while [89] found 151,244151{,}244 candidates up to z=1.5z=1.5.

Most recently, [94] produced a catalog of 1.58 million clusters using stellar-mass overdensities in the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Legacy Imaging Surveys [27]. These unprecedentedly large samples offer the potential for refining cosmological constraints (e.g., Sartoris et al. 2016 and references therein) and for quantitatively assessing the impact of environmental quenching processes over cosmic time. However, a key challenge remains in characterizing the cluster catalogs generated by these extensive surveys. For these catalogs to support cosmological and environmental studies, both their selection functions and mass calibration must be well quantified, including completeness and contamination as functions of mass and redshift, the mass-observable relation, and the projection and photometric-redshift effects that bias these quantities.

In this paper, we focus on the Boötes field: a 9.3 deg2 region near the North Galactic Pole that was originally targeted by the NOAO Deep Wide-Field Survey [51, NDWFS,]. This field has since been extensively observed across the electromagnetic spectrum and was used by the ISCS to identify 335 galaxy clusters, including 106 at z>1z>1, based on data from the IRAC Shallow Survey [33]. ISCS clusters have been the focus of a number of follow-up studies that examined the properties of galaxies in high-redshift environments. These include investigations of star formation in galaxy clusters [17, 8, 9, 6], the effects of dust obscuration on star formation [7, 61], brightest cluster galaxy evolution [58], AGN activity and black hole growth [59, 9], emission-line spectroscopy of star-forming members [99], and quenching in cluster galaxies [87, 75, 73].

papers.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
papers.abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.

Compressing the past into a bounded recurrent state avoids the scan, but the compression is performed before all future information needs are known. The positions of the current context and the retrieval heads aim to hold the information about the current expected value of the to be retrieved memories, as all memories in ϵ\epsilon distance will be retrieved.

Our proposal differs from semantic retrieval in one important respect: addresses should be shaped by the decision value of retrieving memory contents, rather than by similarity between the contents themselves. This distinction matters because two semantically similar memories may be redundant, whereas two dissimilar memories may only be useful together.

External differentiable memories have long separated computation from stored state. Neural Turing Machines combine content and location addressing [3]. Differentiable Neural Computers add dynamic allocation and temporal links [4]. Lie-access Neural Turing Machines are particularly close in mechanism. Here, memories occupy a continuous address manifold and read heads move by relative transformations [12]. Neural Map instead uses physical position as an external memory index [8]. Modern sparse-attention and retrieval systems use hashing, learned routing, nearest-neighbor search, or retrieval indices to avoid attending to every stored item [5, 9, 11, 6]. We ask instead whether the address space itself can be organized by the expected utility of future retrieval and then traversed persistently across related queries.

papers.title: Exact Competitive Ratios of Index Rules for Scheduling with Obligatory Testing
papers.abstract: We revisit scheduling with obligatory testing, where each job consists of two operations: a test with an initially known time and an operation whose processing time is revealed upon completion of the job's test. We develop an iterative competitive-ratio-preserving instance-reduction method that enables us to compute exact competitive ratios directly on highly structured instances for various index rules. Our main result is a clean analysis showing that the competitive ratio of the algorithm $1$-SORT is exactly the Golden Ratio $\varphi\approx 1.618$, improving the recent best-known upper bound of $1.861$ for arbitrary testing times. We further leverage this method to obtain near-tight bounds for a simple randomized algorithm on instances with uniform testing times.
papers.intro:
This paper studies scheduling under explorable uncertainty, where some job parameters are initially unknown but can be revealed through time-consuming tests. This uncertainty reduction comes with a trade-off towards the completion of jobs for which full information is already available. Thus, the model bridges classical offline and online scheduling settings, augmented with testing as a layer of active information acquisition at the cost of time investment. The paper follows a line of research on scheduling with testing that originated in the foundational works of [5, 9] and provides a competitive analysis that characterizes the exact performance guarantee of the studied scheduling rules.

papers.title: Converting a superseded Raith electron beam pattern generator into an unattended Critical Dimension SEM
papers.abstract: Design-based metrology of academic electron beam lithography (EBL) is bottlenecked by low-throughput imaging. For integrated photonics, where nanometre-scale structural variation can significantly limit device performance, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is the standard tool for critical dimension (CD) metrology, revealing the structure of devices that is not available from optical measurements. Manual SEM imaging on a wafer-scale is time-intensive, can feature operator-dependent distortions, and yields too few data to reliably close the nanofabrication calibration loop. The following details a methodology that utilises existing hardware in an academic cleanroom: a GDSII-to-SEM software workflow that converts a facility's superseded pattern generator into a CD-SEM for unattended image acquisition and efficient CD and line edge roughness (LER) extraction. This is shown for a Raith eLine Plus, and is expected to be applicable to other pattern generators running Raith's NanoSuite. Presented are results demonstrating its three use cases within a facility: accelerated calibration of two photoresists' process windows; chip-scale metrology of integrated photonic devices to track CD variation; and mass dataset acquisition for convolutional neural network training to predict process distortion. This methodology enables foundry-style, metrology-driven process calibration in academic cleanrooms, generalisable beyond photonics to any EBL nanofabrication that requires nanometre-scale CD control.

papers.intro:
Metrology workflows in electron beam lithography (EBL) rely on scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for top-down critical dimension (CD) measurements of structures. In semiconductor manufacturing and EBL foundry services, design-based metrology (DBM) workflows marry a floorplan layout to the physical structures on a chip/wafer surface, enhancing quality control. Measurements in these settings are performed by critical dimension SEMs (CD-SEMs) that automatically image large datasets of structures on the wafer-scale [1], with DBM workflows setting up these imaging recipes directly from design data [2]. In shared nanofabrication facilities, where the cost of CD-SEMs is often not an option, metrology relies on manually operated SEMs. For facilities with access to commercial nanofabrication software suites, such as GenISys ProSEM, Tracer and Beamer [3, 4, 5], image analysis and process-aware design are no longer the bottleneck towards achieving best practice fabrication. In our experience, the largest obstacle for academic cleanrooms is the volume of time required to manually image samples, as manual SEM set-up is time-consuming and image quality depends strongly on user ability [6]. While after-market upgrades exist that can add layout-driven automation to a manual SEM column [7], the following shows how traditional bottlenecks towards achieving automated imaging workflows may be alleviated by utilising existing hardware in a facility. By combining a superseded Raith eLine Plus electron beam (E-beam) pattern generator, image analysis software ProSEM [3], process calibration software Tracer [4], and custom automation scripts, we achieve an automated DBM workflow within an academic cleanroom.

This is possible since Raith E-beam pattern generators share many of the same components as CD-SEMs. Both consist of an SEM column with an in-lens/through-lens secondary electron detector [8, 9], the same through-lens detection used by CD-SEMs for high-resolution measurement [1]. The accuracy of CD-SEM measurements is calibrated with reference samples [1]. Similarly, a Raith pattern generator completes writefield alignment and correction with a laser-interferometer stage on a standard calibration chip (a ‘chessy’) with checkerboard structures. These remain on an eLine Plus sample holder and are used to align pattern generation writefields for EBL, and for calibrating SEM magnification, X and Y scaling and distortion. Combined with three-point rotation and working distance correction of the sample itself (Section 2.1.3), every scanframe imaged through the pattern generator is spatially and focally corrected, and the eLine Plus can be operated as a functionally equivalent CD-SEM. Semi-automated imaging is available on the eLine Plus by defining scanning routines with the same position list structures used for pattern generation, but these lists typically require manual structuring and are the largest bottleneck towards automated metrology within our facility.

Native automation on Raith EBL tools is designed for exposure [10], and we find no prior work that generates Raith position lists for unattended imaging directly from a design floorplan. In response, we present AutoSEM, an open-source, website application-based program that converts a GDSII design floorplan into ready-to-scan position lists. This allows unattended image acquisition on a Raith eLine Plus. With acquired images passed to GenISys ProSEM, Tracer and Beamer for process calibration and proximity effect correction (PEC) of future exposures, the result is an automated DBM workflow within our facility. By shifting the focus of users from manual imaging at the tool to defining scanframes at the design stage, we enable faster training, consistent image quality regardless of the user’s SEM operation skills, and wider adoption of metrology workflows. The software and analysis methodology are detailed in Section 2. Section 3 demonstrates the workflow across three use cases: accelerated process calibration of two EBL photoresists; chip-scale metrology of silicon photonic devices planned at the design stage; and large-scale dataset acquisition enabling next-generation process calibration with convolutional neural networks. Limitations in the methodology, remaining open challenges, and visions for generalisations across nanofabrication are discussed in Section 4.

papers.title: Local neoclassical calculations using a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space basis with advanced collision operators
papers.abstract: We present radially local neoclassical (NC) calculations based on a Hermite-Laguerre (HL) velocity-space polynomial expansion combined with advanced linearized collision operators, including the exact Fokker-Planck-Landau (FPL) operator. The implementation is verified against the NC code SFINCS using both a multi-species Lenard-Bernstein-Dougherty-like (LBD) operator and the FPL operator, the NC fluxes agreeing to within 3% in the Pfirsch-Schl\"uter regime. The accuracy of the HL basis is then assessed by convergence studies against the Legendre-Laguerre (LG) basis. At an equal number of spectral coefficients, neither basis is uniformly more accurate. In the plateau regime, the LG basis is more accurate on the particle and heat fluxes, which are sensitive to the trapped-passing boundary, whereas the HL basis is more accurate on the bootstrap current, carried by the parallel flow. In the banana regime, both bases converge slowly. Finally, we compare the LBD and the original (OS) and improved Sugama (IS) operators against the FPL operator. The IS operator retrieves the NC fluxes to within 6% over four decades of collisionality, whereas the LBD operator overestimates the ion heat flux by a factor of 2.6 to 4.7. The OS operator overestimates the ion heat flux by 4 to 33%, while retrieving the particle flux and the bootstrap current to within 9% and 18%, respectively. The convention adopted for the LBD collision frequency also changes the bootstrap current by up to two orders of magnitude. The present work extends the use of the HL basis, previously used in turbulent calculations, to NC physics and, to the knowledge of the author, these are the first NC calculations using the HL basis.

papers.intro:
Neoclassical (NC) transport is the collisional transport that survives in tokamaks [52] and stellarators [22] once all fluctuations are removed, and it therefore sets the irreducible transport level of these devices [23, 24, 21]. It originates from the banana orbits of trapped particles, whose width, much larger than the Larmor radius, sets the step of the collisional random walk associated with small-angle deflections. The same trapped–passing collisional coupling also generates the bootstrap current and the parallel and poloidal flows of each species [23, 39].

Neoclassical (NC) transport is the collisional transport that survives in tokamaks [52] and stellarators [22] once all fluctuations are removed, and it therefore sets the irreducible transport level of these devices [23, 24, 21]. It originates from the banana orbits of trapped particles, whose width, much larger than the Larmor radius, sets the step of the collisional random walk associated with small-angle deflections. The same trapped–passing collisional coupling also generates the bootstrap current and the parallel and poloidal flows of each species [23, 39].

The role of NC physics is particularly important in the pedestal of high-confinement (H-mode) plasmas, where the gradients are steepest and the collisionality varies strongly across the pedestal. There, the radial electric field well is dominated by the main-ion diamagnetic contribution, the poloidal flow being close to its NC value [50, 51], and its shear suppresses the edge turbulence [5, 7] and is connected to the access to H-mode [40, 6, 38]. The bootstrap current drives the peeling–ballooning modes that limit the pedestal [41], while the ion poloidal Larmor radius approaches the pedestal width [26, 28, 44]. In fact, in the H-mode pedestal, where turbulence is strongly suppressed, the ion heat transport is expected to approach its NC level [49].

In these conditions, describing the self-consistent interactions between turbulent and NC transport becomes unavoidable, and full-ff gyrokinetic (GK) simulations provide a first-principles framework to model both [27, 35]. However, full-ff GK simulations resolving the interplay between turbulent and NC transport are computationally expensive. To alleviate this cost, spectral approaches in velocity space have received renewed attention [33, 17, 32, 19]. These investigations have focused on turbulent (linear and nonlinear) calculations, for which advanced linearized multi-species collision operators have been developed and implemented using the Hermite–Laguerre (HL) basis, including the original Sugama (OS) [43], the improved Sugama (IS) [42, 16], and the exact Fokker–Planck–Landau (FPL) collision operators [25, 14]. We remark that the HL basis has also been extended to full-ff GK simulations in X-point geometry [19]. While these previous investigations have shown the computational efficiency of the HL basis and its ability to retrieve the turbulent transport, its ability to capture the NC physics remains to be addressed.

To alleviate this cost, spectral approaches in velocity space have received renewed attention [33, 17, 32, 19]. These investigations have focused on turbulent (linear and nonlinear) calculations, for which advanced linearized multi-species collision operators have been developed and implemented using the Hermite–Laguerre (HL) basis, including the original Sugama (OS) [43], the improved Sugama (IS) [42, 16], and the exact Fokker–Planck–Landau (FPL) collision operators [25, 14]. We remark that the HL basis has also been extended to full-ff GK simulations in X-point geometry [19]. While these previous investigations have shown the computational efficiency of the HL basis and its ability to retrieve the turbulent transport, its ability to capture the NC physics remains to be addressed.

The goal of the present paper is therefore twofold. First, we assess the accuracy of the HL basis to describe NC transport and bootstrap current. Second, leveraging the HL advanced collision operators [14, 16], we test the multi-species Lenard–Bernstein–Dougherty (LBD) collision operator [31, 10], used in full-ff GK codes [46, 12], against the OS, IS and FPL operators. We solve for the steady-state solution of the drift-kinetic (DK) NC equation in the absence of a radial electric field. To test the convergence of the HL basis, we also solve the DK NC equation using the Legendre–Laguerre (LG) polynomial basis, the Legendre expansion of the pitch-angle dependence being widely used in NC solvers [48, 3, 4, 29]. Indeed, the LG basis is a natural choice to describe the trapped–passing boundary, which is a structure in the pitch angle (Legendre) at fixed energy (Laguerre). papers.title: Playing CHESS with stars II. Homogeneous analysis of high-resolution optical spectra for a sample of 135 giants in 14 bulge globular clusters
papers.abstract: Bulge globular clusters are key tracers of the complex formation history of the Galactic bulge, as they retain information on its past star-formation episodes. Their chemical abundances serve as empirical `fossil records'' of the early evolution of the bulge. We present a homogeneous analysis of archival high-resolution UVES spectra for 135 giants in 14 Galactic bulge globular clusters. We explore the results in the context of the phenomenon of multiple stellar populations and discuss what the abundances reveal about the chemical evolution of the bulge. We employed the CHEmical Survey analysis System (CHESS) pipeline to derive atmospheric parameters on an accurate scale defined by reference stars. Abundances for Li, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Sc, Y, Zr, Ba, Ce, Nd, and Eu were derived by spectrum synthesis. Deviations from local thermodynamic equilibrium (i.e., non-LTE or NLTE) were taken into account for Na, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Y, Ba, and Eu. We serendipitously discovered a Li-rich giant with A(Li) = 1.68 (after 3D NLTE corrections) in NGC 6723, which was hidden in the archival data. Our sample includes both first- and second-generation stars, as indicated by the observed spread in Na abundances. Compared to halo clusters, the bulge clusters show a lower [{\alpha}/Fe] plateau at low metallicity and a more gradual decline in [{\alpha}/Fe] toward higher metallicities. The Sc abundances are below solar and lower than in disk stars of the same metallicity. This difference could be important for solving open questions about the nucleosynthesis of this element. None of the clusters exhibit any significant spreads in heavy elements. Most clusters exhibit [Ba/Eu] \sim 0.0, indicating a contribution from both s- and r-processes. Clusters with [Fe/H] < -0.5 show negative [Ce/Nd] ratios, supporting the idea that these elements were predominantly produced by the r-process in these clusters.

papers.intro:
The Galactic bulge was recognized as a distinct structural component of the Milky Way eight decades ago (Baade 1946; Stebbins & Whitford 1947). Since then, the processes driving its formation, evolution, and chemical enrichment have been a topic of growing interest (Barbuy et al. 2018; Zoccali 2019, see reviews by). Processes such as gas accretion, early mergers, and inward migration of thick-disk gas clumps are likely to have played a significant role in its formation, operating at different timescales. Nevertheless, there is still no fully self-consistent model for the Galactic bulge formation (Barbuy et al. 2018). The inner regions of the Milky Way are difficult to investigate as a result of severe interstellar extinction and stellar crowding. Recent progress in understanding the bulge is being driven by modern large photometric (VISTA Variables in the Vía Láctea, VVV and VVV eXtended, VVVX; Minniti et al. 2010; Borissova et al. 2018, respectively), astrometric (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016; Gaia Collaboration et al. 2023, Gaia;), and spectroscopic (Majewski et al. 2017, Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment, APOGEE;) surveys, some of them exploring infrared wavelength ranges where the effects of extinction are less pronounced. The new instrument MOONS (Cirasuolo et al. 2020, Multi-Object Optical and Near-infrared Spectrograph,) will contribute to that in the near future.

The bulge stellar population seems to consist of two main components, a metal-poor one ([Fe/H]11 1 [X/Y]=log⁡(NX/NY)∗−log⁡(NX/NY)⊙\mathrm{[X/Y]=\log(N_{X}/N_{Y})_{*}-\log(N_{X}/N_{Y})_{\odot}} ∼\sim −-0.5) distributed as a spheroidal and a metal-rich one ([Fe/H] ∼\sim +0.3) that dominates in the mid-plane and is responsible for the boxy/peanut shaped bar (Hill et al. 2011; Rojas-Arriagada et al. 2017; Johnson et al. 2022). Miller et al. (2026) compared APOGEE data with a two infall Galactic chemical evolution model implemented in the OMEGA++ code and found evidence that the bulge formed as a combination of a classical collapse followed by a later star formation episode that produced a younger stellar component. Similarly, the chemical evolution modeling of Molero et al. (2024) could reproduce the metallicity distribution of bulge stars with two in situ bursts of star formation. On top of that, there is an extended distribution of stars towards the very metal-poor regime ([Fe/H] << −-2.0) likely dominated by a contribution from accreted galaxies (Ardern-Arentsen et al. 2024).

Studies of bulge globular clusters (GCs) have played a key role in improving our understanding of the formation scenarios and chemodynamical properties of this Galactic component. For GCs, distances and ages can be better determined than for field stars. Early discussions of the connection between inner Galaxy GCs and the bulge focused on their metallicities and radial velocities (Minniti 1995; Côté 1999). Among these early studies, it is worth mentioning Ortolani et al. (1995), who demonstrated that bulge GCs are old and used this to infer that the bulge had been part of the halo formation process and that it had undergone rapid chemical enrichment. Since then, numerous studies have focused on examining the properties of these clusters. Valenti et al. (2007); Valenti et al. (2010) presented a homogeneous photometric survey to derive magnitudes, reddening, distances, and photometric metallicities for almost 80% of bulge clusters22 2 http://www.bo.astro.it/~GC/ir_archive/. Similarly, Geisler et al. (2025) presented a catalog of homogeneous chemical abundances derived from high-resolution spectra of stars in 18 bulge GCs.

There are several open issues concerning the origin and properties of the bulge clusters. The nature of several recently discovered candidate GCs still needs to be confirmed, while ages and spectroscopic metallicities are also missing in many cases (Bica et al. 2024). In addition, there is the problem of identifying the in situ and ex situ GCs. Interactions with the harsh and crowded environment of the Galactic center and the general orbital evolution of GCs complicate such efforts (Ishchenko et al. 2023; Ishchenko et al. 2024; Pagnini et al. 2023). Recently, Origlia et al. (2025) showed that Terzan 5 displays evolutionary, kinematic, and chemical properties that support the hypothesis of its in situ formation. Using the chemical abundances of V and Zn as markers, Bartolomei et al. (2026) favoured an in situ origin for NGC 6553, one of the most metal-rich GCs in the bulge. However, identifying the origin of a cluster is not an easy task, since about 30% of the bulge clusters could, in fact, be an inner halo or thick disk clusters passing through the bulge location (Pérez-Villegas et al. 2020).

The recent bulge GC census by Bica et al. (2024) listed 83 GCs possibly associated with the bulge. That same study also confirmed that the bulge GCs exhibit a bimodal metallicity distribution. This suggests that we are tracing multiple star formation episodes. In particular, the lack of an age-metallicity relationship for old clusters supports an situ origin for these systems (Bica et al. 2024). A similar bimodal metallicity distribution is also observed in bulge field stars again suggesting different star formation episodes (Lian et al. 2020; Molero et al. 2024).

The presence of multiple populations (MPs) and variations in the chemical abundances of light elements (e.g., C, N, O, and Na) is a defining characteristic observed in Milky Way GCs (see reviews by Gratton et al. 2012; Bastian & Lardo 2018; Milone & Marino 2022, and references therein). Globular clusters mainly host two distinct populations: stars that have abundances similar to those of halo stars of the same metallicity (so-called first-generation stars) and stars that have enhanced abundances of N and Na and depleted abundances of O and C (second-generation stars). These chemical differences likely come from the evolution of stars from the first generation, but the nature of these polluters has not been determined thus far (e.g. Bastian & Lardo 2018, and references therein). Multiple populations can also be seen as distinct photometric sequences that are directly linked to the spectroscopic observations (Dondoglio et al. 2025). In their work, Dondoglio et al. (2025) also reported that more massive GCs seem to have higher iron and barium spreads. The need for homogeneous spectroscopic data was very clear in their work, being necessary for a robust comparison of so many clusters.

papers.title: Ionization and Dissociation Energies of Molecular Hydrogen
papers.abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the simplest neutral molecule and its ionization and dissociation energies are key benchmarks for testing first-principles calculations of nonadiabatic, relativistic, quantum-electrodynamic and finite-nuclear-size effects in molecules. To obtain improved H$_2$ ionization and dissociation energies, we performed precision measurements of 15 transition frequencies in para-H$_2$. They connect the X $^1\Sigma_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ ground state, the long-lived EF $^1\Sigma_g^+(v=0,N=0)$ excited state, and several high members of the $n$p and $n$d Rydberg series with principal quantum number $n$ in the range between 48 and 70. The new data by itself leads to a five times more accurate value of the ionization energy of the ground state of para-H$_2$, equivalent to a relative frequency accuracy of $5\times 10^{-11}$. Combined with a global network analysis of 45 energy intervals in para- and ortho-H$_2$ that have been measured in the past three decades, we obtain new statistically robust values for the ionization energy [$E_{\rm I}(0,0)/(hc)= 124\,417.491\,1573(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] and the dissociation energy [$D_0^{N=0}=36\,118.069\,6646(58)$~cm$^{-1}$] of H$_2$. These values have an unprecedented accuracy equivalent to 175 kHz. The network analysis also leads to improved term values and dissociation energies of the excited states involved in the analysis. By comparing the results with first-principles calculations of the level structures of H$_2$ and H$_2^+$ , a significantly reduced upper bound of 540 kHz is derived for putative beyond-the-standard-model contributions to the energy difference between para- and ortho-H$_2$.

papers.intro:
For more than 100 years, the ionization and dissociation energies of molecular hydrogen (H2) have served as benchmark quantities to test first-principles calculations of molecular structure. The first determination of the dissociation energy of H2 relied on chemical thermodynamic and kinetic measurements [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. By the time modern quantum mechanics was introduced 100 years ago, these measurements had converged to a value in the range between 100 and 110 kcal/mol (corresponding to about 36 750 cm-1) for the dissociation energy of H2, with a precision in the range between 5 and 10 kcal/mol (1750-3500 cm-1), sufficient to unambiguously establish the strength of the chemical bond between two H atoms. In 1913, Bohr calculated a value of 60 kcal/mol (about 21 000 cm-1) for the dissociation energy of H2 using an extension of his model of the hydrogen atom to molecules [6]. He was confident enough in his result to write concerning the marked deviation from the early experimental result of Langmuir (550 kJ/mol; about 46 000 cm-1 [1]): “On account of the indirect [experimental] method employed, it seems difficult to estimate the accuracy to be ascribed to the latter value” [6]. Only a year after Schrödinger’s articles on wave mechanics [7, 8, 9, 10, 11], Heitler and London, also in Zurich, provided a rigorous explanation of the chemical bond by applying Schrödinger’s equation to the hydrogen molecule. With a minimal basis of only two orbitals they calculated a dissociation energy of about 2.2 eV (see their Fig. 1; about 18 000​cm−118\,000\penalty\ {\rm cm}^{-1}) [12]. In 1926, spectroscopic determinations of the dissociation energy started superseding chemical methods in precision and accuracy. Witmer [13] and Dieke and Hopfield [14] independently obtained values around 4.35 eV (≈35100\approx 35100 cm-1). papers.title: NORI: a GPU-accelerated code for simulating self-gravitating and self-interacting dark matter
papers.abstract: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can form cores in dark matter haloes and later drive their gravothermal collapse, raising their central densities far above those of NFW haloes. Simulating this collapse is computationally demanding, requiring increasingly short time-steps and a large particle number to resolve the shrinking core. We present NORI, an $N$-body code that runs on CPUs and GPUs and simulates isolated self-gravitating systems with elastic, isotropic self-interactions using a Monte-Carlo method. To avoid MPI communication in the tree walks, each compute node in CPU mode, and each GPU or group of GPUs in GPU mode, holds a copy of all particles and its own Morton-ordered tree. A fixed evaluation order makes the results bitwise identical on CPUs and GPUs. Applying scattering events sequentially conserves the momentum and energy of each pair to round-off and allows multiple scatterings per particle per step. With global time-steps in both codes, NORI is several times faster on CPUs than our AREPO-2 implementation. One four-A100 GPU node is up to 60 times faster per time-step than AREPO-2 on a 112-core CPU node. For a full core-collapse simulation, where AREPO-2 uses individual time-steps, the speed-up is $\sim 30$ for the central density to reach $10^3$--$10^4$ times the NFW scale density, $\rho_{\rm s}$. We follow a halo with $10^8$ particles within $r_{200}$ to a central density of $10^4\,\rho_{\rm s}$. Within the limit of about $2\times10^9$ particles set by data replication, NORI provides an efficient tool for isolated SIDM simulations, including gravothermal collapse and cluster collisions.

In the standard Λ\LambdaCDM cosmological model, cold dark matter (CDM) is non-relativistic, does not interact with electromagnetic radiation, and is effectively collisionless. The CDM model provides a successful description of structure formation on cosmological scales. On galactic and sub-galactic scales, however, comparisons between gravity-only CDM simulations and observations have revealed several possible tensions. These include the “cusp–core” and “missing satellites” problems, the finding that the most massive predicted subhaloes are too dense to host the observed bright satellites (“too big to fail”), and the diversity of dwarf-galaxy rotation curves (Flores and Primack, 1994; Moore, 1994; Klypin et al., 1999; Boylan-Kolchin et al., 2011; Boylan-Kolchin et al., 2012; Oman et al., 2015). The significance of these tensions remains actively debated, since baryonic processes, selection effects, and uncertainties in inferring halo properties can alleviate at least some of them (Bullock and Boylan-Kolchin, 2017).

The significance of these tensions remains actively debated, since baryonic processes, selection effects, and uncertainties in inferring halo properties can alleviate at least some of them (Bullock and Boylan-Kolchin, 2017).

One widely studied solution to these tensions is self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), in which dark matter particles undergo non-gravitational scattering (Spergel and Steinhardt, 2000). Repeated scattering transports energy through a halo, providing an effective mechanism for heat conduction. During the early evolution, heat flows from the dynamically hotter outer halo into the colder central cusp, lowering the central density and producing an approximately isothermal core. At the relatively low velocities of dwarf galaxies, cross-sections of σ/m∼1​–​10​cm2​g−1\sigma/m\sim 1\text{--}10\,\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}} produce kpc-sized cores and substantially lower the central densities of haloes, potentially alleviating some of the tensions discussed above (Vogelsberger et al., 2012; Rocha et al., 2013; Elbert et al., 2015; Kaplinghat et al., 2016; Tulin and Yu, 2018). In galaxy clusters, however, where velocities are much higher, the density profiles and shapes of cluster haloes and merging clusters constrain the cross-section to considerably smaller values (Randall et al., 2008; Peter et al., 2013; Kaplinghat et al., 2016; Sagunski et al., 2021). This motivates velocity-dependent models in which the interaction is strong at low velocities but suppressed at high velocities. A velocity-dependent cross-section is also natural for interactions mediated by a light force carrier (Feng et al., 2010; Buckley and Fox, 2010; Loeb and Weiner, 2011; Tulin et al., 2013).

(2025) derived an effective interaction between simulation particles from the microphysics in the short-mean-free-path regime. They are also used to calibrate the simpler models (Outmezguine et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Mace et al., 2026). Their numerical accuracy therefore directly affects the predictions made with these models.

papers.title: A double debris disc around a white dwarf sculpted by two planetary bodies
papers.abstract: Many planetary systems survive the metamorphosis of their hosts stars into white dwarfs, as demonstrated by the detection of dusty circumstellar discs around these stellar remnants as well as chemical signatures of planetary debris in atmospheres of these stars. A small fraction of these circumstellar discs also contain gas, detected in the form of emission lines from various ionic transitions (most commonly the near-infrared Ca ii triplet). All of the 21 known gas discs exhibit double-peaked line profile characteristic of a rotating flat disc. The mechanism behind the the generation of gas is still debated, but for at least one system it has been linked with the presence of a surviving planetesimal embedded within the dust disc. Here we report the discovery of WD J132800.85-145019.95, a new gas disc system which exhibits quadruple-peaked instead of double-peaked line profiles. These emission lines originate from two separate gaseous rings extending from 0.14 Rsun to 0.34 Rsun and from 0.54 Rsun to 1.93 Rsun. We propose that this structure results from the presence of two distinct planetary bodies within these discs, ranging in size from a few km to the size of Pluto. The detection this stable double-disc presents a new challenge for the current models of debris disc formation and evolution.

papers.title: The Carousel Lens III: Joint lens convergence and source kinematic modeling
papers.abstract: We introduce a new, independent modeling component to the Carousel Lens series by exploiting the spatially-resolved kinematics contained within the lensed arcs, which so far has remained rather underexplored in strong-lensing analyses. We present an end-to-end forward-modeling framework that reconstructs an integral-field spectroscopic datacube from a parameterization of the lens convergence profile together with the line-of-sight velocity, velocity dispersion, and surface brightness profiles of the unlensed source. The kinematic structure of the source acts as an additional set of ray-traceable markers distributed across every lensed image, inaccessible from imaging data alone. Furthermore, by generating an [OII] emission-line datacube, we isolate a single source redshift and remove lens and line-of-sight light contamination. We apply this framework to deep VLT/MUSE observations of the Carousel Lens, modeling the [OII] emission of the quadruply-imaged star-forming galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$ that anchors the system's cosmography constraints. We measure an Einstein radius $\theta_{\rm E} = 12.816''^{+0.005}_{-0.007}$ and a logarithmic slope $\gamma = 1.412^{+0.002}_{-0.002}$, tightening the statistical uncertainties on both by roughly a factor of $2-2.5$ relative to the corresponding flat emission-line map model. We find that the source galaxy exhibits a strong rotation, lies confidently along the star-forming main sequence, and has an inferred central black hole mass of $\log M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot} = 7.89 \pm 0.51$. These results establish datacube-level forward modeling as a practical and independent route to traditional image-based lens models in the current systematics-limited regime, and one that extends naturally to this system's other lensed sources and to other lens systems.

papers.intro:
Strong gravitational lensing is a leading probe in observational cosmology. Measuring the time delays of variable sources allows for an independent late-time measurement of the Hubble constant, with the potential precision to break the Hubble tension (TDCOSMO Collaboration et al., 2025; Pascale et al., 2025; Sheu et al., 2026; Galan et al., 2026, e.g.,). By using the properties of compound lenses (i.e., lenses with multiple sources at different redshifts), it is also possible to constrain the dark energy equation-of-state and the matter density of the universe (Caminha et al., 2022; Urcelay et al., 2026; Ballard et al., 2026, e.g.,). By measuring flux and time-delay anomalies for lensed quasars, one can also assess the dark matter fraction and substructure (Xu et al., 2015; Gilman et al., 2024; Paugnat et al., 2025, e.g.,). And perhaps in the most direct application, strong lensing allows us to study magnified, high-redshift sources (Treu et al., 2022, e.g.,). All these applications rely on being able to model the lens mass profile precisely and accurately. In other words, tighter constraints on these lens models would propagate as tighter constraints on all these fields of cosmology.

Despite these applications, we posit that strong-lensing IFU information is still underutilized. Rather than providing external constraints to the lens modeling pipeline, the idea of using the spatially-resolved kinematic information within the arcs themselves is rarely pursued. This methodology uses the kinematic markers within the source galaxy as lens modeling constraints, introducing additional velocity dimensionalities to the process (in our manuscript, a “marker” is defined as an identified feature on the lensed images that should ray-trace to the same location on the source). In addition to relying on high-resolution imaging to identify flux-based markers within each lensed image, leveraging this extra dimension can achieve the same effect with kinematics-based markers. Additionally, IFU data can be used to isolate light from a single source galaxy redshift, often removing nearly all lens and field galaxy light contamination. This significantly reduces, if not eliminates, degeneracies between the lens and source light, and crucially, reveals radial and demagnified central images overwhelmed by the lens galaxy in imaging data. These central images provide tight constraints on the lensing mass slope near the cluster core, well within the tangential critical curves, that are challenging to obtain in other ways, enabling critical tests of the cold dark matter model and alternatives such as the self-interacting dark matter (Sagunski et al., 2021; Andrade et al., 2022; O’Donnell et al., 2026a). Lastly, by forward-modeling the lens profile with the unlensed kinematic profile of the source, we can build a precise dynamical map of the source, incorporating data from all the lensed images. Having such a precise model makes it possible to even probe the black hole mass within the source galaxy, which would not be possible with imaging data alone (Newman et al., 2026).

papers.title: Tayler Instability and Its Saturation in Rotating Stars
papers.abstract: In stably stratified regions of rotating stars, magnetic instabilities play a key role by enabling dynamo and angular momentum transport. In particular, the Tayler instability of wound-up toroidal fields has long been considered to drive the Tayler-Spruit dynamo. However, the nonlinear saturation of the instability is poorly understood, despite its central role in the dynamo loop. In this paper, we use global simulations to verify the recently completed linear theory of the Tayler instability and determine its saturation. We confirm the picture of overstability of magnetostrophic and inertial waves, which grow on similar magnetostrophic timescales but oscillate with different frequencies. We find that magnetostrophic waves saturate with large amplitudes $\delta B/B\sim 1$ and dissipate the toroidal field on magnetostrophic timescales, while inertial waves saturate with $\delta B/B\ll 1$ and erode the toroidal field over much longer timescales. Moreover, magnetostrophic waves efficiently regenerate axisymmetric poloidal fields through nonlinear couplings while inertial waves do not. Our results indicate that the Tayler-Spruit dynamo can operate only through the magnetostrophic wave branch and that its steady-state may follow the scenario proposed by \cite{spruit2002dynamo}, ruling out the small-amplitude saturation scenario proposed by \cite{fuller2019slowing}. Implications for angular momentum transport and magnetic field amplification in evolving stars and nascent neutron stars are discussed.

It operates via the Tayler instability (TI) of strong toroidal fields [43], which are generated by the winding of weak poloidal fields. The nonlinear saturation of the TI, accompanied by regeneration of the poloidal fields, closes the dynamo loop.

It operates via the Tayler instability (TI) of strong toroidal fields [43], which are generated by the winding of weak poloidal fields. The nonlinear saturation of the TI, accompanied by regeneration of the poloidal fields, closes the dynamo loop.

The TSD has been invoked to explain efficient AM transport inside evolving stars [11, 2, 14], predict the natal spins of compact objects [13, 23, 15], and magnetize nascent neutron stars [25, 5, 33, 30]. However, the efficiency of the TSD remains highly uncertain due to the poorly understood properties of the TI, including its saturation and ability to regenerate poloidal fields.

The linear theory that determines the instability conditions and identifies the unstable modes was recently completed in [37] [37]. The analysis demonstrated that the TI in a rotating star is typically diffusively enabled: instability requires a dominant diffusive process to help overcome stabilization by the Coriolis force. As a result, the TI develops on length scales where diffusive and Coriolis timescales are comparable. This picture was not evident from the original marginal stability analysis in [41], and numerically testing the new linear theory is one of the goals of this paper.

Exponential growth of the unstable modes is followed by their saturation, which is strongly affected by rotation. When rotation is slow, TI saturation is well-understood: magnetic loops slip freely in opposite directions from the poles and saturate through parasitic Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities on Alfvénic timescales ∼1/ωA\sim 1/\omega_{\rm A} [19]. This generates magnetic field fluctuations comparable in magnitude to the background field δ​B∼B\delta B\sim B that dissipate through a turbulent cascade [8, 45, 17, 26]. The TSD, however, operates in the limit of fast rotation (Ω≫ωA\Omega\gg\omega_{\rm A}) where Coriolis forces restrain latitudinal slipping on Alfvénic timescales. In this case, the unstable eigenmodes are overstable waves—they oscillate with a real frequency while growing in amplitude on the magnetostrophic timescale ∼Ω/ωA2\sim\Omega/\omega_{\rm A}^{2} [32, 41, 9]. Their saturation amplitude is a key unresolved question, as it controls the dynamo outcome and AM transport.

Their saturation amplitude is a key unresolved question, as it controls the dynamo outcome and AM transport.

Two theoretical models predict different saturation levels based on disjoint possibilities. [42] argued that Tayler modes saturate through large-scale, latitudinal displacements of magnetic loops in the unstable polar regions. In this picture, toroidal fields migrate across the pole on magnetostrophic timescales and easily reconnect with opposite polarity fields, resulting in large saturation amplitudes δ​B/B∼1\delta B/B\sim 1 and efficient dissipation of the background toroidal field. [14] instead argued that saturation occurs with small displacements of magnetic loops. Then, energy transfer can occur only through interactions between local perturbations of the background field, resulting in a lower saturation level δ​B/B∼ωA/Ω≪1\delta B/B\sim\omega_{\rm A}/\Omega\ll 1 and less efficient dissipation. The lower saturation level and reduced dissipation predicted in [14] relative to [42] leads to a TSD model that builds up stronger dynamo fields and transports AM more rapidly.

In this paper, we aim to (1) numerically verify the linear instability theory developed in 37 and (2) resolve the question of TI saturation. Our global numerical model of a stably stratified fluid ball is described in Section II. Tests of the linear theory are presented in Section III, using simulations with different diffusivity ratios to isolate different TI modes. These modes are either overstable magnetostrophic waves (MW) or inertial waves (IW); the unstable IWs in particular are a new prediction of 37. We then examine their saturation and find qualitatively different outcomes. The unstable MW saturate with large-scale loop displacements, large amplitudes (δ​B∼B)(\delta B\sim B), and dissipate the background field on instability timescales, consistent with the picture in [42]. By contrast, the unstable IW saturate with smaller displacements, smaller amplitudes (δ​B≪B)(\delta B\ll B), and slower dissipation of the background field, similar to the picture in [14] originally proposed for MW. These findings are paralleled in a complementary paper, [12], that uses local simulations in a cylindrical geometry. In Section V, we present analytical arguments that account for both MW and IW saturation by examining the nonlinear timescales for energy transfer between different modes. Implications for the TSD and AM transport in evolving stars and nascent neutron stars are discussed in Section VI.

papers.title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger
papers.abstract: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.

papers.intro:
Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, MBH∼102M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{2}–105​M⊙10^{5}\,\rm M_{\odot}) bridge the gap between stellar-mass black holes (BHs) and supermassive black holes (SMBHs with MBH>106​M⊙M_{\rm BH}>10^{6}\,\rm M_{\odot}, see Greene et al., 2020, for a review). While their origin is still debated, they are the missing link to understand where the SMBHs that reside at the centres of most massive galaxies form.

Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs, MBH∼102M_{\rm BH}\sim 10^{2}–105​M⊙10^{5}\,\rm M_{\odot}) bridge the gap between stellar-mass black holes (BHs) and supermassive black holes (SMBHs with MBH>106​M⊙M_{\rm BH}>10^{6}\,\rm M_{\odot}, see Greene et al., 2020, for a review). While their origin is still debated, they are the missing link to understand where the SMBHs that reside at the centres of most massive galaxies form.

Although they are difficult to detect, growing observational samples provide evidence for accreting IMBHs and BHs just above the IMBH mass range (∼105{\sim}10^{5}–106​M⊙10^{6}\,\rm M_{\odot}), in dwarf galaxies (Filippenko & Ho, 2003; Baldassare et al., 2015), including more than 150 optical candidates in the SDSS (Reines et al., 2013), X-ray-selected IMBH candidates out to z∼2.4z\sim 2.4 (Mezcua et al., 2016; Mezcua et al., 2018), X-ray selected active galactic nuclei (AGN) in local dwarfs from eROSITA (Bykov et al., 2024; Sacchi et al., 2024), and dynamical measurements (Nguyen et al., 2019). Recently, DESI spectroscopy has tripled the census of AGN candidates in dwarf galaxies, including several hundred IMBH candidates (Pucha et al., 2025). One of the most robust IMBH candidates resides in the star cluster ω\omega Centauri and has a dynamically measured mass of ≳8200​M⊙\gtrsim 8200\,\rm M_{\odot} (Häberle et al., 2024). Nevertheless, the occupation fraction and mass distribution of IMBHs, particularly in low-mass galaxies that are expected to host this BH population, remain uncertain.

Nevertheless, the occupation fraction and mass distribution of IMBHs, particularly in low-mass galaxies that are expected to host this BH population, remain uncertain.

IMBHs might also be important as progenitors of SMBHs observed today. Indeed, JWST has uncovered a vast population of massive black holes at high redshift (Übler et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2023; Kocevski et al., 2023; Matthee et al., 2024), with some candidates close to the IMBH range (Maiolino et al., 2024b; Fei et al., 2026). However, most BHs with masses below 105​M⊙10^{5}\,\rm M_{\odot} are likely still missed by current observations. While some IMBHs at high redshift are expected to grow into SMBHs, some of them will be in environments where IMBHs do not grow efficiently. Hence, studying their evolution might help to understand what information their demographics retain about the formation of the first BHs (Greene et al., 2020; Volonteri et al., 2021).

Hence, studying their evolution might help to understand what information their demographics retain about the formation of the first BHs (Greene et al., 2020; Volonteri et al., 2021).

IMBHs can grow via gas accretion (including the disruption of stars) or mergers with other BHs. Especially at high redshift, mergers between galaxies are frequent (Fakhouri et al., 2010; Deason et al., 2014), but for BHs to grow via galaxy mergers the BHs brought into the galaxy must coalesce. Whether this process is efficient for IMBHs is therefore central to models of hierarchical black hole growth.

IMBHs can grow via gas accretion (including the disruption of stars) or mergers with other BHs. Especially at high redshift, mergers between galaxies are frequent (Fakhouri et al., 2010; Deason et al., 2014), but for BHs to grow via galaxy mergers the BHs brought into the galaxy must coalesce. Whether this process is efficient for IMBHs is therefore central to models of hierarchical black hole growth.

Coalescence proceeds through dynamical-friction-driven sinking, stellar hardening, and finally gravitational-wave (GW) emission (Peters, 1964; Begelman et al., 1980; Quinlan, 1996). Each stage can be inefficient for IMBHs. As dynamical friction depends on the mass of the sinking body (Chandrasekhar, 1943), pairs in low-mass haloes and gas-poor galaxies may remain off-centre for more than a Hubble time (Tremmel et al., 2018; Bellovary et al., 2019; Pfister et al., 2019; Bortolas et al., 2020; Bellovary et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2024; Partmann et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025), particularly in the cored density profiles common in dwarfs (Read et al., 2006; Tamfal et al., 2018). Even after a bound binary forms, stellar scattering must remove orbital energy from the binary for its separation to shrink (also called “stellar hardening”). However, the scattering of stars can be inefficient outside of dense star clusters and the binary can stall once it depletes the stellar orbits available for three-body scattering (Milosavljević & Merritt, 2003; Khan et al., 2024). In this case, more complex interactions, e.g. with a third BH, are required to trigger a BH merger (Partmann et al., 2024). Finally, as the Schwarzschild (1916) radius is BH mass dependent, the separation of IMBHs must be smaller than for SMBHs for gravitational waves to drive the BHs to merge (Peters, 1964).

Each stage can be inefficient for IMBHs. Even after a bound binary forms, stellar scattering must remove orbital energy from the binary for its separation to shrink (also called “stellar hardening”). However, the scattering of stars can be inefficient outside of dense star clusters and the binary can stall once it depletes the stellar orbits available for three-body scattering (Milosavljević & Merritt, 2003; Khan et al., 2024). In this case, more complex interactions, e.g. with a third BH, are required to trigger a BH merger (Partmann et al., 2024). Finally, as the Schwarzschild (1916) radius is BH mass dependent, the separation of IMBHs must be smaller than for SMBHs for gravitational waves to drive the BHs to merge (Peters, 1964).

Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) may alleviate both the sinking and hardening problems, by enhancing the mass of the sinking body and by providing high stellar densities for the scattering of stars. Direct NN-body simulations find that IMBH binaries embedded in sufficiently massive NSCs can form hard binaries and merge within a few hundred Myr (Khan & Holley-Bockelmann, 2021; Khan et al., 2026). When each black hole is initially carried by its own NSC, the interaction and merger of the clusters can further accelerate the early orbital decay (Ogiya et al., 2020; Mukherjee et al., 2025, see also Mastrobuono-Battisti et al. 2025). NSCs are common in low- and intermediate-mass galaxies, with nucleation fractions peaking around M⋆∼109​M⊙M_{\star}\sim 10^{9}\,\rm M_{\odot} (Sánchez-Janssen et al., 2019; Neumayer et al., 2020; Hoyer et al., 2021), although the fraction that also hosts massive black holes remains poorly constrained due to observational limitations (Hoyer et al., 2024). Dense clusters also provide a plausible scenario for the formation of IMBH seeds through runaway stellar collisions, tidal disruption of stars, and hierarchical black hole mergers (Portegies Zwart & McMillan, 2002; Giersz et al., 2015; Stone et al., 2017; Antonini et al., 2019; Rizzuto et al., 2021; Fujii et al., 2024; Rantala et al., 2024). If IMBH seeds indeed form in such clusters, the IMBHs delivered by dwarf-galaxy mergers arrive embedded in exactly the stellar systems that can both carry them to the centre and harden their binary, which motivates studying the two together. In addition, their potential well can enhance the mass growth of IMBHs via gas accretion (Partmann et al., 2025; Shin et al., 2025), allowing even IMBHs of ∼100​M⊙{\sim}100\,\rm M_{\odot} to grow fast (Partmann et al., 2025). BHs in NSCs are also predicted to be the dominant source of tidal disruption events (TDEs), which are relevant both as a BH growth channel and as a tool to identify IMBHs observationally (Polkas et al., 2024).

papers.title: The extragalactic science of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey II: Discovery of a galaxy cluster at z = 0.089 behind the Galactic plane
papers.abstract: The Zone of Avoidance (ZoA) continues to represent the most significant incompleteness in the extragalactic census of the Local Universe. It is evident that photometric surveys alone are insufficient to establish whether the galaxy overdensities detected therein are physical systems or projections along the line of sight. We present the first spectroscopic results of the extragalactic science area of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, demonstrating how near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy can reveal and dynamically characterise galaxy clusters hidden by the Milky Way. A photometric overdensity of 19 galaxy candidates was identified in the VVV NIRGC III catalogue, centred at $(l,b)=(274.05^\circ,+2.85^\circ)$ with a mean interstellar extinction of $A_{K_s}=0.2$ mag; 16 of these candidates were observed with VLT/KMOS in the $HK$ grating and yielded spectra with reliable cross-correlation radial velocities. A total of 14 galaxies form a compact structure with a mean redshift of $\langle z \rangle = 0.089 \pm 0.001$, which corresponds to a mean radial velocity $\langle cz \rangle = 26660 \pm 170$ km/s, while two are foreground galaxies. The rest-frame line-of-sight velocity dispersion is $\sigma_v = 560^{+110}_{-120}$ km/s, implying an indicative dynamical mass of $M_{200} = 1.9^{+0.7}_{-1.1} \times 10^{14} M_\odot$ (based on members within the cluster core $\sim 0.4 r_{200}$) and placing the system in the poor-cluster regime. Of these 14 cluster members, 13 also lie within the $2\sigma$ scatter of the fitted near-IR red sequence. The other two galaxies are foreground objects that lie outside this range.

papers.intro:
A reliable map of the mass distribution in the Local Universe requires a whole-sky galaxy census, yet roughly one-tenth of the sky remains poorly explored. Along the Galactic plane, interstellar dust, and (at the lowest latitudes) severe stellar crowding obscure background galaxies, even in the NIR. This region, called the Zone of Avoidance (ZoA), intersects with some of the richest structures in the nearby Universe, including the Great Attractor (Lynden-Bell et al. 1988) as well as the Norma (Kraan-Korteweg et al. 1996) and Vela (Kraan-Korteweg et al. 2017) superclusters. Recovering the galaxies hidden behind the Galactic plane is therefore essential for reconstructing the local mass distribution and velocity field.

Deep NIR imaging from the VISTA Variables in the Vía Láctea survey (Minniti et al. 2010, VVV;) and its extension VVVX (Saito et al. 2024) has substantially increased the number of galaxies detected in this region, yielding catalogues of more than 200000200000 galaxy candidates (Baravalle et al. 2021; Daza-Perilla et al. 2023; Duplancic et al. 2024; Alonso et al. 2025). Using the VVV NIRGC I catalogue, Soto et al. (2022) identified photometric overdensities that may extend known superclusters into the obscured region. These NIR surveys have also supported cluster studies behind the Galactic plane along two complementary lines. VVV/VVVX photometry has been used to characterise clusters previously known from X-ray observations, such as a cluster detected with Suzaku (Coldwell et al. 2014) and the Ophiuchus cluster (Galdeano et al. 2022). In addition, Baravalle et al. (2019) and Galdeano et al. (2023) identified new cluster candidates from VVV near-infrared (NIR) photometry, which were subsequently confirmed as physical structures through long-slit spectroscopic observations with Gemini South. As these cases show, photometry alone cannot determine whether an apparent overdensity corresponds to a physical structure or to a chance alignment of galaxies at different distances along a crowded line of sight. Redshift measurements are needed to turn the 2D catalogue of galaxies into a 3D view of the galaxy distribution.

The KMOS VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey (Arnaboldi et al. 2026, ESO programme ID 116.29EF;) is designed to deliver NIR spectroscopy of Galactic and extragalactic sources at low Galactic latitudes, exploiting the multiplexing capability of the 24 integral field units (IFUs) of KMOS at the VLT (Sharples et al. 2013). The survey design, target selection, observing strategy, data reduction, and redshift-measurement methodology for the extragalactic science area of the survey are fully described in the companion Early Data Release (EDR) paper (Baravalle et al., in prep.), which releases the first 161 galaxy spectra and validates the end-to-end pipeline.

papers.title: Detailed chemo-dynamical characterization of four elusive Milky Way star clusters
papers.abstract: A variety of faint and observationally challenging stellar systems has been discovered in the Milky Way in the last decades. Unveiling their kinematic and chemical properties is crucial to understand their nature and to assess their role in the history of our Galaxy. In this paper, we present a chemo-dynamical analysis of four elusive stellar systems (BH 140, Garro 01, BLISS 1, and Kim 3) using spectra collected with the X-shooter medium-resolution spectrograph at the VLT. We derived precise line-of-sight velocities and chemical abundances for all targets. Specifically, we provide the first spectroscopic characterization of metallicity and {\alpha}-element content for BH 140, the first comprehensive chemical characterization for BLISS 1 and Garro 01, and the first spectroscopic metallicity determination for Kim 3. BH 140, Garro 01 and BLISS 1 are relatively metal-rich systems with [Fe/H] ~ -0.7 dex and have enhanced {\alpha}-element abundances, whereas Kim 3 is notably metal-poor with [Fe/H] ~ -1.8 dex. We also performed an orbital analysis to investigate their origin as accreted or in situ systems. We found that Garro 01 and BH 140 have orbits confined within < 1.5 kpc from the Galactic plane, the former having also a remarkably circular orbit. They were likely born in situ, although the high orbital eccentricity of BH 140 and its mild deficiency in {\alpha}-elements leave other possibilities open. Although undoubtedly accreted, BLISS 1 does not exhibit a clear dynamical association with any known progenitor, lying in a high energy (E) - high vertical angular momentum (LZ ) prograde orbit reaching a maximum height from the Galactic plane of zmax ~ 8 kpc. Its chemical properties seem to favor an in situ origin, which might be connected with the Aleph sub-structure. Finally, we tentatively link the high energy and low LZ orbit of Kim 3 to the Elqui stream.

The advent of large-scale photometric and astrometric surveys, such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS; York et al. 2000), the Dark Energy Survey (DES; Collaboration 2005), the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS; Skrutskie et al. 2006), the VISTA Variables in the Vía Láctea and its eXtension (VVV, Minniti et al. 2010; VVVX, Saito et al. 2024), and the Gaia mission (Gaia Collaboration et al. 2016), has revolutionized our census of Galactic star clusters (Garro et al. 2024, e.g.,). In recent years, these surveys have led to the discovery of numerous faint or highly obscured stellar systems residing in both the Galactic halo and the disk/bulge (e.g., Balbinot et al. 2013; Kim et al. 2015; Kim et al. 2016; Koposov et al. 2017; Torrealba et al. 2019; Mau et al. 2019; Garro et al. 2020; Garro et al. 2022a; Garro et al. 2022b, and references therein).
