In recent years, these surveys have led to the discovery of numerous faint or highly obscured stellar systems residing in both the Galactic halo and the disk/bulge (e.g., Balbinot et al. 2013; Kim et al. 2015; Kim et al. 2016; Koposov et al. 2017; Torrealba et al. 2019; Mau et al. 2019; Garro et al. 2020; Garro et al. 2022a; Garro et al. 2022b, and references therein).

The nature of a significant fraction of these new systems remains ambiguous. Indeed, many of these ultra-faint stellar systems are rapidly filling the gap between globular clusters (GCs) and ultra-faint dwarf (UFD) galaxies in the size–luminosity plane (see Fig. 1), making this diagnostic diagram less effective in determining their true physical nature (Gilmore et al. 2007; Belokurov et al. 2014; Laevens et al. 2014; Contenta et al. 2017; Cerny et al. 2026, hereafter C26 ). To properly classify these faint systems, detailed chemo-dynamical characterization is essential. Indeed, the fundamental distinction between a UFD galaxy and a GC relies on the presence of a dark matter halo and variations in the iron content. The UFD galaxies are dark matter dominated systems; consequently, they exhibit dynamically resolved velocity dispersions that are too high to be explained by their visible stellar mass alone, leading to extremely high mass-to-light ratios (Simon 2019, e.g.,). Conversely, GCs are purely baryonic systems (Gratton et al. 2019, see,). Chemically, the deep potential well of UFD galaxies allowed them to retain supernova ejecta and sustain multiple bursts of star formation, resulting in a measurable, intrinsic spread in their iron content ([Fe/H]\rm[Fe/H]) (Willman and Strader 2012). In contrast, GCs generally display a homogeneous iron abundance. Furthermore, measuring precise and detailed abundance patterns serve as key discriminants to further classify these faint stellar systems into open clusters (OCs) and GCs. Indeed, GCs are traditionally more metal-poor than OCs (Carretta et al. 2009; Spina et al. 2021; Dal Ponte et al. 2025, e.g.,), and are characterized by the presence of multiple stellar populations exhibiting characteristic chemical inhomogeneities in light-elements, the most widespread example being the Na-O anticorrelation (Carretta et al. 2009), a feature generally absent in OCs. It has been proposed that many of these faint clusters, particularly those residing in the Galactic halo, were accreted into the MW following the disruption of their host satellite galaxies (Searle and Zinn 1978; Koposov et al. 2007; Leaman et al. 2013). Determining their birth environment can be key to untangle the ambiguous nature of these systems.

In this context, the Hubble Missing Globular Cluster Survey (MGCS; Massari et al. 2025) aims to shed light on these newly discovered objects. Specifically, the MGCS provides homogeneous two-band photometry and astrometry (Libralato et al. 2026) for all those kinematically confirmed clusters that were never observed by Hubble before. One of the main goals of this new survey is to determine the age and the distance of these systems, which will be combined with their chemo-dynamical properties in order to robustly assess their nature and origin (Massari et al. 2023).

papers.title: The origin of UV emission in extremely low-mass satellite galaxies: Insights from Leo T
papers.abstract: Leo T, a Milky Way (MW) satellite, is the lowest-mass gas-rich galaxy known to show recent star formation, making it an excellent laboratory for investigating star formation in the ultraviolet (UV) regime within a low-density, metal-poor environment. We present a far-UV (FUV) study using Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) data, aiming to characterize FUV star-forming clusters (SFCs), identify FUV-emitting stars, constrain their properties, and explore star formation in an extremely low-mass, metal-poor galaxy. We examined the galaxy's FUV extent and compared it with the H I distribution. We extracted thirty SFCs and derived their properties, including area, luminosity, and star formation rate (SFR), and compared them with previous studies. FUV-emitting stars and their stellar parameters were identified through cross-matching with catalogs from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE). We also estimated the global SFR and star formation efficiencies (SFEs) associated with previously identified CO clouds. The FUV luminosities of the SFCs confirm the absence of massive O and B-type stars in Leo T. The FUV-emitting stellar population consists of main-sequence (MS) stars, blue loop (BL) stars, horizontal branch stars, and emission-line (EM) stars. The upper MS and EM stars are concentrated near the optical center, whereas the lower MS and BL stars are more spatially extended. We find that five out of the six FUV-emitting stars with MUSE spectroscopy are extremely metal-poor ([Fe/H] $\leq$ -3). The (NUV - r) color profile indicates that the UV emission is dominated by stellar populations younger than 1 Gyr out to a radius $\lt$ 185 pc. Despite the recent detection of CO(1-0) emission, no SFCs are associated with the molecular clouds, which exhibit extremely low SFEs. The spatial distribution of the SFCs suggests a directional interaction with the MW.

papers.intro:
Milky Way (MW) dwarf satellite galaxies are broadly classified as either gas-rich or gas-poor systems (Jones et al., 2024). Gas-rich, low-mass satellites typically exhibit ongoing or recent star formation, whereas quenched galaxies are largely devoid of gas. Among these, the faintest satellites are highly compact, making them some of the smallest known galaxies in the Universe (Belokurov, 2013). They are dynamically overwhelmingly dark matter-dominated (Wolf et al., 2010; Walker and Peñarrubia, 2011; McConnachie, 2012; Di Cintio et al., 2014; Brook and Cintio, 2015; Bullock and Boylan-Kolchin, 2017; Read et al., 2019; Orkney et al., 2021, e.g.,). Chemically, they are extremely metal-poor and are considered to be some of the least evolved stellar systems in the local Universe (Vargas et al., 2013; Simon, 2019). These extreme properties make them unique cosmological laboratories for investigating the formation of the first galaxies and for placing stringent constraints on the nature of dark matter. Over the past two decades, the advent of large-scale digital sky surveys has driven a surge in the discovery of these faint systems (see review by Simon, 2019, and references therein).

Chemically, they are extremely metal-poor and are considered to be some of the least evolved stellar systems in the local Universe (Vargas et al., 2013; Simon, 2019). These extreme properties make them unique cosmological laboratories for investigating the formation of the first galaxies and for placing stringent constraints on the nature of dark matter. Over the past two decades, the advent of large-scale digital sky surveys has driven a surge in the discovery of these faint systems (see review by Simon, 2019, and references therein).

Recent studies of the star formation histories (SFHs) of faint dwarf galaxies, based on deep and accurate Hubble Space Telescope (HST) photometry, have shown that their stellar populations are predominantly old, with a substantial fraction of their stars having formed in the early Universe (Brown et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2014; Weisz et al., 2014). The blue stars observed in these systems have often been attributed to blue stragglers rather than recent star formation (Santana et al., 2013). These galaxies may therefore be regarded as fossil remnants that preserve information about the early stages of galaxy evolution (Simon, 2019). In addition, several studies have suggested that some faint dwarf galaxies may have shallower initial mass function (IMF) slopes than the canonical Salpeter IMF, corresponding to a bottom-light IMF (Geha et al., 2013; Gennaro et al., 2018). If such an IMF is extrapolated to higher stellar masses, it would imply a relatively larger population of massive stars and hence a higher supernova (SN) rate for a given total stellar mass. The resulting enhanced stellar feedback could have important consequences for the retention of gas and metals as well as for the chemical evolution and subsequent star formation in these systems.

The resulting enhanced stellar feedback could have important consequences for the retention of gas and metals as well as for the chemical evolution and subsequent star formation in these systems.

The metallicity distributions of faint dwarf galaxies also provide important insights into their chemical evolution. Spectroscopic studies have revealed a broad range of stellar metallicities (Martin et al., 2007; Simon and Geha, 2007), including extremely metal-poor stars with [Fe/H]<−3\mathrm{[Fe/H]}<-3 (Kirby et al., 2008). Several faint dwarf galaxies also show indications of multiple peaks in their metallicity distribution functions, suggesting the presence of chemically distinct stellar populations (Brown et al., 2014). Different chemical evolution models are used to explain the different metallicity distribution functions (Lai et al., 2011). Together, these observations highlight the interplay between stellar feedback, gas retention and accretion, and metal enrichment in shaping the evolution of faint dwarf galaxies.

Observationally, the vast majority of extremely low-luminosity satellites detected are MW satellites. While a few have been discovered around other nearby massive galaxies (Martin et al., 2016, e.g.,) and in the broader Local Volume as diffuse low surface brightness objects (Bennet et al., 2017; Danieli et al., 2018, e.g.,), performing detailed stellar population analyses on such faint systems remains highly challenging. Examining their SFHs reveals a stark contrast with more massive dwarf galaxies, where star formation is typically quenched by environmental effects (Geha, 2012). Even systems that were only recently accreted onto the MW halted their star formation billions of years ago (Fritz, T. K. et al., 2018; Simon, 2018). This early quenching is widely attributed to the cosmic epoch of reionization (Brown et al., 2014; Fitts et al., 2017; Rodriguez Wimberly et al., 2018), implying that star formation in these extremely low-mass systems was suppressed globally, regardless of their proximity to a massive host galaxy. An exception to this general picture of early quenching is the nearby satellite galaxy Leo T, which exhibits clear signatures of intermediate and even recent star formation.

Leo T is a low-mass, gas-rich MW satellite galaxy, with a brightness of Mv=−8\mathrm{M_{v}}=-8. This galaxy is slightly brighter than ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (Simon, 2019, UFDs; Mv>−7.7\mathrm{M_{v}}>-7.7;). It is considered a transitional galaxy, with properties of both dwarf spheroidal (dSph) and dwarf irregular (dIrr) galaxies (Irwin et al., 2007). Leo T is at a distance of 407kpc−27+29{}^{+29}_{-27}\,\mathrm{kpc} (Clementini et al., 2012), and has a stellar mass of 2×105​M⊙2\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}} (de Jong et al., 2008). Deep H i observations have revealed that the galaxy is gas-dominated, with a gas mass that is twice that of the stellar mass (Adams and Oosterloo, 2018, MHI=4×105​M⊙\mathrm{M_{HI}=}4\times 10^{5}\,\mathrm{M_{\odot}};). Therefore, Leo T is one of the faintest star-forming, gas-rich galaxies. Such features are more commonly associated with dIrr galaxies (Amrutha et al., 2024; Hunter et al., 2012).

Several studies have explored the SFH of Leo T (Irwin et al., 2007; de Jong et al., 2008; Weisz et al., 2012; Clementini et al., 2012; Vaz et al., 2023). In particular, optical photometry from HST (Weisz et al., 2012; Clementini et al., 2012) has revealed multiple distinct episodes of star formation within the galaxy. While 50% of the stellar population formed more than 7 Gyr ago, a younger population with an age of less than 500 Myr is also present. Star formation activity has also been detected at early epochs (between 10 and 13 Gyr ago), although with lower star formation rates (SFRs) compared to later episodes.

papers.title: High-Field Heat Capacity of Atacamite Cu$_2$Cl(OH)$_3$ for $\mathbf{H} \parallel b$ axis: From Antiferromagnetic Order to Correlated Disorder
papers.abstract: We present the heat capacity of the frustrated sawtooth-chain compound atacamite Cu$_2$Cl(OH)$_3$ in high magnetic fields up to 35 T for $\mathbf{H} \parallel b$ axis. We clearly observe the change from antiferromagnetic long-range order, indicated by a sharp transition anomaly shifted to lower temperatures when increasing field, to a field-induced spin-liquid-like state with the absence of any transition anomaly. Here, in highest magnetic fields above 32 T a broad anomaly is present which is shifted to higher temperatures as the field is increased. The low-temperature heat capacity in the high-field region can be described well by an exponential behavior indicating a thermal activation over a spin gap. The findings are consistent with our scenario for the high-field state in atacamite for $\mathbf{H} \parallel c$ axis, where we proposed the sawtooth chains to decouple into two spin subsystems, basal and apical spin sites, leading to a partially polarized state with $M \sim M_\mathrm{sat}/2$.

papers.title: SDSS-V LVM: Mapping of plasma temperatures in the Lagoon Nebula reveals the origin of long-standing chemical abundance discrepancies
papers.abstract: Knowing the chemical composition of interstellar gas is essential for understanding the chemical evolution of galaxies. Ionized nebulae provide key laboratories for this purpose, where chemical abundances are commonly derived from emission lines of heavy ions such as doubly ionized oxygen, $O^{++}$. Abundances can be inferred either from collisionally excited lines (CELs) or from recombination lines (RLs). However, for more than 80 years, the former have yielded systematically lower abundances than the latter. We map this ''abundance discrepancy'' using the first spatially resolved integral field unit (IFU) observations of $O^{++}$ RLs and CELs across a Milky Way H II region: the Lagoon Nebula (a.k.a. M8). Modeling the data using a plasma temperature perturbation model, we present unequivocal evidence that electron temperature ($T_e$) fluctuations drive the abundance discrepancy in M8. We find a tight correlation between the abundance discrepancy and the difference between $T_e$ derived from the classical CEL method and a hybrid RL/CEL approach. We identify this Te discrepancy as an observational proxy for the amplitude of the thermal fluctuations, providing a new, direct way to quantify their effect on nebular abundances. The correlation constrains the mean electron temperature of the gas. Adopting this mean temperature reconciles CEL and RL abundances, effectively eliminating the abundance discrepancy.

The chemical composition of galaxies reflect the cumulative history of star formation, stellar nucleosynthesis, astration, supernova explosions, gas and dust chemical redistribution and depletion processes, and the inflow, mixing, and dispersal of gas in and out of galaxies across cosmic time. These processes underpin a wide range of phenomena in astrophysics, making chemical abundances a key parameter in stellar and galaxy evolution models [45, 36, 44, 27, 8, 28].

In star-forming galaxies, H ii regions mark sites of recent star formation, where radiation from young massive stars ionizes the surrounding neutral gas. The resulting plasma emits a spectrum rich in emission lines from multiple elements, whose relative intensities provide primary diagnostics of the physical conditions – electron density (nen_{e}), and electron temperature (TeT_{e}) – and chemical composition of the ionized gas.

The abundance of heavy elements in the interstellar medium (ISM), measured with respect to that of hydrogen (H), provides a fundamental tracer of galaxy evolution. Oxygen, the most abundant heavy element, is widely used as a proxy for measuring the overall heavy element content of the ISM [27, 8, 35, e.g.]. The strong collisionally excited lines (CELs) of O++ are readily detected in the optical spectra of H ii regions. Faint auroral CELs, historically hard to detect in many galactic and nearby H ii regions, are now detected out to a red-shift, z∼10\sim 10, thanks to the James Web Space Telescope (JWST), while the extremely faint recombination lines (RLs) of O++ can only be reliably measured in the brightest nearby regions [16, 21, 38, 11, 57, 59].

Gas-phase O++ abundances are commonly derived using the so-called “direct method”. In which, the electron temperature is inferred from ratios of CELs with different excitation energies, while the electron density is obtained independently from ratios of CELs with close-lying upper levels, whose relative populations are set by the density-dependent competition between radiative decay and collisional de-excitation. Given TeT_{e} and nen_{e}, the emissivities of O++ CELs can be calculated directly, allowing the O++/H+ abundance ratio to be determined by comparing their brightness to that of hydrogen RLs [45].

In which, the electron temperature is inferred from ratios of CELs with different excitation energies, while the electron density is obtained independently from ratios of CELs with close-lying upper levels, whose relative populations are set by the density-dependent competition between radiative decay and collisional de-excitation. Given TeT_{e} and nen_{e}, the emissivities of O++ CELs can be calculated directly, allowing the O++/H+ abundance ratio to be determined by comparing their brightness to that of hydrogen RLs [45].

Because CEL emissivities depend exponentially on TeT_{e}, the direct method is intrinsically sensitive to the thermal structure of a nebula. Hotter regions contribute disproportionately to the observed emission, while cooler regions contribute comparatively little once collisional excitation becomes inefficient. As a result, if present, unresolved temperature variations along the line of sight can bias the inferred TeT_{e} toward higher values, leading to systematically underestimated O++ abundances from CELs [52, 38].

RLs of elements heavier than Helium (“metals” in astrophysical lingo) provide an alternative abundance diagnostic that is largely insensitive to temperature fluctuations. Because the emissivities of O++ and H+ RLs have a very similar temperature dependence, their ratio provides an almost temperature-independent measure of the O++ ionic abundance [45, 51]. However, O++ RLs are intrinsically 3 to 4 orders of magnitude fainter than their CEL counterparts, restricting their detection to the brightest and nearest H ii regions.

Since the early work of [65], it has been recognized that abundances derived from heavy-element RLs systematically exceed those obtained from CELs in H ii regions, often by factors of up to 3 [50, 16, 18, 21, 15, 7, 38, 59]. This long standing offset is quantified through the abundance discrepancy factor (ADF), defined as the logarithmic difference between RL- and CEL-based abundances. Despite decades of observational and theoretical effort, this discrepancy has persisted as a fundamental obstacle to the accurate determination of chemical abundances in ionized nebulae for more than 80 years.

Resolving this discrepancy is imperative. If heavy-element abundances in star-forming regions are underestimated by a factor of 2–3, the metal content of galaxies and the cosmic heavy-element budget would be systematically biased [47]. Such an offset would propagate across a wide range of astrophysical inferences, directly impacting constraints on physical processes associated with metal production [28, e.g., nucleosynthesis, ], ISM enrichment [44, 24, heavy element stellar yields, stellar winds and supernovae feedback, ], the baryon cycle on galactic scales [63, 53, gas inflows and outflows, ]) and heavy element depletion [14, e.g. dust formation and metal capture in stellar remnants]).

The metallicity of the ISM further regulates gas cooling and the resulting star formation, shaping the stellar initial mass function both in theoretical models [23, 12] and observations [66, 32], with further implications for models of the Galactic habitable zone, shifting our expectations of where and when a galaxy like the Milky Way, is most likely to form life-hosting planets like Earth [33, 26, 37]. Furthermore, since direct-method (i.e. CEL) abundances underpin most of the strong-line diagnostics used to infer chemical abundances in galaxies across cosmic time [7, 27, 35, 56], any systematic bias in the local CEL abundance scale would propagate into our understanding of galaxy chemical evolution [42].

The physical origin of the abundance discrepancy remains debated. Several hypotheses have been proposed, including shocks and turbulence by stellar feedback [49, 6, 54]; chemically enriched high density inclusions embedded within the ionized gas [62, 60], and departures from a Maxwellian electron energy distribution in the ionized ISM [43]. papers.title: Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS) VIII. First interstellar detection of fully deuterated methyl cyanide
papers.abstract: Deuteration is a powerful metric to gain insight into the formation pathways of interstellar molecules in star forming regions. Our primary goal is to search for the fully deuterated form of methyl cyanide, CD3CN, in the ISM. We used a sensitive imaging spectral survey of the protostellar system L1551 IRS5 in the Taurus molecular cloud performed as part of the Large Program carried out with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) called Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (COMPASS). We derived the column densities of methyl cyanide and several of its less abundant isotopologs, including deuterated ones, under the assumption of local thermodynamic equilibrium. All three deuterated isotopologs of methyl cyanide were detected toward the northern binary component of L1551 IRS5. In particular, we report the first interstellar detection of CD3CN. The measured D/H ratio increases by about half an order of magnitude from one deuterated isotopolog to the next, in a similar way as what was measured for methanol in several other low-mass protostars. This suggests that methyl cyanide predominantly forms like methanol on the surface of dust grains during the cold prestellar phase. However, the measured factor of 2 difference between the D/H ratios of methyl cyanide and methanol may either indicate that gas-phase processes during the warm-up stage contribute approximately equally to the production of methyl cyanide, or that methyl cyanide and its deuterated isotopologs are formed during the prestellar phase at a somewhat earlier time than methanol. Multiply deuterated isotopologs are crucial to understand the formation and inheritance of molecules in the ISM by coupling observations and astrochemical models. Unfortunately, no model has so far investigated the deuteration of methyl cyanide up to the fully deuterated form. [Abridged]

papers.intro:
In the field of astrochemistry, complex organic molecules (COMs) are defined as carbon-bearing species made of at least six atoms (Herbst and van Dishoeck 2009). Understanding how and when these molecules form in the interstellar medium (ISM) and if the chemical composition of the material involved in star formation is inherited or altered from one evolutionary phase to the next are some of the main goals of astrochemistry (Jørgensen et al. 2020, see, e.g.,). One property of COMs that can help us decipher their origin is their degree of deuteration. Molecules get enriched in deuterium during the cold and dense prestellar phase thanks to the exothermicity of the reaction of the main molecular ion, H+3{}_{3}^{+}, with the molecular reservoir of deuterium, HD (Ceccarelli et al. 2014, e.g.,). Measuring the deuterium fractionation of a molecule (that is the column density ratio of its deuterated form to its hydrogenated form) can thus tell us about the time when, and conditions (e.g., temperature) under which, a molecule has formed.

In this work, we are interested in the deuteration of methyl cyanide, CH3CN. This species is one of the simplest COMs in the family of nitrogen-bearing molecules. Both solid-phase and gas-phase processes have been proposed for the formation of methyl cyanide. For instance, in the astrochemical models of Aikawa et al. (2012) and Taquet et al. (2014), it predominantly forms on the surface of dust grains, both during the cold, prestellar phase and later during the warm-up phase once the protostar has started to heat up its envelope. The tentative identification of methyl cyanide in interstellar ices gives some support to these model predictions (Nazari et al. 2024). In contrast, in the astrochemical model of Garrod et al. (2022), gas-phase reactions significantly contribute to the formation of methyl cyanide during the warm-up phase, during which deuteration is expected to be inefficient. Measuring the deuteration level of methyl cyanide in protostellar envelopes can thus allow us to discriminate the reaction schemes proposed by these models and better understand the formation of this molecule. So far, two of its three deuterated isotopologs have been detected in the ISM: CH2DCN and CHD2CN (Gerin et al. 1992; Calcutt et al. 2018, e.g.,).

The Large Program performed with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) called Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys (Jørgensen et al. 2026, COMPASS;) is an unbiased spectral survey of 11 low-mass Class 0 and I protostellar sources that are known to be chemically rich and reside in diverse environments. The goal of the COMPASS project is to characterize the chemical composition of these sources and investigate the impact of the environment and physical evolution of a star forming core on its chemical evolution. One of the targeted sources is the Class I protostellar system L1551 IRS5 (see Jørgensen et al. 2026, for an overview of its properties). This binary system is located in the Taurus molecular cloud at a distance of 145 pc (Zucker et al. 2020; Jørgensen et al. 2026). The binary components, called L1551 IRS5N and IRS5S (Lim et al. 2016), are separated by about 50 au and each one possesses a compact (radius of about 10 au) circumstellar disk (Rodríguez et al. 1998). The system is surrounded by a circumbinary disk or flattened inner envelope with a radius of ∼\sim150 au (Cruz-Sáenz de Miera et al. 2019; Takakuwa et al. 2020) and a larger scale (radius ∼\sim0.1 pc) ∼\sim1–2 M⊙M_{\odot} envelope (Jørgensen et al. 2002; Chou et al. 2014). L1551 IRS5 is known to have a relatively high D/H ratio of water compared to other protostars (Andreu et al. 2023). From a preliminary analysis of the methyl cyanide emission in the COMPASS sources, L1551 IRS5 stood out as a particularly interesting source with respect to the deuteration of this molecule. This motivated a detailed study of methyl cyanide and its isotopologs toward L1551 IRS5, which is presented in this article.

papers.title: PRISMS GHZ8: Evidence for a Young Burst and Potential Merger Activity at z=10.23
papers.abstract: UV-bright galaxies in the early Universe provide important constraints on the rapid build-up of stellar mass and the sources responsible for cosmic reionization. However, the physical processes that drive their high UV luminosities remain unclear. Here we report JWST/MIRI LRS spectroscopy of GHZ8, a UV-bright galaxy at z=10.23 with a magnification $\mu=1.23$. The spectrum shows a $\sim 5\sigma$ detection for the $\rm H\beta$-[OIII] complex and $\sim 4\sigma$ for $\rm H\alpha$ line, with fluxes of $3.2\pm0.9\times10^{-18}$ and $\rm 1.7\pm0.4\times10^{-18}\,erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}$, respectively. Based on JWST/NIRCam imaging, we find that GHZ8 consists of two components separated only by 0.16" ($\approx600$ pc): a bright, extended main component and a faint, compact southeastern clump, hereafter referred to as GHZ8-main and GHZ8-SE. Through morphological decomposition, we find demagnified $M_{UV}=-19.91\pm0.10$ and $-18.03\pm0.15$ mag for GHZ8-main and GHZ8-SE, with blue UV slopes of $\beta_{UV}=-2.53\pm0.22$ and $-3.45\pm0.49$, respectively, indicating that both components host young stellar populations. In particular, the extremely blue UV continuum of GHZ8-SE requires an extremely young, ISM-poor stellar population with a high ionizing photon escape fraction, $f_{esc}= 0.6-1.0$. Combining the UV and $\rm H\alpha$ luminosities with the results from the spectro-photometric SED fitting, we constrain the star-formation activity of GHZ8-main, and find either a recent, short-lived burst of star formation that is now in its final phases, or continuous star formation over a relatively short period ($<50\,{\rm Myr}$). GHZ8 therefore provides observational evidence for bursty star formation in a UV-bright galaxy. Globally, GHZ8 may be undergoing a merger-induced starburst, although deeper imaging or spatially resolved kinematic information is required for a more definitive interpretation.

JWST deep-field and lensing-field imaging surveys have identified a large number of galaxy candidates at z>10z>10 [60, 67, 115, 123, 53, 41, 11, 85, 115, 61, 44, 39, 116], many of which have been subsequently confirmed by spectroscopic follow-up observations [49, 64, 6, 61, 72, 108, 149, 4, 3, 104, 141, 136, 35, 71]. A subset of these galaxies shows very high UV luminosities, leading to an apparent excess at the bright end of the UV luminosity function [61, 38, 42, 66, 44, e.g.,]. This exceeds the expectations of pre-JWST models and poses a challenge to galaxy-formation theory [17]. Within the standard framework of hierarchical structure formation, producing a large population of UV-bright galaxies at such early cosmic times is not straightforward, and may involve the earlier dark-matter halo assembly, higher star-formation efficiency, and the lack of feedback [52, 61, 67, 86].

Several physical mechanisms have been proposed to explain the population of UV-bright galaxies at z>10z>10. One possibility is a bursty star-formation history (SFH), in which intense star formation over a short timescale temporarily boosts the UV luminosity and makes galaxies easier to detect [98, 129, 134, 92, 135, 112, 38, 83]. Young, metal-poor stellar populations with less dust can also produce brighter UV continua and higher ionizing photon production efficiencies [59, 58, 57, 67, 54, 24]. Binary stellar evolution, or a top-heavy IMF, can further enhance the hard ionizing spectrum and UV output [67, 146, 74, 78, 127, e.g.,]. These mechanisms are not mutually exclusive, and multiple processes may operate simultaneously within the same system.

In this paper, we report JWST/MIRI LRS rest-frame optical spectroscopy of GHZ8 and combine it with existing NIRCam imaging and NIRSpec/prism spectroscopy for a joint analysis. In Section II, we describe the observations and data reduction. In Section III, we measure the Hα\alpha, Hβ\beta+[O iii], and rest-frame UV emission lines, and use line ratios and the Balmer decrement to constrain its properties. Section IV presents the image decomposition and the clumpy morphology of GHZ8, consisting of GHZ8-main and GHZ8-SE. In Section V, we describe the configuration of the decomposed SED fitting. Sections VI and VII present the fitting results for GHZ8-SE and GHZ8-main, respectively. In Section VIII, we discuss the physical origin of the clumpy structure of GHZ8 and its implications for ionizing photon escape. Finally, we summarize our conclusions in Section IX. papers.title: Memorization Capacity of Invariant Convolutional Neural Nets
papers.abstract: Neural networks are powerful memorizers which are often able to interpolate their training data even when the labels have been randomized. While there exists an extensive literature on the memorization capacity of fully connected networks, in practice more specific architectures with problem-dependent properties are preferred, such as convolutional networks for image classification. In this paper we consider convolutional networks which are invariant with respect to a given arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations, which may include translations, reflections, and/or rotations of images and invariances of higher order tensors. We prove upper bounds on the size of an invariant convolutional neural network with threshold activations that is required to interpolate a given dataset with two classes. Our bounds are formulated in terms of a complexity measure that takes the invariant structure into account and is instance-specific, i.e., it is related to the mutual arrangement of the classes in the given dataset and their geometric properties rather than the number of samples. Our proof is constructive: for given input data, instances of an interpolating network can be computed via a randomized algorithm with high probability. In numerical experiments we investigate the practical effectiveness of this algorithm.

papers.intro:
The memorization capacity of a neural network architecture quantifies the number of parameters and neurons needed for the architecture to be able to interpolate any NN data points for any assignment of labels (for a suitable setting of the weights). The study of this capacity has a long history—dating back all the way to the 1960s—and its importance experienced a recent revival due to the double descent phenomenon (Belkin et al., 2019). According to the long-standing bias-variance trade-off (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014; Hastie et al., 2009), the complexity of a machine learning model needs to balance underfitting and overfitting to achieve good generalization performance. It should be rich enough to express the underlying patterns in the data but still be simple enough to avoid picking up any spurious patterns. This classical viewpoint is at odds with modern practice in deep learning, where highly over-parameterized neural networks are trained to achieve a (nearly) perfect fit on the training data (Canziani et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017, see, e.g.,). In spite of this apparent overfitting, however, these models perform well on test data. This behavior is described by the double descent curve, where increasing the models complexity beyond the interpolation threshold—where the model is just complex enough to interpolate its training data—results in a second descent of the test error. This behavior is well documented for deep neural networks as well as a wide variety of other machine learning models, see, e.g., Belkin et al. (2019); Belkin (2021); Nakkiran et al. (2021); Mei and Montanari (2022); Hastie et al. (2022). As was argued by Dirksen et al. (2024), in practical applications the model size is tailored to a given data set. Memorization capacity, however, studies the reverse situation, requiring a model of fixed size to interpolate any dataset of NN samples. This results in bounds that necessarily grow with the number of samples. However, for a problem with a ‘nice’ structure, such as linearly separable classes in the simplest case, this should certainly not be necessary.

A prominent example are convolutional neural networks for the processing of sequential or image data. Additionally, those models are frequently endowed with special problem-dependent properties such as translation-invariance, e.g., through data augmentation in the training process or the use of global pooling operations, see, e.g., Biscione and Bowers (2021); Blything et al. (2021). This leads to the question: What is the memorization capacity of a translation-invariant neural architecture? We recall that memorization capacity requires an architecture to be able to interpolate any NN samples for any assignment of labels. When two samples are the same up to translation, interpolating any label assignment simply becomes impossible. At the very least, one would need to identify these samples and assign them the same label. At the same time, instead of the total number of samples one should then consider only the number of unique samples up to translation, as any translated copies are correctly classified automatically.

(2021). This leads to the question:

What is the memorization capacity of a translation-invariant neural architecture?

We recall that memorization capacity requires an architecture to be able to interpolate any NN samples for any assignment of labels. When two samples are the same up to translation, interpolating any label assignment simply becomes impossible. At the very least, one would need to identify these samples and assign them the same label. At the same time, instead of the total number of samples one should then consider only the number of unique samples up to translation, as any translated copies are correctly classified automatically.

In this paper, we remedy the above issues via an instance-specific approach which additionally respects the translation-invariant property of the model. Specifically, we build upon the prior work of Dirksen et al. (2024) who derived an instance-specific result for fully-connected networks. Our main contributions are the following: 1. Memorization capacity of translation-invariant neural nets. In Section 2, given a binary classification data set, we prove upper bounds on the required number of parameters and neurons for a translation-invariant convolutional neural network to be able to interpolate the data. The bounds are linked to a new complexity measure that respects both the translation-invariant property of the model, as well as the mutual arrangement of the two classes and their geometric properties. 2. Randomized interpolation algorithm for convolutional neural nets. Our proof is constructive: we introduce a randomized algorithm that, given a binary classification data set, with high probability, outputs a translation-invariant convolutional neural network which interpolates the data and has at most the asserted size. In numerical experiments, we investigate the effectiveness of our algorithm both in controlled experiments and on real image data, and compare its performance to previous work. 3. Beyond just translations. In Appendix A, we prove our results in a more general framework, which supports invariance with respect to a given, arbitrary finite group of orthogonal transformations. Apart from translations, this also includes, for example, reflections and rotations of image data, and invariances of higher order tensor data. We have chosen to present our results first in the special setting of translation-invariant neural nets to keep the exposition accessible. We develop our results for networks with threshold activations, as this is a challenging setting in memorization theory. We expect that our results can be extended to other activations that zero out negative inputs and assign positive values to positive inputs, such as the ReLU.

papers.title: Countable unions of intervals without Riesz spectra
papers.abstract: We prove that every set $S = \bigcup_{n \geq 0} [ t_{2 n + 1} , t_{2 n} )$, where $t_0 > t_1 > \cdots > 0$ and $t_n \to 0$, admits no Riesz spectrum. This extends the result of Kozma, Nitzan, and Olevskii \cite{KNO} to a wide class of countable unions of intervals.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Super and Lightning: Open, Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, open and efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic workloads. Super is a 120B-parameter, 12B-active multimodal model, while Lightning is a smaller 30B-parameter, 3B-active text model; both designed for efficient deployment. Both models combine large-scale distillation, long-context training, and native speculative decoding, while Super further incorporates Indic continued pretraining and agentic software-engineering mid-training. We develop a comprehensive post-training pipeline spanning supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RLVR and RLHF), complemented in Super by specialized teacher training and multi- teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). This transforms Super from a text-only base model into a multimodal agent capable of reasoning over text, images, video, and interactive tool environments. We further explore test-time scaling through parallel agent execution and self-verification. Across training and deployment, we jointly optimize capability and efficiency. Indic continued pretraining improves Indian-language benchmarks by up to 9.82 percentage points, while agentic mid-training strengthens software-engineering capabilities and robustness across agent harnesses. The post-trained Super model achieves 51.78% on SWE-bench Pro, surpassing Nemotron 3 Ultra despite using approximately 4.6x fewer active parameters. Post-training MTP boosting improves speculative- decoding acceptance length by up to 21.8% under probabilistic draft sampling, while NVFP4 quantization achieves 99.62% median accuracy recovery relative to BF16. Inference optimizations enable up to 4,856 output tokens/s/GPU on GB200 while sustaining at least 50 tokens/s/user.

papers.intro:
We present Nemotron 3.5 Super and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, efficient Mixture-of-Experts Hybrid Mamba-Transformer models designed for reasoning, multimodal understanding, and long-running agentic workloads. Nemotron 3.5 Super is a 120 billion total and 12 billion active parameter model initialized from Nemotron 3 Super (NVIDIA, 2026b), while Lightning 3.5 is a 30 billion total and 3 billion active parameter model initialized from Nano 3 Base (NVIDIA, 2025c). As LLM applications increasingly move toward long-horizon agents that write code, interact with tools, reason over large contexts, and operate across multimodal environments, both model capability and inference efficiency become increasingly important. Nemotron 3.5 targets this regime through efficient hybrid architectures, native speculative decoding with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) (Gloeckle et al., 2024), large-scale distillation, specialized continued pretraining and mid-training, agent-focused post-training, and NVFP4 quantization.

Nemotron 3.5 targets this regime through efficient hybrid architectures, native speculative decoding with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) (Gloeckle et al., 2024), large-scale distillation, specialized continued pretraining and mid-training, agent-focused post-training, and NVFP4 quantization.

We begin by adapting the MTP architecture for efficient recursive speculative decoding. Nemotron 3.5 Super consolidates two non-shared MTP heads into a single recursively shared head, while Lightning initializes its MTP head from Nemotron 3 Super Base through architecture-aware projection fusion and pruning. Both models undergo a dedicated 100 billion token MTP warm-up with the backbone frozen. For Super, we additionally introduce hidden-state mixing to mitigate the train–inference conditioning mismatch during recursive drafting. We subsequently distill both models for 1 trillion tokens using the next-larger Nemotron form factor as teacher: Ultra 3 Base (NVIDIA, 2026) for Super and Super 3 Base (NVIDIA, 2026b) for Lightning. Following distillation, Lightning undergoes long-context training, while Super proceeds through additional continued-pretraining and agentic mid-training stages.

We further improve Nemotron 3.5 Super through targeted continued-pretraining and mid-training stages. First, we perform 100 billion tokens of Indic continued pretraining, incorporating 10 billion tokens of synthetic and natural Indic data alongside 90 billion tokens from the preceding training mixture. We then extend the model to a 1M-token context length using 35 billion tokens of continued pretraining, followed by 65.4 billion tokens of agentic software-engineering mid-training at 256K context. papers.title: Extending Higher-Order Critical Pairs
papers.abstract: Confluence is a fundamental property of computation which implies that the nondeterminism of a system does not affect its outcomes. A key concept of confluence research in rewriting theory is the notion of critical pairs which captures the potential local sources of non-confluence. In this paper, we lift the definition of higher-order critical pairs to a more expressive class of higher-order rewrite systems. Thereby, we facilitate confluence analysis of rewrite systems which can express complex one-step computations as well as program transformations from functional programming.

Nipkow lifted the “critical pair approach” to confluence from first-order rewriting to rewriting on simply-typed λ\lambda-terms [19, 20]. The corresponding TRSs are called higher-order rewrite systems (HRSs). In HRSs, terms are viewed modulo the meta-theory of β​η\beta\eta-conversion in the simply-typed λ\lambda-calculus. papers.title: Going deep, reaching further: What can Boltzmann machines efficiently represent?
papers.abstract: While universal approximation theorems theoretically underpin the representation capabilities of machine learning models, they have two shortcomings: They do not focus on efficient representations and they tend to be insensitive to depth and other heuristically important properties. In this work we show that these two shortcomings are intertwined. We prove that machine learning models which are deeper or have higher-order interactions can efficiently represent a larger set of functions, i.e. have larger efficient reach. It follows that deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) sub-maximal, and k-body generalizations of RBMs form a hierarchy between the two, even though all are universal. More generally, (i) we provide a full characterization of machine learning models with maximal efficient reach; (ii) we derive separations between deep and shallow models for three representation tasks; and (iii) we prove that the efficient reach of shallow models constitutes an infinite hierarchy indexed by the interaction order. The proofs draw on different methodologies, namely on (i) a recent characterization of universal spin models; (ii) computational complexity bounds for spin models; and (iii) communication complexity bounds applied to shallow models. This work shows that universal machine learning models can strongly differ in their efficient representation capabilities, and provides a theoretical foundation for heuristic observations.

papers.intro:
Several machine learning models are theoretically supported by so-called universal approximation theorems (UATs), that is, proofs that the respective model can represent or approximate any function from a certain function class. Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs), deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) and deep belief networks (DBNs) are universal approximators of probability distributions [26, 27, 33], feedforward neural networks with at least one hidden layer are universal approximators of continuous functions with compact support [20, 9], and transformers are universal approximators of sequence-to-sequence functions [47].

Several machine learning models are theoretically supported by so-called universal approximation theorems (UATs), that is, proofs that the respective model can represent or approximate any function from a certain function class. Restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs), deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) and deep belief networks (DBNs) are universal approximators of probability distributions [26, 27, 33], feedforward neural networks with at least one hidden layer are universal approximators of continuous functions with compact support [20, 9], and transformers are universal approximators of sequence-to-sequence functions [47].

Although theoretically foundational, practically, these UATs have two major shortcomings. First, they do not consider the efficiency of the representation. For instance, the UATs for RBMs, DBMs and DBNs, require exponentially many hidden units and hence exponentially many parameters to represent a generic target function [26, 27, 33]. Consequently, they provide limited insight into the representation capabilities of efficient models. Second, these UATs often are insensitive to heuristically important model hyperparameters such as depth. For example UATs exist for feedforward networks with just one hidden layer as well as for both RBMs and DBMs. They therefore do not explain the widely observed superiority of deep models [32, 43, 45, 42]. This raises two questions: Are all universal machine learning models equal with regard to their efficient representation capabilities? (Q1) If not, what properties characterize “efficient universal models”? (Q2) For (Q2), we are thinking of properties such as depth or other model hyperparameters.

For (Q2), we are thinking of properties such as depth or other model hyperparameters.

Recently, we have shown that UATs of certain, energy-based machine learning models such as RBMs, DBMs and generalizations thereof can be proven by means of a characterization of so-called universal spin models [40]. The latter are spin models which can encode arbitrary energy functions in their low-energy sector. This way of deriving UATs has two main advantages for addressing (Q1) and (Q2). First, the characterization of universal spin models provides a handle on the resource requirements of UATs in the following sense. Spin models have a local structure that is respected by the universality characterization. If the target is compatible with this local structure, the derived UAT will only require a polynomial overhead. Second, the characterization of universal spin models is fundamentally based on a notion of composition. As a consequence, the resulting UATs should favour deep models, since depth arises by constructing representations in a compositional way, layer by layer.

In this work, we leverage the characterization of universal spin models to tackle (Q1) and (Q2). We find the following answers: No, they have different efficient representation capabilities, forming a rich landscape (see Fig. 1). (A1) The properties that determine the efficient representation capabilities are depth (or, more precisely, visible closure) and interaction order. (A2) Our work provides a theoretical underpinning for the heuristic observation that deep models perform better. It also shows that the two shortcomings of UATs mentioned above are deeply intertwined. More generally, it illustrates how insightful connecting different fields through a common notion of universality can be — the characterization of universal spin models gives us an edge in the study of “efficient universality” of machine learning models.

We study the efficient reach, i.e. the efficient representation capabilities, of machine learning models from three different angles. (i) Characterization of maximal models. Models which have maximal efficient reach are called maximal. Here we provide a characterization of maximal models. More precisely, we study the efficient reach of spin and machine learning models through the notion of simulations (that is, encoding target functions in the low-energy sector) and the characterization of universal spin models, using that simulations imply approximations (in terms of marginal distributions). We prove that, for spin models, universality and maximality are equivalent (Theorem 10), so the characterization of universality also applies to maximal efficient reach. In contrast, for machine learning models with visible and hidden spins (or units) another property becomes decisive: visible closure (Definition 12), which formalizes the intuition that hidden-hidden interactions are required to compose simulations and approximations. We then prove that any two of the three properties of universality, visible closure and maximality imply the third (Theorem 16, see also Fig. 2). Thus, among universal machine learning models, visible closure precisely characterizes those with maximal efficient reach. This extends the connection between universality and universal approximation established in [40] to the setting of polynomial resources. It follows that DBMs with at least two hidden layers are maximal (Corollary 17). (ii) Separation between shallow and maximal models. We establish separations for three representation tasks: simulating functions (in the low-energy sector), approximating functions as unnormalized visible spin marginals, and approximating functions as normalized visible spin marginals (see Table 1). All three are based on reasonable assumptions on computational complexity, namely the non-collapse of the polynomial hierarchy.11 1 This is in a similar spirit as the 𝖯≠𝖭𝖯\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP} conjecture; for details see Section A.1. For the first task, we show that maximal models can efficiently simulate certain 𝖭𝖯\mathsf{NP}-hard functions that shallow models cannot (Theorem 20). For the latter two tasks, on the one hand we show that maximal models can approximate certain #​𝖯\mathsf{\#P}-hard functions up to a common positive factor, and the corresponding normalized distributions to arbitrary uniform relative precision, provided that the respective maximal models are visible closed in a strong sense. On the other hand, shallow models cannot achieve these two approximations efficiently (Theorems 24 and 26). Consequently, these separation results imply that shallow models such as RBMs do not have maximal efficient reach. (iii) Separation hierarchy for shallow models. We establish that the efficient simulation reach of shallow models is described by an infinite hierarchy indexed by their interaction order, that is, their maximal number of spins per local interaction (see Fig. 3). Namely, for each k≥2k\geq 2 there exist functions that shallow kk-local models cannot efficiently simulate (Theorems 32 and 33) but shallow k+1k+1-local models can (Theorem 36), under reasonable assumptions on the size of the model weights. To derive these results, we relate the efficient reach of shallow kk-local models to sums of polynomial threshold functions (PTFs) of degree at most k−1k-1 (Lemma 28), and use communication complexity bounds to exclude efficient simulations of certain target functions, such as the kk-party inner product modulo 22 (Theorems 31 and 32). We then prove that increasing the interaction order from kk to k+1k+1 allows one to efficiently simulate these targets, by first characterizing the efficient reach of RBMs through sums of small ridge functions (Lemma 34), and then extending them to shallow kk-local models (Lemma 35).

We study the efficient reach, i.e. the efficient representation capabilities, of machine learning models from three different angles.

papers.title: Steering interfacial molecular structures by substrate-molecule charge transfer
papers.abstract: Intermixed self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) provide a powerful approach for tuning inorganic-organic interfaces, but their local structure and energetics often remain elusive. Here, an intermixed stripe phase of fullerene $C_{60}$ and Zn(II)-5,10,15,20-tetrakis(4-aminophenyl)porphyrin (Zn-TAPP) on a Ag(111) surface is identified, establishing a direct link between molecular assembly and charge transfer. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS) and Kelvin probe force spectroscopy (KPFS) have been used to map electronic states and local contact potential differences (LCPD). Compared to close-packed $C_{60}$ islands, the stripe phase exhibits a larger interfacial dipole and increased occupation of previously unoccupied $C_{60}$ states, consistent with enhanced charge transfer from Ag(111) to $C_{60}$. Analysis indicates that larger $C_{60}$ spacing in the stripe geometry reduces Coulomb repulsion, stabilizing the intermixed phase and enhancing charge transfer with respect to close-packed domains. These results provide direct evidence of charged $C_{60}$ molecules in stripe structures and guidelines for engineering intermixed SAMs with tailored interfacial electronic properties.

papers.title: From photons to neutrinos : Advancing multi-messenger modeling with Gammapy
papers.abstract: In recent years, several astrophysical objects have been identified as potential multi-messenger photon-neutrino emitters. New instruments dedicated to the study of these two messengers have been and are still being built, achieving unprecedented sensitivity. This observational improvement increases the need for more sophisticated and precise analysis tools. Multi-wavelength and multi-messenger data fitting is crucial to constrain astrophysical models of particle acceleration and radiation mechanisms at work in these extreme environments. In this contribution, we present a novel framework dedicated to multi-wavelength and multi-messenger modeling, built within the open-source software Gammapy. The framework enables data analysis from optical up to very-high-energy gamma rays, and fitting physical models directly to instrumental counts in these wavebands, without the need of computing flux points. Focusing on blazars as a first example of a multi-messenger candidate, we showcase the performance of this tool in constraining multi-wavelength emission models, and how it reduces fitting biases. We show the results of a leptonic model that can be fitted on the fly, due to the short computing time needed. For more computing-intensive emission codes, we explore a grid-fitting approach. We evaluate the performance of the new fitting tool and present its first application to leptonic modeling of blazars. By fitting directly on photon and neutrino events, this novel approach will enable, for the first time, statistically sound constraints on the physics of multi-messenger sources.

papers.intro:
The study of extreme particle accelerators requires collecting and analyzing data from a large number of instruments, covering a large part of the photon spectrum, or combining photons with additional messengers such as neutrinos or gravitational waves. Current approaches for multi-wavelength and multi-messenger analyses typically involve the computation of flux points estimated in each waveband, followed by fitting a physical model with χ2\chi^{2} statistics. This method has, however, several limitations. First, flux points are derived with the assumption that the flux in each energy band follows a functional form (such as a Power Law or a Log Parabola), which is different from the model that will later be fitted to these flux points, introducing a bias. Additionally, upper limits (ULs) are often only used as strict thresholds, to ensure that the model does not overshoot them.

papers.title: "It Would Make a Geordie Feel at Home": Regional Accent Perceptions and Speech Accommodation in Voice AI
papers.abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems often perform less accurately for speakers of regional dialects, but less is known about how users respond to these limitations and how regional voices produced by voice assistants (VAs) are evaluated through a sociolinguistic lens. This study investigates these issues among speakers of Newcastle English (Geordies), examining both linguistic accommodation to voice technologies and perceptions of regional versus mainstream-accented VA voices. Participants interacted with a simulated VA that spoke either Newcastle English or Standard Southern British English (SSBE). They subsequently completed semi-structured interviews about their experiences with the experimental VA and voice technologies, language use, accent attitudes, and place orientation. The findings reveal a two-way process of sociolinguistic bias. The Geordie VA was associated with familiarity, warmth, personality, and local belonging, but also with concerns about professionalism and authority, whereas the SSBE voice was perceived as more neutral, clear, and credible. Participants also reported adapting their speech when voice technologies failed to recognise them, most commonly by shifting to a more mainstream accent, enunciating more clearly, and speaking more slowly. These strategies are similar to accommodation in human-human interaction and reflect users' perceptions of what technologies can recognise, also known as perceived intelligibility pressures. Overall, the findings demonstrate that voice technologies can reproduce existing accent biases both by encouraging users to suppress regional features and by activating established social stereotypes through synthetic voices. The study positions sociolinguistics as a bridge between understanding human-AI interaction and designing inclusive technologies around users' own linguistic priorities.

papers.title: Models of n-dimensional categories as $n\to\infty$
papers.abstract: We verify that saturated complicial sets model the right limit of the $\infty$-categories of $(\infty,n)$-categories, whereas the canonical comparison with the left limit is not an equivalence. By contrast the category of strict $\omega$-categories is equivalent to both the right and left limits of the categories of strict $n$-categories.

papers.title: The vanishing viscosity limit for the inhomogeneous incompressible Navier-Stokes equations around a small obstacle
papers.abstract: We investigate the interaction between a vanishing obstacle and the vanishing viscosity limit in the setting of the inhomogeneous incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions. We work in the space exterior to a small obstacle in three dimensions. We prove quantitative convergence rates, assuming that the obstacle is sufficiently small, namely smaller than a constant times the viscosity. The convergence holds as long as the solution to the limit problem is known to exist and stays sufficiently smooth. This extends the results of Iftimie, Lopes Filho and Nussenzveig Lopes to the inhomogeneous Navier-Stokes equations. Moreover, we can show improved convergence rates and convergence of the gradient in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

papers.title: On equivariant affineness in elliptic cohomology
papers.abstract:
We investigate equivariant affineness in spectral algebraic geometry: the phenomenon where $\infty$-categories of quasi-coherent sheaves of a spectral stack are equivalent to $\infty$-categories of modules over an equivariant ring spectrum. In the nonequivariant case, this is known as 0-affineness, and has been studied by Gaitsgory, Mathew--Meier, amongst others. Allowing for equivariant phenomena opens up a much wider class of spectral stacks to be studied through the lens of spectra.
  The spectral stacks at the heart of our analysis are oriented elliptic curves, their associated Hilbert schemes, and related constructions. When working over the universal base, so the moduli stack of oriented elliptic curves, we show that these spectral stacks are $U(1)$-, $U(n)$-, and $SU(n)$-equivariantly affine, with associated $G$-ring spectrum Gepner--Meier's equivariant topological modular forms $\mathrm{TMF}_G$. Our results also encompass the groups $Sp(n)$ as well as all finite products of such groups. Our most general result is a relative statement over an arbitrary base stack. These results can be viewed as an integral and global refinement of Greenlees' algebraic model for modules over rational $U(1)$-equivariant elliptic cohomology.

papers.title: Solid Arithmetic D-modules
papers.abstract: We introduce a solid ring of arithmetic differential operators analogue to Berthelot's D-dagger, and its derived infinity-category of solid quasi-coherent modules. We show that there is a fully faithful functor from Berthelot's derived category of bounded complexes of D-dagger-modules with coherent cohomology into our new category.

papers.title: CSO: Refining Robotic Policies via Skill Distribution Alignment and Skill-Grained Optimization
papers.abstract: Discretizing continuous actions into discrete skills using methods like VQ-VAE has emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, quantization errors yield a suboptimal distribution for the skill prior, degrading its performance. While reinforcement learning offers a path for refinement, its direct application faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. To address these challenges, we introduce Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. First, Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the model's observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning. Second, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes an independent, clipped importance ratio for each complete skill, enabling stable and efficient updates. With a lightweight QueST-style policy, CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks. Additional comparisons with FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL further validate the effectiveness of our two-stage post-training strategy.

A promising direction is to learn structured action representations through Transformer-based architectures [3, 29]. Temporal action chunks provide useful abstractions for control [43]; skill-based approaches additionally map continuous trajectories into discrete latent representations [17]. This hierarchical framework simplifies the problem, enabling an autoregressive policy to tackle complex tasks by sequentially composing tokens to generate a skill [28].

However, while this discretization paradigm is powerful, policies trained purely via imitation learning (IL) with these discrete skills exhibit a notable limitation. The VQ-VAE’s discretization process introduces inherent quantization errors, meaning the skills are only approximations of the expert’s continuous actions [17]. These reconstruction errors compound with policy errors during online execution. On one hand, the inherent imprecision of the tokens that constitute a skill can cause the decoded action to fail the task. On the other hand, these quantization errors can accumulate over an episode, progressively pushing the agent into states outside the expert data distribution. This resulting distribution shift severely hinders the generalization of the IL-trained policy [15].

To overcome the limitations of the initial policy, a natural remedy is to refine it with online reinforcement learning (RL) [11, 22, 37]. However, directly applying RL to this setting presents several challenges. A primary issue is the unstable update of the observation encoder. Online data collection often yields an imbalanced mix of task outcomes (e.g., many successes on easy tasks, many failures on hard ones). This provides inconsistent gradient signals to the crucial observation encoder, leading to inefficient training and often requiring complex hybrid frameworks to stabilize [11, 6]. A second structural challenge arises from a mismatch between the unit of decision-making (a skill) and the unit of optimization (a token). Token-level methods apply a separate importance ratio to each generated token [34, 24], which treats the components of a jointly executed skill separately. Episode-level methods such as GSPO instead use one length-normalized ratio and a shared clipping decision for the complete sequence [44]. Robotic episodes exhibit length asymmetry: time-outs are often longer than successes. This motivates skill-level optimization, which assigns each complete skill its own ratio and clipping decision while sharing the terminal advantage. We compare token-, skill-, and episode-level optimization from the same R-SFT checkpoint.

papers.title: New muon transfer cell for muonic x-ray spectroscopy on microgram-quantity targets based on liquid hydrogen
papers.abstract: The muon transfer method allows access to radioactive/rare atomic nuclei for determining their charge radii via muonic x-ray spectroscopy. In this study we present a new muon transfer cell based on liquid hydrogen optimized for low-energy x-ray spectroscopy by employing a thin-walled Mylar cell for the container of the liquid hydrogen. Based on simulations, the present liquid hydrogen cell achieves competitive efficiencies compared to existing devices using the muon transfer method. Additionally, the liquid-hydrogen-based muon transfer setup provides a short timescale for the diffusion process of the muonic hydrogen atoms in the cell, well below 200~ns.

papers.intro:
Nuclear charge radii can be measured by different means such as elastic scattering with leptonic probes or spectroscopy of atomic transitions in electronic and muonic atoms [1]. The implications of precision charge radii determination range from benchmarking state-of-the-art ab initio nuclear theory models [2, 3], learning about the link of nuclear radii to the equation of state of the nuclear matter [4, 5], and even testing deviations from the standard model of particle physics [6, 7]. X-ray spectroscopy of muonic atoms, i.e. atoms with electrons replaced by a muon, is a well-established method for extracting absolute charge radii with high precision and has been applied to almost all stable nuclei [8].

For studying unstable nuclei, however, traditional muonic x-ray spectroscopy methods involving a muon beam bombarding a thick target cannot be applied. A muon transfer cell based on hydrogen gas was developed by the muX collaboration [9] in order to bring muonic x-ray spectroscopy measurements on microgram target materials within reach [10]. The muon transfer method is based on the pioneering work in Refs. [11, 12]. In the muon transfer method, the muon is first stopped in a hydrogen–deuterium mixture and captured on a hydrogen atom. Upon encountering deuterium, the muon transfers to form muonic deuterium (μ​d\mu d) with eV-range kinetic energy, whose diffusion is strongly enhanced by the Ramsauer–Townsend effect [10]. The neutral μ​d\mu d atom then diffuses to the target of interest, transferring the muon to a higher-ZZ atom via the chain μ−→μ​p→μ​d→μ​Z\mu^{-}\rightarrow\mu p\rightarrow\mu d\rightarrow\mu Z. While the muX collaboration [9] focuses on heavy nuclei studies, the QUARTET collaboration [13] aims at improving the precision of charge radii for the low-medium-Z elements (Z≤12Z\leq 12) in combination with the use of metallic magnetic calorimeters (MMC) reaching a resolving power of up to 6000 [14].

In this technical design report we present the development of a new device for muonic x-ray spectroscopy on microgram target materials via the transfer method operating with liquid hydrogen (LH2). In Section 2 we discuss in details the processes happening in the muon transfer cell, we present Monte Carlo simulations performed to evaluate the muon transfer rate for different configurations of geometry and hydrogen properties, and we conclude by comparing the transfer cells based on liquid hydrogen and gaseous hydrogen. In Section 3 we describe the mechanical design of the cryogenic LH2 system, followed by Section 4, where we detail the integration of the cryogenic system with the full experimental setup including two configurations: MMC detectors and a high-purity Ge (HPGe) detector array. In Section 5, we present the commissioning and the performance of the LH2 target system, and lastly we discuss the conclusions and the physics outlook with the newly developed LH2 transfer cell.

papers.title: Tracing the Influence of Retrieved Literature on Scientific Ideation in LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate research ideas from scientific literature. Existing systems combine literature retrieval with search, generation, and refinement, making it difficult to determine how the retrieval strategy itself shapes the ideas generated. We isolate this contribution by comparing five retrieval strategies and a No Literature baseline under a shared generation protocol, using 45,000 ideas across 15 machine learning topics and ten open-weight models. Relative to no literature basline, all five retrieval strategies reduce diversity among ideas generated from the same set of papers by $5.6\%$--$17.9\%$, while most increase diversity by $10.2\%$--$18.1\%$ when ideas from different sets are pooled. Effects on idea quality and novelty are modest on average but vary across topics. We further apply a JSD-based attribution method to trace the influence of individual input papers on each idea's motivation, core idea, approach, and validation. In $79.3\%$ of ideas, only one or two distinct papers receive the highest attribution scores across these four parts. These leading sources often recur across ideas generated from the same set of papers, and groups with more varied source attribution contain more diverse ideas ($r=0.70$). These findings motivate various sets of literature and the use of attribution to guide the choice of sources for subsequent ideas.

papers.title: Gaussian Distillation of Flow Policies
papers.abstract: Flow policies are among the strongest robot controllers and are well suited to modelling multimodal action distributions. Our analysis shows that the continuous-action distributions of the studied flow policies are well approximated by Gaussians. We propose the Gaussian Action Readout (GAR), which replaces a flow policy's final layer with a Gaussian readout trained on just 0.02% of eligible states, while keeping the rest of the network frozen. It samples with one action-network pass, gives closed-form likelihoods, and achieves near-teacher task success at up to twice the inference speed.

papers.intro:
Diffusion and flow-matching policies achieve strong performance in robot manipulation (Chi et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025). An appealing feature is their ability to model multimodal action distributions, capturing the different valid ways to act in human demonstrations (Chi et al., 2023). Generating actions, however, requires iterative sampling with repeated network evaluations, making inference computationally costly. Their action likelihoods are also unavailable in closed form. This raises the question: is this distributional flexibility needed for task performance, or could a simpler policy perform just as well while allowing cheaper direct sampling and closed-form likelihoods?

To explore this possibility, we fit separate Gaussians to the translation and rotation action-chunk distributions of Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (Xiaomi Robotics Team et al., 2026) and GR00T (NVIDIA et al., 2025) at fixed inputs. We find small approximation errors for both models (Section 3). These results motivate us to look for a simple, inexpensive way to convert these models into Gaussian policies while retaining their task performance.

papers.title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns
papers.abstract: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors' communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations.

Text-based online counselling has gained increasing prominence as a flexible and accessible alternative to traditional face-to-face therapy, especially in reaching diverse populations with unique needs [5, 13]. Within counsellor education, role-playing exercises are central to developing crucial communication competencies [15, 14], offering trainees controlled, practice-oriented scenarios to explore, reflect on, and refine their skills [18, 20]. However, role-plays with human peers often face logistical constraints such as coordinating schedules and achieving consistent complexity across multiple sessions [22], while also being limited by the role-play partner’s availability, engagement level and ability to maintain character depth and consistency throughout the interactions [12].

This paper examines text-based role-play counselling sessions, comparing interactions between human counsellors and human clients with those between human counsellors and LLM-simulated clients. We draw on a specialised categorisation framework for counselling communications, analysing the distribution and temporal evolution of specific interaction patterns in both settings. Our findings highlight significant similarities and differences in how clients disclose their concerns and how counsellors respond and structure the session. In doing so, this study provides insights into the potential of LLM-based role-plays to augment — and possibly transform — the way future counsellors are trained, while also identifying areas where further development is needed to narrow the gap between virtual and human clients.

papers.title: Blind Video Denoising for Vocal Tract rtMRI using a Self-Supervised Ensemble
papers.abstract: Real-time magnetic resonance imaging of the vocal tract makes speech articulation directly observable, but the trade-off between temporal resolution and signal quality introduces substantial noise and obscures fine articulatory detail. Since clean references cannot be acquired for a moving vocal tract, supervised denoising approaches are not applicable in this setting. We propose a self-supervised denoising framework that combines spatiotemporal super-resolution learning with pseudo-supervision derived from a variance-stabilized non-local means filter. A dual-model fusion strategy balances noise suppression and preservation of high-frequency articulatory structure. Experiments on the USC-75 multi-speaker dataset under natural noise conditions show that the ensemble raises the signal-to-noise ratio by 11.9 dB on unseen subjects while attaining more high-frequency articulatory content in the frames. Among tuned implementations of anisotropic diffusion, block-matching filtering, non-local means and pre-smoothed non-local means, every configuration that achieves comparable noise suppression does so at the cost of high-frequency content or of structural fidelity. Under severe added Gaussian, Rayleigh and Rician noise, peak signal-to-noise ratio improves by 7.6 to 11.8 dB and structural similarity roughly triples. An ablation shows that the variance-stabilized pseudo-supervision is an essential element for denoising, and that the effect is attributable to the hard thresholding contained in the stabilization transform.

Nevertheless, a recurring limitation identified in the current literature is the heavy reliance on supervised training with large paired datasets.
