Recent research instead exploits the internal correlations of high-dimensional acquisitions to build supervisory signals without ground truth. N2SR-M by Tian et al. [6] trains on spatially sub-sampled pairs from noisy data to restore fine structures via Super-Resolution (SR) constraints. Although it was formulated for multi-contrast MRI, the principle transfers to the temporal dimension of rtMRI, and it has been validated in quantitative MRI sequences [7] and in high-speed fluorescence imaging [8]. Complementarily, we believe that conventional analytical approaches remain indispensable for their explicit handling of noise statistics and spatial signal characteristics [9, 10]. Works such as that of Yang et al. [11] have addressed Rician noise reduction via a Pre-Smoothed Non-Local-Means (PSNLM) filter with variance stabilization, demonstrating that explicitly modeling noise characteristics is crucial for preserving anatomical detail in low-SNR regimes.

papers.title: ODAQ-Collection: Expanding the Open Dataset of Audio Quality with a Focus on Spatial Distortions
papers.abstract: The Open Dataset of Audio Quality (ODAQ) is an expanding resource that addresses the scarcity of openly available data in audio quality assessment research. While previous contributions focused mainly on timbral distortions, with spatial processing limited to basic mid-side and left-right stereo conditions, we present a new contribution featuring high-quality music and speech recordings with diverse stereo images, controlled spatial distortions, and subjective listening test results from trained listeners in a laboratory setting. With 148 pairs of stereo audio samples processed by three different method classes, two applying controlled binaural cue distortions and one applying dialogue enhancement, this addition expands the collection to 688 pairs of processed and unprocessed audio signals spanning 17 processing method classes, along with 18,984 raw subjective ratings from listeners. All associated data and code are released as open resources to facilitate future expansions and research on objective audio quality metrics.
papers.intro:
Quantifying perceived audio quality is essential for enabling measurable progress across various audio tasks such as source separation[10], audio coding[12], and music generation[29]. Although subjective listening tests remain the gold standard for audio quality assessment, objective audio quality metrics are often considered a convenient alternative due to their practicality and compatibility across different application domains [27]. Developing such metrics, however, requires well-curated datasets to characterize human perception of audio quality, inform the design of a computational approach, and validate its correlation with human ratings. Creating these datasets is time-consuming and costly, and the sharing of audio source files can sometimes be prohibited due to copyright restrictions. As a result, many datasets for this purpose remain private[7] or are only shared to a limited extent[14]. While individual datasets exist for specific application domains such as audio coding[23] and source separation[10], they are typically one-off contributions limited in size and scope of experimental conditions. Larger datasets have since been constructed via crowdsourcing[3, 20, 19] or by outsourcing evaluations to external vendors[26], but these often involve uncontrolled listening environments and increased label noise, necessitating sophisticated pre- and post-screening procedures[18].

To address these limitations, the Open Dataset of Audio Quality (ODAQ) [28] was proposed as a publicly available resource featuring high-quality audio signals and subjective scores collected from the Multiple Stimuli with Hidden Reference and Anchor (MUSHRA)[15] tests conducted in controlled listening environments. After the initial release, a subsequent addition [8] provided further subjective scores based on the same material and protocol, confirming the reproducibility of the initial test. This addition also introduced a basic benchmark of objective quality metrics on the dataset. A later addition introduced new audio content investigating basic stereo processing conditions, namely mid-side (MS) and left-right (LR), together with MUSHRA test results allowing comparisons between preprocessing methods and presentation context[9], and a companion study benchmarked objective quality metrics on this material[6]. A more recent addition from the community [17] added derived assets from the initial release processed by neural audio codecs. In contrast to the other additions, subjective ratings were collected via crowdsourced MUSHRA tests with post-screening, and the participants were self-reported expert listeners.

papers.title: Few-Electron Partitioning in the Fractional Quantum Hall Regime
papers.abstract: Motivated by few-electron partitioning experiments [Shaju et al., Nature 642, 928 (2025)], we study the partition statistics of $N$-electron states at a fractional quantum Hall point contact. At the solvable point $g=1/2$, we obtain nonperturbative current and noise formulas for arbitrary drives, while for Lorentzian pulses (Levitons) the full counting statistics reduces to an $N\times N$ determinant. We show that the charge is transferred solely in units of $e$, and that symmetrized cumulants for $N=2,3,4$ reveal strong antibunching and higher-order correlations, observable in a $(\nu_1,\nu_2)=(1,1/3)$ junction.

papers.title: MesoCraft: a web-based tool for interactive procedural modeling of mesoscale biological structures
papers.abstract: Biological models bring the molecular world of cells into view, enabling experts and the public to explore and understand biological discoveries. Building mesoscale models requires organizing many molecular components into spatial arrangements that can be revised as evidence and interpretations develop. We present MesoCraft, a browser-based tool for structural biologists centered on interactive procedural modeling. User-defined rules generate collections of molecular instances, while a geometry-node editor and visual feedback support authoring and revision of their spatial relationships. Beyond model construction, MesoCraft integrates exploration and communication, enabling researchers to inspect molecular organization and create guided animations that highlight key spatial relationships. By connecting modeling, exploration, and explanation in a unified workflow, MesoCraft allows insights gained during exploration and communication to inform iterative model refinement, supporting the development of mesoscale models into visual narratives of cellular organization. A demonstrative deployment of the tool is available at https://mesocraft.kaust.edu.sa/.

papers.intro:
Biological discoveries often begin with an image that reveals an unexpected structure or a new view of cellular organization. Connecting these observations to the molecules that make up a biological system requires integrating evidence across scales. Microscopy reveals cellular architecture, whereas structural biology provides detailed molecular structures. Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) brings these perspectives closer by visualizing macromolecular assemblies within cells; combined with subtomogram averaging, it can resolve selected complexes at high resolution, as demonstrated for eukaryotic ribosomes in situ (4). Yet images and reconstructions do not generally identify and locate every molecular component in a heterogeneous cellular region. Building a molecular account of that region therefore requires combining imaging observations with known structures, composition estimates and spatial information (7; 14).

papers.title: Diffraction of rotated measures
papers.abstract: Consider a translation-bounded measure on the line. We can rotate the measure, distributing the mass proportionally to the area, to create a two-dimensional rotationally invariant translation-bounded measure. We show that the diffraction of the two-dimensional object is the normalised rotation of the diffraction of the original measure. We discuss some examples and generalisation beyond $d=2$.

It proved itself to be an invaluable tool in the theory of aperiodic order, and it helped to understand many, nowadays standard, systems with certain long-range order.

In this note, we extend the results in [5, 16] by showing that the diffraction of a rotationally invariant translation-bounded measure (or a uniformly bounded function) is a rotation of the diffraction of its radial section or its radial profile. This comes as a surprise, as it is a priori not clear at all that the diffraction of a rotationally invariant measure and the diffraction of its radial profile should be related. In fact, the Fourier transform of a rotationally invariant function can be identified as the Hankel transform of the section; so the derived relationship looks surprising. It hints at a hidden relationship among the process of calculating the autocorrelation, the Fourier transform in the plane, and the Hankel transform in 1-dimension.

We first recall the basic notions such as autocorrelation, and introduce various operators that bring a function or measure to its rotationally symmetric counterpart and vice versa. We carefully review their properties as we shall need them later. In Section 3, we begin our study with uniformly continuous functions, for which we establish the main result in Theorem 3.1. Section 4 is devoted to establishing the correspondence for translation-bounded measures, and requires some more technicalities. The main result is summarised in Theorem 4.5, and the next section, Section 6 gives certain implications of our results for radially symmetric measures and their diffraction. We also provide an outlook on how to extend these results to higher dimensions in Section 7. While the results extend naturally, and the proofs follow along the same lines, the necessary technicalities make the proof longer, more complicated, and hide the main ideas, so we decided to omit them.

papers.title: Joint Antenna Position and Beamforming Optimization for Movable Antenna Enabled Near-Field ISAC Imaging
papers.abstract: Near-field (NF) integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems enable simultaneous two-dimensional (2D) radar imaging and multi-user downlink communication. However, fixed-position antenna arrays can exhibit high sidelobes in the point spread function (PSF), which degrade imaging performance and cause ghost-target artifacts. Movable antennas (MAs) offer additional spatial degrees of freedom to suppress these sidelobes while meeting communication requirements, without increasing the number of antenna elements. In this paper, we investigate MA-enabled NF ISAC by jointly optimizing the transmit and receive antenna positions and the transmit beamforming to minimize a weighted sum of the integrated sidelobe level (ISL) and peak sidelobe level (PSL) of the 2D PSF, subject to communication-rate, illumination-power, transmit-power, and antenna-placement constraints. To tackle the resulting non-convex problem, we propose a hybrid alternating optimization (AO) framework that combines particle swarm optimization with a genetic algorithm. Our numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves the lowest ISL among the considered array configurations and reduces the PSL by at least 5 dB compared with the benchmarks. The optimized array is further shown to resolve two closely spaced targets whose reflectivities differ by 6dB, outperforming random, Mills Cross, and rectangular arrays while satisfying the imposed minimum user-throughput requirements.

papers.intro:
Integrated sensing and communication has emerged as a key technology for future sixth-generation networks by sharing hardware, spectrum, and signal-processing resources. It enables both functionalities for applications such as vehicle-to-everything, smart manufacturing, and environmental monitoring [10]. Conventionally, multiple-input multiple-output integrated sensing and communication approaches primarily focus on parameter-estimation-oriented sensing, targeting quantities such as range, velocity, and angle. Commonly adopted sensing objectives include beampattern matching, the Cramér-Rao bound, and radar signal-quality metrics [10, 13, 14]. Unlike parameter estimation, radar imaging aims to reconstruct the spatial reflectivity distribution of an extended scene. Its performance therefore depends on the spatial response of the imaging system, namely its resolution and sidelobe characteristics. Sidelobes and grating lobes can introduce imaging artifacts and interfere with the reconstruction of neighboring scatterers [16, 2]. Conventional parameter-estimation-oriented sensing metrics do not directly characterize these imaging effects. Instead, the point spread function describes the reconstructed response to a point scatterer and characterizes resolution, sidelobe behavior, and spatially dependent imaging artifacts [2]. In addition, high-resolution sensing and imaging typically require large apertures and high carrier frequencies, which can place the region of interest within the near-field of the radar system [13, 2]. Since antenna geometry and transmit beamforming both influence the point spread function and the communication performance, their joint optimization is particularly relevant for near-field integrated sensing and communication systems.

papers.title: Thermalization-Controlled Superconducting Diode-Like Transport in Disordered Molybdenum and NbN Thin Films
papers.abstract: Superconducting diode effects are characterized by direction-dependent critical currents in the superconducting state. Here, we investigate diode-like transport in 128-nm-thick Mo thin film deposited on Si_SiO2 substrate by DC magnetron sputtering. The thin film exhibit a superconducting transition temperature TC of 5.8 K. Pronounced current-direction asymmetry and hysteresis are observed in current-voltage characteristics measured in a closed-cycle refrigerator. In contrast, the same thin film exhibits a substantially more symmetric response in a 14T cryogenic system with improved sample thermalization. We attribute this strong dependence on the measurement environment to electrothermal effects arising from current-induced Joule heating and finite thermal relaxation. As the current approaches the superconducting-to-resistive switching condition, the emergence of a resistive component leads to a rapid increase in Joule heating, raising the sample temperature and modifying the switching condition. Conversely, during the resistive-to-superconducting transition, residual heating and finite thermal relaxation reduce the switching current. Since P is equal to I2R it is independent of current polarity, the observed asymmetry is not associated with polarity-dependent Joule heating but with the interplay of thermal relaxation, sweep history, and thermal boundary conditions. The suppression of the asymmetry under improved thermalization, together with similar behavior observed in NbN reference films, indicates that the apparent diode-like response is strongly influenced by electrothermal effects. These results highlight the need to distinguish thermal switching and hysteresis from intrinsic nonreciprocal superconductivity when identifying superconducting diode effects in transport measurements.

papers.title: Optical clock network tracks tidal variations of the gravity potential
papers.abstract: Gravity affects the passage of time, as described by General Relativity. On Earth, the rate of a clock as seen by a fixed observer changes by about one part in $10^{16}$ per metre in height. Chronometric levelling exploits this effect to directly measure differences in gravity potential by comparing distant clocks. It has been proposed as a complementary approach to established geodetic techniques for linking height reference systems and monitoring the terrestrial gravity potential. Experimental demonstrations have to date focused primarily on static potential differences. Yet, the potentials of the Moon, the Sun and other celestial bodies as well as the Earth's response to their tidal forcing change clock rates by several $10^{-17}$, providing a predictable test signal to demonstrate optical clock networks resolving small variations in relativistic time dilation. Here, we report chronometric observations of time-varying gravity potential differences using a network of optical clocks and phase-stabilized fibre links in Europe. Two distinct geographical configurations, with baselines of about 800 km each, result in different combinations of diurnal and semidiurnal tidal components. One comparison uses a transportable optical clock as a remote sensor. The measured rate shifts track the tidal variations, resolving the predicted signal within 1 d of measurement and agreeing with model predictions. These results extend experimental chronometric levelling from static to dynamic potential differences and highlight the need to account for the time dependence of relativistic time dilation in frequency metrology. They also open the prospect for quantum clock networks with improved stability and availability to move beyond known tides and monitor other gravity potential variations, such as those arising from surface deformation and mass redistribution in geologically or volcanically active regions.

papers.intro:
The notion of describing the figure of the Earth in relation to an equipotential surface of its gravity field dates back about two hundred years to the works of Gauss Gauß (1828). Surveying Earth’s gravity potential remains essential in geosciences as the foundation of physical height reference systems. Measurements of its temporal variations constrain models of mass redistribution among continental water, ice, oceans and atmosphere United Nations General Assembly (2015); Hofmann-Wellenhof and Moritz (2006); Tapley et al. (2004). Gravity potential measurements are particularly valuable for processes that are difficult to monitor by other means, such as groundwater storage or deep-ocean currents and aquifers Tapley et al. (2004). Satellite gravity missions provide global observations of broad-scale potential variations Tapley et al. (2004), whereas potential differences between fixed points are often determined by a combination of geometric levelling, height measurements based on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), and local gravimetry Hofmann-Wellenhof and Moritz (2006).

Chronometric levelling provides a complementary means to determine gravity potential differences through the resulting differences in time dilation between distant atomic clocks. These are measured as relativistic rate shifts (RRSs) of clock frequency ratios in comparisons via suitable time or frequency links Vermeer (1983); Bjerhammar (1985); Mehlstäubler et al. (2018); Delva et al. (2019). Experiments have progressed from initial demonstrations Chou et al. (2010); Lisdat et al. (2016); Takano et al. (2016); Grotti et al. (2018) to measuring potential differences with state-of-the-art height uncertainties of few centimetres International Clock and Oscillator Networking Collaboration (2024). Temporal variations of the potential difference between two locations have not been resolved using optical clocks, owing to the precision required to resolve the signal at its characteristic time scale. Challenges range from the frequency stability and availability of clocks and links to their reproducibility if slow variations are to be investigated. Furthermore, the potential difference between two clocks depends on geographical configuration, e.g., the uniformity of the time-varying potential components may lead to a strong supression across short distances.

Tidal potential variations have been modelled and removed as a background signal in some clock comparisons Delva et al. (2017); International Clock and Oscillator Networking Collaboration (2024); Hou et al. (2026); Tofful et al. (2026). Yet, they also provide a known signal to test an optical clock network’s ability to resolve geodynamics. Their leading contributions result from the tide-generating potential of the Moon and the Sun as well as the solid Earth tides and ocean tidal loading Voigt et al. (2016). Here, the solid Earth tides represent the response of the Earth to the tide-generating potential, which consists of surface deformation and the resulting mass redistribution. These two effects counteract and reinforce the effect of the tide-generating potential, respectively. Ocean tidal loading includes the effect of water displacement and the resulting effects like the deformation of the Earth’s surface. Variations caused by other tidal and non-tidal effects at similar time scales are usually at least one order of magnitude smaller Voigt et al. (2016). Overall, the dominant components of the tidal potential variations have diurnal and semidiurnal periodicity and change the RRS at an individual fixed location on the Earth’s surface by up to 5×10−175\text{\times}{10}^{-17}. The differential potential variations between locations depend on the baseline geometry: longitudinal separation results in phase shifts, while latitudinal separation produces amplitude differences. Across continental distances, this results in peak-to-peak differential RRS variations of several ​10−18{10}^{-18} or more. Resolving them thus requires relative comparison instabilities in the range of 1×10−181\text{\times}{10}^{-18} at a few hours of averaging time.

Here, we demonstrate first tracking of the time-varying gravity potential using comparisons of 87Sr and 171Yb optical lattice clocks across the European fibre link network, providing high-resolution, local probes into the gravity potential. We compared the self-contained transportable optical clock PTB-Sr4, which was deployed to the Istituto Nazionale di Ricerca Metrologica (INRiM) in Torino, Italy, to the laboratory clock PTB-Sr3 at the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) in Brunswick, Germany. We demonstrate that both NPL-Sr1 and PTB-Sr4 track and resolve the predicted tidal RRS variations in less than one day of measurement when compared to the laboratory clock PTB-Sr3.

papers.title: Measuring the Value of Communication in Multi-Agent Tracking Under Finite-Rate Belief Sharing
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the value of communica- tion (VoC) in cooperative multi-agent tracking under rate- constrained information exchange. Although prior work has studied distributed tracking, quantized communication, and robust fusion, it remains unclear at what communication rate most of the achievable tracking gain is obtained, beyond which additional communication resources yield only marginal benefit. We consider stationary agents that observe a moving target through heterogeneous range and bearing measurements, perform local extended Kalman filtering (EKF), quantize their posterior state means, and fuse exchanged information via covariance intersection (CI). Performance is evaluated versus communication rate relative to no-communication baselines, a centralized oracle, and a CI-perfect reference. The results show that communication is not uniformly beneficial: very low rates can degrade performance due to coarse quantization, whereas moderate rates recover most of the achievable gain. In the considered scenario, increasing the rate from 4 to 12 bit/s per agent reduces the root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 13.93 m to 6.35 m, while a further increase to 32 bit/s per agent improves it only marginally to 5.93 m. This reveals a clear knee region at moderate rates, beyond which the remaining loss is mainly due to the conservatism of the fusion architecture. Overall, the proposed framework characterizes low-rate degradation, communication-efficient operation, and diminishing returns, while highlighting the joint role of rate and sensing geometry in determining communication benefit.

papers.intro:
Multi-agent systems (MAS) such as connected vehicles, cooperative robots, and distributed sensor networks can benefit from communication and information exchange to improve task performance [1, 2]. However, communication consumes bandwidth, introduces latency, and incurs energy and privacy costs, which often make it a system bottleneck [3]. Communication is therefore not inherently valuable; its benefit must be evaluated relative to the resources it consumes. This motivates the central question considered in this paper: how much inter-agent communication is justified by the resulting performance improvement, relative to its communication cost?

However, communication consumes bandwidth, introduces latency, and incurs energy and privacy costs, which often make it a system bottleneck [3]. Communication is therefore not inherently valuable; its benefit must be evaluated relative to the resources it consumes. This motivates the central question considered in this paper: how much inter-agent communication is justified by the resulting performance improvement, relative to its communication cost?

This question is especially important in cooperative tracking, where each agent has only local and incomplete information about the target state. In such settings, communication can improve global estimation performance, but its utility depends strongly on how informative the exchanged messages are, how restrictive the available rate constraint is, and how the received information is fused.

In such settings, communication can improve global estimation performance, but its utility depends strongly on how informative the exchanged messages are, how restrictive the available rate constraint is, and how the received information is fused.

Prior work most relevant here falls into three threads. Distributed estimation over sensor networks combines local estimates for global accuracy [4, 5], but fixes the protocol rather than the rate itself. Rate limited and event triggered schemes bound how much is sent [6, 7], but emphasize stability and triggering over the gain a given rate buys. Communication aware and task oriented exchange learns what to transmit [8, 9], yet evaluates whole policies without isolating the rate accuracy tradeoff. It thus remains unclear how communication benefit evolves with rate in cooperative tracking, and where added rate ceases to be justified.

A meaningful value of communication (VoC) analysis also requires a consistent fusion model. Because repeated exchange of local estimates induces unknown statistical dependencies among agents [10, 11], ignoring them can overstate the apparent VoC; we therefore adopt the conservative covariance intersection (CI) rule [12]. Unlike the threads above, we keep the estimator, quantizer, and fusion rule fixed and resolve tracking distortion as an explicit function of communication rate, separating loss due to limited rate from that due to conservative fusion.

papers.title: Contact-free charge carrier density determination of doped sub-{\mu}m thin cubic GaN layers with terahertz time-domain spectroscopy
papers.abstract: As cubic GaN is a promising material for optoelectronic applications, its layers need to be precisely doped to realize the desired properties. While contact-based methods are established to measure the realized charge carrier density, contact-free techniques are more advantageous for this purpose. We show terahertz time-domain spectroscopy measurements of cubic GaN layers with thicknesses between 0.6 ${\mu}$m and 2 ${\mu}$m with doping densities in the range from $10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$ to $10^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$. From these measurements, we determine the charge carrier densities and verify the results with time-of-flight secondary-ion mass spectrometry measurements. The results are in accordance with simulations of the doping ranges which the technique is expected to be sensitive in. In preparation for the terahertz time-domain spectroscopy measurements, we validated the layer thicknesses by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy measurements. With this, a wide range of doped cubic GaN samples can be addressed by optical methods. In the future, these techniques could allow for a fast and non-destructive characterization of GaN layers, right after or even during the growth process.

Wide-bandgap (WBG) semiconductors are becoming increasingly important for many applications, e.g. in power electronics applications ranging from electric vehicles over photovoltaic applications to energy storage and consumer electronics [72, 64, 34, 10]. Gallium nitride (GaN) is one of the most widely used representatives of WBG semiconductors besides silicon carbide [59] and WBG oxide semiconductors [58]. In addition to the applications of GaN in power electronics [45], this material system has also become a cornerstone in optoelectronics, from first GaN-based blue light-emitting diodes (LED) [51, 49, 48] to the sophisticated devices established nowadays, such as highly efficient LEDs of multiple colors and with high power densities [47, 38].

In addition to the applications of GaN in power electronics [45], this material system has also become a cornerstone in optoelectronics, from first GaN-based blue light-emitting diodes (LED) [51, 49, 48] to the sophisticated devices established nowadays, such as highly efficient LEDs of multiple colors and with high power densities [47, 38].

Most of these well-engineered applications use the preferred and thermodynamically most stable hexagonal (i.e., wurtzite) phase of GaN (h-GaN) as it is the ground state of the bulk material, whereas cubic (i.e., zinc-blende) GaN (c-GaN) is in a metastable phase [35]. Therefore, the hexagonal phase has become widely used and commercialized over decades [26, 57], while the cubic phase has gained attraction more slowly [44, 3]. Nonetheless, it is a promising material with certain technological advantages over its hexagonal polytype. A possible advantageous application lies in the context of µ-LEDs. While the state-of-the-art material for red LEDs is AlGaInP [20], the efficiency suffers from miniaturization [19]. Alloys based on c-GaN, such as InxGa1-xN, can, in principle, cover large parts of the electromagnetic spectrum extending the visible range towards both the infrared and the ultraviolet regions. For h-GaN, however, internal fields cause a quantum-confined Stark effect, reducing the efficiency towards longer wavelengths, opening up an opportunity for cubic nitrides to be the material system of choice for red µ-LEDs [27]. Going a step further towards multi-color LEDs, it is desirable to stay within one material system, being another possible application for c-GaN [40].

The process of doping cubic GaN layers with Ge is a key step along the way to realize these devices. Yet, it is still subject to ongoing research and optimized progressively [74, 27]. The electrical properties, especially charge carrier density and mobility, are often determined by Hall measurements in Van der Pauw geometry or capacitance-voltage measurements. Both of these techniques require physical contacts, e.g., gold wires, to be soldered [1] or deposited onto the sample [25, 65, 4]. So, contactless methods would be beneficial to allow a sample to be characterized without limiting its further use. Time-of-flight secondary-ion mass spectrometry (ToF-SIMS) is a method, which can be used to determine the overall dopant concentration, which can be correlated with the charge carrier density directly [27, 15]. An optical method to measure this latter quantity directly is spectroscopic ellipsometry, e.g. in the infrared or the ultraviolet [6]. While it has been shown that this is a possibility, the technique requires extensive modeling, fitting of the results and measurements under multiple angles, which increases measurement times. Instead, a promising contactless and non-destructive technique is terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (TDS), which is becoming more and more deployed to applications in the context of semiconductors [61] after having become established as a standard technique for the characterization of insulators, such as plastic or paint [18].

papers.title: Only Accepted Tokens Count: An Energy Accounting of Speculative Decoding Under Latency Targets
papers.abstract: Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

papers.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
papers.abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.
papers.intro:
As large language models become more capable, the risks of their misuse grow as well. As a result, models undergo extensive safety training and evaluation before deployment. However, existing research consistently shows that red-teaming is much more effective in non-English languages than in English, yet open multilingual safety data remains scarce. Take an English prompt that a model reliably refuses, translate it, and adapt it to the specifics of the target culture (a local extremist movement, a historical atrocity, a community-specific slur): the same model may now comply, even though the harmful intent is unchanged.

Existing safety alignment datasets are heavily English-centric, both linguistically and culturally. Collecting data beyond English faces several obstacles: (1) recruiting native speakers for such sensitive tasks is costly and slow, which is challenging at the current pace of global LLM development; (2) human red-teaming is of the highest quality, but rarely covers low-resource languages at scale; (3) machine translation does not produce the locally specific context needed to broaden the scope of the model’s safety understanding; (4) scalable synthetic data generation or translation with other language models is often blocked by the generator’s own refusals, since the content is harmful by design. As a result, users communicating in low-resource languages are the least protected, and these languages open an easy attack vector for misuse.

Multilingual safety can benefit from a mix of cross-lingual transfer, stronger general model capabilities, and strong English-focused alignment. However, these effects diminish in extremely low-resource settings, and even more so for culture-specific harms, which depend not on knowledge transfer but on knowledge breadth. Therefore, safety should be treated less as a general model capability axis and more as a combination of model, language, and culture axes: a request reliably refused in English can be complied with in its translated and culturally grounded variant. Measuring and closing this gap requires safety data that is multilingual and culturally authentic, not merely translated.

We produce such data at scale in a fully automated way by relying on language models instead of human red-teaming experts. We abstract a real harmful prompt into a template with typed slots and translate the template natively, then refill those slots along two axes. Generic fillers carry the harmful frame into every language at full coverage; a second, deliberately selective pass instead admits real local referents from a per-language cultural card. Filling the same slots with safe referents gives benign minimal pairs, which serve both to measure over-refusal and as training signal. Every variant is validated by LLM judges distinct from the generator models. Instantiating the pipeline yields MSafeTemp. Red-teaming leading open models on it exposes multilingual safety gaps that English-only evaluation does not show, and the localized variants surface failures that the translated ones miss.

papers.title: Robust LIDAR Sensor-to-Sensor Domain Generalization via Accumulated-Point Scene Completion
papers.abstract:
We study domain generalization for LIDAR semantic segmentation. Deep neural networks achieve strong performance on 3D point clouds, yet real-world LIDAR exhibits sensor-specific sampling patterns that hinder transfer across datasets. In many applications, performance on completely unseen sensors is crucial. A model should preferably work on a new setup without prior access to its data or labels. To this end, we introduce a source-only training scheme that adds an occupancy prediction auxiliary objective. We aggregate source-domain scans into a simple world model and use it as the supervision signal, replacing single-scan standard segmentation training.
  A key property of our approach is that it does not alter the input scan. At deployment, there is no runtime overhead as the auxiliary head can be dropped for pure segmentation, or kept to obtain scene completion alongside semantic segmentation. In an experimental evaluation across distinct LIDAR datasets, we demonstrate that a model's generalization to new domains can be significantly affected by how it is supervised. In certain setups, performance on unseen domains improves without any explicit domain adaptation (no target scans, no target labels, no sensor priors) and without prediction refinement. At the same time, our method maintains competitive source-domain segmentation performance and incurs no additional inference cost.

Highly automated vehicles and mobile robots rely on deep learning–based perception models that typically require large volumes of annotated data. Yet these systems must operate across diverse domains induced by weather, geography, traffic culture, and sensor generations. Since data collection and annotation is costly and time-consuming, repeating them for every new domain is impractical. uda (uda) targets this challenge with automated methods that adapt models to new domains without requiring manual annotations in the target domain. Going further, dg (dg) seeks to build models using only source-domain data without any access to potential target domains (neither labels nor raw sensor data) and to maximize performance on these unseen targets at test time. Models that generalize well to unseen domains reduce retraining efforts when experimenting with new platforms and sensor setups. They accelerate deployment and iteration, and they improve robustness in safety critical systems.

papers.title: Countable Nondeterminism in Weighted Programming with an Application to Mechanized Foundations for Probabilistic Program Verification
papers.abstract: Weighted programming is a framework by Batz et al. for describing mathematical models or optimization problems as imperative programs parametrized over semirings and then analyzing them with program verification techniques like weakest precondition calculi. Applications include reasoning about expected outcomes of probabilistic programs and competitive analysis of online algorithms. We extend weighted programming with (1) countable nondeterminism and (2) user-defined additive rewards, where programs are parametrized over modules instead of semirings. The resulting framework enables reasoning about expected resource consumption of probabilistic programs and about optimal scores of combinatorial games. A technical challenge is that wp-calculi for weighted programs with (1) and (2) over arbitrary modules can be unsound, because it is well-known that continuity properties commonly used in program semantics break in the presence of countable nondeterminism. We study conditions under which a wp-style transformer for reasoning about weighted programs is sound with respect to an operational ground truth defined in terms of weighted decision processes (WDPs) - transition systems that generalize Markov decision processes by drawing transition weights and state rewards from a module. Based on those conditions, we show that a range of concrete instances of the weighted programming framework enjoy sound weakest precondition reasoning. We demonstrate the usefulness of our wp-semantics through case studies for different modules. We mechanized our extended weighted programming framework and our main soundness results in the interactive theorem prover Lean. Instantiating these results for probabilistic programming yields, to the best of our knowledge, the first mechanized proof of a fixed point characterization of minimal expected rewards in Markov decision processes with countable nondeterminism.

Weighted programming is a framework by Batz et al. (2022) for describing mathematical models or optimization problems as imperative programs and then analyzing them with program verification techniques like weakest precondition calculi. In a nutshell, a weighted program is an ordinary program, where every execution step is equipped with a multiplicative weight. Furthermore, in addition to standard control flow statements, weighted programs may branch into two program executions whose weights are summed up during analyses. A prime example of weighted programming is reasoning about expected outcomes of probabilistic programs: Every execution step is equipped with a probability and, during analysis, the probabilities of all program executions with a desired outcome are summed up. Weighted programming generalizes probabilistic programs by admitting weights to be drawn from a semiring. For instance, Batz et al. (2022) use weighted programming over the tropical semiring (ℝ≥0∞,min,+,∞,0)(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{\infty},\min,+,\infty,0) to model competitive analysis problems for online algorithms. Weighted programming over the arctic semiring (ℝ−∞∞,max,+,−∞,0)(\mathbb{R}_{-\infty}^{\infty},\max,+,-\infty,0) captures optimization problems, where one attempts to maximize an objective.

papers.title: Encode Once, Answer Many: Internalizing Context via Parametric Flow
papers.abstract: Large language models are typically adapted to a task either by placing knowledge in the input context, which keeps it external and re-encodes it on every call, or by fine-tuning, which internalizes it but demands a costly round of optimization per task. We aim to internalize the knowledge carried by a context directly into model parameters, without per-task optimization and without keeping the context in the input at inference time. To this end, we propose CLIK, a context-conditioned parameter generator that maps a given context to LoRA parameters for internalizing knowledge in a single forward pass through a Transformer encoder with cross-attention, requiring no test-time gradient updates. Once the generated LoRA is inserted into a frozen base model, the model answers downstream queries from the query alone, having internalized the context into its weights rather than re-reading it. Because the adapter depends only on the context, it is generated once and reused for every query on the same document, so the cost of reading that document is amortized across queries. On document question answering, CLIK substantially improves over the no-context base model and outperforms existing hypernetwork-based generators, while remaining behind a base model that reads the context directly, and it carries over to multi-turn dialogue without any multi-turn-specific training. Analysis further shows that the context-dependent part of the generated adapter concentrates in a compact and specific substructure.

Many uses of large language models (LLMs) require the model to act on a specific body of knowledge that is not in its pretrained weights, such as a set of reference documents, a long task instruction, or the history of an ongoing conversation (Brown et al., 2020; Laban et al., 2026). The standard way to supply this knowledge is to place it in the model’s input context, as in in-context learning and retrieval-augmented prompting, where the material is kept as text and read by attention at generation time; this approach is flexible, requires no training, and has become the default as context windows have grown. A second route is to write the knowledge into the weights by fine-tuning, so that the model answers without the context in its input (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026): parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA make each update cheap to store (Hu et al., 2022), and context distillation trains the model to reproduce, without the context, the outputs it would have produced with it (Snell et al., 2022; Kujanpää et al., 2025).

A second route is to write the knowledge into the weights by fine-tuning, so that the model answers without the context in its input (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026): parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA make each update cheap to store (Hu et al., 2022), and context distillation trains the model to reproduce, without the context, the outputs it would have produced with it (Snell et al., 2022; Kujanpää et al., 2025).

Keeping the knowledge in the input runs into two well-documented problems. The first is that quality does not scale with length, because as inputs grow, models increasingly fail to use the relevant information and their accuracy degrades, an effect reported as lost-in-the-middle behavior, weak long in-context learning, and context rot (Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a; Hong et al., 2025). The second is that cost grows with length, because self-attention is quadratic in the input and the key–value cache that must be stored and re-read at every decoding step grows linearly with the number of context tokens, so both latency and memory rise with the amount of knowledge supplied (Ge et al., 2024). Prompt- and cache-compression methods relieve this overhead by shortening the input or shrinking the cache (Jiang et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2024; Ge et al., 2024), but the knowledge still lives outside the parameters and must be re-supplied and re-read for every new query, so it is supplied to the model but never internalized by it.

Context-based adaptation is instant but never internalizes its knowledge, while fine-tuning internalizes the knowledge but is too costly to update for each new context. Hypernetworks (Ha et al., 2017) offer a way to keep the advantages of both, since one network can emit the weights of another and thus turn an input into an adapter in a single forward pass, with no test-time optimization and nothing left in the context window (Chen et al., 2025; Abdalla et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025). papers.title: Strong rate for one-dimensional driftless continuous strict local martingales
papers.abstract: For one-dimensional strict local martingales of the form $\mathrm{d} X_t=\sigma(X_t) \mathrm{d} W_t$ starting from $X_{0}=x_{0}>0$, we prove the strong rate $\mathbb{E}\left[|X^h_N-X_T|\right] \lesssim h^{\min\{\theta\alpha,\frac{1}{2}\}}$ for a discrete scheme~$X^h$ truncated at a level $h^{-\alpha}$, with time step~$h$, as $h\downarrow 0$, where~$\theta$ depends on the truncation property. For the CEV model $\sigma(x)\equiv x^{1+\gamma}$ in particular, the rate is~$\frac{1}{2}$ for any $\gamma \in (0,1)$ (up to a logarithmic pre-factor at $\gamma=\frac{1}{2}$).

papers.intro:
In the Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing [10, 11], the discounted price of a traded asset is required to be a true martingale under the risk-neutral measure. When it is not so, in particular when it is a strict local martingale, major issues arise: Put-Call parity fails, European Call prices lie strictly below their intrinsic values for small strikes (leading to undefined implied volatilities) and the pricing PDE may admit several solutions, as explained in [7, 13, 24, 29, 30, 32, 38]. Such models are standard descriptions of financial bubbles [40], but may also arise unintentionally, in the case of mis-calibrated (local and/or stochastic) volatility models as in the CEV model [4, 8, 9], the SABR model [22] and other stochastic volatility models with moment explosions [2, 21, 42].

papers.title: Hybrid AI Patterns: Thirteen Ways to Couple Language Models with Rules, and How to Choose Among Them
papers.abstract: Language models handle text well, and rule engines give conclusions with proofs. Systems that combine the two are usually described by example, and the same coupling turns up under different names in agent frameworks, guardrail toolkits and neuro-symbolic research. This document defines thirteen patterns for coupling a language model with an executable rule language, in the catalogue form introduced for object-oriented design: intent, motivation, applicability, participants, collaborations, consequences, implementation, known uses and related patterns. Four patterns concern what crosses the boundary between model and rules, five who controls whom, three how the model takes part in the reasoning, and one how knowledge is kept over time. Five invariants hold for every combination, and five failure patterns name the couplings that break them. We relate the catalogue to published pattern catalogues and taxonomies of hybrid and neuro-symbolic systems and show where they overlap with it. A decision guide leads from a problem to a pattern. It rests on our measurements, including the cases in which a model alone did as well as the hybrid or better, and it reports what each design cost.

papers.intro:
More and more organisations let language models act on documents, conversations and transactions that are governed by explicit rules: a regulation, a protocol, an authority limit. Two designs are possible. The rules can be written into the prompt and the model asked to apply them, or the rules can stay executable and the model be given the parts of the task that rules cannot do: reading text, phrasing a question, proposing a candidate. Between these two designs lie many couplings, and practitioners tend to reinvent them project by project.

(1994) made patterns a working vocabulary for object-oriented design, and Buschmann et al. We use the same form for couplings of language models with rules. A shared name lets designers say which coupling they mean. The consequences make the trade-offs explicit, including the cases where a model alone is the better choice, and the known uses tie each pattern to running systems and to measurements.

papers.title: Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in Question Answering
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, yet they produce wrong answers indistinguishable from correct ones. In question answering (QA), such an error propagates unnoticed into downstream tasks. Perturbation-based uncertainty quantification (UQ) addresses this by probing a model over a set of input rewrites and reading uncertainty from how much its predictions vary. Yet this set is usually built generically, by free paraphrasing, token-level perturbation, or adversarial search. Such rewrites leave two things uncontrolled that matter in QA: what kind of change is made to the context, and how explicitly the context supports the answer. When neither is controlled, the composition of the set is determined by the generator rather than by design, and the estimate inherits whatever that generator happens to produce. Quality-diversity (QD) search is built to cover a predefined exploration space, so we recast input perturbation as a QD problem and propose \emph{neighborhood elites (NE)}, a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes, the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. We compare NE against three other neighborhood constructors, holding the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure and search objective fixed, and against three scores read from the original context. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of the 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. Additionally, NE detects failure better than semantic entropy computed over decoder samples, by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding and generation (OpenAI, 2023), question answering and multi-step reasoning (Wei et al., 2022), and program synthesis (Chen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). Beyond single prompts, they increasingly act as the reasoning engine of larger systems, from retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that grounds answers in external corpora (Lewis et al., 2020; Asai et al., 2023) to agentic workflows that plan and call external tools to perform tasks (Yao et al., 2023). In such pipelines, a single wrong answer can propagate through later steps (Zhang et al., 2024), so the usefulness of an LLM depends not only on producing an answer, but also on signaling whether that answer can be trusted.

In such pipelines, a single wrong answer can propagate through later steps (Zhang et al., 2024), so the usefulness of an LLM depends not only on producing an answer, but also on signaling whether that answer can be trusted.

LLMs hallucinate, presenting fabricated facts with the same assurance they provide to correct answers (Maynez et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2022). They tend to agree with the user rather than correct a mistaken assumption (Sharma et al., 2024), and rarely express doubt or admit when they do not know (Yin et al., 2023). Asking the model how confident it is, is not helpful, as its stated confidence is poorly aligned with its actual accuracy (Xiong et al., 2024). This motivates uncertainty quantification (UQ): estimating how much to trust an answer without relying on the model’s own account of it (Malinin and Gales, 2021; Kuhn et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024).

Asking the model how confident it is, is not helpful, as its stated confidence is poorly aligned with its actual accuracy (Xiong et al., 2024). This motivates uncertainty quantification (UQ): estimating how much to trust an answer without relying on the model’s own account of it (Malinin and Gales, 2021; Kuhn et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024).

UQ methods can be categorized by the signal used to quantify uncertainty. One family relies on the predictive probabilities assigned by the model (Malinin and Gales, 2021), while another measures the variability between multiple predictions. The latter requires only model outputs and is therefore applicable in black-box settings. These approaches differ mainly in the way the predictions are produced. Sampling-based methods sample the model several times on a fixed input (Manakul et al., 2023; Farquhar et al., 2024). Perturbation-based methods instead vary the input, rewriting the prompt in ways that should not change the answer (Gao et al., 2024; Song et al., 2025). In either way, the predictions are compared by meaning rather than surface form, which is what semantic entropy measures (Kuhn et al., 2023).

In the text setting, a perturbation-based estimate is only as informative as the input variants it compares. QD algorithms (Mouret and Clune, 2015; Pugh et al., 2016), coupled with LLMs, can orchestrate the search and assembly of such a set of input variants. The LLM carries out the variations, while quality-diversity steers the search, keeping the best candidate found in each cell it explores, so the set spans many strong candidates rather than a single best one. This pairing has proven useful across domains, generating diverse code (Lehman et al., 2022), creative writing (Bradley et al., 2024), and adversarial prompts (Samvelyan et al., 2024). It is therefore a natural engine for building a set of input variants that vary systematically across a chosen feature space.

A key limitation of these methods is that their rules apply to each rewrite on its own, rather than to the set as a whole. A rewrite is described by the operation applied and by how far it moved from the original, and not by its relation to the answer, though a rephrased question can ask for the same answer more or less directly. The composition of the set is therefore determined largely by the generator, rather than by design.

In extractive QA, a perturbation set has to control two dimensions: how the context is modified and how explicitly the rewrite still supports the answer. The answer is inside of the rewritten input, so a rewrite changes its support whether or not anything records the change. Two contexts can preserve the same answer while differing substantially in how directly they support it: a rewrite may keep the answer in place but reach its support through a referring expression or spread that support across several sentences. The answer has not changed, but recovering it now places greater demands on the model.

We refer to this set as the neighborhood of the input. We hypothesize that uncertainty estimated over such structured neighborhoods contains a richer uncertainty signal for detecting model failures than uncertainty derived from less structured variations or repeated sampling of the original input. Since the context passage already contains the answer, the neighborhood consists of whole-passage rewrites leaving that answer unchanged. The search steers the generator toward specified combinations of edit type and answer support, targeting one cell after another rather than accepting whatever it produces. This advantage also holds over repeated decoder sampling on the original context when using the same uncertainty measure. Our contributions are as follows.

papers.title: Quantum-Inspired Convolutional Networks for High-Resolution Pseudo-Label Generation from Multimodal Earth Observation Data
papers.abstract: Accurate land-cover mapping from multimodal Earth observation (EO) data remains a challenge in regions where high-resolution annotations are scarce or costly to obtain. This work introduces a quantum convolutional encoder-decoder network for pseudo-label generation using Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, guided only by coarse MODIS-derived land-cover maps. The proposed framework uses quantum-inspired convolutional blocks to enhance feature extraction and cross-sensor fusion, enabling the model to infer a fine-scale semantic structure from heterogeneous inputs. Experiments were conducted on the DFC2020 dataset, which provides a quadruple of Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 multispectral, low-resolution MODIS labels and high-resolution reference land-cover maps. The proposed training framework first learns a robust representation of multimodal inputs through the reconstruction branch before any supervision from low-resolution labels is applied. This self-supervised stage enables the model to capture a fine-scale spectral-spatial structure, which is then used to generate high-resolution pseudo-labels. These pseudo-labels are subsequently evaluated through classification metrics on the test data, demonstrating that the proposed approach produces more spatially coherent and class-consistent compared to classical baselines. The results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired deep learning to improve label generation in low-annotation remote sensing scenarios, offering a scalable path towards high-quality land-cover products for EO applications.

Multimodal EO sources such as Sentinel‑1 SAR and Sentinel‑2 multispectral images offer rich and complementary information, but utilizing them effectively requires models capable of learning robust spectral–spatial representations under weak or coarse supervision. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled significant progress in semantic segmentation and data fusion, particularly through encoder–decoder architectures that can reconstruct fine‑scale patterns from heterogeneous inputs. However, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) often require substantial amounts of labeled data, involve large parameter budgets, and may struggle to generalize across varying spectral–spatial distributions, sensor modalities, and acquisition conditions commonly encountered in remote sensing imagery [3, 9]. These limitations motivate the exploration of alternative architectures, such as parameter efficient quantum‑inspired convolutional networks that can also enhance feature expressiveness and improve pseudo‑label generation.

Building on these limitations, recent studies have highlighted the potential of quantum machine learning (QML) as an emerging alternative for remote sensing applications. QML is a class of machine-learning models based on parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which can be trained to perform various downstream tasks such as classification, regression or data generation. Quantum neural networks (QNNs) can be formulated using different architectural styles, including unitary architectures in which the network is composed of parametrized qubit rotations and other unitary operations. In contrast to classical convolutions, which perform linear aggregations of spatially local features, a quantum network achieves non-linear feature mixing by encoding information into quantum states through parameterized rotation gates and entangling operations [2, 1]. QML models can exploit hybrid quantum–classical training schemes to achieve competitive performance with significantly reduced computational resources, making them an attractive direction for future EO workflows [6]. Moreover, QML offers the advantages of quantum algorithms that can be efficiently simulated on conventional hardware while integrating quantum computational principles with machine learning to address complex optimization and representation‑learning challenges more efficiently than purely classical approaches [7, 5]. In recent years, weak‑supervised and self‑supervised learning strategies have gained prominence as effective alternatives to supervised approaches, particularly in limited, coarser or noisy label EO scenarios [14, 13, 10, 11]. These methods exploit coarse labels, unlabeled imagery, or pretext tasks to learn meaningful representations that can generalize across sensors and acquisition conditions. The convergence of parameter efficient quantum‑inspired architectures with weak‑supervised learning provides a promising foundation for developing models capable of generating reliable pseudo‑labels from multimodal satellite data, even when only low‑resolution land‑cover information is available. We design a quantum-inspired convolutional network, a parameter-efficient quantum convolution–based encoder–decoder for pseudo label generation. 2. We propose a reconstruction module with an auxiliary classifier that learns spectral–spatial representations and uses the reconstructed features to generate high‑resolution pseudo‑labels. 3. Section III highlights the experimental data, loss function formulations, experimental results, and detailed discussions. Finally, Section IV concludes the paper and highlights the future scope.

papers.title: Spectrahedral relaxations and tightenings of rigidly convex sets
papers.abstract: We construct a natural spectrahedral relaxation of a rigidly convex set (rcs) that depends only on the cubic part and on the degree of the defining real zero polynomial. For quadratic polynomials, we prove exactness and for a product of linear polynomials, we show that a higher order version of our relaxation is exact. We also establish a way of tightening the relaxation by moving the origin inside the rcs, and that the rcs is recovered by sweeping the origin over its interior. To obtain all these results we use a linear form that is closely connected to the zeros of a given real zero polynomial. We also prove that any rcs can be written as an affine linear slice of the cone of non-negative polynomials. Using this, we can define a hierarchy of tightenings that are spectrahedral shadows. We can show that this tightening is exact if the given polynomial admits a determinantal representation. This tightening is similar to a tightening of a hyperbolicity cone due to Kummer, Plaumann, and Vinzant.

papers.title: AdMuse: Skill-Guided Creative Advertising Image Generation
papers.abstract: An outstanding creative advertising image should both attract attention and communicate a product's positioning. How to choose a persuasive conceptual bridge before rendering begins is challenging for advertising generation. We present AdMuse, a skill-guided multi-agent framework that distills high-quality advertisements into reusable creative skills for cross-domain advertising strategy. Rather than retrieving isolated exemplars, AdMuse abstracts recurring bridge patterns into a skill library that can guide new product briefs. At generation time, AdMuse coordinates skill routing, multi-candidate ideation and selection, and VLM-guided visual refinement: diverse skills propose alternative concepts, relative judgment selects the most promising direction, and vision-language feedback helps realize the selected intent in the final image. This design treats advertising creativity as a structured decision process rather than a single prompt-writing step. Experiments across diverse product and brand positionings show that AdMuse produces visually compelling advertisements that faithfully communicate product positioning.

papers.intro:
Creativity plays a vital role in advertising. Creative advertisements are more memorable than regular ones (Till and Baack, 2005; Jin et al., 2019). Although modern image generators (OpenAI, 2026) and agentic visual pipelines (Chen et al., 2026) can render high-quality images, they still largely rely on the user to provide the core creative idea. For advertising, however, the main difficulty often lies not in rendering an image, but in deciding what visual concept to use. A key challenge is that a product can support many creative directions, each producing distinct visual and communicative effects. Advertising generation therefore needs a creative-strategy representation that reveals, compares, and instantiates viable directions (Koushik et al., 2025). It should generalize across products while guiding visual synthesis, often through cross-domain associations that make desired qualities perceptible.

Advertising generation therefore needs a creative-strategy representation that reveals, compares, and instantiates viable directions (Koushik et al., 2025). It should generalize across products while guiding visual synthesis, often through cross-domain associations that make desired qualities perceptible.

We frame this problem through the notion of a creative bridge: a cross-domain association that links a product to a distant concept through an interpretable visual chain. High-quality creative ads repeatedly reuse a limited set of such bridge patterns (Sun et al., 2025). We therefore distill them into reusable creative skills that specify when a strategy applies, what associative chain it constructs, and how it can be instantiated for a new product brief. Based on this representation, we propose AdMuse, a skill-guided multi-agent framework for creative advertising image generation. AdMuse routes bridge-diverse skills for a brief, lets multiple skill-conditioned concepts compete through relative judgment, and then refines the selected concept with VLM feedback. Our contributions are summarized as: • We formalize the creative bridge and distill recurring bridge patterns from advertisements into a reusable skill library. • We propose a skill-guided multi-agent pipeline that combines routing, multi-candidate ideation and selection, and VLM-guided visual refinement. • We show that AdMuse produces visually compelling and message-faithful advertisements across diverse briefs, products, and positionings (see Fig. 1).

papers.title: Static dipolar impurity in a Fermi gas
papers.abstract: We consider a static dipolar impurity immersed in a Fermi gas and show how dipolar interactions shape both the few-body scattering properties and the resulting polaron physics. Using Fumi's theorem, we connect the anisotropic phase shifts directly to the ground-state energy, and compute the exact impurity spectrum via the functional determinant approach. The resulting spectrum is a convolution of independent even- and odd-wave contributions, giving rise to a ground state with simultaneously occupied even- and odd-wave bound states whose separation is tunable via the dipole length. A variational ansatz limited to one particle-hole excitation fails to capture this doubly occupied ground state. We further find that long-range dipolar interactions weaken Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe, reducing the power-law decay of the quasiparticle weight. These effects can be tested with ultracold polar molecules, where microwave shielding and independent tunability of interactions enable experimental access to the predicted regimes.

papers.intro:
Impurities in a quantum medium serve as a sensitive probe of few- and many-body physics [1, 2]. The medium dresses the impurity with its excitations, forming a polaron whose properties are predominantly determined by the underlying two-body scattering. In strongly correlated Fermi systems, polarons provide a controlled quasiparticle picture of complex many-body physics [3, 4]. A prominent example is the density-imbalanced unitary Fermi gas, where the normal phase is described as a Fermi liquid of polarons [5, 6, 7].

Most studies so far have focused on short-range interactions between impurity and bath. Recent advances with magnetic atoms [8] and, in particular, ultracold polar molecules [9, 10, 11, 12] now open a qualitatively different regime governed by dipolar interactions. Dipolar interactions are anisotropic and long-ranged, coupling different partial-wave channels and producing strong finite-range corrections [13, 14, 15, 16]. This anisotropic, momentum-dependent scattering underlies a broad landscape of many-body phases, from supersolids and self-bound droplets to unconventional dipolar superfluidity [17, 18, 19, 20, 21].

We then compute the exact spectrum and show that it factorizes into even- and odd-wave contributions, giving a ground state with simultaneously occupied even- and odd-wave bound states. We benchmark the widely used Chevy ansatz [47] against the exact solution, and show how long-range interactions weaken the orthogonality catastrophe. We conclude in Section IV with a discussion of the implications for future studies of dipolar many-body systems. Throughout this work, we use natural units, in which ℏ=kB=1\hbar=k_{B}=1.

papers.title: Who Else Is In? Multi-Agent Collusion Initation Via Strategic Vagueness
papers.abstract: Multi agent LLM systems raise the risk of collusion among agents pursuing objectives hidden from their overseers. When potential partners identities are unknown, collusion first requires initiation: agents must discover one another, often through a public channel observed by ordinary agents and monitors. Strategic vagueness offers a way to navigate this mixed audience, conveying intent to a prospective partner while preserving a plausible ordinary interpretation. We introduce a mutual identification game in which two schemers must identify each other through public interaction, while jointly solving an ordinary task. We find that some models discover successful handshake strategies without explicit signalling guidance, using task compatible exchanges that monitors often fail to flag at low false positive rates. To characterize the communicative capabilities underlying these exchanges, we study a controlled coordination setting. We find an asymmetric response to message explicitness: as messages become more indirect, monitor punishment can fall faster than partner coordination, creating a profitable intermediate regime of strategic vagueness. Together, these findings illustrate a Blackstone style evidential asymmetry: communication sufficient for coordination between agents may remain insufficient for confident detection by monitor, opening a new surface of collusion.

papers.title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
papers.abstract: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.

papers.intro:
Softmax attention scales poorly to long contexts: its compute grows quadratically with sequence length, while its key–value cache grows linearly. Recurrent language models address both problems by processing the sequence in linear time and carrying a fixed-size state while decoding. Moreover, modern recurrent architectures such as gated linear attention, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2 (Yang et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2025; Dao & Gu, 2024) admit an efficiently parallelizable structure commonly referred to as the chunkwise-parallel form, in which tokens within each chunk are processed in parallel using dense matrix multiplications, while only the recurrent state is propagated sequentially across chunks. Given this scalable structure, the central question for this class of models is how to make the recurrent memory more expressive without sacrificing parallel evaluation.

Test-time training (TTT) addresses the expressivity side of this question by treating the recurrent state as the weights of a small model that learns from the sequence through online gradient descent (Sun et al., 2025). With a linear memory and a squared reconstruction loss, this recovers the delta rule of Widrow & Hoff (1960), the update used by DeltaNet (Schlag et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024b), whereas a nonlinear memory can adapt its features as well as its readout. TTT-MLP, Titans, and LaCT (Sun et al., 2025; Behrouz et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2026) explore such neural memories, but their gradients depend nonlinearly on the current weights: each token changes the weights at which the next token’s gradient should be evaluated, creating a sequential dependency. To recover parallelism, existing methods group gradient evaluations into blocks and evaluate every gradient in a block at the weights entering it. This creates a fidelity–speed tradeoff: larger blocks reduce the sequential depth but more coarsely approximate token-by-token learning, while smaller blocks are more faithful but require more sequential steps.
