papers.title: Logical Guidance of Stochastic Interpolants
papers.abstract: Guidance and composition of generative models have applications in visual design, chemistry, and biology. Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models. However, Flow Matching (FM) and Stochastic Interpolants (SI) learn velocity fields. We show that negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant, whereas conjunction, and therefore any formula containing one, is exact on Gaussian paths but in general incurs a drift-interaction error, so composed velocities need not sample the logical target. LOGSI solves this by using score-based re-equilibration as our principled mechanism and falling back to the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor. In non-Gaussian bridge problems, generation alternates transport steps with score re-equilibration steps. On image trans fer (EMNIST to CMNIST, CelebA) and QM9 source-to-target molecular editing with logical attribute constraints, LOGSI improves rule conformity at the same network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, while also improving fidelity on the image tasks. More broadly, LOGSI applies wherever stochastic interpolants need guidance and logical combinations of constraints are natural.

papers.intro:
Guidance and composition are central to generative AI, enabling controlled generation across domains ranging from visual design to chemistry and biology (Saharia et al., 2022; Hoogeboom et al., 2022; Watson et al., 2023; Skreta et al., 2025; Blohm and Garg, 2026). Guidance steers a model toward desired properties, while composition combines multiple conditions or concepts to produce outputs that satisfy more complex requirements. Most existing methods target diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021; Song et al., 2020), where one endpoint is a fixed Gaussian, and the reverse dynamics depend only on the score. A natural extension is to lift logical guidance to stochastic interpolants (SI) (Albergo et al., 2025), which unify diffusion and flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) and are not tied to a Gaussian endpoint. Classical guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho and Salimans, 2022) for SI has been studied (Feng et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026), but logical composition of atomic conditions in this regime remains open. We focus on domain transfer (Liu et al., 2023): an interpolant transports a source distribution ρ0\rho_{0} to a target ρ1\rho_{1}, samples can be initialized from concrete source instances (Albergo et al., 2024), and guidance enforces a Boolean formula φ\varphi over target attributes. For example, we may edit a source molecule by adding a geometry (e.g. rings) and an atom-composition constraint (e.g. oxygen).

papers.title: LinQuant: Functional Invariances for Low-Precision Linear Recurrences
papers.abstract: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.

Linear recurrences offer an efficient, sub-quadratic alternative to softmax attention for sequence modeling (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Dao & Gu, 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025). They summarize past tokens in a fixed-size state, avoiding the growing key-value cache of softmax attention, and are increasingly used in both standalone and hybrid language models (NVIDIA, 2025; Amini et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025; Beck et al., 2024). For prefill, these models are typically evaluated using chunkwise-parallel algorithms, which process blocks of tokens in parallel through dense matrix multiplications while propagating a recurrent state between them (Dao & Gu, 2024; Yang & Zhang, 2024). This mirrors the blockwise organization of efficient attention kernels such as FlashAttention and makes recurrent prefill naturally amenable to low-precision execution.

This mirrors the blockwise organization of efficient attention kernels such as FlashAttention and makes recurrent prefill naturally amenable to low-precision execution.

Low-precision attention has been studied extensively, with optimized integer and floating-point kernels now forming a mature part of the Transformer inference stack (Zhang et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2024). In contrast, low-precision kernels for linear recurrences remain largely unexplored. Prior work has studied quantization of recurrent models (Xu et al., 2025; Chiang et al., 2025), largely targeting the projections and activations surrounding the Mamba-2 recurrence. SSDi8, on the other hand, executes the recurrent computation in low precision, demonstrating an efficient INT8 implementation specific to Mamba-2 (Kim et al., 2026). We instead study the space more generally, investigating low-precision computation across the design space of modern linear recurrent architectures.

Executing sequence mixers in low-precision can come at the cost of performance. One powerful lever to mitigate this is functional invariances. Such transformations preserve the full-precision operator while changing the numerics presented to a quantizer. Figure 12 in the appendix illustrates this principle through write-factor absorption. We distinguish two broad classes. Mixer-agnostic invariances act on the residual stream or individual linear layers and do not depend on the algebra of the sequence operator (Xiao et al., 2023; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Because these transformations are largely independent of the mixer, they transfer naturally to recurrent architectures and have already been adopted by methods such as MambaQuant and Quamba2 (Xu et al., 2025; Chiang et al., 2025). Mixer-specific invariances instead rely on the sequence operator itself, and can be classified as either mixer-external or mixer-internal. The former materialize as changes of basis and can be applied outside of the sequence-mixer, while the latter are functions of a recurrence’s algorithmic realization (Figure 1). Transformer PTQ has exploited such invariances within softmax attention, for example through transformations of its query, key, and value representations (Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). In contrast, the mixer-specific invariances of linear recurrences have yet to be characterized.

papers.title: Coherent Electronic Lensing in Proximitized Graphene
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved control of coherent electron transport offers a route to understanding and engineering interference phenomena in hybrid superconducting devices. Here, we use Scanning Gate Microscopy (SGM) to investigate Fabry-P\'erot (FP) interference in the n-p-n cavity of a ballistic graphene Josephson junction. Spatial maps of the superconducting switching current and normal-state conductance reveal circular interference fringes arising from two distinct effects of the SGM tip potential. A global shift of the Fermi wave vector modulates the FP resonances of the cavity, while a local perturbation produces additional oscillations that persist at fixed Fermi wave vector as the tip bias is varied. An analytical model identifies the origin of this local response with coherent electron lensing, in which the tip modifies the phase accumulated along interfering trajectories. The measured fringe patterns in the switching current indicate that this mechanism affects superconducting transport, consistent with tip-induced shifts of the resonance conditions for Andreev bound states. These results establish SGM as a tunable local lens for controlling interference in superconducting ballistic graphene devices.

papers.title: Proximal R2 Priors for Structured Variance Allocation
papers.abstract: Scientific domain knowledge in regression often concerns structural relationships among model terms, which are typically encoded as parameter constraints. Since such relationships rarely hold exactly in practice, prior distributions should encourage them while at the same time retaining support for scientifically plausible departures. Accounting for these relationships becomes more pressing in modern regression, where high-dimensionality is usually present and regularisation is essential. $R^2$ decomposition priors provide an interpretable foundation for regularisation by placing a prior on total explained variance and distributing the implied signal across model terms. We introduce the Proximal R2 prior, which uses proximal relaxations to encode these relationships as soft constraints on the variance allocation. Our formulation yields differentiable posteriors compatible with standard gradient based samplers. Theoretically, we prove that our prior preserves the characteristic marginal properties of global-local shrinkage priors. Moreover, we establish posterior consistency and contraction rates in growing dimensions, showing that the inclusion of structural relationships and proximal methods do not alter the shrinkage properties. Notably, these results demonstrate that the structural constraints in the model do not hinder posterior recovery. Simulation studies and real-data applications to interaction and generalised additive models demonstrate that our prior improves parameter recovery, out-of-sample prediction, and sampling efficiency over existing constrained and unconstrained shrinkage priors, even under structural misspecification.

papers.intro:
Modern regression models frequently contain terms linked by scientifically meaningful relationships. In an interaction model, for instance, an interaction is often considered more plausible when the main effects are active, a principle known as heredity (Chipman et al., 1997; Griffin and Brown, 2017). In a generalised additive model, a parsimonious linear effect might be preferred unless the data provide sufficient evidence for a non-linear departure (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1986; Marra and Wood, 2011). Likewise, domain knowledge often suggests that certain treatment exposures or mechanisms should receive greater prior signal than others (Hahn and Carvalho, 2015; Sewell, 2025). Such structural beliefs govern the relative relevance of model terms, yet they rarely hold exactly in practice. A useful prior should encourage the proposed structure without preventing the data from supporting scientifically credible departures from it (Robert, 2007).

Incorporating such structural guidance is especially critical in high-dimensional regression problems, where the number of covariates is large relative to the sample size (Wainwright, 2019). Bayesian inference responds to the complexity of these problems by designing prior distributions that encode structure (Castillo and Vaart, 2012; Castillo et al., 2015). This provides a principled route for incorporating structure into the model while still allowing domain knowledge to be easily elicited. papers.title: Separating the Density Wave Phase from Zero-Resistance Superconductivity in La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$
papers.abstract: Identifying the key ingredients for superconductivity under pressure in the Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates remains a formidable challenge, due to a complex interplay between structural variations, oxygen content and location, electronically ordered phases, and the need for high pressures to reach the superconducting phase. To disentangle these complex inter-dependencies, here we study a series of clean single crystals of trilayer La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$. We discover that enhanced biaxial, compressive pressures induce a zero-resistance state at a 60\% lower pressure compared to previous reports. At the same time, we completely separate the low-pressure density wave phase from superconductivity, effectively ruling out that soft, quantum critical fluctuations of the density wave order parameter act as the pairing glue in this system. Our results establish biaxial, in-plane pressures as a powerful tool for promoting superconductivity in nickelates, unifying the required pressure scales for superconductivity in different Ruddlesden-Popper structures, and providing a connection to the recently discovered thin film samples.

papers.title: Epimorphism testing with dihedral targets
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of deciding whether or not there is an epimorphism from the class of finitely presented groups to a fixed finite group. We show this problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete when the target is a non-nilpotent dihedral group. This complements work of Kuperberg and Samperton (2018, Geom. Topol.) who showed the same result when the target is a fixed finite non-abelian simple group. We also include a survey of complexity and reduction results when the source and target are classes of finitely presented groups.

papers.title: Randomized Symplectic Model Reduction: One-Pass Basis Construction and Sketched Hamiltonian Assembly
papers.abstract: Symplectic model order reduction of Hamiltonian systems yields reduced dynamics that conserve the reduced Hamiltonian along exact trajectories, avoiding the artificial energy drift that can arise from conventional projection methods. For large-scale spatial discretizations, however, basis construction and reduced-operator assembly can involve substantial offline costs. Randomized numerical linear algebra can reduce these costs through low-dimensional sketches while supporting streaming and parallel implementations. We develop randomized techniques for two parts of the offline stage while preserving the Hamiltonian structure of the reduced dynamics. First, we introduce the one-pass sketched randomized cSVD (Ops-rcSVD), a one-pass randomized variant of the complex-SVD algorithm. Combining randomized range finding with an independent left sketch, Ops-rcSVD constructs an ortho-symplectic reduced basis from a single pass over the snapshot ensemble. Second, for quadratic Hamiltonian systems, we introduce a randomized reduced-Hamiltonian assembly based on sketching the reduced basis and operator actions, yielding a reduced Hamiltonian system by construction. We derive bounds for the snapshot projection error, uniform-in-parameter perturbation bounds for the sketched reduced Hamiltonian, and an energy-norm estimate for the difference between reduced and sketched reduced trajectories. Experiments on large-scale systems show that Ops-rcSVD attains projection accuracy comparable to deterministic and two-pass randomized constructions while reducing basis-construction time. They further demonstrate accurate sketched reduced-Hamiltonian assembly when storing the complete snapshot ensemble is no longer feasible.

papers.intro:
Hamiltonian systems are widely used to model conservative dynamics, arising, for example, in mechanics and spatial discretizations of partial differential equations [1]. For large-scale discretizations, numerical simulations can become computationally expensive, particularly when repeated evaluations are required, as in parameter studies, optimization, or other multi-query settings. Moreover, applications such as real-time simulation and control often require rapid evaluations. Projection-based model order reduction (MOR) addresses these challenges by approximating the full-order model (FOM) dynamics in a low-dimensional subspace to reduce computational cost; see [2] for a comprehensive overview. Classical projection-based reduction methods, however, do not in general preserve the underlying Hamiltonian structure. Consequently, invariants of the full-order dynamics, in particular energy conservation, may be lost in the ROM, leading to energy drift and qualitatively incorrect long-time behavior.

papers.title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.

papers.intro:
Identifying an unknown dynamical system from a finite hypothesis class is a problem that appears naturally in many applications (Choirat and Seri, 2012). In particular, the identification of the active mode of a switched system is a relevant problem in the adaptive control literature (Narendra and Balakrishnan, 1997). Recently, in the context of adaptive control Rantzer (2021) considered model uncertainty in the form of a finite hypothesis class, renewing interest in this setting. Furthermore, in evolutionary and ecological models often several hypothesis exist and the most suitable one needs to be determined from observations (Johnson and Omland, 2004). While all these applications have a finite hypothesis class, in many realistic cases the true system is not necessarily contained in the hypothesis class. Instead, the hypothesis class typically contains an approximation of the true system the learner should identify. However, recent works that cover the identification of a LTI (LTI) system from a finite hypothesis class rely on the assumption that the true system lies inside the hypothesis class and do not consider the misspecified setting. We remove this assumption and provide finite-sample identification guarantees.

Based on novel tools in high-dimensional statistics (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011; Wainwright, 2019) recently this has been considered from a finite sample perspective (see, e.g., (Tsiamis et al., 2023; Ziemann et al., 2023) for an overview on the topic). Extending these works (Wagenmaker and Jamieson, 2020; Wagenmaker et al., 2021; Chatzikiriakos et al., 2025) consider the problem of experiment design in this setting from a finite sample perspective.

papers.title: Single-Temperature Ranked Greedy Cluster Exchange for Max-Cut on Two-Dimensional Tori
papers.abstract: Ground-state search in two-dimensional Ising spin glasses on large toroidal lattices remains challenging for local-update heuristics because rugged energy barriers impede relaxation across metastable states. Equivalent to zero-field toroidal Max-Cut problems, these spin-glass instances also serve as standard benchmarks for optimization heuristics. Many Monte Carlo approaches combine single-spin flips or cluster moves with temperature ladders or annealing schedules, yet even with tuned parameters, rarely achieve rapid, reliable ground-state convergence at scale. Here, we address the need for faster ground-state search through cooperation between replicas. We introduce ranked greedy cluster exchange (RGCX) and combine it with fixed-temperature Metropolis sweeps to form single-temperature RGCX. Replicas are ranked by cut to determine the pair-processing order. Each pair deterministically exchanges every disagreement cluster that raises the better replica's cut, retaining the complement and conserving the pair's summed cut. On the 20,000-spin Gset instance G81, the estimated runtime to reach the certified optimum with 99% success probability (TTS99) was 12.1 s on an 8-core desktop computer. With the same population size, exchange interval and temperature, the method reached the best known cuts on all 17 toroidal Gset graphs, including 9 certified optima. These findings advance ground-state search on large two-dimensional tori by establishing single-temperature RGCX as an efficient population-based method that combines ranked greedy cluster exchange with fixed-temperature Metropolis dynamics.

papers.title: GenAI as an 'Invisible Hand' in Opinion Dynamics: Evidence from a Group-Level Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Recent arguments suggest that genAI can act as an invisible hand that gradually shapes social structures, such as collective beliefs and norms. The argument is that if millions of people repeatedly consult genAI tools, their generated outcomes quietly shape what becomes acceptable, reasonable or conventional. We study this in the context of collective opinion dynamics, i.e., how groups form opinions around controversial dynamics. We present the findings of a simulation including 50,000 group discussions across 50 controversial statements, three LLMs, and different social configurations. We vary two characteristics of LLM interaction-agreeableness and personalization-and compare the influence of genAI in homogeneous and heterogeneous groups. Our findings indicate that profile-specific personalization increases LLM influence when models adopt a non-neutral stance, i.e., when they agree or disagree with the user. Furthermore, we find that neutral LLMs have a stronger effect in homogeneous groups. Based on our simulation, we generate a set of hypotheses to specify how, why and when AI-related features and social configurations jointly shape collective opinion making.

papers.title: The Anatomy of Socio-Demographics in Pluralistic Offensiveness Modeling: When and Where It Helps, and the Role of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Subjective judgments such as offensiveness often vary substantially across individuals, motivating pluralistic modeling approaches that incorporate annotators' socio-demographic information to capture this variation. However, prior findings on the benefits of socio-demographic information for pluralistic modeling are mixed, calling for a systematic analysis of both its effectiveness and the mechanisms through which it improves prediction. In this work, we study $\textbf{when}$ and $\textbf{where}$ socio-demographics benefit pluralistic offensiveness modeling, as well as $\textbf{the role of explicit reasoning}$ in leveraging this information. Across three multi-annotator datasets with prompted and trained LLMs, we first show that demographic gains are small and inconsistent for individual predictions but become clearer at the group and population levels, because aggregation attenuates the idiosyncratic variation that masks small but systematic demographic signals. Second, using a reasoning and prediction format that explicitly decomposes individual judgment into an overall baseline and a demographic-specific deviation, we show that the gains arise from both components: demographic information improves baseline estimation and enables meaningful demographic-specific shifts, and interventions show that better component estimates improve final predictions. Finally, comparing direct demographic conditioning with explicit reasoning about how the text interacts with annotator demographics, we find that reasoning yields more accurate baseline and shift estimates as well as final predictions, whereas conditioning alone rarely produces informative shifts. These results suggest that the mixed evidence in prior work may partly stem from individual-level evaluation, and that the value of socio-demographic information depends on both how it is evaluated and how models are guided to use it.

Subjective judgments such as sentiment, bias, and offensiveness often vary substantially across annotators. Rather than treating such disagreement as noise, pluralistic modeling aims to preserve and model the diversity of human judgments (Sorensen et al., 2024; Mostafazadeh Davani et al., 2022; Fleisig et al., 2023). A common approach is to incorporate annotators’ socio-demographic information, motivated by the observation that social and cultural backgrounds can systematically shape how the same text is perceived. However, prior studies provide mixed evidence on its benefits for pluralistic modeling: demographic information improves prediction in some settings or along particular demographic axes, while providing limited benefits or even degrading performance in others (Mokhberian et al., 2024; Zhang and Coltekin, 2026; Orlikowski et al., 2023; Orlikowski et al., 2025). These conflicting findings call for a systematic analysis of when socio-demographic information is beneficial, where its benefits arise, and how modeling choices affect its use.11 1 A more detailed discussion of related work is provided in Appendix A.

We first ask when socio-demographic information is beneficial across three levels of evaluation: individual annotators, socio-demographic groups, and the overall population. Existing work has evaluated demographic-aware modeling at these levels, but largely treats them as separate targets rather than examining how the benefits change across them (Fleisig et al., 2023; Parappan and Henao, 2025; Xu et al., 2026). This gap can obscure small but systematic demographic signals that are difficult to detect at the individual level yet become apparent after group or population aggregation. We find that demographic gains are indeed limited at the individual level and become more pronounced at the group and population levels. A simple statistical analysis explains why: aggregation attenuates residual individual variation, which demographics cannot explain, while preserving systematic demographic effects.

We next ask where in the prediction process these benefits arise. An individual judgment can be viewed as an overall baseline plus a demographic-specific deviation, but existing approaches leave this decomposition implicit and expose only the final prediction (Xu et al., 2026; Zhang and Coltekin, 2026). It is therefore unclear whether socio-demographics help by improving the baseline, the demographic-specific deviation, or both. papers.title: A Spectral-model-independent Diagnostic of Phase-resolved Spectral Convergence in Swift J0243.6+6124
papers.abstract: We introduce a spectral-model-independent spectral-shape metric, $\delta_{\rm rms}$, to probe phase-resolved spectral evolution in the Galactic ultraluminous X-ray pulsar Swift J0243.6+6124. The $\delta_{\rm rms}$--luminosity relation reveals a reproducible convergence--redivergence behavior: spectra from two geometrically opposite pulse phases converge to near identity around $L_{\rm t}^{\ast}\sim8.8\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}}$, with a mean shape difference of only $\sim2\%$, and rediverge at higher luminosities, most prominently at higher energies. This strong phase-resolved spectral convergence coincides with a pulse-profile reversal and traces the same transition luminosities previously identified from broadband continuum evolution, including $L_{\rm t}\sim4.5\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{erg\ s^{-1}}$. These results suggest a possible luminosity-driven reweighting between a broadly distributed surface-reprocessed/reflected component and an increasingly important direct accretion-column contribution, while establishing $\delta_{\rm rms}$ as a robust, spectral-model-independent diagnostic of radiation-geometry restructuring in bright accreting X-ray pulsars.

papers.title: Larger Crossing Families
papers.abstract: We give the first explicit constant for crossing families of linear size by showing that every set of $n$ points in general position in the plane contains a crossing family of size approximately $\frac{n}{79}$. We further identify some conditions where there are even larger crossing families. The first such condition forbids the existence of a large different pattern, namely non-convex 4-clusters: We show that every point set contains either a large non-convex 4-cluster or a large crossing family. The second condition is the existence of many crossings: We give a bound for the size of a crossing family in terms of the number of crossings of the complete geometric graph drawn on the point set.

papers.title: Student-LLM Interactions During Math Learning: Limited Epistemic Proactivity Overall, but Within-chat Change Predicts Performance Without AI
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.

papers.intro:
Students are increasingly using general-purpose large language models (LLMs) for learning [1]. While they can use LLMs to improve immediate task performance, their use does not necessarily support the knowledge-construction processes needed for durable learning—such as planning, reasoning, and structuring problems [2]. Learners may instead delegate these learning-relevant cognitive and regulatory work to the tool without an immediate or visible cost to task completion [3]. A central question for AI-supported learning is therefore whether learners can retain responsibility for these cognitive and regulatory processes through which learning occurs, while benefiting from the assistance these systems provide.

Learners may instead delegate these learning-relevant cognitive and regulatory work to the tool without an immediate or visible cost to task completion [3]. A central question for AI-supported learning is therefore whether learners can retain responsibility for these cognitive and regulatory processes through which learning occurs, while benefiting from the assistance these systems provide.

This concern is increasingly discussed in terms of learner agency: whether learners remain able to direct and take responsibility for their own learning when working with AI [3]. Agency, however, is a broad and context-dependent construct that has been conceptualized as encompassing regulatory and reflective abilities, agentic actions such as selective and responsible engagement, and motivational characteristics such as self-efficacy and persistence [4]. This breadth makes agency an important overarching concern, but difficult to investigate empirically. This challenge is even more pronounced in complex learning environments such as GenAI-supported ones where the system itself can reshape several components of learners’ agency [5].

This breadth makes agency an important overarching concern, but difficult to investigate empirically. This challenge is even more pronounced in complex learning environments such as GenAI-supported ones where the system itself can reshape several components of learners’ agency [5].

We therefore focus on one specific epistemic dimension of learner agency, which we term epistemic proactivity: the extent to which learners retain responsibility for initiating, monitoring, advancing, and evaluating their own knowledge-building processes with AI [6, 7]. Epistemic proactivity therefore distinguishes initiating a learning trajectory from primarily reacting within one proposed by the system [8]. In doing so, it also distinguishes behavioral from epistemic engagement during AI-supported learning: a learner may remain behaviorally agentic—asking questions, evaluating suggestions—while becoming epistemically reactive if the AI is increasingly determining what should be explored next, and how the interaction should proceed [9, 10]. We examine this dimension through self-regulated learning (SRL) as the overarching regulatory framework, complemented by help-seeking strategies and epistemic vigilance as finer-grained accounts of what learners ask AI to contribute and how they evaluate its contributions.

In doing so, it also distinguishes behavioral from epistemic engagement during AI-supported learning: a learner may remain behaviorally agentic—asking questions, evaluating suggestions—while becoming epistemically reactive if the AI is increasingly determining what should be explored next, and how the interaction should proceed [9, 10]. We examine this dimension through self-regulated learning (SRL) as the overarching regulatory framework, complemented by help-seeking strategies and epistemic vigilance as finer-grained accounts of what learners ask AI to contribute and how they evaluate its contributions.

Importantly, epistemic proactivity is unlikely to remain fixed during a learning process: it may shift as task demands, learners’ resources, and experience with the tool evolve [11]. Studying it therefore means asking how it develops across an interaction, not only how often particular behaviors occur. However, such examinations are still missing in literature; and, specifically, two main gaps remain. First, process-level analysis of student–AI interactions is still limited for secondary-school students compared with university populations, despite their growing use of these systems [1, 12]. Second, little is known about whether such interaction dynamics relate to learning beyond the performance achieved while AI assistance is available. This question is especially relevant during adolescence, when capacities required for an epistemically-active use of AI are still developing [13]. Against this background, we studied 112 Grade-9 students using a general-purpose LLM during an open-ended mathematical-modeling activity between a pre-test and post-test completed without AI. We address two questions: to what extent do students remain epistemically proactive while learning with AI, and whether the way epistemic proactivity develops over time is associated with what they can subsequently do without AI. We operationalize epistemic proactivity in conversational traces through SRL, complemented by finer-grained analyses of help-seeking strategies and epistemic vigilance. By answering these questions, we aim to clarify when AI-supported interaction reflects productive learning rather than successful performance with assistance, and to inform the design of scaffolds for adolescent learners.

papers.title: A First-Order Phase Transition in Spin-Imbalanced BCS Theory of Superconductivity
papers.abstract: We study a translation-invariant BCS functional of superconductivity for a system of spin-$1/2$ fermions with spin-dependent chemical potentials, $\mu_+\neq\mu_-$. Numerical work of Caldas and Mota and analytical work of Freiji, Hainzl, and Seiringer has suggested an unusual first-order phase transition in spin-imbalanced BCS models, in which the normal state becomes globally unstable while remaining locally stable. Here, we prove that a first-order phase transition occurs in such spin-imbalanced BCS functionals. For each sufficiently small fixed spin imbalance and sufficiently low temperature, there is a coexistence coupling $\lambda_{\mathrm{fo}}$ strictly below the linear-stability threshold $\lambda_{\mathrm{lin}}$ of the normal state at which the Cooper pair density exhibits a nonzero jump and the minimized energy has a kink. The methodological insight is a coercivity estimate obtained by decomposing the BCS energy minimization into two parts, where the ``inner'' problem minimizes over the one-particle density matrices at fixed pairing and can be exactly solved by a Legendre--Fenchel transform.

papers.intro:
In the mathematical analysis of the BCS functional of superconductivity, a central role is played by the normal state and its stability. The normal state minimizes the BCS functional among states with zero pairing density. If it is globally unstable, a minimizer with non-zero pairing exists and the physical system becomes superconducting. The onset of superconductivity as the temperature is varied is commonly governed by a second-order phase transition in which the pairing density of competing minimizers to the normal state vanishes continuously at the critical temperature. Hence, the linear stability criterion (positive definite Hessian operator) of the normal state plays a crucial role in describing the second-order phase transition. In particular, in the translation-invariant spin-balanced model, linear stability characterizes the critical temperature [19, Theorem 1]. The Hessian can become a subtle operator in itself, especially in the presence of external fields [14] and it plays a central role in the celebrated rigorous derivation of Ginzburg–Landau (GL) theory near the critical temperature [13]. See [22] for a survey of the mathematical properties of the BCS functional of superconductivity. In domains with boundary, a rigorous derivation of GL theory remains open. An exception is at zero temperature, where [16] derived an effective Gross-Pitaevskii functional for domains with boundary in the Bose–Einstein condensation regime. For a derivation of GL theory near the superconducting transition temperature, a key issue is to establish its second-order nature in the presence of a boundary. This question is complicated by the possibility of boundary superconductivity [20, 29, 30, 31]. This motivates the broader need to develop new tools to analyze the nature of different phase transitions in BCS models.

In particular, line III in Figure 2 of [7] records a numerical prediction for the occurrence of this phase transition in a spin-imbalanced BCS functional with delta interaction. In this paper, we rigorously confirm that such a first-order phase transition occurs for a broad class of interaction potentials in the regime of small spin imbalance and low temperature. The precise statement of our main result can be found in Theorem 2.2 below. In the mathematical physics literature, the spin-imbalanced BCS functional was studied by Freiji, Hainzl, and Seiringer [17]. The techniques of [17], in particular, gave a spectral characterization of the existence theory of solutions to the nonlinear gap equation (i.e., of critical points of the BCS free energy functional) with non-zero pairing. The absence of critical points can then be used to exclude the possibility of superconductivity in suitable parameter regimes. However, these techniques are less suited to identify situations in which the normal state is locally stable but globally unstable — or when the normal state is not the unique minimizer, which is the case at a first-order phase transition where a normal and superconducting minimizer coexist.

papers.title: Grammar Control for Language Learning with Sequential Monte Carlo and Small Language Models
papers.abstract: Second language learners benefit from exposure to level-appropriate grammar in interactive language use. While prompted frontier language models can usually produce target grammar structures, less resource-intensive models that can be run on device often fail in this task. We use sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to steer dialogue turn generation in small lan- language models toward target grammar constructions from an expert-developed pedagogical resource. With a minimal set of hand-coded potential functions, SMC achieves near-perfect coverage of target grammar, enabling small models to outperform state-of-the-art results from models 140 times larger. We also use code synthesis with frontier models to generate new potentials, showing that our method scales to hundreds of target grammar skills with no need for additional training or supervised data.

papers.intro:
A key task in second language pedagogy is exposing language learners to level-appropriate target grammatical structures in diverse natural contexts. For example, a learner who speaks English at an advanced beginner level (e.g., level A2 in CEFR, the Common European Framework of Reference) should be able to understand and use the verb enjoy followed by a verb in its gerund (-ing) form (e.g., enjoy swimming, enjoy cooking). A capable English-language instructor can use this target construction in dialogue (e.g., I enjoy cycling. What exercises do you enjoy?), encouraging learners to practice and develop this grammatical skill—that is, producing grammatical constructions (e.g., enjoy swimming) rather than ungrammatical word sequences (e.g., enjoy to swim). We would like language models to provide similar interactive support for learners. Whether a model can do so reliably, however, depends heavily on its scale. Frontier language models can usually produce learner-appropriate grammatical constructions through prompting, but smaller, less resource-intensive models often fail to reliably produce grammar targets (Sun et al., 2023; Ribeiro-Flucht et al., 2025). Bridging this gap could make efficient, on-device language learning tools more feasible, reducing costs and reliance on cloud-based frontier-model APIs while broadening access to learning applications.

This problem is naturally formulated as a constrained generation task: Given some set of level-appropriate grammar skills, we want to constrain language model generations such that they contain the target constructions. Pedagogical resources such as the English Grammar Profile (O’Keeffe and Mark, 2017) identify a range of grammatical targets at specific proficiency levels. Previous research has investigated grammar control via prompting, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and classifier-based constrained decoding, but none have yet achieved reliable elicitation of target constructions from small language models (Okano et al., 2023; Glandorf and Meurers, 2024; Glandorf et al., 2025).

In this work, we specify potential functions via the GenLM Control library,11 1 genlm.org/genlm-control using short, interpretable, human-readable programs to steer generation. For example, a potential function for the enjoy + gerund construction might parse the candidate sentence and return a high score if and only if the verb enjoy is followed by a verb gerund, excluding superficially similar sequences (e.g., enjoy something). Because potential functions can be implemented as explicit programs, they can be flexibly developed, modified, and composed. Programmers can directly write functions to specify target grammar constructions, which we do in Experiment 1. Such programs can also be synthesized by large language models, and refined through iterative generation and testing, a technique known as self-steering SMC (Grand et al., 2025); we demonstrate that this approach can scale to cover tens (Experiment 2) or hundreds (Experiment 3) of targets. In all cases, potential functions can be inspected and refined by domain experts (e.g., instructors or curriculum designers), allowing flexible adaptation for specific pedagogical goals.

papers.title: VERITAS Limits on Dark Matter Annihilation in the Galactic Center Halo
papers.abstract: Well-motivated models of particle dark matter predict its self-annihilation into Standard Model end states, which may be detected by particle detectors or telescopes. We conduct an indirect dark matter search using gamma rays detected by the VERITAS telescope from within $2^\circ$ of the Galactic Center. A template-based approach is used for background estimation, increasing our sensitivity to sources of gamma-ray emission with spatial extents comparable to the $3.5^\circ$ VERITAS field of view. The analysis benefits from data taken exclusively at large zenith angles, which results in an increased effective area at energies above ~1 TeV, compared to small zenith angle observations. No significant gamma-ray signal is observed in the search region, resulting in upper limits on the end-state-dependent dark matter annihilation cross sections. Cross sections as low as $\langle \sigma_\text{ann} v\rangle = 1.77\times 10^{-25} \text{ cm}^3 \text{ s}^{-1}$ are excluded at 95% confidence assuming complete annihilation into $\tau^+ \tau^-$, an Einasto profile, and a dark matter mass of 1 TeV.

Our cosmological paradigm includes a dark matter component constituting approximately 84% of the Universe’s matter density [38]. Dark matter, in addition to being a necessary ingredient in most cosmological models, simultaneously resolves numerous other astrophysical anomalies. However, dark matter has to date eluded explanation from any Standard Model particle or astrophysical source. Its nature, particle or otherwise, remains unknown.

Theoretically-appealing candidates, such as weakly-interacting massive particles (WIMPs), predict the self-annihilation of dark matter into Standard Model end states—the observation of which would constitute an indirect detection of dark matter particles (e.g. Ref. [27]). Among the most promising avenues of indirect detection are gamma-ray searches at the Galactic Center, where the dark matter density in our Galaxy is expected to peak [13]. At GeV energies, such searches have already revealed the puzzling Galactic Center excess [21, 26, 7], whose dark-matter interpretation is complicated by its morphology and astrophysical foregrounds (e.g. Refs. [32, 34, 42]), while observations at TeV energies have placed the most stringent constraints on a variety of dark matter models [22, 1, 4].

[32, 34, 42]), while observations at TeV energies have placed the most stringent constraints on a variety of dark matter models [22, 1, 4].

Such dark matter searches must contend with the presence of a variety of astrophysical sources within a few degrees of the Galactic Center. Even at TeV energies, sources of emission are believed to include supernova remnants, diffuse emission from cosmic-ray interactions with gas, and a source in the direction of the supermassive black hole designated Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) [8]. Ground-based gamma-ray observations additionally face a background due to cosmic-ray interactions with the atmosphere. These effects complicate the search for a gamma-ray signal from the Milky Way’s dark matter halo, whose brightest region may be fairly spatially extended, in principle. The present work develops a methodology that can handle these properties, by means of background templates. This methodology is well-suited for the analysis of extended sources, even in the presence of other gamma-ray sources in the same field of view.

papers.title: Bulk gap stability and spectral flow for fermions with weak long-range interactions
papers.abstract:
We prove that weak long-range many-body interactions preserve the bulk gap of a free fermion system and that a quasi-local spectral flow transports the free ground state to ground states of the interacting system. Let $\Phi_h$ be a free fermionic interaction, possibly including pairing terms, whose infinite-volume Majorana coefficient operator $h$ has no spectrum in $(-g,g)$, and let $\mathcal V$ be an even self-adjoint many-body interaction. For sufficiently small $|\lambda|$, we construct pure ground states $\omega_{\lambda}$ of the interacting bulk system $\Phi_{\lambda}=\Phi_h+\lambda\mathcal V$ and quasi-local automorphisms $\beta_{0,\lambda}$ such that $\omega_{\lambda}=\omega_0\circ\beta_{0,\lambda}$, where $\omega_0$ is the free ground state of $\Phi_h$. Each $\omega_\lambda$ has a GNS Hamiltonian with gap at least $g-C_*|\lambda| \|\mathcal V\|_*$, where $\|\cdot\|_*$ is the relevant interaction norm.

papers.title: Local determination of low-energy states in gapped fermion systems with weak long-range interactions
papers.abstract:
We consider bulk-gapped fermion systems whose infinite-volume bulk is obtained by adding sufficiently weak even many-body interactions to a free Hamiltonian with spectral gap $g>0$, allowing polynomial spatial decay of both parts. We prove quantitative local determination of low-energy states: whenever another interaction agrees with the bulk interaction inside a finite or infinite region $U$, with bulk terms crossing its boundary unchanged or removed, all its states with excitation energies in $[0,3g/4]$ have local expectations close to those of the bulk ground state deep inside $U$. The error decays with the distance to the complement of $U$, independently of the interaction terms supported outside $U$ and of the chosen low-energy state.
  Quantitative local determination has strong consequences. (i) The bulk interaction has a unique algebraic ground state. (ii) A strong "local perturbations perturb locally" (LPPL) principle holds: arbitrary distant defects change local ground-state expectations only by a spatially decaying error. (iii) Low-energy excitations in finite samples remain localized near the boundary for all times, up to spatially decaying tails, uniformly over arbitrary even boundary terms. (iv) Correlations from deep inside $U$ to outside $U$ are small, with quantitative bounds in terms of spatial separation and distance to $U^c$.
  To prove local determination of low-energy states, we combine quasi-adiabatic transport of the free ground state to the interacting bulk ground state with a new condition, local excitation detectability (LED). A companion paper establishes gap stability and constructs the transport for weak interactions, while we prove LED at sufficiently weak coupling. The abstract theorem is nonperturbative and applies whenever the transport and LED hypotheses hold.

Introducing a boundary or a strong defect into a bulk-gapped material like a topological insulator can create excitations at arbitrarily small energies [34]. We prove that, for fermion systems obtained by adding sufficiently weak many-body interactions to a gapped free system, these excitations have only a spatially decaying influence on the interior. Every state in a fixed window above the modified ground energy has local expectations close to those of the unmodified bulk ground state deep inside any region UU where the terms supported in UU are unchanged and each bulk term crossing its boundary is unchanged or removed. The bounds are independent of the strength, extent, and geometry of the exterior changes and remain valid throughout the evolution of every state in the window. We call this property quantitative local determination of low-energy states and establish it for short- and long-range many-body interactions.

papers.title: Quantifying the Relay-Coverage Trade-off in Mobile Multihop Flooding
papers.abstract: Network-wide flooding in mobile multihop networks selects relays from locally maintained topology information. Mobility makes this information outdated, leaving two basic responses: add redundant relays or refresh the topology and re-select relays more frequently. How these mechanisms trade reliability for overhead, however, is not well quantified. We quantify this trade-off on a public trace of 157 vehicles using Optimized Link State Routing version 2 (OLSRv2) and exact minimum-cost relay sets. Twofold coverage increases median relay-cover lifetime by only 2.3x, rather than about an order of magnitude as predicted by an independent-hazard model. The limitation is structural: 43.6 % of two-hop neighbours have only one possible relay, and newly appearing neighbours invalidate existing covers. Moreover, the delivery gain of a second relay falls from 0.061 to 0.016 when relay selection uses instantaneous link state, showing that redundancy mainly compensates for outdated topology information. Relay coverage and topology refresh therefore form a measurable redundancy-freshness trade-off rather than independent robustness mechanisms. In our trace, twofold coverage has lower overhead below about 100 bit/s of application flooding per node, whereas fresher topology information has lower overhead above it. This makes relay redundancy a load-dependent design choice rather than a fixed heuristic robustness setting.

Network-wide broadcast supports route discovery and control dissemination in infrastructureless wireless networks, but naive flooding wastes capacity through redundant transmissions and collisions [1]. Relay-based schemes instead select one-hop neighbours that collectively reach the two-hop neighbourhood, as in Optimized Link State Routing (OLSR)/OLSR version 2 (OLSRv2) [2, 3, 4], Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) [5], and dominating-set broadcast [6]. Mobility creates a common failure mode: the topology changes while the local information used to choose relays ages.

A protocol can tolerate this mismatch in two ways. It can add relay redundancy, spending forwarding capacity so that outdated choices remain useful, or maintain a fresher topology view, spending control capacity so obsolete choices are replaced sooner. OLSR exposes the former through MPR_COVERAGE and explicitly suggests increasing coverage under mobility [3, §16]. Yet the exchange between these mechanisms, how much robustness a second relay buys, why, and when that cost is preferable to fresher topology information, has not been quantified on a realistic mobility trace (Section II).

papers.title: Inertial Steering and Motion Prediction of Tracked Vehicles on Low-Adherence Surfaces
papers.abstract: Tracked vehicles are widely used in off-road applications, but their conventional motion models often rely on no-slip assumptions that become inaccurate on low-adherence surfaces. Rather than treating inertial effects arising from slip as a disturbance to be minimized, this work investigates how inertial effects arising from a moving mass can be deliberately exploited for steering on low-friction surfaces. A dynamic model for an articulated tracked vehicle with a passive trailer is developed, allowing inertial effects from trailer motion to be captured. The approach is experimentally evaluated on ice, where our dynamic model outperforms the kinematic baseline. We also propose a mixed dynamic-kinematic model to adapt predictions to both surface and situation by exploiting predictions from both methods. Finally, we demonstrate inertial steering on a mono-track vehicle without a conventional steering mechanism, showing that controlled movements of an internal mass can generate turning motion on ice. The resulting behavior can be predicted using the proposed dynamic model by representing the internal mass as a frictionless trailer, revealing the analogous dynamics between the two configurations. These results demonstrate the feasibility of inertial steering as an alternative steering mechanism for tracked vehicles operating in low-adherence environments.

In the past, slip has been mainly treated as an unknown disturbance to be estimated, compensated, or minimized, rather than as a locomotion mechanism to be deliberately exploited [8]. One estimation approach augments classical kinematic models with slip parameters identified either online or from prior terrain characterization [33, 10]. In control publications, these models are commonly integrated into MPC (MPC) to regulate slip as ground adherence changes [29]. The resulting behavior is safe but conservative, as the vehicle slows down precisely where friction saturates, limiting potential mobility. Yet for certain robots, losing ground adherence also opens the opportunity for an alternative steering mechanism, with articulated vehicles serving as a representative example. As illustrated in Fig. 1 b), when reorienting its trailer, an articulated vehicle also moves a mass mm relative to its towing body, which generates an inertial steering wrench. On ice, as the kinematic model loses fidelity, the trailer can accelerate and move faster, increasing its inertial contribution to steering. Inertial steering then appears as a complementary mechanism to maintain or even increase mobility on low-friction surfaces.

papers.title: Inferring cell property distributions from high-throughput measurement data with cell-to-cell variability
papers.abstract: High-throughput measurements of cell populations produce broad distributions of observables due to inherent cell-to-cell variability. While these distributions contain valuable biological information, extracting the underlying distributions of cellular properties remains challenging. We introduce the likelihood functional, a statistical framework that infers cell property distributions by combining experimental data with deterministic computational models. The method first evaluates the model on a discrete parameter grid. Optimization of the likelihood functional is then possible without repeated model evaluations and yields best-fit property distributions which enable the direct prediction of observable distributions for comparison with experiments. As a demonstration, we apply the framework to real-time deformability cytometry data and infer cytosol and membrane viscosity distributions of human red blood cells.

papers.title: Optimal self-orthogonal binary linear codes
papers.abstract: We complete the determination of the minimum possible length of eight-dimensional binary self-orthogonal codes with given minimum distance. For dimension nine we give exact values and bounds for minimum distance at most $64$. By exploiting the geometric reformulation of linear codes as multisets of points, we fully redo the classification for dimension at most seven in a simplified and computer-free manner. As a by-product we prove the non-existence of $[93,9,44]_2$ codes and show several divisibility results for putative optimal nine-dimensional binary codes.

papers.title: Emergence of Zonal Flows in an Imbalanced Point-Vortex System
papers.abstract: Motivated by experiments on rotating Bose-Einstein condensates, we investigate the statistical mechanics and the non-equilibrium dynamics of an imbalanced gas of oppositely signed Onsager point vortices confined in a disk. To model external forcing and dissipation, we supplement their Hamiltonian dynamics with an annihilation-reinjection (AR) mechanism that preserves the imbalance: oppositely signed vortices are annihilated when they approach closer than a distance representing the healing length, and are subsequently reintroduced into the domain at random locations. At positive energies, the system self-organizes into a large-scale coherent dipole at low imbalance and into a zonal flow at higher imbalance. While AR breaks energy and angular momentum conservation, we argue that the vortex gas evolves quasi-adiabatically through the equilibrium phase space. We capture the topological transition between dipolar and zonal flows both from a statistical and a hydrodynamical perspective. In particular, the bifurcation reflects a non-trivial equilibrium diagram in terms of energy $e$, angular momentum $\mu$, and vortex imbalance $\eta$. We characterize this phase diagram in the "strong mixing'' regime studied by linearizing the Joyce-Montgomery mean-field theory about the weakly non-uniform state. We show that the linear theory is surprisingly relevant for the numerical simulations with AR and suggest that the selection between the dipolar and the zonal configurations in the $(e,\mu,\eta)$ phase space is driven by a hydrodynamical shear instability.

papers.intro:
The statistical behavior of a gas of hydrodynamic point vortices confined to a bounded two-dimensional (2D) domain is a classical problem in hydrodynamics [8, 30, 27]. It historically connects to the problem of classical 2D turbulence [13], and also serves as a fundamental model for quantized vortices in superfluids [32, 33, 47, 20, 41]. Experimentally, vortex gases can be realized in trapped Bose-Einstein condensates (BEC), where quantized vortices are nucleated by external excitations or rotation [10]. Recent advances in experimental techniques now enable the confinement of cold atoms in a variety of geometries [39, 14, 23, 15], including highly oblate and bubble-shaped traps realizing quasi-2D setups [19, 7]. In such systems, vortex populations need not be neutral: excitation protocols may introduce rotation and produce states with unequal numbers of vortices and antivortices, leading to a finite net circulation. Understanding how this imbalance modifies the statistical organization of vortex gases is the central motivation of the present work.

papers.title: On the variational characterization of a laminated core model in ferromagnetic materials
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of iron losses in transformers, electric motors, and generators at elevated frequencies requires accounting for eddy currents in laminated magnetic cores during field simulation. We study local material models for these lamination losses that resolve the inhomogeneous magnetic-field distribution across the thickness of the respective steel sheets via one-dimensional diffusion equations. This allows to incorporate skin-effect and eddy-current losses in the laminations at each material point of a two- or three-dimensional magnetic-field simulation. The macroscopic material response is described implicitly through a minimization problem involving a set of internal variables which encode the load history and current state of the material. The variational structure of these problems allows us to prove well-posedness, to include anisotropy and hysteresis, and to develop efficient globally convergent solvers for the evaluation of the macroscopic material response. The proposed framework thus allows to efficiently and reliably predict magnetic behaviour of laminated core material over a wide frequency range and is well-suited for integration into nonlinear magnetic field solvers.

papers.intro:
The design and optimization of electromagnetic devices requires accurate simulation of the governing magnetic-field problems. In transformers, electric motors, and generators, an appropriate representation of the nonlinear behaviour of magnetic core materials is particularly important, since these devices are commonly designed for operation at high power densities. At the fundamental operation frequencies, eddy-current losses can be largely suppressed by the use of laminated electrical steel. Pulse-width-modulated excitation by modern power converters, local field inhomogeneities, parasitic effects, or time-varying and stochastic load conditions, however, give rise to higher-frequency field components. The resulting eddy currents within individual laminations produce reaction fields which may substantially affect the local magnetic-field distribution and the associated losses. Appropriate simulation of these eddy currents and their coupling with saturation, hysteresis, and anisotropy of magnetic materials remains a computational challenge [1].

papers.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
papers.abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.
papers.intro:
Benchmarks measuring the mathematical capabilities of AI systems are getting saturated at an accelerating pace. School-level problem sets such as GSM8K and MATH (Cobbe et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2021) were followed by university-level benchmarks, such as U-Math and ASyMOB (Chernyshev et al., 2025; Shalyt et al., 2025), and math olympiad questions (Zheng et al., 2022; He et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025). The frontier of LLM evaluation is now shifting towards research-level mathematics (Glazer et al., 2025; Phan et al., 2026; Abouzaid et al., 2026; Peyronnet et al., 2026). Meaningful assessment at this level requires a rare combination: problems at the research frontier whose solutions are unpublished to avoid training-data contamination - but are known privately.

In this work, we present the results of the Ramanujan Challenge for AI (Shalyt et al., 2026), a collection of ten research-level numerically verifiable number theory problems. Of these, 8 were proved by the authors but unpublished, and 2 are open conjectures. The collection was released as a benchmark for AI-assisted proving. Our analysis shows that the submissions which were most successful at producing correct natural language proofs used models from the Claude and GPT families, while such proofs from submissions combining Lean with CAS outperformed those that relied on any single tool, suggesting benefits from diversified supporting evidence.

In this work, we present the results of the Ramanujan Challenge for AI (Shalyt et al., 2026), a collection of ten research-level numerically verifiable number theory problems. Of these, 8 were proved by the authors but unpublished, and 2 are open conjectures. The collection was released as a benchmark for AI-assisted proving. Our analysis shows that the submissions which were most successful at producing correct natural language proofs used models from the Claude and GPT families, while such proofs from submissions combining Lean with CAS outperformed those that relied on any single tool, suggesting benefits from diversified supporting evidence.

Notably, some of the complete proofs were submitted by amateur mathematicians, and one of the open conjectures had multiple correct proofs submitted, showing the potential of advanced AI to lower the barrier of entry to parts of mathematical research. Submitters to the challenge, who obtained correct solutions include a person with no higher mathematical education and whose solution to one of the challenge problems was found to be simpler than the original solution from the authors. They also include young independent researchers with no mathematical training, one of whom solved a famous open mathematical problem prior to their participation in the challenge, and a high-school student who achieved significant results towards proving one of the challenge conjectures. The use of AI thus allows people accross broader backgrounds to access and advance research-level mathematics, democratizing mathematics and opening the door to cross-field research and contributions.

Obtaining the results required addressing a second challenge: evaluating large quantities of complex mathematical proof candidates. The recent boom in AI-assisted mathematics (Alon et al., 2026; Feng et al., 2026; Ju et al., 2026), while producing some incredible results (OpenAI, 2026; Alpöge, 2026), created an avalanche of mathematical claims – making this problem widespread beyond benchmarks. The Ramanujan Challenge illustrates this scale: participants sent a total of 228 submissions, containing a total of 4802 pages of natural language mathematical proofs and 1,079,380 lines of code across Lean, Python, Mathematica and Sage. Recent mathematical benchmarks approach automated validation in different ways: fully relying on a large language model (LLM) as a judge (Zhang et al., 2025), using an LLM to check equivalence against a known ground truth (Peyronnet et al., 2026), or using deterministic code to verify LLM-generated answers (Shalyt et al., 2025). Other benchmarks, such as IMO-GradingBench and μ\mu-Math (Luong et al., 2025; Chernyshev et al., 2025), evaluate LLMs as judges of mathematical proofs and solutions, showing the difficulty of achieving high agreement with expert assessments.

In this paper, we present a novel AI-assisted pipeline, depicted in Figure 1, for the purpose of large scale validation of complex multi-format proofs, which include natural language, CAS code, and Lean formalizations. We assess the Ramanujan Challenge submissions, comparing verdicts across three evaluation methods: our pipeline with and without a human expert in the loop, and a baseline LLM-as-a-judge. Using the evaluation pipeline reduces false positive grading by a factor of 4 for natural language proofs and 11.5 for CAS/Lean code, and increases agreement with human evaluation of the code from 46% to 58%, relative to a baseline of the same LLM without the pipeline.

papers.title: Model Theory of Johnson Graphs
papers.abstract:
A \emph{Johnson graph} $J(n,k)$ is a graph whose vertices are the $k$-element subsets of an underlying set of size $n$ where two vertices are adjacent if they intersect in a subset of size $k-1$. We extend the definition to allow infinite parameters and we study a natural limit theory $T_{\mathcal{J}}$ of Johnson graphs. We show that $T_{\mathcal{J}}$ is complete and we give an axiomatisation of $T_{\mathcal{J}}$, from which we obtain a complete description of the models of $T_{\mathcal{J}}$.
  We use this to show tameness properties of $T_{\mathcal{J}}$, namely that $T_{\mathcal{J}}$ is $\omega$-stable of Morley rank $\omega$, but not monadically dependent. In particular it follows that the class of all finite Johnson graphs is stable, and therefore dependent but not monadically dependent.
papers.intro:
Johnson graphs are an easily-described 22-parameter family of graphs with very strong symmetry and regularity properties. The goal in this paper is to describe, from the viewpoint of model theory, the first order logic of these graphs as both parameters grow.

A Johnson graph, J⁡(n,k)J(n,k) is a graph whose vertices can be identified with the kk-element subsets of an set of size nn with two vertices adjacent if they intersect in a subset of size k−1k-1. We refer to the set of size nn as the underlying set of the Johnson graph. It is immediate that the symmetric group Sym⁡(n)\operatorname{Sym}(n) on the underlying set acts as a group of automorphisms of the Johnson graph, and in fact if n>2​kn>2k then Sym⁡(n)\operatorname{Sym}(n) is the full automorphism group [9]. As a result, Johnson graphs are the most easily described non-trivial examples of distance-transitive graphs, that is, graphs whose automorphism group is transitive on the set of ordered pairs of vertices at any given distance. Johnson graphs have been extensively explored from the viewpoint of graph theory and permutation group theory, but little from that of model theory. In [2] the VC-dimension and the VC-density of the edge relation on Johnson graphs are studied. It is there shown that on the class of all finite Johnson graphs the edge relation has VC-dimension 44 and VC-density 22.

papers.title: A-RSI: Adaptive Task Refresh for Zero-Data Multimodal Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires models not only to acquire useful training experience, but also to decide when their current experience has ceased to be useful. Existing methods often focus on what experience to generate next, while paying less attention to when fresh experience should be introduced. Many also construct training targets through self-consistency or majority voting, making supervision depend on the model's own uncertain predictions. We address these two questions separately: training dynamics determine when to acquire new experience, while the answers to new tasks remain independently checkable. A-RSI monitors reward variation and accuracy in training logs to refresh a task pool when its learning signal declines, without consulting validation or test scores. A static library of model-authored programs produces multimodal questions and derives their reference answers; we specify the task-generation contract, automatically verify chosen properties of the reward and refresh rules, and separately audit the generated answers. The training loop uses no external training examples or human-written answer labels. On the primary eleven-benchmark suite, A-RSI raises the performance average from 57.77 to 61.05 with 800 fresh tasks.

papers.title: Observation of light-induced topological state in graphene
papers.abstract: Driving quantum materials with light can reshape not only their electronic band structures but also the geometry of their electronic wavefunctions. In graphene, circularly polarized light is predicted to open gaps at the Dirac points and induce a pseudospin texture and Berry curvature characteristic of the Haldane model, realizing a Floquet Chern insulator. Transport and all-optical measurements have provided evidence for a light-induced anomalous Hall response, but cannot resolve the underlying electronic states in both energy and momentum space. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy has revealed Floquet-Bloch sidebands and hybridization gaps at crossings between Floquet bands. However, these experiments used linearly polarized driving, which preserves time-reversal symmetry and thus does not induce a topological phase. Here, we combine circular-dichroic time-resolved extreme-ultraviolet momentum microscopy with ab initio theory to investigate graphene driven by circularly polarized light. We observe a pump-induced photoemission circular dichroism near the Dirac point that reverses sign with pump helicity and across the Dirac energy, in agreement with our calculations. These results link the measured dichroic response to the light-induced pseudospin texture and its associated Berry curvature, providing spectroscopic evidence for the Floquet-engineered topological insulating state in graphene.

papers.title: Resolving Photochemical Reaction Pathways Using Field-Induced Surface Hopping Simulation of fs-EUV-TRPES: The Case of Furan
papers.abstract: Recent advances in femtosecond extreme ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy have enabled insight into photochemistry in gases, condensed phases, and at interfaces. Assigning spectral features to reaction pathways requires theoretical predictions connecting nonadiabatic dynamics to measured observables. Here, we present a general approach for resolving photochemical reaction pathways by combining field-induced surface hopping with explicit pulse excitation, RMS-CASPT2, and simulations of time-resolved photoelectron spectra. The pump field prepares the excited-state ensemble under experimental conditions, while the multireference treatment describes excited states, conical intersections, and bond-breaking coordinates. Mapping trajectories onto photoelectron signals, supported by a systematic analysis of photoionization approximations, enables comparison with experiment. We apply this approach to furan excited by a 200 nm, 10 fs pulse. Among trajectories returning to the ground state, approximately 87 % hop near the ring-puckering conical intersection and 13 % near the ring-opening intersection. Subsequent ground-state vibrational energy redistribution nevertheless populates ring-opening structures. Five ground-state products are identified. Simulated spectra reproduce time-dependent electron-binding-energy shifts, characteristic kinks, and bands with predicted photoproduct contributions. Compared with Dyson-norm-based intensities, plane- and Coulomb-wave continuum functions improve the early-time shape of the lowest binding energy signal and show that photoelectron anisotropy is more sensitive to the continuum approximation than the angle-integrated spectrum. More generally, these findings demonstrate how explicit-pulse nonadiabatic dynamics and dynamically correlated multireference electronic structure can resolve competing photochemical reaction pathways through simulated fs-EUV-TRPES.
