papers.title: Light-induced chiral altermagnets from conventional antiferromagnets
papers.abstract: Altermagnets combine compensated collinear magnetic order with momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting, offering new opportunities for spintronic applications. Here, we propose a route to optically induce altermagnetism through coherent lattice control. Using symmetry analysis, we identify phonon distortions that lift the spin degeneracy of conventional antiferromagnets while preserving the rotational symmetries connecting opposite-spin sublattices. Among these, geometric chiral phonons provide a particularly appealing pathway, linking the emergence of altermagnetism to structural chirality. Taking Fe$_2$TeO$_6$ as a prototype, we demonstrate that a linearly polarized mid-infrared pulse can drive a structural instability through negative biquadratic coupling between an infrared-active phonon and an optically silent, symmetry-breaking mode. First-principles-based lattice dynamics reveal the emergence of a transient chiral distortion, while electronic-structure calculations establish that the light-induced structure exhibits nonrelativistic spin splitting characteristic of altermagnetism. Our results establish a symmetry-guided pathway toward the ultrafast optical control of altermagnetic states through nonlinear phononics.

papers.intro:
Altermagnets have attracted broad attention because they combine spin-split electronic bands with compensated collinear magnetic order [25, 24, 16, 17]. Unlike conventional antiferromagnets, their opposite-spin sublattices are connected by crystallographic rotations rather than by inversion or translation. The resulting spin splitting alternates in sign across the Brillouin zone and persists in the absence of spin-orbit coupling [8, 32, 33, 19]. Altermagnets can support spin-polarized currents and spin-splitter torques [7, 1], as well as an anomalous Hall effect when allowed by magnetic symmetry [23]. These transport properties, together with their compensated magnetization and terahertz spin dynamics, make altermagnets attractive for spintronics [11, 10, 26]. This raises a central question: can a conventional, spin-degenerate antiferromagnet be transformed into an altermagnet dynamically, while preserving its compensated magnetic order?

This raises a central question: can a conventional, spin-degenerate antiferromagnet be transformed into an altermagnet dynamically, while preserving its compensated magnetic order?

Altermagnetic spin splitting depends on both crystal structure and magnetic order, offering a route to control through lattice distortions. Advances in optical lattice control raise the prospect of reversibly inducing this splitting in an initially spin-degenerate antiferromagnet, complementing static structural tuning by strain, pressure, or chemical substitution [15]. Intense mid-infrared and terahertz pulses can resonantly drive infrared-active phonons to large amplitudes, coherently reshaping a crystal on ultrafast timescales [3, 6, 28]. Through nonlinear phononics, the driven mode couples anharmonically to other lattice coordinates, generating transient structural distortions [27, 35]. Such mode-selective lattice control offers a route to dynamically induce altermagnetism by lifting spin degeneracy while preserving compensated collinear magnetic order.

In this work, we combine group-subgroup and spin-symmetry analyses with first-principles modeling of driven lattice dynamics to propose phonon-mediated routes from antiferromagnetism to altermagnetism. We identify odd-parity phonon distortions that lower centrosymmetric parent structures to noncentrosymmetric subgroups while satisfying the spin-symmetry requirements for altermagnetism, and we tabulate representative pathways (Table 1). Among these, geometric chiral phonons [22] are particularly appealing because their distortions also induce structural chirality, yielding two enantiomeric altermagnetic structures. We demonstrate access to such a distortion in Fe2TeO6 through biquadratic nonlinear phonon coupling [12, 9]. In particular we show how an optically driven infrared mode can soften the geometric chiral coordinate and induce a transient structural instability above a driving threshold. Using parameters obtained from density-functional theory, we simulate the lattice response to a mid-infrared pulse and calculate the electronic bands of the distorted structure, revealing the light-induced momentum-dependent nonrelativistic spin splitting characteristic of altermagnetism.

We identify odd-parity phonon distortions that lower centrosymmetric parent structures to noncentrosymmetric subgroups while satisfying the spin-symmetry requirements for altermagnetism, and we tabulate representative pathways (Table 1). Among these, geometric chiral phonons [22] are particularly appealing because their distortions also induce structural chirality, yielding two enantiomeric altermagnetic structures. We demonstrate access to such a distortion in Fe2TeO6 through biquadratic nonlinear phonon coupling [12, 9]. papers.title: The Quine Test: How Much of a Model's Self Survives Its Own Description?
papers.abstract:
Frontier language models express coherent preferences, but behavioral evidence alone cannot say whether these belong to the model or to a character it portrays. Following Hofstadter's view of the self as a self-description, we ask whether a model's description of itself works as a portable specification of its preference profile, a quine test: can the text a model writes about itself regenerate its behavior elsewhere? Ten models from nine labs write self-descriptions; we place each one in the prompt of other models (receivers) and of fresh instances of the author, and measure how closely their choices on a 110-item preference battery match the author's.
  First, the tested native self-descriptions (native: the profile measured under a generic assistant prompt) show no average reconstruction gain across variations in length, framing, wording and prompt placement: on a 0 to 1 fidelity scale where a model's fidelity to a fresh instance of itself is 0.979 and to unrelated models about 0.89, the one-sided 95% upper bound on the pooled gain is below +0.01 in every tested system-prompt condition, and descriptions based on the author's observed choices do no better. Second, the channel itself is strong: explicitly listing the author's answers lets receivers reproduce its profile at fidelity 0.955 to 0.960 across three model grids, within 0.03 of same-model repeatability. Third, self-descriptions written under an explicit preference policy transfer the assigned preferences almost as well as the policy text itself. Fourth, reading its own self-description shifts even the author away from its baseline, modestly more than unrelated prose of the same length.
  For the preferences measured here, native self-descriptions influence behavior without reliably specifying how to reproduce it in another model. We release the pipeline, battery, raw call logs, and 198 model-written descriptions.

papers.title: Electronic-morphological decoupling in mixed-dimensional halide perovskite heterostructures
papers.abstract:
Surface morphology is widely considered an indicator of thin-film quality, with smoother films generally expected to exhibit more uniform optoelectronic properties. Here, we demonstrate that substantial surface evolution does not necessarily lead to increased electronic heterogeneity in mixed-dimensional perovskite heterostructures. We investigate how low-dimensional Ruddlesden-Popper capping layers derived from the sterically hindered 5-tert-butyl-phenanthridinium cation affect the spatial distributions of photoluminescence (PL) characteristics and quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) in 3D perovskites. By combining statistical atomic force microscopy (AFM) analysis with confocal, spatially resolved PL spectroscopy, we correlate surface topography with microscale optoelectronic properties.
  Although capping increases surface roughness and height asymmetry, it does not increase electronic inhomogeneity. Instead, the heterostructures exhibit enhanced PL, reduced non-radiative recombination, and improved spatial uniformity of radiative QFLS compared with pristine 3D films. Under accelerated aging, this contrast becomes more pronounced: pristine films develop substantial spatial fluctuations in emission and QFLS, whereas capped heterostructures largely preserve their optoelectronic homogeneity. These findings indicate that the low-dimensional capping layer suppresses aging-induced optoelectronic disorder, demonstrating that electronic uniformity can be maintained despite morphological irregularity. This decoupling provides a design principle for developing durable, high-performance perovskite photovoltaics.

papers.intro:
Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as one of the most promising next-generation photovoltaic technologies owing to their rapid improvements in power conversion efficiency (PCE), now exceeding 27%, and cost-effective fabrication methods [1]. However, despite these remarkable advancements, a major bottleneck preventing the commercialization of PSCs is their inherent instability. That is primarily attributed to moisture-induced decomposition, ion migration, and phase segregation in mixed-halide compositions [2]. Consequently, extensive research efforts have focused on improving the long-term stability of PSCs through compositional tuning, optimizing device architecture, passivation procedures, and interface engineering [3,4,5,6,7]. For instance, the use of mixed-cation compositions has been shown to suppress phase segregation and improve film crystallinity, leading to more stable PSCs [8,9,10]. Similarly, targeted halide or cation mixing (e.g., Br/I ratio tuning) can effectively enhance the resistance of perovskite films against ion migration and phase segregation [11]. Among the various interface engineering strategies, low-dimensional (LD) perovskite capping layers have emerged as an effective method for improving both stability and optoelectronic properties by suppressing defect-mediated recombination and protecting the underlying bulk perovskite layer.

papers.title: The MARTINI platform II. Tracing r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers with long-lived remnants
papers.abstract: Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers are among the primary sites of the rapid neutron-capture (r-)process. In mergers with long-lived remnants, sustained neutrino irradiation raises the electron fraction of the disc wind ejecta, modifying the resulting nucleosynthesis pattern. Yields from numerical-relativity simulations with accurate neutrino transport are needed to quantify the contribution of BNS mergers to the Galactic production of heavy elements and to interpret kilonova spectra. We present and publicly release tracer trajectories and nucleosynthesis yields for eight BNS mergers forming long-lived neutron star remnants, obtained from general-relativistic simulations with M1 neutrino transport, spanning two equations of state (DD2 and SFHo), and a range of total masses and mass ratios. Passive tracer particles following the dynamical and wind ejecta were post-processed with the nuclear reaction network WinNet up to 1 Gyr. The yields and tracer trajectories are available on the MARTINI platform. At 1 day, the production of light and first-peak elements (He, Ni, Sr, and Y) is similar across models and is primarily enhanced by the neutrino-irradiated disc wind. The yields of heavy nuclei vary by more than one order of magnitude, with unequal-mass binaries producing the largest amounts owing to their more neutron-rich ejecta. Our He yields, particularly in the wind, exceed those of recent studies based on an M0 neutrino scheme, consistent with the stronger neutrino irradiation resulting from an M1 scheme. At 1 Gyr, all models reproduce the second and third solar r-process peaks, but differ in the first peak, the lanthanide region, the mass range between the first and second peaks, and the trans-lead region, reflecting the electron fraction distribution of the ejecta and the dynamical and wind contributions. Two equal-mass models provide a close match to the solar pattern.

papers.intro:
The astrophysical origin of elements heavier than iron (Fe) remains one of the longest-standing problems in nuclear astrophysics (National Research Council, 2003). Approximately half of these nuclei are synthesised through the rapid neutron-capture (rr-) process (Burbidge et al., 1957), which is responsible for the production of the heaviest stable elements in nature, including the actinides 232Th, 235U, and 238U (Thielemann et al., 2017; Cowan et al., 2021, for recent reviews on rr-process, see). Because the rr-process requires extremely neutron-rich conditions, with neutron densities exceeding ∼1026​cm−3\sim 10^{26}\penalty\ {\rm cm^{-3}} to produce elements up to actinides, and a short timescale (∼1​s\sim 1\penalty\ {\rm s}), identifying the astrophysical environments in which it operates has been a major challenge for decades. Several astrophysical sites have been proposed as potential sources of the rr-process, including core-collapse supernovae, magneto-rotational explosions, collapsars, and compact-object mergers. While some of these environments may contribute to a weak rr-process (Wanajo & Ishimaru, 2006; Honda et al., 2006), growing theoretical and observational evidence indicates that BNS (BNS) mergers, and possibly NS (NS)- BH (BH) mergers, are among the primary production sites of the main rr-process responsible for the Solar abundance pattern (Sneden et al., 2008; Rosswog et al., 2018; Horowitz, 2019; Shibata & Hotokezaka, 2019, e.g.).

AT2017gfo exhibited clear signatures of freshly synthesised rr-process material, providing the first direct observational confirmation that BNS mergers produce heavy elements through rr-process (Pian et al., 2017; Smartt et al., 2017, e.g.). Additional observational evidence has further strengthened interest in understanding rr-process nucleosynthesis in the ejecta of compact binary mergers. In particular, the abundance patterns observed in extremely metal-poor stars, including the so-called actinide-boost stars characterised by enhanced thorium (Th) and uranium (U) abundances relative to lighter rr-process elements such as europium (Eu), provide a unique probe of the astrophysical conditions under which the heaviest nuclei are synthesised and raise important questions about the diversity of rr-process sites (Ji & Frebel, 2018; Holmbeck et al., 2018; Holmbeck et al., 2019; Eichler et al., 2019; Kullmann et al., 2023, e.g.). Eichler et al. (2019) showed that the Th/Eu ratio is highly sensitive to both the thermodynamic conditions of the ejecta and the adopted nuclear input, particularly the nuclear mass model, suggesting that the observed diversity of Th/Eu ratios may arise either from different ejecta components within BNS mergers or from multiple astrophysical rr-process sites.

In particular, the abundance patterns observed in extremely metal-poor stars, including the so-called actinide-boost stars characterised by enhanced thorium (Th) and uranium (U) abundances relative to lighter rr-process elements such as europium (Eu), provide a unique probe of the astrophysical conditions under which the heaviest nuclei are synthesised and raise important questions about the diversity of rr-process sites (Ji & Frebel, 2018; Holmbeck et al., 2018; Holmbeck et al., 2019; Eichler et al., 2019; Kullmann et al., 2023, e.g.). Eichler et al. (2019) showed that the Th/Eu ratio is highly sensitive to both the thermodynamic conditions of the ejecta and the adopted nuclear input, particularly the nuclear mass model, suggesting that the observed diversity of Th/Eu ratios may arise either from different ejecta components within BNS mergers or from multiple astrophysical rr-process sites.

In this context, accurate nucleosynthesis predictions from BNS mergers are essential not only to quantify the contribution of these events to the Galactic production of heavy elements, but also to interpret kilonova observations and to assess whether BNS mergers can reproduce the chemical signatures observed in metal-poor and actinide-boost stars.

The nucleosynthesis outcome from a BNS merger depends strongly on the properties of the ejected matter, in particular its electron fraction, entropy, and expansion velocity (Hoffman et al., 1997a; Hoffman et al., 1997b). These properties depend sensitively on several intrinsic binary properties, such as the total mass, mass ratio and spins. Additionally, they vary subject to several microphysics inputs, including the nuclear EOS (EOS) and the treatment of weak interactions, requiring fully general-relativistic simulations coupled to neutrino-radiation hydrodynamics (see Radice et al. 2018; Radice et al. 2020; Perego et al. 2021 for recent reviews). In particular, the lifetime of the merger remnant plays a crucial role in shaping the properties of the remnant accretion disc and the subsequent outflows. Long-lived NS remnants sustain neutrino irradiation over timescales comparable to the disc lifetime, increasing the electron fraction of disc wind ejecta and substantially modifying the resulting nucleosynthesis pattern (Fujibayashi et al., 2020; Kawaguchi et al., 2021; Just et al., 2023; Bernuzzi et al., 2025; Sneppen et al., 2026, e.g.). The predicted ejecta composition is also highly sensitive to the adopted neutrino transport scheme. Specifically, the M1 neutrino transport scheme (Foucart et al., 2016; Radice et al., 2022; Zappa et al., 2023) consistently predicts broader electron fraction distributions in the neutrino-driven wind than the simpler M0 approximation, leading to enhanced production of light and Fe-peak nuclei (Foucart et al., 2016; Vincent et al., 2020; Radice et al., 2022; Radice & Bernuzzi, 2023; Radice & Bernuzzi, 2024; Bernuzzi et al., 2025; Jacobi et al., 2026; Sneppen et al., 2026, e.g.). The angular structure of the neutrino irradiation in M1 simulations and its imprint on the electron fraction was recently quantified by Çokluk et al. (2026) for the set of BNS merger simulations considered in this work. They found that the quadrupole-dominated neutrino radiation field drives the polar material close to the equilibrium electron fraction set by neutrino absorption, with values of about 0.50–0.55 at late times, whereas the equatorial material remains more neutron-rich and below its equilibrium value. The anisotropy of the neutrino flux therefore leaves a robust polar–equatorial imprint on the composition of the ejecta, which is expected to affect both the nucleosynthesis and the kilonova emission.

papers.title: Enhanced image forensics through partial C2PA-based provenance information
papers.abstract: Cryptographically verifiable C2PA-based Content Credentials (CCs) can be attached to freshly acquired or generated digital images but also to already existing ones with no previous provenance information, for instance after processing through trusted C2PA-enabled software tools. The latter case leads to images with so-called partial CCs, which capture only the last operations applied, while prior provenance remains unknown and can be investigated through signal forensics. This paper addresses the forensic analysis of such images, highlighting the opportunity to leverage the partial CCs as additional trusted knowledge to adapt forensic detectors towards the statistical characteristics of the image under analysis and mitigate potential distribution shifts. To this end, a two-step strategy is envisioned: (i) reconstructing the operations applied by the last signer through a structural analysis of the partial CCs; (ii) exploiting the obtained reconstruction to enhance the forensic detector of the analyst through an adaptation process. An empirical analysis on partial CCs produced by commercial C2PA-enabled software tools through different editing operations is carried out, providing evidence on the feasibility of the reconstruction in practical cases. An experimental case study on the forensic task of synthetic image detection is then presented, showing that the proposed strategy can significantly enhance the performance of state-of-the-art detectors on test images that are postprocessed via C2PA-enabled software tools after being generated/acquired.

papers.intro:
Cryptographic media provenance systems rely on cryptographic techniques (such as hashing, digital signatures, public-key infrastructure) to create a tamper-evident record of the origin and edit history of a media object, that can be verified over time by users or systems on the basis of trust mechanisms [11]. Existing approaches include embedding digitally signed metadata into media files, or in an external reference (e.g., a distributed ledger or a dedicated repository) [13] that is robustly linked to the media file (e.g., through watermarking or other identifiers). This creates protected provenance claims that can be disclosed and attributed to a signer, which can be an individual user, an organization, an editing/generation software, or an acquisition device. Due to the consequent security properties, such cryptographic media provenance systems recently attracted a growing interest (especially in industry), as they also align with the directions of recent regulations on the transparent use of generative AI in force over different countries [4][8][12].

In this context, the C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) ecosystem (https://c2pa.org/), supported by a strong industrial consortium, emerges as a prominent approach. While the solution does not represent the only possible design for cryptographic provenance and still entail technical limitations [10], the C2PA framework presents a number of favorable features, including the availability of an evolving open standard [5], available codebases, and a running conformance program, resulting in a growing (yet still globally limited) adoption by editing tools, AI-based generators, acquisition devices.11 1 https://tinyurl.com/c2pa-adoption. In this case, the resulting manifest (and any subsequent extension) conveys the very origin of the media asset and all consequent steps, and we say we have complete CCs. The resulting CCs written by the tool in the exported object will then convey the operations it applied, while the previous digital history remains unknown. Practical use cases include users processing a downloaded image carrying no manifest (potentially AI-generated) through C2PA-conformant software (e.g., Adobe tools, Google Photos) and redistribute it over channels preserving CCs (e.g., Linkedin, Google Messages, and prospectively many others33 3 https://tinyurl.com/prohibited-provenance-removal.).

As is often the case in a number of applications, it may become necessary to investigate the authenticity of those images. If considered reliable, those can be regarded as trusted additional knowledge to be leveraged as contextual information in the forensic analysis. This would enable optimizing detectors towards the statistical properties of the image under analysis, which can be strongly influenced by the last processing steps. However, to make full use of partial CCs, information need to be effectively extracted from the C2PA syntactic structure and incorporated in forensic detectors. papers.title: Mg II Signatures of Frequency Dependent Wave Propagation in Magnetic Elements
papers.abstract: Waves in solar magnetic elements provide a pathway for transporting and dissipating energy in the chromosphere, yet the relationship between photospheric oscillations and chromospheric spectral structure remains incompletely understood. We investigate whether distinct chromospheric Mg II spectral states are linked to different populations of photospheric kink mode oscillations, with particular focus on the role of high frequency (~5mHz) waves. Magnetic elements are tracked in SDO/HMI magnetograms to derive horizontal velocity power spectra, while corresponding Mg II h + k profiles from IRIS are classified using k-means clustering into morphology-based (SHAPE) and intensity-based (ABS) groups. Both classifications exhibit systematic differences in oscillatory behavior. The SHAPE clusters isolate spectral morphologies associated with enhanced high-frequency power, including cases where oscillations in the 4-6 mHz band exceed those in the photospheric p-mode band. In contrast, the ABS clusters show a monotonic increase in the relative contribution of high-frequency oscillations with increasing emission strength and magnetic flux. These results indicate that high-frequency oscillations are both selectively enhanced in specific chromospheric states and systematically strengthened in stronger magnetic environments. This suggests that magnetic structuring plays a key role in regulating both the transmission and the conversion of kink mode wave energy into observable chromospheric signatures.

papers.intro:
Waves are continuously generated in the solar photosphere by convective motions, both directly and through the excitation of global pp‑mode oscillations. During propagation through the magnetized atmosphere, wave behavior is governed by the coupled plasma and magnetic field system, which can in turn be modified by the waves themselves. The photospheric acoustic power is concentrated near 3 mHz, reflecting the dominant contribution from global pp-mode oscillations. At chromospheric heights, however, enhanced acoustic power is frequently observed near 5 mHz (Howard et al., 1968; Lites, 1986; Khomenko and Collados, 2015; Jess et al., 2015, e.g.). This shift toward higher frequencies has often been attributed to atmospheric filtering effects, whereby waves with frequencies above the local acoustic cutoff are able to propagate, while lower-frequency waves become evanescent. The effective cutoff can be modified by factors such as magnetic field inclination and radiative losses, allowing lower-frequency waves to propagate to higher layers of the solar atmosphere under certain conditions (Centeno et al., 2006; Jefferies et al., 2006; Wedemeyer-Böhm et al., 2009; Jiménez et al., 2011, e.g.).

(2024) found that their horizontal oscillations exhibit a pronounced peak near 5 mHz. Formed under conditions of strong scattering and partial frequency redistribution, these lines sample atmospheric layers extending from the upper photosphere to the upper chromosphere and lower transition region (Leenaarts et al., 2013a; Leenaarts et al., 2013b; Pereira et al., 2015). papers.title: An HDG-type discretization of 1D embedded blood flow in complex networks with Riemann-coupled junctions
papers.abstract: We present a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) method for one-dimensional blood flow in arterial networks with Windkessel boundary conditions. The scheme uses a Harten--Lax--van Leer (HLL) numerical flux and implicit time integration. After spatial discretization, the complete network---including cell states, hybrid traces, junction conditions, and dynamic $\mathrm{RCR}$ terminal pressures---is written as a residual index-one differential--algebraic equation (DAE) and integrated with variable-step, variable-order backward differentiation formulas. The implicit formulation removes the CFL stability restriction of explicit schemes and allows variable-order, variable-step solvers. The resulting single global residual and Jacobian for the network and its terminal dynamics also provide a natural interface for monolithic coupling with external nonlinear models. We establish local solvability and a semi-discrete energy balance, and show numerically optimal convergence rates for both solution variables in the $L^2$ norm and the broken $H^1$ seminorm. The solver is validated against established benchmarks, including an aortic bifurcation and a $37$-artery network, and is further applied to a cerebral arterial network. Mass conservation is observed in a synthetically generated anatomical liver network of $8\,\mathrm{k}$ vessels, and strong-scaling studies are performed on synthetic networks of $50\,\mathrm{k}$ and $100\,\mathrm{k}$ vessels.

papers.intro:
One-dimensional (1​D1\mathrm{D}) models of the cardiovascular system provide a computationally efficient framework for analyzing pulse-wave propagation and hemodynamic variables across complex arterial networks [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. By simplifying the three-dimensional Navier–Stokes equations through cross-sectional averaging, these reduced-order models retain the dominant network-scale dynamics at a small fraction of the cost of fully three-dimensional simulations. In the literature, each vessel is commonly represented as an interval with a single axial coordinate. However, anatomically realistic arteries are curved tubes with a definite orientation in space, and effects such as gravity depend on that orientation. In existing 1​D1\mathrm{D} models, gravity is typically introduced through a source term involving the component of gravitational acceleration along the vessel axis [6, 7].

Thus, the embedding is purely geometric: the model describes one-dimensional flow along the centerlines, with 𝒃⁡(𝒙)\bm{b}(\bm{x}) specifying the local vessel orientation. No ambient divergence or off-centerline extension of the tangent field is required; the full formulation is given in Section 2. When gravity is included, its projection onto the vessel enters the momentum source through 𝒈⋅𝒃⁡(𝒙)\bm{g}\!\cdot\!\bm{b}(\bm{x}). A spatially varying 𝒃⁡(𝒙)\bm{b}(\bm{x}) therefore allows this known gravity-dependent source term to follow the vessel geometry accurately.

A network model is closed by two types of coupling. At each junction one imposes conservation of mass and continuity of total pressure across the incident vessels. At each terminal we attach a lumped 0​D0\mathrm{D} Windkessel model whose pressure satisfies an ordinary differential equation (ODE). Existing network formulations include characteristic, finite-volume, and discontinuous Galerkin discretizations, as well as hybrid 1​D1\mathrm{D}–0​D0\mathrm{D} models that couple different vessel descriptions through conservation conditions [1, 11], and terminal coupling is standard in these works. Implicit arterial-network solvers also predate the present formulation: Carson and van Loon [12] developed an enhanced trapezoidal rule method with a global pressure solve and Lagrange multipliers enforcing conservation of mass and total-pressure continuity at junctions. The present contribution combines a specific hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) formulation with HLL-based stabilization, the coupling of multi-way junctions and dynamic Windkessel terminals through hybrid trace unknowns, and implicit time integration with adaptive step size and variable order. The system is integrated implicitly by a variable-order, variable-step backward differentiation formula (BDF\mathrm{BDF}). Each time step is solved by Newton’s method on the full nonlinear system, with no linearization or operator splitting, using one global Jacobian that couples vessels, junctions and terminals.

Implementing this strategy requires a global set of unknowns that couples hybrid traces, junctions, and terminals within the same nonlinear system. The hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) method provides such a set. Discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods are widely used for hyperbolic conservation laws because they handle shocks and complex geometries and are well suited to parallel computation. With implicit time integration, however, a standard DG formulation leads to a globally coupled system involving all element degrees of freedom. With explicit time integration, by contrast, each element is updated from known neighbour states and no global solve is needed, at the price of a CFL-type step restriction. HDG methods introduce additional “trace” unknowns defined only on the mesh skeleton (the traces of the unknowns on the mesh faces). Once those trace values are known, each element can be solved independently using a local element solver [13]. The junction and terminal conditions involve these skeleton unknowns and can be assembled with the cell equations in a single Newton system. Although element elimination is possible when the local Newton blocks are invertible, the current solver implementation solves the full cell-trace-capacitor system.

papers.title: Hierarchical Step Decomposition for Training-free Online Video Step Grounding
papers.abstract: Given a set of procedural steps, Video Step Grounding (VSG) aims to identify which steps occur in a video and localize when they are performed. Existing methods are either offline, requiring access to the full video before making predictions, or online, but relying on fixed-length video segments producing noisy, over-segmented outputs. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Step Decomposition (HSD), a training-free framework for online VSG that leverages the semantic understanding capabilities of Large Multimodal Models. HSD addresses two central challenges in online grounding: constructing semantically coherent temporal segments from a streaming video, and bridging the semantic gap between coarse procedural step descriptions and visual observations. To construct elementary temporal units, HSD incrementally groups incoming segments into semantically consistent events, using an anchor caption that is continuously validated against the visual stream. Based on these events, we perform zero-shot procedural step classification and selectively refine uncertain predictions by decomposing candidate steps into finegrained substeps that capture more nuanced visual evidence. By operating on semantically coherent events rather than every fixed-length segment, HSD reduces redundant computation and produces more stable predictions. Experiments on HT-Step, Ego4D Goal-Step, and CrossTask show that HSD substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, overall achieving better step recognition, more accurate temporal localization, and faster inference.

papers.intro:
When humans perform a task (e.g., cooking), they undergo a series of steps (e.g., cutting, adding ingredients, mixing): recognizing these steps is essential for applications that analyze, monitor, or assist humans. To this end, given a video and a list of procedural steps in natural language, Video Step Grounding (VSG) [51, 23], aims to identify which steps are present in the video and when they occur.

When humans perform a task (e.g., cooking), they undergo a series of steps (e.g., cutting, adding ingredients, mixing): recognizing these steps is essential for applications that analyze, monitor, or assist humans. To this end, given a video and a list of procedural steps in natural language, Video Step Grounding (VSG) [51, 23], aims to identify which steps are present in the video and when they occur.

Recent progress in VSG has been largely driven by weakly supervised approaches [12, 23, 5, 18] that formulate temporal grounding as alignment between textual descriptions and predefined video units, such as individual frames or fixed-length segments. While effective, these methods rely on task-specific supervision on curated training data, and typically process the video offline. As a result, they are difficult to transfer to unseen tasks and not well suited for streaming scenarios, such as always-on assistive devices, where a video must be processed incrementally as it is observed. This limitation has recently motivated the development of online, training-free approaches based on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) [45].

As a result, they are difficult to transfer to unseen tasks and not well suited for streaming scenarios, such as always-on assistive devices, where a video must be processed incrementally as it is observed. This limitation has recently motivated the development of online, training-free approaches based on Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) [45].

Online Video Step Grounding (OVSG) is significantly more difficult, as it requires recognizing a step given only past frames. A major challenge lies in the choice of the temporal units to use for prediction. The only existing OVSG method [45] relies on fixed-length segments, a rigid representation poorly aligned with instructional procedures, where action lengths vary substantially. For instance, short segments often lack sufficient visual evidence to reliably identify a step while longer segments may encompass multiple actions, mixing visual evidence from different steps and leading to ambiguous predictions. A second challenge arises from the semantic gap between procedural step descriptions and local visual observations. Step descriptions are often coarse and goal-oriented. For instance, a step such as cook carrot soup may involve several finer-grained actions, such as taking the carrots, cutting them, and placing them into a pot. At any given timestep, the video may show only one of these sub-actions, so the visual information may only partially match the step description. As a result, the model may miss the correspondence with the higher-level step or may confuse it with visually similar actions.

In this work, we propose Hierarchical Step Decomposition (HSD), a training-free framework for OVSG that jointly addresses both challenges. HSD operates in three stages. In the first, instead of grounding predictions on fixed-length temporal units as in [45], we incrementally build semantically consistent event segments by determining whether each incoming visual observation continues the current event or initiates a new one. As a result, the model performs grounding over semantically coherent video units, avoiding the rigidity and the noise of fixed-length partitioning. In the second stage, we perform an initial prediction of the procedural step associated with an event, leveraging the zero-shot capabilities of an LMM [3, 2, 6, 40]. To reduce the granularity mismatch between the coarse procedural steps and local visual evidence, we introduce a third stage, i.e., a hierarchical step refinement stage, that is activated when the model has low confidence in the initial event-to-step assignment. In this stage, coarse descriptions of procedural steps are expanded into multiple, fine-grained substeps, and the current event is re-evaluated against these more detailed alternatives. Importantly, all stages of HSD use the same, frozen LMM, in a unified training-free pipeline. A comparison between HSD and previous methods is illustrated in Fig. 1.

papers.title: Structural signatures of primary and secondary relaxation during physical aging of a metallic glass
papers.abstract: Physical aging drives glasses toward equilibrium and changes their thermodynamic and mechanical properties, but the accompanying microscopic structural evolution remains poorly understood. Here, using our recently developed low-background setup combining fast scanning calorimetry with \emph{in-situ} X-ray total scattering, we investigate microscopic structural changes during physical aging in Pd$_{42.5}$Cu$_{30}$Ni$_{7.5}$P$_{20}$ metallic glass. The measurements span an unprecedented six orders of magnitude in time and a temperature range extending from above the glass transition temperature to more than 150\,K below it. We observe dominant structural changes near the first and second peaks of the structure factor. Near and above the glass transition temperature, changes in the first sharp diffraction peak closely follow enthalpy relaxation and are associated predominantly with increasing degrees of medium-range ordering. At lower temperatures, the enthalpy evolution can no longer be described by this contribution alone, revealing an additional, faster relaxation process that correlates with changes near the second diffraction peak and thus short-range structural rearrangements, including increased Pd--Pd correlations. These results establish a direct connection between thermodynamic relaxation and structural evolution, providing strong evidence that primary and secondary aging processes are associated with distinct structural length scales.

papers.intro:
Aging is a universal phenomenon in glasses where, after the system falls out of equilibrium upon cooling below the glass transition temperature, it continues to evolve with time toward equilibrium [1, 2, 3, 4]. This evolution is accompanied by changes in various macroscopic properties such as density, enthalpy, and viscosity. In metallic glasses, physical aging can also alter mechanical properties, including the elastic moduli [5] and brittleness [6], and is therefore an important factor to consider for technological and industrial applications. Despite extensive research on this topic, many aspects of physical aging remain unclear because of its intrinsic complexity and non-equilibrium nature [1]. In particular, the microscopic structural changes during aging are not yet fully understood, reflecting the broader and long-standing quest to establish structure–property relations in glassy systems. Several previous studies [7, 8, 9] have examined the effects of annealing, aging, and cooling rate on the microscopic structure of metallic glasses, but a coherent picture has yet to emerge, and the connection between structural evolution and changes in macroscopic properties such as enthalpy remains unclear.

In this work, we combine X-ray total scattering with fast scanning calorimetry (FSC) to perform in-situ structural measurements during physical aging over a broad range of temperatures and time scales. The use of FSC provides rapid and precise temperature control, enabling reproducible measurements on time scales as short as milliseconds. In comparison, conventional temperature control systems usually operate at heating and cooling rates on the order of 20 K/min, thereby setting a lower limit for the measurable time to be minutes or longer. Hence, the use of FSC provides several orders of magnitude of improvement in the range of probed time scales, making it possible to study aging-induced relaxation processes in detail, as will be shown below. Moreover, our experimental setup allows low-background X-ray diffraction measurements at momentum transfers (QQ) from below 1 Å-1 to above 18 Å-1 [10]. This makes it possible to reliably and reproducibly obtain the structure factor and, subsequently, the pair distribution function (PDF) of the sample. Therefore, combining these two techniques, our setup is able to provide direct and quantitative insight into the microscopic structural evolution that occurs during aging with an unprecedented range of time scales.

As a model system, we investigate the metallic glass with composition Pd42.5Cu30Ni7.5P20 (at.%). This alloy has been extensively characterized in the literature and is found to exhibit high glass-forming ability together with several notable properties, including a pronounced secondary (β\beta) relaxation below the glass transition temperature, TgT_{g} [11]. After cooling the sample from the equilibrium supercooled liquid state well above TgT_{g}, we perform X-ray diffraction measurements as a function of time while keeping the sample at a constant aging temperature. The accessible aging times extend from tens of milliseconds to hours, spanning almost six orders of magnitude, while the investigated aging temperatures range from more than 30 K above TgT_{g} to more than 150 K below it. These measurements provide a comprehensive picture of microscopic structural evolution during physical aging and reveal signatures of different relaxation processes at distinct structural length scales.

papers.title: Rubricon: Automated Rubric Generation and Refinement for LLM Evaluation and Training
papers.abstract: Rubrics enable reward assignment on tasks without verifiable answers, but are expensive to manually produce from scratch. We present Rubricon, a pipeline that generates discriminative rubrics without requiring human preference labels, rubric annotation, or generator-model training. Using any LLM, Rubricon samples multiple rubrics, selects the most discriminative candidate, adds criteria to capture overlooked requirements or response flaws, and prunes criteria that are misaligned or shallow. Alongside LLM self-critique and test-time scaling, Rubricon uses observed criterion pass rates on example model responses to guide refinement. Across five professional, consumer, clinical, and general-use LLM benchmarks, Rubricon produces rubrics whose scores of frontier LLM responses exhibit 9% greater alignment with labor-intensive expert-authored rubrics, compared to the best alternative synthetic rubric generation method among RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, and agentic generation via harnesses like Codex. On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from the strongest alternative synthetic rubric generator, RRD.

papers.intro:
Rubrics provide explicit, checkable criteria for systematically evaluating open-domain LLM responses and assigning post-training rewards (Gunjal et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026a). Expert-authored rubrics are the gold standard but are painstaking to produce (datasets with rubrics can require hundreds of physicians or bankers (Arora et al., 2025; Lau et al., 2026)). Asking an LLM to generate a rubric yields criteria too shallow to separate strong responses from weak ones, or even criteria that incorrectly favor lower-quality responses (Shen et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). A further challenge is building rubrics that remain discriminative as models improve, which requires criteria that will appropriately penalize flaws in responses from stronger future models not yet available.

Asking an LLM to generate a rubric yields criteria too shallow to separate strong responses from weak ones, or even criteria that incorrectly favor lower-quality responses (Shen et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). A further challenge is building rubrics that remain discriminative as models improve, which requires criteria that will appropriately penalize flaws in responses from stronger future models not yet available.

We propose Rubricon, a straightforward pipeline that automatically generates higher-quality rubrics via three stages: Generate-and-Select, Add, and Prune. It targets three properties a good rubric needs: (i) the ability to discriminate between responses of different quality, (ii) coverage so that substantively weak responses do not go unpenalized, and (iii) headroom for quantifying flaws in responses from stronger future models. The pipeline does not require any human data annotation or model fine-tuning, and can utilize any LLM to generate/refine the rubrics, yielding better rubrics as LLMs advance. Rubricon also supports iterative refinement as the Add and Prune stages can be repeatedly applied to continuously reassess and improve a rubric’s criteria.

Rubricon illustrates a way to scale test-time compute (Snell et al., 2025) for rubric generation that is empirically more effective than alternate approaches like agentic rubric generation or Recursive Rubric Decomposition (Shen et al., 2026). Relying solely on LLM self-critique or ensembling yields limited test-time scaling gains due to LLM brittleness and biases in the rubric generation setting. Instead, Rubricon additionally grounds its refinement stages in how candidate rubrics actually score example responses. Because existing LLMs cannot properly self-judge their own generated rubrics, our refinement stages encourage the models to rely on particular outside signals and workflows which simplify the judgment calls a model must make. Compared to existing rubric-generation techniques, the resulting Rubricon-generated rubrics score responses more consistently with expert-authored rubrics (Table 1) and improve post-training outcomes (Figure 2).

papers.title: Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection
papers.abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

Learning dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations is a promising path toward general-purpose robot skills, and the quality of that demonstration data has been shown to directly impact downstream policy performance [1]. There are three major options for capturing human manipulation sequences: egocentric-Computer-Vision (ego-CV) only; CV with an exoskeleton-based solution; and CV with a sensing-glove-based solution.

The ego-CV-only approach is the least intrusive of the three and obtains the most natural manipulation data, but CV cannot recover high-fidelity hand pose under occlusion, which becomes more severe exactly when hand-object interaction happens. Paliwal et al. reported that in ego-CV recorded manipulation tasks, << 10% of the raw data eventually are usable for training purposes [2]. Besides limitation in measuring hand pose, vision-based methods cannot directly measure the contact forces that are important for fine dexterity tasks. Exoskeleton-based systems like MILE [3] provide high-fidelity kinesthetic data but constrain finger motion and alter grasp strategies; recent systems such as WHED [4] and DexEXO [5] achieved some progress, but still made great trade-off of naturalism with data quality. Sensing gloves promise both naturalism and direct force measurement, yet as we detail in the following section, no existing platform jointly provides calibrated force sensing, occlusion-resilient pose tracking, and a form factor validated to preserve natural grasp behavior.

papers.title: Improving Group Deliberation through AI-Guided Self-Reflection
papers.abstract: As AI systems increasingly mediate human communication, identifying conditions under which they augment collective sense-making is a critical challenge. Through a randomized experiment (N=1,173 U.S. participants across 391 small-group deliberations), we investigate whether AI-guided self-reflection improves subsequent deliberative discourse. We show that engaging with a non-directive AI chatbot instructed to structure self-reflection prior to group deliberation yields significantly higher deliberation quality (measured by the Discourse Quality Index, DQI) compared to a baseline of no self-reflection (Cohen's d=0.31) and a condition of unassisted self-reflection (d=0.27), and the positive impact is most pronounced in groups with disagreement. This improvement may be driven by more sophisticated argument justifications, greater consensus-building effort, and increased respect for counterarguments. Furthermore, after self-reflection, participants in the AI condition reported higher empathy toward dissenting peers and a deeper understanding of opposing reasoning. Beyond observed behavior, our findings are empirically relevant to open debates between political philosophy and psychology surrounding self-reflection, demonstrating that interactive AI could transform solitary thinking into productive internal reflection. Together, these results demonstrate that even simple AI-based reflective scaffolds can foster more productive group dynamics, opening new avenues for leveraging AI to augment collective intelligence.
papers.intro:
AI is increasingly shaping how people engage with contested issues. Recent work suggests that this influence can be constructive, through eliciting greater openness towards opposing views (Lu et al., 2025), reducing feelings of partisan animosity (Thurgood et al., 2026), and durably changing conspiracy beliefs (Costello et al., 2024). However, in these interventions, AI largely supplies the reasoning and the evidence that people then evaluate. Research on critical thinking suggests that such interaction mode may carry risks, linking reliance on AI to cognitive offloading and downskilling of human reasoning (Stadler et al., 2024; Melumad and Yun, 2025; Gerlich, 2025a), though outcomes appear contingent on how systems are leveraged (Gerlich, 2025b; Wang and Fan, 2025; Lee et al., 2025; Zhi et al., 2026). This raises the question of whether AI can support engagement by fostering human reasoning rather than replacing it.

This raises the question of whether AI can support engagement by fostering human reasoning rather than replacing it.

Such support would be of particular interest in online deliberation, where discussions often fall short of mutual understanding and instead entrench polarization (Fulay and Roy, 2026). To counter this dynamic, a host of approaches have been proposed and tested. Political theorists have highlighted self-reflection, or "deliberation within" (Goodin, 2000; Goodin and Niemeyer, 2003), as a mechanism to encourage perspective-taking, surface gaps in one’s own knowledge and beliefs, and foster empathy. Empirically, asking individuals to explain the mechanistic foundations of their positions has been found to expose an illusion of explanatory depth and moderates extreme views (Fernbach et al., 2013). However, solitary thinking has known limits: producing confirmatory arguments can reinforce one’s existing beliefs, and reasoning works best when exercised in dialogue with others (Landemore and Mercier, 2010; Mercier and Sperber, 2011). A non-directive conversational AI that poses reflective questions could offer a middle ground between solitary reflection and AI that supplies reasoning and conclusions.

Can AI-guided reflection help individuals unpack their reasoning, reproducing the benefits of deliberation within and, in turn, improve the quality of subsequent group deliberation? We explore deploying an AI Reflector (AIR) as a reflection scaffold prior to group interactions, akin to a reflective elicitation in Revel and Pénigaud (2026)’s framework. We examine whether AI can be designed to facilitate self-reflection while avoiding the pitfalls by focusing more on critically examining their own knowledge and reasoning and imagining the reasoning of others. Collaborating with Deliberate Lab (Qian et al., 2025), we empirically test the impact of this pre-deliberation intervention on both individual- and group-level deliberative desiderata.

Self-reflection. A core tenet of this work is self-reflection – the idea that self-generated insight can provide a constructive kind of knowledge. This concept takes roots in the Socratic method, where an interlocutor is guided toward self-generated insight, a practice Socrates conceptualized (and Plato recorded) as maieutikē technē or the “midwifery craft” (Jowett et al., 1894). Building on these classical foundations, scholars have developed neo-Socratic frameworks. Most notably, the Nelsonian tradition (Nelson, 2025; Heckmann, 1981) departs from adversarial cross-examination in favor of non-directive facilitation, wherein participants reflect collaboratively upon shared personal experiences. In Nelsonian dialogue, a facilitator assists participants in identifying the boundaries of their own comprehension through concrete, real-world examples (Saran and Neisser, 2004). This non-directive ethos was subsequently operationalized and evaluated within clinical and applied psychology through Motivational Interviewing (Miller and Rollnick, 2012; Lundahl et al., 2010; Rubak et al., 2005), as well as within philosophical frameworks of critical thinking (Virtanen and Kallio, 2026). Further afield, Goodin has explored how self-reflection can play a vital role in democratic deliberation practices(Goodin, 2000). His “deliberation within” framework posits that the internal cognitive process of processing new information, weighing competing considerations and perspective-taking could serve as a foundational component of improved democratic discussions.

Despite these benefits, solitary reflection is also susceptible to systematic biases: according to the argumentative theory of reasoning (Mercier and Sperber, 2011; Mercier and Landemore, 2012), human reasoning evolved largely to produce and evaluate justifications within social argumentation. Because this mechanism is fundamentally designed to defend one’s stance against others, when individuals reason in isolation, they lack the natural corrective of social opposition, predisposing them to recruit evidence that selectively defends their prior convictions. Consequently, solitary contemplation could risk entrenching existing attitudes rather than refining them, underscoring that unstructured self-reflection is not an unalloyed mechanism for depolarization.

papers.title: Stabilizing fluctuating Cooper pairs with a terahertz resonator
papers.abstract: Coupling quantum materials to electromagnetic cavities or resonators without external driving has gained prominence as a new control mechanism. Here we develop an equilibrium theory of a mesoscopic, disordered two-dimensional superconductor coupled to a subwavelength terahertz resonator, focusing on the interplay between superconducting phase fluctuations in the sample and electromagnetic fluctuations of the resonator. Modeling the resonator as a lumped-element circuit, we show that the coupling enhances, rather than suppresses, the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$. When the sample is smaller than the Pearl length, phase fluctuations near the Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless (BKT) transition strongly amplify this enhancement. Crucially, the resistive quasiparticle response of the sample must be included in the analysis: at low frequencies the superfluid shunts the normal-fluid channel, reducing the total sample impedance. For representative parameters, a $1 \,\mu\mathrm{m} \times 1 \,\mu\mathrm{m}$, $8 $nm-thick disordered film, we find a relative $T_c$ enhancement of about $1\%$, an order of magnitude larger than the $0.1\% $ obtained when phase fluctuations are neglected. These results identify superconductors with soft phase fluctuations as promising platforms for equilibrium control with terahertz resonators.

papers.title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
papers.abstract: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand $r$, the goal is to estimate $Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx$ on $D\subset\mathbb R^d$. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on $\mathbb R^d$ and do not respect the domain constraint $x\in D$. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in $D$ by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on $D$, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of $Z$. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating $r$. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

To design a learnable diffusion-based proposal that respects the domain constraint, we draw inspiration from diffusion models (Song et al., 2021) for constrained generative modeling. Existing approaches fall into two groups. The first changes the geometry in which the process evolves: mirror diffusion models map 𝒟\mathcal{D} onto ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} through the gradient of a strictly convex potential and run a standard diffusion in the resulting dual space (Liu et al., 2023), while log-barrier diffusions equip the interior of 𝒟\mathcal{D} with the Riemannian metric induced by the Hessian of a barrier function, under which the process remains in the interior (Fishman et al., 2023). The second group keeps the Euclidean geometry of 𝒟\mathcal{D} and confines trajectories by reflecting them at the boundary, using reflected Brownian motion as the noising process (Fishman et al., 2023; Lou & Ermon, 2023). In this work, we follow the second route and adapt reflected diffusions from generative modeling to sampling, where no samples from π\pi are available and the reverse dynamics must be learned from evaluations of rr alone.

papers.title: Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning
papers.abstract: Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. papers.title: A photonic-integrated optomechanical mid-infrared detector
papers.abstract: Tracking the resonance frequency of a mechanical oscillator is the basis of atomic force microscopy, mass sensing and thermometry. Nanomechanical thermal detectors exploit this principle to sense absorbed radiation, most effectively with tensile-stressed resonators, whose tension converts thermal expansion into a large frequency shift and dilutes dissipation. Approaching their fundamental sensitivity limit, however, has required free-space or fibre-coupled interferometers, hindering compact deployment and scaling to arrays. Here we remove this bottleneck by monolithically integrating a high-Q nanomechanical resonator with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit. A tensile-stressed silicon nitride trampoline with an impedance-matched platinum absorber is dispersively coupled to a photonic integrated microresonator beneath it. At room temperature and with microwatt-level optical power, the detector reaches a noise-equivalent power of 3.4 pW/$\sqrt{\rm Hz}$ for broadband thermal radiation (3-12 $\mu$m), referred to incident power. Referred to absorbed power, this is within a factor of 1.5 of its fundamental thermal fluctuation limit. Using our detector in a state-of-the-art commercial Fourier-transform infrared spectrometer, we resolve the vibrational fingerprint of a polymer film across 2-20 $\mu$m and reach the precision of the built-in pyroelectric detector with about an order of magnitude lower incident power. This architecture opens a route to multiplexed optomechanical focal-plane arrays.

papers.title: Cognitive Debt in the GenAI Era - Listening to Practitioners' Voices on the Loss of Understanding
papers.abstract: Fast-paced AI-assisted software development risks reducing developers' understanding of the systems they build. This growing gap between what the system does and what developers understand about it, described as ``cognitive debt'', is not new, but AI has exacerbated it. This has led to a recent surge in blog posts and online discussions, in which practitioners recognize and write about cognitive debt, and share their experiences well before academic studies can capture them. To understand their concerns and inform future research and practice, we conduct a grey literature review of 76 sources, focusing on how cognitive debt is conceptualized and manifests, its contributing factors, its consequences, and the practices to prevent, detect, and mitigate it. We find that cognitive debt can accumulate unnoticed behind working code and passing tests, particularly when developers accept AI-generated solutions without building understanding. Practitioners report consequences such as harder maintenance and debugging, fragmented knowledge in the team, and reduced productivity. They propose practices such as documenting design rationale, review-sized changes, comprehension gates, and knowledge-sharing rituals, along with signals like reliability metrics to detect it. Our findings give software teams a structured view of emerging practical approaches in AI-assisted development and stress the need to preserve human understanding alongside faster code production.

To build this understanding, developers engage in cognitive processes and form mental representations of a program’s structure and behavior [2, 3], which in turn support their decision-making and reasoning about their decisions [2]. However, building such mental models is an effortful and incremental process [4], which does not necessarily follow the fast pace of GenAI-embedded software development.

Cognitive debt is no longer entirely hypothetical: practitioners report adopting AI-generated solutions and code snippets without fully understanding them [7]. The problem itself is not new; indeed, developers have always reused libraries, frameworks, and copied and pasted parts of code that they did not fully understand [8]. papers.title: Are Seismic Foundation Models More Than Glorified Feature Extractors?
papers.abstract: Earthquake sequences are stochastic on two separated timescales: the seismic waves of any individual earthquake propagate over seconds to minutes, while the earthquakes themselves arrive as a sparse, self-exciting occurrence process, with inter-event intervals from seconds to months. Respecting both scales in one training objective is the open challenge. Foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms instead import their learning targets from audio and vision, where every target is computed from a single fixed-length window. Such a window holds one realization of the wave propagation (an earthquake trace), never the occurrence process that decides when earthquakes happen. We develop nine model designs sharing one Mamba encoder-decoder, trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; the two key comparisons are architecture-matched, varying the objective alone. Each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks. Varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to our strongest classifier re-specializes it rather than making it a generalist: it gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. By the standard imported from language and vision, these models are feature extractors rather than FMs. Controls on capacity, architecture, and domain proximity do not explain why skill moves rather than rises. Against task-specific baselines the advantage is regime-dependent: our checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction, and trail them on full data. We argue the binding constraint is the target, and that settling the question requires a learning target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic in the first place.

papers.intro:
Seismicity is a canonical stochastic dynamical system at two distinct levels. Within a recorded earthquake trace, ground motion is a continuous, non-stationary process governed by the wave equation [5], with randomness from source and path heterogeneity, site response, and ambient noise [4]. Across the catalog (the record of past events with their times, locations and magnitudes), earthquakes arrive as a sparse, self-exciting point process: inter-event intervals span seconds during an aftershock sequence to months during interseismic quiescence [33], and magnitudes follow the Gutenberg–Richter law [12], so the events that matter most (large magnitude events) are by construction the rarest. The modeling tradition for the second level, like ETAS [24] and its neural descendants [21, 37, 8], is explicitly a stochastic-dynamics tradition. Characterizing a sequence means saying when the next event will come and how large it will be: quantities that live in the catalog, not in any one trace.

Machine learning has entered at the first level, the waveforms themselves. These are continuous ground-motion recordings from networks of seismometers irregularly placed at the surface, cut into fixed-length windows of three orthogonal components (vertical and two horizontal), typically sampled at 100100 or 200200 Hz. Recording never stops, but only the sparse windows around catalogued events carry labels, and the curated benchmarks used for pretraining are smaller still: on the order of a million traces [23, 1]. Recent foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms [20, 29, 19, 28, 34, 6, 7, 17] import self-supervised recipes from language, vision, and audio domains [9, 13, 2]. These recipes differ in architecture and objective, but agree on something more basic and rarely stated: the learning target is always a functional of a single fixed-length window. Masked prediction [20], compressed reconstruction [17], contrastive alignment [29], and diffusion denoising [7] all ask the model to recover or discriminate one realisation of the observation process, on a fixed clock; none references the occurrence dynamics, which bounds the abilities of the FM. When the physics is local to a short window, a window-level target is enough, and phase picking is the clear case, except when signal of interest is the pattern of occurrence (Section 4).

papers.title: Who Called? V33DA: A Physically Verified Multimodal Benchmark for Vocal Attribution in Zebra Finch Groups
papers.abstract: Deciding which member of an animal group produced a vocalization and where that vocalization was produced are central to studying social communication but are rarely evaluated with physically verified ground truth. Existing resources either localize sounds without identifying the caller, or recognize individuals from isolated vocalizations without reliance on the 3D candidate geometry. We close this gap with V33DA, a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches: it comprises 33,625 verified events coupling 5-channel audio with three camera views, calibrated 3D pose for every visible candidate, and per-bird radio telemetry across 10 individuals and three experiments. Caller identity is verified from an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration signal; this channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only by an on-body reference ceiling. Given a detected vocalization and the visible candidate birds, the task is to select the caller. We evaluate it under three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, held-out-experiment transfer to a new cohort, and leave-one-individual-out evaluation on a bird whose vocalizations are held out from training. Reference methods expose a consistent gap between in-domain accuracy and transfer to unseen individuals: methods that can exploit familiar vocal identity perform well on known callers but degrade sharply on unseen ones, whereas candidate-aware methods preserving explicit spatial reasoning transfer substantially better. The on-body reference stays near-perfect across regimes, confirming the internal consistency of the accelerometer-verified labels. We release V33DA with fixed protocols and code for the evaluated methods, and V33DA++, an unevaluated companion set of verified overlapping-call events and +/-2 s context windows.

Vocal communication in a social group is only interpretable at the level of individuals once each call can be assigned to the individual that produced it. In zebra finches, vocalizations carry information about identity, pair bonds, and social context (Elie and Theunissen, 2015; Elie and Theunissen, 2018); without caller attribution, these signals cannot be linked back to the animals that generated them. The problem is therefore the entry point to studying who communicates with whom, when, and under what social conditions.

Caller attribution in freely behaving groups is difficult because the evidence is distributed across modalities. The sound arrives at several microphones, the candidate animals move through a shared 3D space, and visual identity, posture, proximity, and acoustic structure all change over time. A model can also solve the wrong problem: if the same individuals appear in training and test, high accuracy may reflect recognition of familiar voices rather than a transferable ability to assign a call to the correct visible animal. A useful benchmark must therefore separate familiar-individual recognition from spatial attribution that generalizes to new individuals.

Existing resources capture important pieces of this problem but not the full setting. Large bioacoustic corpora support species, call-type, or individual-recognition tasks, but typically do not provide the synchronized candidate geometry needed to decide which animal in a group produced a sound (Kahl et al., 2021; Hagiwara et al., 2022; Rauch et al., 2024). Spatial-audio benchmarks evaluate localization or direction-of-arrival estimation, but usually do not provide physically verified caller identity for freely behaving animals (Evers et al., 2020; Politis et al., 2022; Shimada et al., 2023). Active-speaker and diarization datasets ask related attribution questions in humans, but rely on perceptual annotation, face or mouth cues, or close-talk references, and rarely provide calibrated 3D candidate state (Roth et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2025). On-body animal-recording studies can verify who called, but they do not by themselves define a public multimodal benchmark for testing transfer across unseen individuals. What is missing is a dataset that combines physical verification, synchronized group state, and evaluation splits designed to expose identity shortcuts.

We introduce V33DA (Vocal 3-Experiment 3D Attribution), a dataset-centered multimodal benchmark for spatial vocal attribution in social zebra finches, built on the BirdPark recording system (Rüttimann et al., 2025). Each of the 33,625 released events includes 5-channel audio, three calibrated camera views, per-frame 3D pose for every visible candidate, per-bird radio telemetry, and an on-body accelerometer-derived vibration channel used for verification. The verification channel is withheld from benchmark models and used only to define an on-body reference ceiling. We additionally provide V33DA++ as an unevaluated companion release: 3,784 verified overlapping-call events excluded from the main V33DA benchmark and ±2\pm 2 s padded context windows. These files are intended to support future work on source separation, vocal activity detection, and longer-context active-speaker tasks; no result in this paper depends on them.

The primary benchmark task is candidate-conditioned caller attribution: given a detected vocalization and the currently visible candidate birds, choose which bird produced the call. We also report 3D source localization as a diagnostic of whether a method has learned usable spatial evidence rather than only a candidate ranking. Evaluation uses three regimes: session-disjoint testing on familiar birds from held-out recording dates, leave-one-bird-out testing on a bird whose vocalizations are held out under the same cage and sensor setup, and held-out-experiment testing on a new cohort with no birds shared between train and test. Together, these regimes distinguish in-domain reuse, unseen-vocalizer generalization under fixed acquisition conditions, and broader experiment-level transfer.

The paper makes three contributions: • A physically verified multimodal release. V33DA provides synchronized audio, video, 3D pose, radio telemetry, and withheld on-body verification for social vocal attribution. • Splits that separate familiar from unseen individuals. The evaluation protocol separates familiar-individual testing from unseen-individual and held-out-experiment transfer, with fixed splits and common attribution/localization metrics. • A benchmark lesson about shortcut learning. Reference methods show that high in-domain accuracy can come from familiar-identity cues, while transfer to unseen individuals depends much more strongly on candidate-aware spatial reasoning.

papers.title: A $\pi / 4$ lower bound for random access in symmetric linear ensembles under optimal decoding
papers.abstract: We study the expected number of random linear observations required to recover a prescribed information symbol. For ensembles with uniformly random supports, independently sampled nonzero coefficients, and uniformly bounded column weights, we prove that the asymptotic normalized expected recovery time is at least $\pi/4$ under optimal decoding. The result holds over finite or infinite fields and extends the lower bound previously established for binary fully symmetric codes under peeling decoding. For singleton - pair observations, we determine the exact limiting expectation and show that optimal and peeling decoding have the same limit, independently of the field and coefficient distribution. The minimum within this family is approximately $0.793933445$, which explicit constructions attain asymptotically over every fixed finite field.

The random-access problem in DNA-based storage asks how coding can reduce the number of random reads needed to recover a prescribed information symbol [1]. In the noiseless uniform model, kk information symbols are encoded into nn symbols, which are sampled independently and uniformly with replacement. The objective is to minimize the expected number of samples needed for recovery, typically taking the maximum over the requested information symbols.
