Related work considers several retrieval goals, including reconstructing the entire message [2, 3], recovering requested files [4] or sets of information symbols [5], characterizing tradeoffs between individual file retrieval times [6, 7], and recovering a fraction of the message using LT codes [8]. Other studies address errors and nonuniform sampling [9, 10, 11], repair of failed storage containers [12], and parallel sampling from multiple containers [13]. Further coverage models consider draws that reveal subsets or windows [14], and repeated observations of composite symbols or motif combinations [15, 16, 17].

papers.title: Inertial flows over the Koch leaf
papers.abstract: The main hypothesis of this paper is that inertial effects known from porous-media flow can be observed even in a simple system consisting of a single channel. The strength of inertia is controlled by the Reynolds number, $Re$. We investigated fluid flow through a channel with a cavity in the shape of a Koch leaf. The Koch leaf of level-6 was chosen because it combines regularity, repeatability, and representativeness with a complex multiscale structure and non-trivial hydrodynamic interactions. We analyzed nonlinear effects through the so-called friction factor and show that its deviation from Darcy's law is very subtle. We further examined the influence of inertia on the flow structure, including the participation number $\pi$ and the backward-flow fraction $\rho^{-}$. In contrast to disordered porous media, the participation number decreases with $Re$, indicating that inertia concentrates kinetic energy in the main through-flow, while recirculation (backward flow) increasingly occupies the Koch leaf cavity. The tortuosity varies non-monotonically with $Re$, the apparent permeability decreases, and in the inertial regime the two are related by a power law with an exponent comparable to that found for natural rock. At the lowest and highest Reynolds numbers, the local kinetic energy followed a power-law distribution, $P(\varepsilon)\propto\varepsilon^{-m}$, over several orders of magnitude with the same exponent, $m\approx0.83$; inertia modified only the tails of the distribution. Our research can be regarded as an investigation of transport in an extremely porous system with porosity $\varphi \approx 1$.

papers.intro:
Fluids flowing through porous media self-organize into preferential flow channels, whose structure is set by the interaction between the moving fluid and the geometry of the fluid–solid interface [1, 2]. When the driving force is large, the flow along these channels may gain enough momentum for inertial effects to appear, even though the flow remains laminar. Understanding how such channels form and how they are modified by inertia is important for subsurface energy storage and CO2 sequestration [3], groundwater abstraction [4], and engineered porous systems such as microfluidic devices [5], porous-medium combustors [6], filters [7], and catalytic and thermochemical reactors [8].

When the driving force is large, the flow along these channels may gain enough momentum for inertial effects to appear, even though the flow remains laminar. Understanding how such channels form and how they are modified by inertia is important for subsurface energy storage and CO2 sequestration [3], groundwater abstraction [4], and engineered porous systems such as microfluidic devices [5], porous-medium combustors [6], filters [7], and catalytic and thermochemical reactors [8].

At low flow velocities, fluid transport through a porous medium is described by Darcy’s law, which establishes a linear relationship between the applied pressure gradient and the flow velocity [9, 10], −∇p=μk​𝐔,-\nabla p=\frac{\mu}{k}\,\mathbf{U}, (1) where kk is the permeability and 𝐔\mathbf{U} is the superficial velocity. As the velocity increases, inertial effects become significant and deviations from linearity emerge. These are commonly captured by the Forchheimer equation, which introduces a second-order correction [11, 12], −∇p=μk​𝐔+β​ρ​|𝐔|​𝐔,-\nabla p=\frac{\mu}{k}\,\mathbf{U}+\beta\rho\,|\mathbf{U}|\,\mathbf{U}, (2) where β\beta is the non-Darcy (inertial) coefficient. The transition between the two regimes is governed by the Reynolds number and involves a number of pore-scale phenomena, including local flow separation, vortex formation, and enhanced drag [13, 14, 15]. Its onset and strength depend sensitively on the properties of the medium, in particular on porosity and heterogeneity [16, 17, 18]. Pore-scale simulations of bead packs and natural rocks have shown that heterogeneous samples can depart from Darcy flow at Reynolds numbers two to three orders of magnitude lower than homogeneous ones of similar porosity [19], and heterogeneity also modifies how inertia affects solute transport [20]. Deviations from Darcy’s law have even been reported at very low Reynolds numbers, in the so-called pre-Darcy regime [21, 22].

A further difficulty is that the onset of inertial effects does not necessarily coincide with a pronounced change in the global pressure–flow relation. Changes in the internal organization of the flow can appear considerably earlier and may remain hidden if only integral quantities, such as the friction factor or the apparent permeability, are considered [18, 23]. Pore-scale measures are therefore needed to resolve the transition. The participation number π\pi quantifies how kinetic energy is distributed over the pore space [2]; the hydraulic tortuosity τ\tau measures how strongly the flow paths deviate from the mean flow direction [24, 25]; and the backward-flow fraction and the formation of vortices characterize recirculation [18, 23]. In disordered media, the transition toward inertia-influenced flow is accompanied by an increase in π\pi, as kinetic energy is redistributed from preferential channels into the surrounding pore space [2, 18], and by a non-monotonic change in tortuosity [18, 23].

Most of these observations come from idealized granular packings or from disordered and natural porous media, in which several geometrical properties—porosity, pore-size distribution, connectivity, tortuosity, and surface roughness—act simultaneously. Consequently, it is difficult to distinguish changes produced directly by fluid inertia from those imposed by structural disorder. In a recent study of low-porosity natural rock samples, we showed that the transition to inertial flow occurs through a distinct mechanism, visible as a change in tortuosity and the early formation of vortical structures, while the friction factor shows no clear departure from Darcy’s law [23]. Rough and self-affine boundaries are likewise known to influence hydraulic transport and permeability [27, 28]. These results raise the question of which features of inertial porous-media flow originate from disorder and which can emerge solely from the nonlinear interaction between fluid momentum and a complex solid boundary.

Deterministic fractal geometries provide a way to address this question in a controlled setting, because they contain geometrical features over several length scales while remaining exactly reproducible. The Koch leaf of any level is a particularly simple example of such a multiscale boundary: at every construction level, smaller geometrical features are introduced according to the same deterministic rule. Higher-order Koch leaf geometries (order n≥3n\geq 3) therefore represent an intermediate level of geometric complexity between simple obstructions and the highly irregular boundaries encountered in natural porous materials, and have already been investigated in transport-related studies. For instance, Adrover showed that convection-dominated dispersion in channels bounded by Koch leaf and Koch snowflakes exhibits a scaling different from that of smooth boundaries [29]. However, comparatively little attention has been devoted to how an increasing contribution of fluid inertia progressively alters the flow structure around an isolated Koch-type obstruction.

papers.title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction. AtomSteer improves molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity. For protein-ligand complexes, AtomSteer reduces ligand E/Z errors relative to experimental reference structures while achieving competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity. Our method provides a unified framework for adding chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models without retraining or architectural changes.

papers.intro:
Atomistic generative models can sample periodic crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein–ligand complexes with broad distributional fidelity (Miller et al., 2024; Hassan et al., 2024; Passaro et al., 2025), yet samples often violate known structural requirements. Recent co-folding models generate wrong ligand chemistry or chirality for more than half of the tested ligands (Goddard & Croll, 2026; Ishitani & Moriwaki, 2025; Luthfi et al., 2026), and crystalline generative models over-sample low-symmetry structures such as P​1P1 that are rare in nature (Levy et al., 2025). Each failure breaks a requirement: molecular graphs specify local geometry and stereochemistry, protein–ligand poses must be chemically valid, and space-group symmetries strongly influence the material properties (Levy et al., 2025; Kazeev et al., 2025).

Recent co-folding models generate wrong ligand chemistry or chirality for more than half of the tested ligands (Goddard & Croll, 2026; Ishitani & Moriwaki, 2025; Luthfi et al., 2026), and crystalline generative models over-sample low-symmetry structures such as P​1P1 that are rare in nature (Levy et al., 2025). Each failure breaks a requirement: molecular graphs specify local geometry and stereochemistry, protein–ligand poses must be chemically valid, and space-group symmetries strongly influence the material properties (Levy et al., 2025; Kazeev et al., 2025).

Existing approaches incorporate structural requirements through specialized representations, architectures, conditioning, or training objectives, while inference-time methods use reward reweighting or differentiable potentials (Section 2). A common way to add heterogeneous structural requirements at test time to pre-trained atomistic generative models is missing. These requirements differ in what they measure and in how the structure should move to satisfy them: an E/Z error is measured on four atoms but corrected by rotating an entire substituent, a protein–ligand clash is measured between atom pairs but can be corrected by moving the ligand as a rigid body, and space-group symmetry is measured across symmetry-equivalent atoms but corrected by moving each orbit with the lattice. Cartesian projection, for example, is suitable for bond lengths, angles, and small torsion refinements but cannot correct an E/Z configuration without displacing the four dihedral atoms and distorting the bonds around them. Therefore, each structural requirement calls for a residual on the atomistic graph paired with a suitable projection.

papers.title: WebMaze: Defending Against LLM-Powered Web Scanners with Functionality-Coupled Deception
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled more effective vulnerability scanning of web applications. However, these capabilities also make it significantly easier for attackers to automate cyberattacks on the web. In this work, we investigate how to divert malicious LLM-based web scanning, with preservation of genuine functionality as a deployment requirement. We systematically study six LLM-based scanners and summarize how they gather information and iteratively select actions based on observations. Guided by the study, we then present WebMaze, a defense that preserves genuine application functionality while diverting LLM-based scanners to a generated decoy world. WebMaze embeds functionality-coupled traps in genuine pages and constructs view-tailored interactive decoy worlds from the application's existing views. The traps blend into genuine components and expose entry points to decoy worlds that sustain exploration through connected pages and interactions without changing genuine functionality. Across 12 web applications and three LLM-based scanners under the default no-disclosure setting, decoy pages account for an average of 93.0% of the distinct pages requested per run. This demonstrates that WebMaze effectively diverts scanners away from genuine application pages and into the generated decoy worlds. Even when explicitly informed about the decoy mechanism and instructed to avoid decoy pages, scanners continue to explore predominantly decoy pages.

papers.intro:
Web scanning is an effective approach for discovering security vulnerabilities in web applications. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have further enhanced its capabilities by integrating LLMs with browsers, direct HTTP requests, and security testing tools. Unlike traditional scanners that primarily rely on predefined rules or exploration strategies, LLM-based scanners can reason about application states, determine subsequent actions, and dynamically adapt their strategies based on observations (Deng et al., 2024; Stafeev et al., 2025). These capabilities have enabled the discovery of security vulnerabilities in widely deployed web applications, including WordPress (Kues, 2026).

These capabilities have enabled the discovery of security vulnerabilities in widely deployed web applications, including WordPress (Kues, 2026).

Despite their benefits for legitimate security testing, LLM-based scanners can also be exploited for malicious purposes. By substantially reducing the expertise and effort required to discover and exploit vulnerabilities, they lower the barrier to conducting sophisticated web attacks. Consequently, attackers have begun leveraging LLM-powered agents to automate and scale their attacks (Anthropic, 2025; Kues, 2026).

There is an urgent need to protect web applications against the growing threat posed by adversarial LLM-based web scanners. Existing defenses are not sufficient. One category of work tries to distinguish legitimate user requests from abnormal scanning via request-pattern detection (Amin Azad et al., 2020; Wan et al., 2019; Searles et al., 2023). However, they have been demonstrated to be easily bypassed or evaded (Deng et al., 2025; Teoh et al., 2025). They also impose friction on legitimate users (Searles et al., 2023). Another line of work employs deception to mislead scanners and divert their exploration toward decoys. Prior work has explored techniques to disrupt or divert automated exploration, including URL marking, honeypot replicas, and misleading webpage content (Wan et al., 2019; Tsouvalas and Nikiforakis, 2025; Li et al., 2026). However, deception still faces two challenges. First, deception uses traps, which are entry points embedded in genuine webpages to divert automated scanners toward decoy functionality. Scanners can identify and filter traps once they know their patterns. For example, hidden-link traps use visually concealed links to decoy pages, which scanners can easily filter by excluding links that are not visibly rendered. Second, even when scanners enter decoy environments, limited functionality and interaction opportunities may cause them to abandon further exploration. Related work on LLM-powered honeypots has independently noted analogous limitations, including insufficient realism, limited adaptability and shallow interaction (Sladić et al., 2024). These challenges motivate two requirements for effective deception: (1) decoy entry points must be difficult to identify and filter, and (2) decoy environments must sustain continued scanner exploration.

Guided by the study, our key insight is that deception becomes more robust when it is coupled to genuine application functionality. If a deceptive element uses a pattern that is absent or different from genuine functionality, a defense-aware scanner can identify and reject it at relatively low cost. In contrast, if the same pattern also appears in legitimate components, rejecting all instances of that pattern may cause the scanner to miss genuine functionality. The scanner must then either accept some decoy interactions or invest additional effort in separating them from legitimate ones. We refer to this tension as the evasion-coverage tradeoff. Moreover, once a scanner enters a decoy, the decoy must provide sufficiently rich and plausible functionality to sustain exploration and consume the scanner’s limited budget.

papers.title: STAR: Scalable TEE-based Anonymous Rate-limiter
papers.abstract: Protecting Internet services from attacks such as TLS/HTTP floods requires rate limiting, yet identifying users to enforce these limits can compromise their privacy. Anonymous rate limiting promises to reconcile these goals, but existing schemes either struggle to scale or assume that services and authorities do not collude. We present STAR, which uses server-side trusted execution environments (TEEs) to overcome these limitations. By enabling lightweight cryptographic operations, TEEs make authentication efficient, but introduce a privacy challenge: malicious services can observe memory-access patterns to infer user secrets. We address this threat through countermeasures against secret-dependent memory accesses and assess our implementation using dynamic analysis. To extend these efficiency gains across servers, we also design a secure sharding mechanism that distributes client requests. We demonstrate that strong privacy guarantees can coexist with efficient authentication at scale; STAR processes authentication requests in tens of microseconds and handles approximately 13.9K requests per second per CPU core.

papers.title: Fully Dynamic All-Pairs Min Cuts on Planar Graphs via Planar Pattern Emulators
papers.abstract:
We study the fully-dynamic all-pairs minimum cut problem on planar graphs. Given an $n$-vertex undirected planar graph $G=(V,E)$ undergoing edge insertions and deletions, the goal is to efficiently process these updates while supporting $s$-$t$ minimum cut queries for any pair of vertices $s$ and $t$. We give a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate dynamic algorithm that supports edge updates and minimum cut queries in $n^{o(1)}$ time, for any $1/\text{poly}(\log n) < \varepsilon < 1$. For general graphs, previous results either are limited to partially dynamic settings or achieve only logarithmic-factor approximations.
  The main conceptual and technical contribution is to show that a suitable adaptation of the planar emulator of Chang, Krauthgamer, and Tan~[STOC'22] satisfies the stronger pattern emulator introduced by Chen and Tan~[ICALP'25]. This leads almost immediately to a nearly linear-time construction of pattern emulators, which, when combined with the recent fully dynamic $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximate all-pairs shortest paths algorithm of Filtser, Goranci, Patel, and Probst Gutenberg~[FOCS'24], yields our result.

papers.title: Skillful and realistic precipitation forecasting with reinforced diffusion
papers.abstract: Accurate precipitation forecasting remains elusive as physics-based models struggle to resolve mesoscale convection and machine learning often yields physically inconsistent, blurred results that consistently underestimate extreme events. We present FitzRoy, the first system that simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art predictive skill and physical realism over the continental United States. Through a reinforced diffusion framework, where a conditional discrete diffusion model is refined via reinforcement learning, FitzRoy effectively resolves the long-standing trade-off between pointwise accuracy and structural fidelity. Across lead times up to 24 hours, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art models while preserving structural realism and capturing extreme events. Its low-latency inference further enables deployment in real-time operational settings. Despite decades of advancement in numerical weather prediction (NWP), short-range forecasts of high-intensity, localized rainfall often lack the precision required for effective emergency response. This stems from a fundamental physical constraint: NWP models typically operate at resolutions too coarse to explicitly resolve key processes such as deep convection, cloud microphysics, and boundary-layer turbulence. Furthermore, precipitation is not a fundamental prognostic variable of atmospheric equations; instead, it is diagnosed from thermodynamic and dynamical fields via highly idealized, heuristic parameterizations. Consequently, even state-of-the-art physics-based systems struggle to capture the sharp gradients and stochastic nature of mesoscale convective systems (James et al., 2022).

Machine learning (ML) has recently matched and even surpassed NWP in predicting smooth variables such as temperature and geopotential height by exploiting reanalysis datasets and flexible architectures (Bodnar et al., 2025; Lam et al., 2023; Price et al., 2025; Pathak et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2025; Bi et al., 2023; Allen et al., 2025; Alet et al., 2025; Kochkov et al., 2024). FitzRoy is, to our knowledge, the first system to surpass operational physics-based models while maintaining high-frequency structural realism at such a long forecast horizon. This is achieved through a reinforced diffusion framework, a generative modeling recipe that combines conditional discrete diffusion with reinforcement learning (RL). We first train a diffusion model to learn the distribution of physically plausible precipitation structures, then fine-tune the system using RL to align these generations with observed outcomes. This is achieved through a reinforced diffusion framework, a generative modeling recipe that combines conditional discrete diffusion with reinforcement learning (RL). By treating the diffusion process as a stochastic policy and ranking realizations against observed events, we apply policy gradients to bias the model toward high-skill trajectories without sacrificing structural fidelity.

We evaluate FitzRoy across held-out data spanning multiple seasons, against both in-situ station observations and radar estimates. Unlike recent models (Price et al., 2025; Lam et al., 2023; Bodnar et al., 2025) that rely on retrospective reanalysis that is unavailable operationally, FitzRoy is trained on heterogeneous data sources and evaluated using operational data streams, ensuring its utility in operational forecasting. Consequently, FitzRoy consistently matches or outperforms strong physics-based and ML baselines in forecasting precipitation probability, rate, and accumulation at lead times up to 24 hours. The system is fully operational and low-latency, generating high-resolution forecasts within seconds. To verify structural realism, we analyze power spectral density and calibration, demonstrating that FitzRoy’s forecast distributions closely mirror the statistical properties of observations. Case studies of high-impact events further demonstrate tangible benefits; notably, during the catastrophic Texas Hill Country floods of July 2025 (Gilbert and Yan, 2025) (Fig. 1) and Missouri floods of July 2026 (Fig. 2), FitzRoy accurately signals the potential for extreme accumulations 18–20 hours in advance, whereas state-of-the-art models underpredict the event’s magnitude and misplace its spatial footprint. Notably, the Missouri floods occurred approximately two years after the cutoff of FitzRoy’s training data, providing evidence of temporal generalization to extreme events well beyond the training period.

papers.title: ARRAKIHS: The observability of tidally stripped satellites in a Milky Way-like halo
papers.abstract: Deep imaging surveys are revealing increasing numbers of low surface brightness stellar streams around Milky Way-like galaxies. These streams trace the orbital evolution and internal structure of their disrupted dwarf galaxy progenitors. We investigate the evolution and observability of tidal features from dwarf galaxies consistent with the $\Lambda$CDM framework and Local Group observations. We performed high-resolution $N$-body simulations of dwarf galaxies orbiting in a static Milky Way-like potential comprising a disc, bulge, and dark matter halo. Each dwarf comprised a Plummer stellar distribution embedded in a cuspy or cored generalised Navarro--Frenk--White dark matter halo. Idealised integrated surface brightness maps were constructed every 0.5 Gyr over 10 Gyr, and detectability was quantified through the projected area of stellar light brighter than limiting surface brightnesses, $\mu_{\rm lim}=29$--$32$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, chosen to span depths relevant to ARRAKIHS, LSST, and Euclid. The detectability of tidal features depends most strongly on progenitor stellar mass, orbital configuration, parameterised by the eccentricity proxy $e_0$, and evolutionary stage. Across this range, extended tidal debris is predominantly recovered for initially more radial configurations, mainly those with $e_0 \gtrsim 0.75$. In the simulated grid, detectable area is dominated by $M_\star=10^8$--$10^9 M_\odot$ progenitors, whereas $M_\star=10^6$--$10^7 M_\odot$ systems can undergo stripping without detectable debris. The detectable area evolves non-monotonically with time, reflecting the competition between stream formation, phase mixing, and the fading of diffuse debris below the adopted surface brightness limits. Cuspy and cored progenitors show similar evolution of the detectable area, with differences smaller than the scatter induced by orbital diversity.

papers.intro:
Stellar tidal streams, shells, and other diffuse structures have already been observed around nearby galaxies through both targeted deep imaging and wide-field surveys (Martínez-Delgado et al. 2010; Fliri and Trujillo 2016, e.g.). These observations have enabled the identification and characterisation of a wide variety of tidal features. Despite this progress, the recovery of the faintest and most diffuse tidal structures remains observationally challenging. Current and forthcoming generations of deep, wide-field imaging surveys will extend these studies by probing fainter structures and providing larger and more systematic samples. Facilities such as Euclid, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will improve the detection of diffuse stellar structures in the outskirts of external galaxies (Borlaff et al. 2022; Montes et al. 2023; Martin et al. 2022, e.g.). Dedicated low surface brightness (LSB) surveys and missions, such as the Large Binocular Telescope Imaging of Galactic Halos and Tidal Structures survey (LIGHTS) and the adopted mission Analysis of Resolved Remnants of Accreted galaxies as a Key Instrument for Halo Surveys (ARRAKIHS), are specifically designed to explore this faint regime (Trujillo et al. 2021, e.g.). Complementary surveys, such as the Stellar Stream Legacy Survey, exploit imaging from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Legacy Imaging Surveys to identify stellar streams around nearby galaxies (Martínez-Delgado et al. 2023). These observations are expected to further expand the known population of faint halo substructures, including streams, shells, and diffuse debris, whose properties provide sensitive probes of the tidal evolution of satellite galaxies (Vera-Casanova et al. 2022; Miró-Carretero et al. 2024; Stoiber et al. 2025, e.g.).

As dwarf galaxies orbit within the gravitational potential of their host haloes, tidal forces remove stars from their outskirts and redistribute them into extended stellar structures. Previous studies have shown that the morphology and spatial distribution of tidal debris are shaped by the satellite’s orbital history, progenitor luminosity, and viewing geometry (Johnston et al. 2008; Hendel and Johnston 2015, e.g.). These properties are also affected by the satellite’s internal structure, including the inner density profile of its dark matter halo, as well as by the global properties of the host potential (Erkal et al. 2016; Errani and Peñarrubia 2019; Errani et al. 2022, e.g.). The inner dark matter profile is particularly relevant in dwarf galaxies because of the long-standing cusp–core problem and because the central dark matter slope can affect the resilience of satellites to tidal stripping (de Blok 2009; Peñarrubia et al. 2010; Pontzen and Governato 2012, e.g.). These dependences motivate a controlled exploration of how orbital configuration, progenitor structure, and observational depth jointly affect the morphology and detectability of tidal debris.

These dependences motivate a controlled exploration of how orbital configuration, progenitor structure, and observational depth jointly affect the morphology and detectability of tidal debris.

To address this problem, simulations are required to investigate the disruption of dwarf galaxies. Among simulation-based approaches, cosmological simulations provide the most complete framework for studying the evolution of satellite galaxies and the debris produced by tidal stripping. High-resolution hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations and cosmological volumes, including Auriga (Grand et al. 2017; Simpson et al. 2018; Riley et al. 2025; Shipp et al. 2025, e.g.), Feedback In Realistic Environments (FIRE) simulations (Panithanpaisal et al. 2021; Shipp et al. 2023, e.g.), FIREbox (Feldmann et al. 2023), and VINTERGATAN (Agertz et al. 2021), follow galaxy assembly in a fully cosmological context, capturing baryonic physics, time-dependent host potentials, and complex merger histories. In these environments, tidal stripping arises self-consistently as satellites orbit their hosts, producing stellar streams, partially disrupted systems, and phase-mixed structures (Panithanpaisal et al. 2021; Riley et al. 2025, e.g.). These studies show that disrupting satellites are common around Milky Way-like haloes and occupy a broad range of orbital and evolutionary states. However, the complexity and computational cost of cosmological simulations make it difficult to isolate the different factors that shape satellite evolution. Beyond the properties of the progenitor and its orbit, satellites are influenced by baryonic components, preprocessing in group environments, interactions with massive companions, and halo-to-halo variations in accretion history (Simpson et al. 2018; Shipp et al. 2025, e.g.). Even when using zoom-in techniques, evolving hydrodynamical simulations to z=0z=0 while maintaining sufficiently high resolution across the relevant dwarf galaxy mass range remains computationally demanding. In addition, many current high-resolution hydrodynamical simulations do not necessarily resolve the internal structure of low-mass dwarf galaxies and their tidal debris at the level required to trace the detailed disruption process, particularly in the mass regime that may contribute substantially to the stream population (Shipp et al. 2023). Predictions from cosmological simulations can also be affected by the adopted subgrid prescriptions for unresolved baryonic physics, including star formation, feedback, and the effective equation of state used to model the unresolved interstellar medium (Shipp et al. 2023; Pakmor et al. 2025, e.g.). These limitations can modify the internal structure of dwarf galaxies and their response to tides, for example, through numerical heating, overly extended stellar components, or enhanced susceptibility to disruption (Cooper et al. 2017). More generally, cosmological simulations may suffer from numerical over-merging, namely the artificial disruption of dark matter subhaloes due to insufficient resolution (van den Bosch and Ogiya 2018; van den Bosch et al. 2018; Errani and Peñarrubia 2019; Benson and Du 2022; Santos-Santos et al. 2025). Disentangling the physical drivers of disruption from these numerical and modelling effects, and connecting them to the observability of the stripped stellar material, remains challenging.

papers.title: Anchored isoperimetry in percolation
papers.abstract: We show that, for any infinite transitive graph $G$, the infinite cluster after supercritical percolation almost surely inherits the anchored isoperimetry of $G$. Moreover, the probability of violating the corresponding isoperimetric inequality decays exponentially in the isoperimetric profile of the host graph. This was previously known only for nonamenable transitive graphs, $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and very recently for transitive graphs of polynomial growth. Our proof combines the thinning-and-sprinkling technique with a novel counting algorithm.

papers.title: Learning Event-based Obstacle Avoidance via Differentiable Simulation
papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe quadrotor flight in unknown environments, yet conventional frame-based cameras remain challenged by motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency under fast motion. Event cameras, with sub-millisecond latency, high dynamic range, and negligible motion blur, offer a promising alternative, but leveraging them for closed-loop control remains difficult. Existing approaches either adopt cascaded architectures that first estimate depth and then map it to control commands, introducing error propagation, or achieve end-to-end control through costly offline pretraining before online fine-tuning can even begin. We address these challenges with a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to render events efficiently within the training loop, integrated into a differentiable simulation pipeline that enables direct gradient backpropagation through the differentiable physics model, improving sample efficiency. This allows us to train an end-to-end policy that maps event frames directly to control commands, without intermediate depth estimation. We validate our approach through zero-shot real-world deployment on a quadrotor, achieving robust obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including under low-light conditions where conventional cameras typically fail.

Quadrotors have been widely adopted in autonomous robotics for applications such as industrial inspection, package delivery, and search-and-rescue, where reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe operation in unknown environments [1]. However, achieving robust vision-based obstacle avoidance remains challenging, particularly during high-speed flight, because conventional frame-based cameras are susceptible to motion blur, limited dynamic range, and sensing latency. Unlike traditional cameras that capture image frames at a fixed rate, event cameras [2], modeled after the biological retina, operate asynchronously. Each pixel functions independently, and an event is triggered only when the change in log-intensity at pixel coordinates exceeds a predefined threshold, with polarity indicating an increase or decrease in brightness. This bio-inspired sensing mechanism inherently minimizes motion blur and provides sub-millisecond latency and a much higher dynamic range, making event cameras highly suitable for agile applications [3, 4, 5]. Most notably, Sony AI’s Ace [3], the first real-world table tennis AI agent competitive with human athletes, uses event-based spin estimation to return high-speed shots.

papers.title: Magnetism in a homometallic square-planar Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$$_4$Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$ metallacrown
papers.abstract: The well-established homometallic metallacrown Cu(II)[12-MC$_\text{Cu(II)N(Shi)}$-4]$^{2-}$, comprising four square-planarly arranged Cu(II) ions surrounding a slightly off-plane central Cu(II) ion, provides an excellent platform for investigating magnetism in exchange-coupled Cu(II) clusters both by experimental and ab initio numerical methods. In the present work, sterically bulky substituents are introduced into the salicylhydroxamate ligand to obtain a modified derivative, Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$[12-MC$_\text{Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$N(L)}$-4]$^{2-}$ (Cu$_4$Cu), thereby effectively suppressing intermolecular magnetic interactions and enabling a detailed investigation of its intrinsic ground-state spin structure and exchange interactions. Static magnetization reveals competing antiferromagnetic exchange interactions of $J_1=-8.1(2)$ THz ($-33.5(8)$ meV) between the central and the peripheral sites and $J_2=-4.40(12)$ THz ($-18.2(5)$ meV) between neighboring sites on the ring of the metallacrown, which are corroborated by ab initio broken symmetry-based density functional theory (DFT). These couplings yield an $S=1/2$ ground state for Cu$_4$Cu at low temperatures, for which X-band and high-frequency/high-field electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) precisely determine the $g$-factors $g_x = 2.028$, $g_y = 2.056$, and $g_z = 2.222$ close to axial anisotropy and in agreement with our DFT results. The ground-state spin-configuration is characterized by $d_{xy}$-character of the unoccupied states. Furthermore, our magnetization data evidence thermal transitions across a doublet-to-quartet gap of $\Delta_{1/2\rightarrow3/2} = 4.8(4)$ THz which is also indicated by the emergence of an excited-state EPR signal.

papers.intro:
One of the most interesting classes of coordination compounds is that of metallacrowns, due to their structural and property versatility [25]. These inorganic analogues of organic crown ethers consist of a repeating sequence, mostly [M–N–O–] or [M–N–N–], forming a macrocyclic ring. The ring size can vary from 9 to 60 atoms. The central cavity may be empty or accommodate transition-metal or lanthanide ions, resulting in a wide variety of structures. Since the pioneering work of Pecoraro and Lah, interest in this class of compounds has steadily increased due to their potential applications [22, 4, 43, 13]. In recent years, the magnetic properties of metallacrowns have become a focus of research, as they can exhibit single-molecule magnetic behavior and could potentially act as qubits in quantum computing [51, 5, 8, 46]. However, in multinuclear systems, understanding and precisely quantifying magnetic properties becomes increasingly challenging as the number of spins and centers increases. A less complex homometallic copper(II)-based metallacrown framework is the copper(II)-centered compound Cu(II)[12-MCCu(II)N(Shi)-4]2-, which has already been studied extensively by some of us [12, 35, 34, 20].

In the present work, we investigate a derivative in which the ring-building salicylhydroxamate ligand carries bulky, silyl-protected tetramethylimidazolinyl side arms. The resulting compound Cu(II)({\mathrm{II})}[12-MCCu(II)({\mathrm{II})}N(L)-4]2- (in short: Cu4Cu) contains four paramagnetic Cu(II) sites at the ring positions and a slightly off-plane central Cu(II) ion (see Fig. 1). The bulky substituents sterically shield the metallacrown cores, suppressing intermolecular magnetic interactions and enabling the magnetic properties of individual Cu4Cu metallacrowns to be investigated in the solid state. Employing X-band and high-frequency/high-field electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and static magnetometry as well as an ab initio-based broken-symmetry approach, we resolve and quantify competing magnetic exchange interactions and gg-factor anisotropy, thereby obtaining a comprehensive magnetic model for this five-spin system.

papers.title: Local Important Separators with Applications to Unbreakable Decomposition and Multicut
papers.abstract:
We present the first local FPT algorithm for finding important separators: Given an undirected graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, vertices $s,t$ and parameters $k$ and $\nu$, we can enumerate all $s$-$t$ important separators of size at most $k$ and volume at most $\nu$ in time $\tilde{O}(\nu 2^{O(k)})$. Known approaches spend either $\Omega(m)$ time (not local) or $\nu^{\Omega(k)}$ time (not FPT).
  Using this local algorithm, we show the following applications.
  (1) The first is an improved construction of unbreakable decomposition, a powerful generalization of tree decompositions. For any $k$, we can compute a $(5k,k)$-unbreakable decomposition with adhesion $4k$ in $\tilde{O}(k^{O(k)}m)$ time. This strictly subsumes the result of Anand, Lee, Li, Long, and Saranurak (SODA 2025) and is faster than the recent $O(k^{O(k^2)}m)$-time algorithm by Korhonen (STOC 2025) when $k = \omega\Bigl(\sqrt{\frac{\log \log n}{\log \log \log n}}\Bigr)$. Our algorithm is also simpler than that of Korhonen (STOC 2025).
  (2) We give a near-linear time algorithm for single-sink important separators. For any sink $t$, we can list all $v$-$t$ important separators of size at most $k$ across all $v \in V(G)$ in time $\tilde{O}(2^{O(k)}m)$. Known approaches trivially compute $v$-$t$ important separators for each $v$, taking $\Omega(4^k k mn)$ time.
  (3) Using the above result on single-sink important separators, we speed up undirected shadow removal and give the first almost-linear time FPT algorithm for Edge Multicut.

papers.title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
papers.intro:
Deep learning models increasingly allocate inference compute adaptively. Learned halting (ACT, Graves, 2016; PonderNet, Banino et al., 2021), confidence-gated early exits (CALM, Schuster et al., 2022), learned routing (Mixture-of-Depths, Raposo et al., 2024; Mixture-of-Experts, Shazeer et al., 2017) and energy-based verification (Gladstone et al., 2025) have established the value of input-conditional escalation. However, these mechanisms generally attach a learned scalar gate to a feedforward stack. Escalation then repeats the standard forward operation and gives no structural guarantee of how the extra computation changes the model’s latent state.

papers.title: CAPTURER: A Dexterous Aerial Manipulator for Dynamic and Precise Grasping across Diverse Environments
papers.abstract: As a representative form of embodied robotic interaction, aerial grasping requires close coordination between the aerial platform and manipulator. Most existing systems perform aerial grasping with static or slowly moving targets under fixed scenarios. Dynamic and precise grasping across different conditions introduces additional challenges, including target motion, localization drift, dynamic coupling, and external disturbances. In this work, we present CAPTURER, a dexterous aerial manipulator for centimeter-level grasping across diverse environments. To achieve the challenging goal, we first develop an onboard perception system for state estimation and target detection. Drift correction and global pose transformation are introduced to improve target localization during flight. A cooperative motion planner is proposed to coordinate the mobility of the aerial platform with the dexterity of the manipulator according to the relative target state. To maintain grasping accuracy under disturbances, we design a disturbance-rejection controller to compensate for dynamic coupling, model uncertainty, and external disturbances. The capability of CAPTURER is validated through indoor and outdoor experiments with both static and moving targets. The results demonstrate that CAPTURER achieves centimeter-level grasping accuracy for a marker pen measuring only 1.5 cm in diameter at flight speeds exceeding 1.5 m/s.

papers.intro:
Aerial robots have evolved from laboratory prototypes into increasingly capable platforms for autonomous operation in complex environments (Aucone and Mintchev, 2025). Their high mobility has enabled applications such as autonomous drone racing (Song et al., 2023), navigation through dense forests (Zhou et al., 2022), and resilient flight under adverse weather conditions (O’Connell et al., 2022). Despite these advances, most aerial robots still primarily serve as sensing and observation platforms. Performing physical interaction remains considerably more challenging, particularly when the task requires both fast motion and precise contact with the external environment.

Despite these advances, most aerial robots still primarily serve as sensing and observation platforms. Performing physical interaction remains considerably more challenging, particularly when the task requires both fast motion and precise contact with the external environment.

Aerial manipulators combine the large-range mobility of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with the local operability of manipulators, enabling physical interactions in difficult-to-access and hazardous environments (Kaya et al., 2025; Khamseh et al., 2018; Ollero et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; Cao et al., 2025b). Early studies have demonstrated aerial interaction using grippers mounted on multirotor platforms (Lindsey et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2014). Soft and compliant grippers are subsequently developed to enlarge the effective contact region and increase grasp tolerance for different target geometries (Appius et al., 2022; Ubellacker et al., 2024). Specialized systems have also achieved millimeter-level accuracy in aerial insertion tasks (Wang et al., 2024b). In addition, coordinated multi-robot systems have demonstrated aerial construction and manipulation over extended workspaces (Zhang et al., 2022).

However, most existing aerial systems operate under quasi-static or near-hovering conditions. Moreover, the grasping motion is often predefined or generated offline. The operating mode does not fully exploit the mobility and agility of the aerial platform during physical interaction. Many systems also rely on external localization infrastructure to maintain accurate positioning. Vision-based approaches reduce this dependence, but they commonly assume that the target is always visible within the camera’s field-of-view (FoV) during operation (Seo et al., 2017; Lai et al., 2022b; Hu et al., 2023). These assumptions are restrictive when the target moves or when the robot operates across different environments.

During a grasping maneuver, the target state may change continuously, while the aerial platform and manipulator move simultaneously. Dynamic and precise aerial grasping introduces three closely coupled technical problems.

The first problem is perception. Precise grasping requires consistent estimation of both the aerial manipulator state and the target state. Unlike conventional aerial navigation, the manipulator moves relative to the floating base during operation. This motion changes the system configuration and induces additional disturbances to the aerial platform. Meanwhile, onboard localization is subject to accumulated drift. The problem becomes more difficult for a moving target because the perception system must continuously update its position while the robot itself is moving (Khamseh et al., 2018; Ollero et al., 2022). When the target leaves the FoV, measurement updates become unavailable and prediction uncertainty increases. Moreover, dynamic grasping requires a consistent target representation that remains usable by the motion planner during platform and manipulator motion.

The second problem is planning. The aerial platform provides large-range mobility, whereas the manipulator provides more precise local adjustment (Ollero et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2026). Different combinations of platform and manipulator motions can satisfy the same end-effector requirement, while resulting in different remaining workspaces for subsequent adjustment. The cooperative planner must allocate motion according to their respective characteristics and the relative target state. Moreover, the attitude information of the aerial platform should be incorporated into the planning process because it directly affects the end-effector state.

papers.title: Online Dense Reinforcement Learning with Planning-Grounding Agent for UI Navigation on Live IOS Apps
papers.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
papers.intro:
UI Navigation agents, which are AI systems designed to perceive graphical user interfaces and autonomously execute sequences of actions to achieve user-specified goals, are gaining traction in both industry and academia. Their applications range from automatically completing tasks for users (Qin et al., 2025a; Gu et al., 2025) to A/B testing (Lu et al., 2026). While frontier models can be quite proficient at UI Navigation (Jang et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2025), they are expensive, often costing several dollars per task (EasyClaw Research, 2026), making them impractically expensive for frequent, everyday use. As a result, there has been a surge in interest for training small models for proficient UI navigation (Yang et al., 2025; Chai et al., 2026). However, current training methods suffer from significant weaknesses. Supervised Fine-tuning (SFT) tends to memorize training trajectories rather than learn generalizable strategies, resulting in brittle execution that struggles to recover from errors (Zhou et al., 2025b; Bai et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2024; Yan et al., 2025). Existing Reinforcement Learning (RL) approaches largely rely on single-step RL that mirrors these same SFT limitations (Yang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025) or rely on only a terminal reward at the end of a trajectory, providing a weak, sparse signal (Bai et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Qi et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2025a).

To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework, trained at a large scale on real iOS applications, that decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning Agent and a UI Grounding Model. Rather than training a single model to jointly handle planning and spatial localization, our architecture allows each component to be optimized for its specific objective. The Planning Agent observes the screen, maintains a history of past actions, and utilizes Chain-of-Thought reasoning to produce both an immediate step and a long-term plan. The immediate step is then passed to the Grounding Model, which translates it into a precise action and corresponding coordinates for on-device execution. Additionally, the Planning Agent’s action space includes an Ask_User primitive to handle underspecified tasks by requesting user preference specifications. Because grounding is a largely deterministic mapping problem effectively solved via SFT, this decoupling allows us to reserve computationally expensive RL for the Planning Agent, where open-ended reasoning and adaptation provide the most benefit.

We optimize the Planning Agent in an online RL setting, centered on a robust LLM-as-a-Judge reward mechanism. To overcome the sparsity of terminal-only feedback, we combine two complementary signals. A Dense Reward evaluates whether each individual step makes meaningful progress while penalizing hallucinations and unproductive loops. A Terminal Reward assesses overall task completion. This dense, step-level feedback provides a rich signal throughout the trajectory, giving the model useful feedback even when terminal success is rare under the current policy. It further encourages exploration and explicitly teaches the agent to recover from unexpected states rather than failing when it deviates from a golden path. To effectively leverage this dense reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE). To prevent the agent from artificially prolonging trajectories to exploit step-level rewards, we use an asymmetric discounting strategy in our reward function that balances local process supervision with discounted dense rewards, combined with a terminal reward for successful task completion. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by incorporating reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories.

papers.title: Near-Field Engineering of Silica-Shelled Plasmonic Nanoparticles toward Enhanced Near-Infrared Fluorescence
papers.abstract: Near-infrared (NIR) fluorescent molecules often suffer from low quantum yields, limiting their applications in sensing and imaging. Their fluorescence can be enhanced by coupling with plasmonic nanoparticles exhibiting resonances in the same spectral region. However, this approach requires precise nanoscale control over the plasmonic near-field. Here, we combine scanning transmission electron microscopy with electron energy-loss spectroscopy (STEM-EELS) and boundary element electromagnetic simulations to engineer silica-coated anisotropic plasmonic nanoparticles. We synthesised three types of nanoparticles, gold nanorods (AuNRs), gold bipyramids (AuBPs), and silver nanorods (AgNRs) with tunable NIR plasmonic resonances. Silica serves as a dielectric spacer, enabling precise control over the distance between the nanoparticle surface and a potential molecular emitter. To assess their suitability for fluorophore attachment, we investigated the dependence of the electric near-field on silica shell thickness. High-resolution STEM-EELS mapping revealed that thin silica shells (4.4 nm for AuNRs and 3.1 nm for AuBPs) allow most of the near-field to extend beyond the dielectric layer. For AgNRs, a thicker shell of 7.0 nm was required to prevent oxidation while maintaining near-field accessibility. Electromagnetic simulations further evaluated the optimal shell thickness and the dependence of fluorescence enhancement on particle geometry, material, fluorophore internal quantum yield, and fluorophore-metal separation. Together, these results provide practical design guidelines for optimizing particle morphology and sub-10 nm silica shells in plasmonic nanostructures for fluorescence enhancement.

papers.title: Symmetry-governed nonlinear metasurface simultaneously enhances circular dichroism, helicity purity, and Q-factor
papers.abstract: Circularly polarized light underpins a broad range of chiroptical and spin-selective photonic technologies, yet extending resonant chirality to nonlinear harmonic emission remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a symmetry-governed mechanism that maps the maximal linear chirality of high-Q degenerate resonances onto the polarization of the generated harmonic. Preserved rotational symmetry protects modal degeneracy and polarization-selection rules, while broken mirror symmetries enable a strong chiroptical response. The metasurface thereby filters the pump polarization and purifies the handedness of the nonlinear output, simultaneously achieving third-harmonic circular dichroism of -0.98, a degree of circular polarization of 0.83, and an effective nonlinear Q-factor of 140. Importantly, the nonlinear emission preserves its handedness even under spatially depolarized excitation, demonstrating robustness to variations in the incident polarization state. These results establish complementary symmetry preservation and breaking as a deterministic route for transferring resonant chirality from linear to nonlinear optical responses, providing a general design principle for nonlinear chiral photonics.

papers.title: Where Do Vision Language Models Fail at 3D Reasoning?
papers.abstract: Vision-language models can get individual judgments right while struggling to recover and consistently use the exact properties of a 3D object. To characterize this gap, we introduce BedBench, a controlled benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks spanning individual judgments and composite answers. Across twelve open-weight and four frontier models, per-color counting exposes a pronounced weakness: humans achieve 93.3% accuracy, compared with 7.2% for the best model. Targeted fine-tuning raises one model's accuracy from 3.0% to 68.6%, but reveals a further difficulty: its answers about the most common colors remain inconsistent with its own per-color counts. Supplying those counts as text improves its judgments, showing that recovering a property does not mean using it consistently. Reasoning, scaling, and added visual cues each improve individual judgments, but none makes exact answers reliable. To locate the difficulty, we probe Qwen3.5-27B: exact per-color counts remain recoverable at the language model's input, yet the model's answers rarely recover them (65.0% for the probe vs. 3.0% for the model). Image-removal controls further show that some apparent successes require no visual evidence. These findings motivate evaluating 3D reasoning by exact correctness, consistent use, and image dependence, rather than accuracy alone. Code and dataset are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/BedBench

papers.intro:
Reasoning about a 3D object from images requires relating its visible parts across views: a model may need to count blocks, identify which parts share a color, or predict the object’s appearance from another direction. Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly evaluated on such spatial and 3D reasoning tasks Liu et al. (2023); Ma et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2026); Yang et al. (2025), yet their scores do not always reveal how they reached an answer. A correct answer may depend on visual evidence, but it may also follow from language priors or cues in multiple-choice options Goyal et al. (2017); Agrawal et al. (2018); Zheng et al. (2024); Balepur et al. (2024). Conversely, a low score may reflect a model limitation, ambiguity in the available views, or a task that is difficult for humans as well.

Building on these works, we ask a more specific question: does success on individual judgments extend to exact answers and consistent use of object properties? Consider a model that can count the distinct colors (T4: Color Count) and estimate the total number of blocks (T1: Volume) in an object. Each is an individual judgment: a single count, comparison, or decision about one property of the object. Such judgments do not establish that the model can report the correct number of blocks of every color (T5: Color Distribution). That requires an exact answer: a structured answer that is correct only when all its quantities, attributes, and their associations are correct together, here every color paired with its correct count. Consistent use adds a further requirement: when asked which colors are most common, the model’s answer should agree with those counts.

We introduce BedBench (short for Blind 3D Benchmark), a benchmark of thirteen procedurally generated tasks using voxel objects (i.e., 3D shapes built from unit cubes) and scenes of geometric primitives. The tasks range from counting blocks (T1) and checking whether an object fits inside a container (T2: Packaging) to reporting per-color counts (T5) and matching an object to its 2D projections (T11: Projection; Figure 1). The generator provides exact ground truth and filters out samples detected as ambiguous at generation time, so individual judgments and exact answers can be compared within one controlled task family. Existing benchmarks include some of these properties (Table 1); BedBench combines exact-answer scoring, consistency checks, image-dependence controls, and frozen-feature probes on the same objects, so it can also locate where a failure arises.

We evaluate twelve open-weight (OW) and four frontier VLMs, with 30 human participants as a reference for task difficulty. We first compare models with humans across tasks to find which exact answers fail most clearly, and test whether simpler queries, a 2D presentation, or task-specific training improve them. Since more reasoning, larger models, and added visual cues are the usual remedies for spatial failures, we then test each of them and probe the frozen visual features to locate where the difficulty arises. Finally, because a high score is meaningful only if it depends on the image, we check whether successful answers require the images. This yields four findings: 1. Exact counting is unreliable, and learning it does not ensure consistent use. Humans reach 93.3% on T5, the best VLM 7.2%. Fine-tuning raises T5 to 68.6%, yet the model identifies the most common colors (T7) only 35.0% of the time from images, versus 74.2% when given its own counts as text (§5.1). 2. Reasoning helps selected tasks but not exact answers. Thinking raises T4 by ++13.9 pp on average, yet T5 stays at 0.7–1.0%, larger budgets lower T1 and T11, and visual misreadings often persist through the reasoning (§5.2). 3. Scaling and visual support leave exact answers unreliable, although visual features hold the counts. Gains from scale and visual cues are selective. A probe at Qwen3.5-27B’s language-model input recovers exact counts on 65.0% of objects, against 3.0% for the VLM, pointing to difficulty in using available visual information (§5.3). 4. Accuracy alone does not establish visual reasoning. Without images, models keep some scores through constant answers, and in a fixed-layout MCQ one model reaches 100% by always choosing the third option (§5.4). Overall, models get individual judgments right while the exact answer stays wrong, and recovering a property does not mean using it consistently.

papers.title: Event-SAMA: Language-Grounded Video Object Segmentation on Neuromorphic Event Streams
papers.abstract: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.

papers.intro:
Referring video object segmentation (RVOS) and grounded video dialogue have progressed rapidly on RGB video, driven by motion-centric benchmarks such as MeViS (Ding et al., 2023) and by models that couple a large language model (LLM) to a promptable segmenter (Yuan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). These models ground language in pixels, which is exactly what real-world deployment of vision-language models requires. All of them, however, assume dense, synchronous RGB frames, and they inherit the failure modes of frame-based cameras: motion blur under fast motion, saturation in high-dynamic-range scenes and noise in low light.

These models ground language in pixels, which is exactly what real-world deployment of vision-language models requires. All of them, however, assume dense, synchronous RGB frames, and they inherit the failure modes of frame-based cameras: motion blur under fast motion, saturation in high-dynamic-range scenes and noise in low light.

Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously with microsecond latency, a dynamic range above 120 dB and no motion blur. They are attractive precisely in the regimes where frame-based cameras degrade, but the language-grounded segmenters that have matured on RGB video cannot consume this modality. To our knowledge, no dataset or model addresses referring segmentation from natural language on event streams. Recording a language-annotated event corpus at the scale that current vision-language models require would mean re-capturing hundreds of hours of video with event hardware and re-annotating it with referring expressions and multi-turn dialogue. We instead follow the standard practice in event vision (Gehrig et al., 2020) and convert an existing, richly annotated RGB corpus into synthetic event streams, inheriting its annotations at no annotation cost.

papers.title: Feeding or Fleeing: The Impact of Enhanced Early Black Hole Growth on Circumgalactic Clumps at $z > 6$
papers.abstract: The circumgalactic medium (CGM) of massive high-redshift galaxies contains inflowing filamentary gas, recycled material, and feedback-driven outflows. We investigate the formation and evolution of dense CGM clumps in two cosmological zoom-in simulations of the same massive halo at $z > 6$: the fiducial Fable model and the modified Fable-SE model, which includes enhanced early black hole growth through mild super-Eddington accretion. We identify dense gas clumps in the CGM and follow their gas properties, stellar content, and radial evolution across cosmic time. At the resolution probed here, the two simulations show broadly similar distributions of clump gas mass, gas size and associated stellar mass. Instead, the clump populations differ mainly in their abundance, metallicity, and radial evolution. Fable-SE produces substantially more metal-enriched clumps, including an outward-moving population during the strong AGN-driven blow-out phase at $z \lesssim 7$. These systems are associated with disturbed HI-rich gas and relatively high gas densities, linking the increased prevalence of dense, metal-enriched CGM structures in Fable-SE to its stronger AGN-driven blow-out phase. Although inward migration dominates overall, Fable-SE also contains an outward-moving clump population during the blow-out phase, with some clumps moving beyond the virial radius. Our results therefore indicate that the distribution of dense CGM clumps around massive high-redshift galaxies reflects both filamentary accretion and feedback-driven CGM evolution, with strong early AGN activity associated with the outward migration of dense, metal-enriched gas structures containing relatively cool gas.

papers.intro:
Galaxies in the early Universe were substantially more gas rich and turbulent than galaxies in the present day (Saintonge et al., 2013; Wisnioski et al., 2015; Zanella et al., 2023; Semenov et al., 2025, e.g.). These conditions are also associated with irregular and clumpy morphologies, where massive star-forming clumps are commonly observed within unstable gaseous discs (Elmegreen et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2015; Shibuya et al., 2016; Harikane et al., 2025; Sok et al., 2025, e.g.). These high gas fractions and turbulent conditions are thought to play an important role in regulating star formation and driving the formation of dense star-forming structures (Renaud et al., 2021; Renaud et al., 2024; van Donkelaar et al., 2022; Ejdetjärn et al., 2022, e.g.). Recent simulations and observations further suggest that galaxies during cosmic dawn may have experienced highly efficient star formation and rapid stellar mass assembly within compact gas-rich environments (Dekel et al., 2023; Bouwens et al., 2023; Harikane et al., 2024; van Donkelaar et al., 2025, e.g.). Understanding how gas inflows, turbulence and feedback interact in these environments is therefore important for understanding galaxy evolution at high redshift.

Understanding how gas inflows, turbulence and feedback interact in these environments is therefore important for understanding galaxy evolution at high redshift.

At the same time, the circumgalactic medium (CGM) around high-redshift galaxies is also unlikely to be a smooth or passive gas reservoir. Instead, these environments contain a complex mixture of dense inflowing gas, satellites, stripped material, feedback-driven outflows and recycled gas interacting within the same halo. Rapid gas accretion from the cosmic web will continuously feed young galaxies (Kereš et al., 2005; Dekel and Birnboim, 2006; Dekel et al., 2009, e.g.), while mergers and interactions between satellites further redistribute gas into the surrounding CGM (Stewart et al., 2011; Anglés-Alcázar et al., 2017; Ginolfi et al., 2020, e.g.). At the same time, the mentioned high gas fractions and intense star formation rates of these early galaxies drive strong galactic winds capable of ejecting dense and metal-enriched material far beyond the central galaxy (Bischetti et al., 2019; Marshall et al., 2023; Ginolfi et al., 2020, e.g.). These different gas components thus coexist within highly dynamic and rapidly evolving environments. Therefore, one may expect that these environments naturally produce compact dense structures embedded within the CGM, including transient star-forming overdensities, stripped clumps, or feedback-compressed gas clouds.

Therefore, one may expect that these environments naturally produce compact dense structures embedded within the CGM, including transient star-forming overdensities, stripped clumps, or feedback-compressed gas clouds.

Feedback from rapidly growing black holes (BHs) can drive powerful outflows (Fabian, 2012; King and Pounds, 2015, for reviews, see), which can reshape the high-redshift CGM (Costa et al., 2015; Bennett et al., 2024, e.g.). Simulations of massive quasar hosts at z>6z>6 show that energetic AGN-driven outflows can expel large amounts of metal-rich gas and dust into the halo, enriching and polluting the CGM out to several virial radii (Sijacki et al., 2009; Costa et al., 2014; Costa et al., 2015; Costa et al., 2022; Bieri et al., 2017; Barai et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2022; Ward et al., 2024, e.g.). These outflows can reach velocities of hundreds to more than 1000​km​s−11000~{\rm km~s^{-1}} and strongly perturb the surrounding gas halo (Costa et al., 2015; Bischetti et al., 2019, e.g.), reducing central gas densities while simultaneously redistributing metal-rich dense gas throughout the CGM (Costa et al., 2018; Costa et al., 2020, e.g.). Rather than simply destroying cold material, recent simulations suggest that AGN-driven feedback can also compress gas within the halo, potentially triggering star formation in outflowing material or long-lived dense clumps (Ishibashi and Fabian, 2012; Zubovas et al., 2014; Costa et al., 2015, e.g.). Such feedback cycles may therefore strongly influence the formation, disruption, and survival of dense circumgalactic structures (Costa et al., 2015; Nelson et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2024; Almeida et al., 2026, e.g.).

Observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (Wootten and Thompson, 2009, ALMA; ) and James Webb Space Telescope (Gardner et al., 2006, JWST;) have been beginning to reveal similarly structured environments around massive high-redshift galaxies and quasars (Ding et al., 2023; Galbiati et al., 2023; Tripodi et al., 2023; Bischetti et al., 2025, e.g.). Extended Lyα\alpha nebulae, metal-enriched gas and large-scale outflows indicate that baryons are already being efficiently cycled between galaxies and their surrounding haloes within the first billion years of cosmic time (Ginolfi et al., 2020; Bischetti et al., 2019; Marshall et al., 2023, e.g.). However, observations provide only instantaneous snapshots of these systems. Simulations are therefore important for connecting these different gas phases and for understanding whether dense CGM structures are transient features, disrupted satellites, recycled outflow material, or long-lived clumps that may survive and evolve within the halo environment (van Donkelaar et al., 2023; van Donkelaar et al., 2026; Ward et al., 2024, e.g.).
