papers.title: Morphology-Aware Channel-Decoupled Mamba Network for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Accurate multi-organ segmentation in computed tomography (CT) is essential for computer-aided diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. However, substantial variations in organ shape and size, together with low tissue contrast and ambiguous boundaries, complicate the modeling of heterogeneous anatomical structures. To address these challenges, we propose a Morphology-Aware Channel-Decoupled Mamba Network (MCDNet), which integrates adaptive local structural enhancement with channel-decoupled long-range modeling. Specifically, we introduce a Morphology-Aware Channel-Decoupled State-Space (MCSS) block that divides feature channels into separate processing groups, allowing differentiated structural representations to be learned within an efficient state-space framework. Within each group, a Morphology-Aware Enhancement Module (MAEM) combines deformable convolutions with channel attention to adapt local feature extraction to anatomical shape variations. Group-wise state-space modeling then captures long-range spatial dependencies, and channel gating adaptively integrates the resulting features. Experiments on the Synapse abdominal CT dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of MCDNet, achieving an average Dice Similarity Coefficient of 81.61% for multi-organ segmentation.

papers.title: Tailoring Infra-Red Filters for Global Mapping of Enceladus' Thermal Environment
papers.abstract: We present the results of an initial study into the feasibility and design of the Enceladus Thermal Mapper (ETM) instrument, designed to provide detailed temperature data for Enceladus, an icy moon of Saturn identified by the Cassini Mission as a prime candidate for astrobiological study due to its subsurface ocean and active cryovolcanism. Building on heritage from previous missions including TechDemoSat-1, Mars Climate Sounder, and Lunar Trailblazer, ETM aims to measure temperature variations across Enceladus' surface, including at the poles during the extreme cold of winter, when they can reach as low as 45 K. Where Cassini provided limited high-resolution flyby data of Enceladus due to its Saturn-centric orbit, ETM, in orbit around the icy moon will offer continuous high-resolution thermal mapping with a 384 x 288-pixel sensor, capable of 80 m/pixel resolution from 150 km altitude. This will improve constraints on the Enceladus' global conductive heat loss, and better characterise and contextualise its active South Polar Terrain. To optimise the instrument's filters for thermal emission measurements, a digital model of the filter assembly was developed. This lightweight, low-power instrument is capable of significantly advancing the understanding of Enceladus' geological behaviour and evaluating its potential habitability by providing comprehensive temperature data essential for interpreting its evolution.

papers.title: Evaluating Visual Realism of AI-Generated Videos with Eye Tracking
papers.abstract: Human evaluation of AI-generated videos has so far relied on explicit human feedback, such as judgments or ratings. While these signals capture the conclusions viewers reach, they fail to offer insights into the perception that leads to them. This paper investigates eye tracking as a complementary human evaluation signal for AI-generated videos. We conducted two Visual Turing Test (VTT) experiments with a total of 90 participants on videos generated by latest generative models, in which participants watched each video twice and then gave their feedback. Across the experiments, we collected 4,286 valid eye-tracking trials on 438 videos. Our analysis indicates that gaze patterns offer informative evaluation signals that align with explicit human feedback. Building on the findings, we propose the first computational method GazeEval to predict the perceived visual realism of AI-generated videos from eye-tracking data. It achieves 71.3% accuracy in prediction, providing evidence that eye tracking data carries informative signals about how people evaluate a video. We release the study data to support further research on eye tracking for evaluating AI-generated video.

papers.title: Random ($\log{n}$)-CNF Formulas Are Hard for Depth-$2$ Frege with Modular Gates
papers.abstract: We prove that, with high probability, refuting a random $k$-CNF formula on $n$ variables with ${M = n2^{k}}$ clauses for $\omega_n(1) \leq k \leq O(\log{n})$ requires polynomial calculus degree at least ${n/2-O(n/\sqrt{k})}$ over every field. Through Pang's recent tradeoff between $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$-Frege size and polynomial calculus degree [Pang 2026, arXiv:2610.00837v2], this implies a size lower bound of $\exp(\Omega_p(\sqrt{k} \log{n}))$ for depth-$2$ $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$-Frege. In this range of $k$, the bound is superpolynomial in $M$ while $M \leq \mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also prove a nearly matching degree upper bound of $n/2-n\ln(k)/{2k} +O(n/k)$, which shows that other formula families are needed to obtain lower bounds for full $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$-Frege through Pang's tradeoff.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Global Climate Policy Cooperation
papers.abstract: International climate policy requires coordination among countries whose mitigation decisions impose local costs but generate global benefits. Classical game-theoretic and integrated assessment approaches can study these incentives, but typically rely on prescribed behavioural assumptions or equilibrium concepts. Recent work has therefore explored Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning as a way to model climate-policy cooperation as an emergent outcome of repeated strategic interaction. We extend an existing MARL climate framework with a multi-stage negotiation mechanism in which agents propose agreements, accept or reject commitments, and face penalties for non-compliance. This allows us to study how agreement design affects learned mitigation behaviour, compliance, and climate outcomes. In an idealized setting with four homogeneous agents, we find that non-binding agreements do little to overcome free-riding, while moderate non-compliance penalties improve cooperation and reduce warming. However, excessively strong penalties discourage ambitious commitments, revealing a trade-off between enforcement and participation. We position the framework as a methodological contribution for testing agreement design rather than a predictive model of real negotiations.

papers.title: AI Cosmos: An Agentic Infra for Situated Learning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can improve task performance during learning, yet these gains do not necessarily reflect learners' ability to thereafter apply the knowledge and skills independently. We present AI Cosmos, an agentic infrastructure for situated learning that organizes learning around two complementary principles: scenario-based participation and cumulative assets of practice. AI Cosmos organizes learners and role-specialized agents within learning scenarios that integrate task-relevant knowledge and, when needed, executable workbenches. An asset-memory loop preserves the processes and outcomes of practice as reusable assets with explicit provenance and dependencies. We evaluate scenario-based interaction through two preregistered randomized controlled studies examining the acquisition of legal reasoning and programming competence, holding the same underlying LLM across conditions. AI Cosmos achieves greater learning gains than a conventional LLM in legal reasoning and higher mastery of unseen programming problems than an LLM-as-Teacher baseline.

papers.title: RepConTUR: A Report-Conditioned Volumetric Multimodal Model for Abdominal Tumor Segmentation
papers.abstract: Tumor delineation is required for radiotherapy planning, yet automatic segmentation is limited by errors, predominantly false positives, that distort dose and increase editing time. The radiology report accompanies the scan and localizes disease at the suborgan level, but existing text-promptable models condition on short referring phrases, and most operate in 2D. We present RepConTUR, a single native-3D early-fusion multimodal model that conditions volumetric abdominal tumor segmentation on the narrative report. We extend AbdomenAtlas 3.0 to a suborgan-level promptable segmentation dataset and generate report-based VQA pairs, yielding four report-derived tasks on the same annotations: referring segmentation (RES), report-grounded segmentation (GSEG), report generation (RRG), and visual question answering (VQA). We train RepConTUR, comprising a 3D CT encoder, an early-fusion language model, and a native-3D segmentation module, jointly on the four tasks. Across liver, kidney and pancreas, RepConTUR attains the highest Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), instance-wise precision, and detection F1 among the text-promptable baselines, and adding the report raises mean precision while leaving recall comparable. Against two vision-only specialists, nnU-Net and the report-supervised R-Super, RepConTUR attains the highest value on every in-domain metric for liver and pancreas and the highest mean DSC, recall, precision, and detection F1 over the four out-of-distribution public cohorts. Ablations indicate that conditioning on the narrative report raises detection F1 from 0.499 to 0.528 within the same model, that joint GSEG training raises RES F1 from 0.450 to 0.482, and that the native-3D segmentation module raises GSEG F1 from 0.139 to 0.528 over its 2D counterpart. Code is available at https://github.com/Oncosoft-Research/RepConTUR.

authors.name: Sangjoon Park
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

papers.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
papers.abstract: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

papers.title: When LLM Architectures Meet Smart Contract Vulnerability Detection: a Replication Study
papers.abstract:
Smart contracts are immutable programs deployed on blockchain platforms, where vulnerabilities can translate directly into financial loss. Among the techniques proposed for their detection, recent work has relied increasingly on Large Language Models (LLMs) guided by carefully crafted prompts. However, the evidence accumulated so far rests almost entirely on the dense Transformer architecture behind the GPT line and on model snapshots already scheduled for deprecation, leaving open the question of whether the reported behaviors reflect a general property of LLMs or an artifact of that specific design.
  This paper presents an extended replication of the empirical study by Chen et al. on LLM-based smart contract vulnerability detection. We replicate the original protocol on GPT-4 as a baseline, followed by a differentiated replication, executing the protocol on representative models based on Mixture-of-Experts and RNN-like designs, together with an attempted preliminary evaluation of State Space Models. The exact replication confirms the findings of Chen et al., including the high-recall, low-precision detection pattern they report on GPT-4. Nevertheless, the differentiated replication shows that this pattern does not transfer uniformly across the evaluated models. Those from the same architectural family may also exhibit different behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the resulting detection profile. We observe the same qualitative dense-Transformer profile in both GPT-4 and Gemma-3, despite a gap of roughly two orders of magnitude in parameter counts, whereas two Mixture-of-Experts models from different lineages exhibit qualitatively divergent behaviors, indicating that architectural family alone is insufficient to predict the detection profile.

authors.name: Gerardo Iuliano
authors.institution: AOU San Giovanni di Dio e Ruggi d'Aragona

papers.title: Neural Compression of Long ADMM Trajectory for Multiparametric Quadratic Program
papers.abstract: Solving large-scale multiparametric quadratic programs (mpQPs) in real time often requires thousands of iterative optimization updates, creating a major computational bottleneck in model predictive control and learning-enabled systems. This paper proposes TQPNet, a self-supervised neural compression framework that learns to compress long ADMM optimization trajectories into a compact neural warm start followed by a few refinement iterations. We derive a low-dimensional ADMM scheme operating on the primal-dual variables $(x,\beta)$ and show that its iteration admits an equivalent ReLU-layer representation, termed ADMM(ReLU). Building on this insight, TQPNet combines a multilayer perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP(ReLU)) and a small number of unrolled ADMM(ReLU) refinement layers. The network is trained offline using an optimality-condition-informed residual loss, eliminating the need for solver-generated labels. The proposed residual-based framework enables both self-supervised training and online solution certification through adaptive ADMM(ReLU) refinement. Experiments on large-scale mpQPs and real-time MPC applications demonstrate that TQPNet achieves high accuracy, strong generalization, and substantially faster inference than conventional optimization-based methods.

papers.title: EditAgent: Rethinking Agentic Image Editing
papers.abstract: Agentic image editors decompose complex requests into steps, but when a step fails, they mostly retry with the same narrow set of tools and a judge that scores each output by eye directly. We argue that such agents are bounded by two spaces: the action space of what the agent can do, and the observation space of what its judge can see. On our expert-annotated benchmark, a general-purpose editor yields no usable result in over 40% of the cases, and no judge is reliable across edit types. We present EditAgent, which expands both spaces. It routes each step to general editors and specialized methods, and attaches to each candidate a verification record. With these records, off-the-shelf VLM judges outperform finetuned reward models. Candidates are generated in parallel and judged in one listwise call: experts prefer this to sequential refinement in 78.5% of decided comparisons, at no more than half the judge calls. EditAgent improves two open-weight editors on three benchmarks and serves as a data engine for training stronger editors.

papers.title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset
papers.abstract: The pursuit of fair and equitable AI in human-centric tasks is critically hindered by the inherent biases and privacy risks of real-world datasets, which offer imbalanced representations of identity and often contain sensitive personal information. Consequently, state-of-the-art generative models trained on this skewed data exhibit unfair performance, particularly in identity-preserving generation. In this work we propose a pipeline for controllable generation of dataset with diverse faces for generative models training and finetuning. We achieve this by expanding foundational Arc2Face diffusion model with a flow matching generative model in the manifold of identity embeddings. We demonstrate that such approach achieves both goals of generative fidelity and label diversity not present in real human-centric datasets. As a result we collect and further contextualize a highly balanced identity-centric dataset of humans named SynthFaces. By design, our released images and identities are synthetic, reducing direct reliance on real personal images; we empirically check identity separation with a nearest-neighbor non-leakage metric. We purpose it for training and tuning of fair models for various downstream tasks, and showcase its usability in finetuning an existing adapter-based method for personalized generation.

papers.title: Tensor products of 2-representations
papers.abstract: In this paper we define comonoidal structures on additive $\Bbbk$-linear $2$-categories which guarantee the existence of a monoidal structure on the corresponding $2$-categories of $2$-representations.

papers.title: Measuring the Inaccessible: Can AI Evaluate Accessibility in Heritage Tourism?
papers.abstract: Accessibility assessment underpins the right to participate in heritage tourism, yet evaluation of archaeological sites remains artisanal: fieldwork does not scale, is often carried out without accessibility training, and is reported in forms that reach neither the sector nor disabled visitors. AI appears to offer a shortcut. We argue that assessment is measurement and inference under sparse, expert-mediated evidence: AI transforms how that evidence is captured and communicated, whereas evaluation, which turns evidence into defensible judgements, demands properties current generative systems lack. In a five-park field study in Spain and Italy, an AI desk audit scored only 66% of dimension-site combinations, could not observe embodied and organisational dimensions, and mirrored sites' online self-presentation. Simple Bayesian models instead quantify the confidence rankings deserve and calibrate desk evidence against fieldwork. We propose a separation of roles between AI and interpretable statistical evaluation as the basis for a reliable accessibility atlas.

papers.title: Inhomogeneous Geometric Last Passage Percolation and the $q$-deformed Jacobi Unitary Ensemble
papers.abstract: We study directed last passage percolation with geometric weights in a spatially inhomogeneous environment. We derive an explicit limit shape and establish fluctuation limits for the passage time, showing that, depending on the strength of the inhomogeneity, the limiting fluctuations are governed by Fredholm determinants associated with either the Airy or Bessel kernel. Our approach is based on an exact relation between the passage time and the smallest particle of the $q$-deformed Jacobi unitary ensemble ($q$-JUE). As part of our analysis, we derive the macroscopic limiting density of the $q$-JUE, which provides a natural $q$-deformation of the classical Wachter distribution, as well as of the limiting distribution of the Meixner ensemble. We further establish Airy and Bessel scaling limits for the smallest particle, which are of independent interest.

papers.title: Representation Complexity Along Learning Trajectories: Trading Width for Precision and Time
papers.abstract: What computational role does overparameterisation play during learning? Information-plane analyses suggest that neural networks can traverse representations substantially more complex than those required by their final predictors. We explore when this transient complexity serves a computational purpose by comparing the representation complexity needed for prediction with that needed to make an unknown target statistically visible through gradient feedback. We introduce an oracle model of neural network learning and use Kolmogorov \(n\)-widths to quantify effective representation complexity. Our main technical result transfers complexity bounds from the forward representation to the corresponding gradient-query features. Combined with statistical-query lower bounds, this gives a task-agnostic lower bound on the initial effective width required for target-dependent gradient information to become detectable. For \(k\)-sparse parity in \(D\) dimensions, a known target admits an \(O(k)\)-width representation, while the general bound already implies a polynomial separation between representation and discovery. We then exploit parity's invariance under coordinatewise sign reflections to identify a sharper unsigned effective width, which removes sign distinctions invisible to the parity information channel. At a transfer-compatible measurement resolution, its critical scale is \(\widetilde{\Theta}_k\left( D^{k-1}\tau^2 \right)\), up to logarithmic factors. Thus, the representation resources required to discover a predictor can substantially exceed those required to represent it once learned. Interpreting precision through accumulation over fresh samples yields a corresponding width-time frontier. Experiments support the predicted dimension dependence and examine how optimisation and generalisation depart from this idealised frontier.

papers.title: Asymptotic distributions of the Betti and Hodge numbers of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$
papers.abstract: We study the asymptotic distributions of the Betti and Hodge numbers of the moduli spaces $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$ of stable pointed curves and the all-light Hassett spaces $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0|n}$, for fixed genus $g\ge1$ as the number of markings tends to infinity. We prove central limit theorems for the full Betti distributions, whose variances grow linearly in $n$ with leading coefficients independent of the genus. For the normalized even Betti numbers, we establish refined local limit theorems with estimates uniform in degree. These local estimates yield asymptotic formulas for individual even Betti numbers and determine the sharp central ultra-log-concavity thresholds $\frac{3(e-2)}{2(3-e)}$ and $3$, respectively. For $g\ge2$, the off-diagonal Hodge components form proportions of exact orders $n^{-1/2}$ and $n^{-1}$ of the total cohomology of the two spaces, respectively. The conditional distributions of the Hodge difference $p-q$ given $p\ne q$ converge, for both spaces, to a single discrete law independent of the genus. We also prove that tautological classes account for all but a proportion of exact order $n^{-1}$ of the even cohomology of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}$. The tautological degree distribution converges to the standard Gaussian under the centering and scaling of the ambient even Betti distribution. An explicit asymptotic formula for the ratio of the ordinary Euler characteristics of the light and heavy spaces answers a question of Kannan, Serpente and Yun. The proofs combine the heavy/light substitution with a stratification of the light spaces by stable cores, singularity analysis of Hodge generating functions, and refined Fourier estimates exploiting Poincar\'e duality.

authors.name: Jinwon Choi
authors.institution: Seoul National University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Comparing metric completions of triangulated categories with Verdier quotients
papers.abstract: Neeman's metric on a triangulated category assigns lengths to morphisms and allows us to construct triangulated metric completions of the category. We prove that the metric completion of a triangulated category with respect to a constant metric is always a subcategory of the Verdier quotient by the thick subcategory generated by cones of zero-length morphisms, and we provide a sufficient criterion for equality. To that end, we define continuous functors between completions which induce triangulated functors between completions. Moreover, we give two applications. First, we show that the additive equivalence discovered by Cummings and Gratz between the Paquette-Yildirim completion and a specific metric completion of an Igusa-Todorov discrete cluster category is, in fact, a triangulated equivalence. Second, we fully classify metric completions of bounded derived categories of coherent sheaves over weighted projective lines of domestic or tubular type.

papers.title: Graphical Models Induced by Irreversible Event Accumulation on Trees
papers.abstract:
Decomposable graphical models are usually adopted for their computational convenience rather than derived from a data-generating mechanism. We show that a special class of them arises naturally from the irreversible accumulation of events along a branching history. Each event is attached to an edge of a latent rooted tree and is inherited by everything below that edge; an observation records which events have occurred at a randomly chosen node, not necessarily a leaf. When the tree is a path, this is the cumulative coding of an ordinal variable, whose indicators form a Markov chain; in the general tree case the Markov chain is replaced by a junction tree.
  The conditional independence graph of the event indicators is always decomposable and, in fact, is the line graph of the tree (maximal cliques correspond to nodes where two or more edges meet and separators are the single events on the edges joining two such nodes). The graph determines the tree up to the choice of root. A connected graph arises in this way if, and only if, it is chordal, any two of its maximal cliques share at most one vertex, no vertex is in three maximal cliques, and the graph is such that any two maximal cliques share at most one vertex. This provides a simple graphical test for compatibility with the mechanism (necessary but not sufficient, as irreversibility also constrains the distribution's support).
  The structure breaks down if we look at just the leaves, and measurement error destroys the exact screening and leads to a denser graph rather than simply a weaker dependence. We discuss inference, provide diagnostics for departures such as recurrent events, illustrate them on some simulated data and discuss their application in the context of mutation accumulation and lineage tracing where both ancestral and descendant types are sampled together.

papers.intro:
Multivariate binary data generated by the accumulation of events along historical trajectories arise in a wide range of scientific areas. Classic examples include the presence or absence of mutations in molecular evolution, somatic mutations in tumour progression, and the transmission of cultural or linguistic traits. In such systems, events typically occur irreversibly and are inherited by everything that descends from the point at which they occurred, producing strong and highly structured dependence patterns among the collected variables.

Multivariate binary data generated by the accumulation of events along historical trajectories arise in a wide range of scientific areas. Classic examples include the presence or absence of mutations in molecular evolution, somatic mutations in tumour progression, and the transmission of cultural or linguistic traits. In such systems, events typically occur irreversibly and are inherited by everything that descends from the point at which they occurred, producing strong and highly structured dependence patterns among the collected variables.

A common approach to modelling dependence in multivariate binary data is through undirected graphical models, and within this system decomposable (or chordal) graphical models play a central role. Their importance stems largely from computational factors: likelihoods factorise according to cliques and separators, statistical inference becomes tractable, and model-selection procedures can be implemented efficiently (Lauritzen, 1996; Edwards, 2000; Abreu et al., 2010). For these reasons decomposable models are often adopted as convenient approximations or as structural restrictions. However, considerably less attention has been paid to the question of when decomposability should arise naturally from an underlying data-generating mechanism.

Their importance stems largely from computational factors: likelihoods factorise according to cliques and separators, statistical inference becomes tractable, and model-selection procedures can be implemented efficiently (Lauritzen, 1996; Edwards, 2000; Abreu et al., 2010). For these reasons decomposable models are often adopted as convenient approximations or as structural restrictions. However, considerably less attention has been paid to the question of when decomposability should arise naturally from an underlying data-generating mechanism.

The present work considers this question in the context of irreversible event accumulation along tree-structured trajectories. We consider a general probabilistic model in which each event may occur at most once on a latent rooted tree and, once realised, is retained by every trajectory that continues past it. Each observation is a single lineage, sampled at an arbitrary stage of its progression, and records the presence or absence of the accumulated events. This abstract formulation incorporates essential features of a broad class of cumulative historical processes while remaining independent of any given application domain.

The present work considers this question in the context of irreversible event accumulation along tree-structured trajectories. We consider a general probabilistic model in which each event may occur at most once on a latent rooted tree and, once realised, is retained by every trajectory that continues past it. Each observation is a single lineage, sampled at an arbitrary stage of its progression, and records the presence or absence of the accumulated events. This abstract formulation incorporates essential features of a broad class of cumulative historical processes while remaining independent of any given application domain.

Because the vocabulary of the applications may be unfamiliar, we state at once what the model is when the vocabulary is removed. A lineage is a directed path in the tree beginning at the root (i.e., the history of one unit) and, since such a path is determined by its endpoint, a lineage is identified with its endpoint node. The model therefore draws a single node ZZ of a tree and reports, for each of the pp arcs, whether that arc lies on the root-to-ZZ path. Equivalently, it reports the indicator vector of a laminar (nested) family of events, of which the tree is nothing but the Hasse diagram. When the tree is a path, this is exactly the cumulative (“thermometer”) coding of an ordinal variable, and the main theorem reduces to the familiar fact that cumulative indicators form a Markov chain; a general tree replaces the ordinal variable by a hierarchical one and the Markov chain by a junction tree. The observation scheme is likewise standard: each unit is inspected once, at a random point in its progression, which is cross-sectional (current-status) sampling of an irreversible progressive process, here with a branching rather than a linear state space. Section 2.2 makes these statements precise; no knowledge of the applications is required at any point before Section 9.

Because the vocabulary of the applications may be unfamiliar, we state at once what the model is when the vocabulary is removed. A lineage is a directed path in the tree beginning at the root (i.e., the history of one unit) and, since such a path is determined by its endpoint, a lineage is identified with its endpoint node. The model therefore draws a single node ZZ of a tree and reports, for each of the pp arcs, whether that arc lies on the root-to-ZZ path. Equivalently, it reports the indicator vector of a laminar (nested) family of events, of which the tree is nothing but the Hasse diagram. When the tree is a path, this is exactly the cumulative (“thermometer”) coding of an ordinal variable, and the main theorem reduces to the familiar fact that cumulative indicators form a Markov chain; a general tree replaces the ordinal variable by a hierarchical one and the Markov chain by a junction tree. The observation scheme is likewise standard: each unit is inspected once, at a random point in its progression, which is cross-sectional (current-status) sampling of an irreversible progressive process, here with a branching rather than a linear state space. Section 2.2 makes these statements precise; no knowledge of the applications is required at any point before Section 9.

Our main result (Theorem 3.1) characterises the conditional independence structure induced by this model. The Markov graph of the observed variables is necessarily decomposable and exhibits a highly constrained clique structure: maximal cliques intersect in at most one variable, and each variable belongs to at most two maximal cliques. In particular, the graph admits a junction-tree representation with singleton separators. Decomposability is therefore not simply a convenient modelling assumption in this setting, but a structural consequence of irreversible event accumulation on a tree.

The Markov graph of the observed variables is necessarily decomposable and exhibits a highly constrained clique structure: maximal cliques intersect in at most one variable, and each variable belongs to at most two maximal cliques. In particular, the graph admits a junction-tree representation with singleton separators. Decomposability is therefore not simply a convenient modelling assumption in this setting, but a structural consequence of irreversible event accumulation on a tree.

Beyond the structural theorem, these results establish a direct correspondence between the topology of the event tree and the structure of the induced graphical model. Maximal cliques correspond to the nodes of the event tree at which two or more edges meet, while the arc-events joining two such nodes act as separator variables linking adjacent clique blocks. Thus, the resulting junction tree reproduces the event tree with its nodes of degree one removed; when every internal node branches, this is exactly the branching skeleton of the accumulation process. We complement this with a converse (Theorem 7.3): the three structural properties of Theorem 3.1 are not only necessary but also sufficient. They therefore characterise exactly the class of graphs realisable by accumulation trees, and turn these conditions into a decidable criterion of graphical compatibility.

It is tempting to model each observation as a complete lineage, that is, a root-to-leaf path. We show in Section 2 that this apparently natural choice is in fact degenerate: complete lineages satisfy exact flow constraints which collapse the induced graph and destroy the clique structure described above. Proposition 2.5 makes the collapse explicit: under leaf-only sampling, the Markov graph reduces to a disjoint union of cliques formed by sibling arcs pointing at leaves, and every other variable becomes an isolated vertex. Allowing each lineage to be observed at an arbitrary stage of progression, so that intermediate states carry positive probability, removes the degeneracy and yields the structure we describe. It is also the more faithful description of applications such as mitochondrial lineage tracing, in which the sample may contain lineages caught at intermediate stages, not only at their endpoints (Amorim, 2019; Ludwig et al., 2019). See Section 9.

These results suggest a theoretical explanation for the empirical success of tree-based and decomposable graphical models in systems driven by cumulative events. They also suggest natural statistical diagnostics: deviations from the structural properties derived here may indicate mechanisms such as recombination, recurrent events, mixtures of populations, or observation noise (Didelot and Maiden, 2010).

papers.title: The Gleason--Kahane--Zelazko theorem: a gentle introduction
papers.abstract: After some personal recollections of Jean-Pierre Kahane, this paper gives a gentle introduction to the Gleason-Kahane-Zelazko theorem. The theorem states that a normalised complex-linear functional on a unital complex Banach algebra is multiplicative whenever it does not vanish on invertible elements. Neither continuity of the functional nor commutativity of the algebra is assumed. We give a detailed account of three proofs: the original argument of Gleason and, independently, Kahane and Zelazko; the polynomial proof of Roitman and Sternfeld; and a proof by the author. We explain the complex analysis behind each: a special case of Hadamard's factorisation theorem, a polynomial argument using the fundamental theorem of algebra, and the P\'olya-Saxer theorem on zero-free entire functions and their derivatives. The elementary entire-function lemma needed for the first proof is proved in full; the P\'olya-Saxer theorem is used without proof. We give full details of the algebraic argument common to the three proofs, which deduces multiplicativity from the preservation of squares, including the non-commutative case. We then discuss applications and counterexamples, and present an extension to Ransford's generalised spectra using the Roitman--Sternfeld argument. We conclude with a brief guide to the more recent literature.

papers.title: MoLRSI: A Recursive Self-Improving AI agent for Molecular Discovery
papers.abstract: Molecular discovery requires navigating vast combinatorial search spaces while balancing competing biological objectives. AI agents can automate expert-defined molecular design protocols, but automation alone does not address how to optimize workflows for new tasks or improve their development through experience. Here we introduce MoLRSI, an AI agent that combines systematic optimization of workflows and model architectures with persistent cross-task memory to recursively improve its search policy for molecular discovery. Workflow performance, refinement outcomes, and execution feedback guide subsequent searches, allowing the agent to improve both its workflows and its strategy for developing them. We evaluate MoLRSI in two challenging molecular discovery settings that require balancing competing properties. In antibiotic discovery, MoLRSI developed a screening workflow balancing antibacterial activity, cytotoxicity and structural novelty, achieving an experimental hit rate of 15.9%, compared with 8.7% for a previous expert-led workflow using the same training data and screening library. In de novo peptide-MHC binder design, MoLRSI developed workflows that jointly consider target binding and specificity, producing eight experimentally validated hits against MART-1 and SARS-CoV-1 pMHCs with preferential binding over tested off-targets while Claude Science completely failed. These findings demonstrate how experience-guided workflow optimization can address competing discovery objectives while improving the search strategies used in subsequent campaigns.

authors.name: James J. Collins

papers.title: Homogeneous polynomial approximation on symmetric convex bodies: A proof of Kro\'o's conjecture
papers.abstract: We resolve Kro\'o's 2004 conjecture on homogeneous polynomial approximation in every dimension, without smoothness or curvature assumptions. For every origin-symmetric convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ with nonempty interior, every continuous real function on $\partial K$ is uniformly approximated by sums of homogeneous polynomials of degrees $n$ and $n+1$ as $n\to\infty$. Moreover, approximation of the constant function by homogeneous polynomials of degree $2n$ is uniform over all such bodies in each fixed dimension. Via homogenization, we also resolve Kro\'o's 2019 weighted approximation conjecture for every convex admissible weight on Euclidean space. The key construction produces homogeneous polynomials with a common Gaussian boundary profile and localization errors controlled by arbitrary polynomial weights. Its analytic core is a weighted Gaussian approximation theorem: for \(d\ge2\), sufficiently broad Gaussians on $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ can be approximated by $e^{-f}F$, where $f$ is nonnegative, convex and Lipschitz with $f(0)=0$, and $F$ is a Schwartz function with Fourier support in an arbitrarily small ball about the origin. Small Fourier support allows Taylor truncation to a lower degree, while the remainder enforces decay through homogenization. We then use positive spherical quadrature and degree raising to yield the full approximation theorem.

papers.title: Spectral isometries of unital $C^*$-algebras
papers.abstract: This paper provides a human digestion of a proof of the spectral isometry conjecture for $C^*$-algebras found by GPT-6 Astra. We prove that every unital surjective complex-linear spectral isometry between unital $C^*$-algebras is a Jordan isomorphism. Without the assumption that the map preserves the identity, it is a central unitary multiple of a Jordan isomorphism. The main step is to show that an entire one-parameter group of unital spectral isometries consists of algebra automorphisms. To prove this, we extend the group to the bidual, which splits into finite and properly infinite summands. On the finite part, we use quadratic and cubic trace identities and on the properly infinite part, we apply a structure theorem for maps that preserve square-zero elements. To show that both summands are invariant, we use holomorphic dependence on the parameter together with a uniform resolvent bound, which ensures that self-adjoint elements have images with real spectrum. We then apply the group theorem to inner automorphisms conjugated by the original spectral isometry. This reduces the problem to the commutative case, where Nagasawa's theorem completes the proof.

papers.title: QMUL_AK at AISA-ArabicFC: Schema-Constrained Function Calling with ALLaM
papers.abstract: We describe the QMUL_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.

papers.title: Embodied at Sea: Imitation Learning for Multi-Task Underwater Manipulation
papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.

papers.title: QSoftCore: A Conceptual Foundation for Quantum Software Engineering
papers.abstract: Quantum software engineering (QSE) requires understanding application requirements, quantum programs and algorithms, quantum computation paradigms, executions, and deployment. However, relevant quantum computing (QC) concepts are often defined across physical, mathematical, and paradigm-specific levels of abstraction, making it difficult for the QSE community and hence proposed methods to refer to them consistently. To this end, we present QSoftCore, a conceptual model that reorganizes established QC concepts from a software engineering perspective and connects quantum applications, computational problems, algorithms, configurations, programs, and paradigm-specific computation specifications with state evolution, execution results, and backends. Our assessment against QSE literature across key software engineering activities indicates that QSoftCore provides shared QC referents for quantum computations, executions, deployment configurations, backends, and measurement evidence across the QSE lifecycle.

papers.title: UniffordInteractor: Reasoning the Unified Affordance for Human and Multi-Object Interaction
papers.abstract: Deriving plausible and dynamic Human Object Interaction (HOI) has gained tremendous progress in Embodied AI and Immersive AR/VR. While existing HOI methods have effectively explored human interaction with individual or fixed objects, they still show limitations in complex multi-object interaction scenes. Meanwhile, previous approaches focus more on the contact information held by human-object relation, overlooking the significance of the contact situation of various entities (i.e., object-object). To address these limitations, we propose UniffordInteractor, a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework that leverages unified affordance for realistic and long-horizon human and multi-object interaction modeling. At the reasoning stage, we devise a Unified Affordance Reasoner (UAR) that employs a fine-tuned 3D Multimodal Large Language Model for unified object-centric affordance prediction. At the interacting stage, we propose Hierarchical Interaction Generator (HIG), which formulates the interaction generation as a hierarchical (e.g., root to body to hand to objects) autoregressive prediction, conditioned on the obtained unified affordance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniffordInteractor surpasses SOTA counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation.

papers.title: Differentiable Electronic Grand Canonical Learning for Electrochemistry
papers.abstract: Electronic grand-canonical density functional theory captures how structure and electronic charge respond to electrode potential and, together with statistical mechanics, how these responses give rise to emergent phenomena. However, its computational cost limits the system sizes and sampling times accessible to first- principles simulations. Here, we introduce a differentiable architecture that represents the grand potential and obtains forces and electronic charge as its derivatives, exactly satisfying the mixed-derivative constraints required for thermodynamic consistency, and implement it within the equivariant MACE framework as GC- MACE. We demonstrate more accurate joint learning across multiple electrochemical interfaces and improved transferability to thicker water films relative to previous models, while enabling constant-potential simulations at substantially larger length and time scales than accessible to ab initio molecular dynamics. With broad training data, the framework offers a route to thermodynamically consistent foundation interatomic potentials for the electronic grand canonical ensemble

papers.title: Bouba Beats Kiki, and Other Regularities in the Subjective Preferences of LLMs
papers.abstract:
Users engage with large language models on tasks that are purely objective ("When was Netflix founded?"), purely subjective ("What should I name my child?") or anywhere in-between. We have rich tools for evaluating model accuracy with respect to objective criteria. However, when it comes to subjective aspects of a task, we do not have similarly developed methodology at hand. In this paper, we take some early steps towards framing the question of subjective evaluation. Rather than measure how often a model is right or wrong on a question, we instead ask, how do models make choices among multiple viable responses without a clear winner?
  To study this question, we restrict our focus to short-form content, and consider comparison tasks among three such content types: numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. We identify 29 aspects of these short-form examples covering many areas of syntax and semantics (length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, spoken sound, etc.). We show first that models tend to have strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects. Second, we show that variations in how the model is asked to express a preference may cause some of these aspects to activate or deactivate in the model's selection. Third, we show that overall preference distributions among pairs may vary radically based on seemingly-unimportant variations in the nature of the question posed to the model, raising new questions about manipulation. And finally, we show that, if models are used both to create lists of alternatives and to rank them, there are unexpected interactions between the two stages that may also drive the models' stated preferences.

papers.title: Learning Graph Beliefs for Active Radio Mapping With Decision-Certified Multi-Step Sensing
papers.abstract: Radio maps provide essential wireless propagation knowledge for network optimization and autonomous platforms. Acquiring dense measurements, however, is prohibitively costly, requiring active sampling to prioritize informative measurements. Existing active sampling methods typically rely on variances from prescribed spatial models or learned pointwise uncertainty, which may not fully capture the spatial correlation of different measurements. This paper proposes GraphBARC, a graph-structured active radio map construction framework that integrates learned spatial modeling with analytical Bayesian inference. A graph network learns correlated node and edge factors using only acquired measurements, inducing a joint full-map belief that supports analytical observation updates without retraining. Rather than immediate one-step acquisition, it adopts a nonmyopic sensing strategy that evaluates joint map-wide Bayes risk reduction over feasible multi-step routes, accounting for information redundancy among planned measurements. We reuse candidate responses and derive residual-based bounds directly on route-value differences, retaining shared response-error structure to avoid uniformly high-accuracy evaluation. An error-aware continuation bound screens unpromising prefixes, after which only responses needed for unresolved comparisons are refined. We further establish a computable decision-gap bound and show that certified exclusions remain valid during refinement. Experiments show that GraphBARC reduces mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) by over 16% relative to the evaluated baselines and core planning time by 56% compared with the fixed-accuracy, unpruned implementation.

papers.title: A $B_{1g}$ phonon unlocks $d$-wave superconductivity in the repulsive Hubbard model
papers.abstract: Using numerically exact finite-temperature quantum Monte Carlo, we demonstrate that a $B_{1g}$ phonon coupled to the doped $t$-$t'$ repulsive Hubbard model produces genuine $d$-wave superconductivity at a substantial transition temperature, in excess of either interaction alone. The observed trends suggest that stronger Hubbard repulsion may cooperate with the phonon to further raise the pairing scale. The enhancement persists at stronger repulsion within the accessible window, limited by the fermion sign problem, and follows a common trend across phonon frequencies $\Omega$ when organized by a retardation scale $2\pi T/\Omega$. We also find a well-defined superconducting dome in doping, echoing a characteristic feature of correlated superconductors. Our results identify the $B_{1g}$ phonon as a plausible microscopic ingredient for robust $d$-wave superconductivity in the Hubbard model and suggest a concrete, physically motivated route toward materials with higher superconducting transition temperatures.

papers.title: Hot off the Stacks: X-rays in Romulus25, Part I - Comparisons to Observations from eRosita
papers.abstract: Recent observations from the from Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA all-sky survey data have helped to illuminate the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) around galaxies at Milky Way-masses and above. In our study, we explore the hot X-ray emitting (T \textgreater 10$^6$ K) component of the CGM in over 750 galaxies from the Romulus25 cosmological simulation (Tremmel et al. 2017) between 10.0 < log(M$_*/M_{\odot}$) < 11.5. We forward-model soft X-ray [0.5 - 2.0] keV observations of our simulated galaxies using pyXSIM and SIXTE to measure the X-ray surface brightness (SB) profiles of the hot CGM. We then compare the average X-ray surface brightness profiles of six stellar-mass selected sub-samples to compare to the observational results from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. 2024a. Broadly, we find that our stacked SB profiles are too bright compared to observations from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al.(2024a) particularly in the inner CGM. Additionally, we calculate the X-ray luminosity (L$_{\chi}$) of the hot CGM for each galaxy and compare the average L$_{\chi}$ across stellar mass to observations from Zhang et al. (2024b) as well as measurements from the EAGLE, TNG, SIMBA simulations. Across stellar mass, the average L$_{\chi}$ of galaxies from Romulus25 are brighter than observations except at the lower, Milky Way-mass end where we are in relative agreement with both observations and most other simulations. We also consider a zero-metallicity emission model, because Romulus25 does not have metal-line cooling, finding the average L$_{\chi}$ decreases by nearly an order-of-magnitude, which better matches observations particularly in the Milky Way-mass regime.

papers.title: DexSuite: An All-in-One Framework for Dexterous Manipulation Across Arms, Hands, and Tasks
papers.abstract: Human-level dexterity remains a central open problem in robotics, yet few simulation frameworks cover the full workflow of dexterous manipulation, from setting up a robot to collecting dexterous demonstrations and evaluating policies. We present DexSuite, an all-in-one simulation framework for dexterous manipulation built on the Genesis simulator. DexSuite provides 30 tasks and assembles its 10 arms and 12 end-effectors, from parallel-jaw grippers to dexterous hands, into more than 100 single-arm robots and thousands of bimanual pairs. It also ships a standardized environment API, integrated teleoperation, and simulated tactile sensing. Moreover, we define a benchmark of 16 task-embodiment pairs spanning diverse contact complexities and horizons, and release a dataset of 4,700 successful episodes in simulation from human teleoperation, scripted experts, and learned policies. We release DexSuite as open source and hope others will build on it. Videos and datasets are available at https://dexsuiteorg.github.io

papers.title: Combining Multiple Incomplete Astronomical Surveys to Estimate Galaxy Flux Distributions
papers.abstract: In astrophysics, the distributions of fluxes or intensities of populations of sources provide insight into the structure and evolution of the universe. We propose a science-driven hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the X-ray flux distribution of a population of galaxies. The distribution is parameterized via a broken power law model, formulated as a mixture of Pareto distributions, and is fit using data from a combination of non-representative X-ray and optical surveys. Because fainter sources are less likely to be detected, astronomical surveys suffer from incompleteness at the low-intensity end, and dedicated survey simulations are used to study the resulting missing-data pattern and determine the form of corrections. We introduce a methodology to combine data from two (or more) surveys with different incompleteness functions. This allows us to leverage deeper surveys (e.g., optical) to more fully characterize the X-ray log(N)-log(S) (where fewer sources are detected). We take advantage of a well-calibrated characterization of the missing-data pattern, particularly in X-ray surveys, to make incompleteness corrections for sources that are not detected in either survey. The proposed model is validated using a simulation study designed to mimic the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), demonstrating accurate recovery of the flux distribution even under high proportions of systematic incompleteness. Finally, we apply our proposed method to data from the CDF-S.

papers.title: TERRA: Task-Oriented Edge AI for Regional Fire Detection with Identity-Free Reporting
papers.abstract: Distributed fire-monitoring systems may involve many sensing devices reporting over a shared uplink, even though the operational objective is often to identify regions exhibiting evidence of fire rather than to recover device-specific measurements. We introduce TERRA (Task-Oriented Edge Representation and Regional Aggregation), an edge-AI framework that combines task-oriented local inference, identity-free region-tagged reporting, and permutation-invariant regional evidence aggregation. TERRA supports two reporting modes: TERRA-Score, in which each device communicates a quantized local fire probability, and TERRA-Feature, in which it communicates a compact learned representation for receiver-side aggregation using a permutation-invariant DeepSets model. Using all 15 numerical sensing modalities of the distributed indoor EN54 fire-alarm dataset as a proof-of-concept testbed, we evaluate regional inference for an episode-level fire-scenario target under repetition-disjoint three-fold cross-validation. We study representation size, task-payload quantization, report availability, and robustness to missed and false recovered messages. With nine reports and perfect message recovery, TERRA-Feature achieves mean AUPRC 0.990 using a 24-bit task payload, while TERRA-Score achieves 0.987 using only 6 bits; both attain an MDR of 1.81% at FAR $\leq$1%. TERRA-Feature achieves slightly higher AUPRC under reliable recovery, whereas the more compact TERRA-Score is less sensitive to increasing false-message contamination.

papers.title: Continuous Representation Theory of the Hierarchical Equations of Motion
papers.abstract: The numerical stability of the hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) depends on the representation of their Liouvillian. Here, we introduce a continuous gauge freedom through a generalized Bogoliubov transformation with the parameter $r$. It subsumes earlier phase space stabilization methods as special cases and explains both their stabilizing mechanism and their limitations. We find that gauge optimization balances the suppression of hierarchy growth against errors in reconstructing the reduced density operator, and show that the factor $e^{2r}-1$ controls the feedback strength, with earlier methods located at the boundary for reconstruction-error amplification, $r=\frac{1}{2}\ln 2$. For spin-boson models, this boundary gauge recovers known stabilizations for undamped and weakly damped modes. In the weakly damped case, an interior gauge further reduces the trace error by more than an order of magnitude. For the Holstein model, interior gauges reduce trace drift by about an order of magnitude relative to the previously adopted fixed representation at the same bond dimension. This improvement stabilizes error-sensitive calculations of equilibrium autocorrelation functions. Our formulation thus extends fixed stabilization methods to a continuous family of HEOM representations generated by linear canonical transformations, and establishes a framework for improving numerical stability and accuracy through continuous gauge selection.

papers.title: Neuroscience of Improvisation Across Music and Other Domains: A Survey and Outlook
papers.abstract: Improvisation (or Improv), the real-time generation of novel, context-appropriate action, occurs in music, dance, theater, sport, education, therapy, and professional practice. Its neuroscience, however, has been studied almost exclusively for music, where most quantitative neuroimaging evidence lies. A PRISMA-style search done by authors quantifies this imbalance: of 111 identified studies, 70.3\% concern musical improvisation or general psychometric creativity. This explains why earlier surveys are either music-centered or confined to a single construct. This survey addresses that gap in two ways. First, for music, it organizes findings from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), hyperscanning, neurofeedback, and brain stimulation, and reports transparently where the evidence agrees (e.g., experience-dependent changes in frontal engagement, increased frontal alpha and theta power) and where it is heterogeneous (e.g., the direction of lateral prefrontal activity, hemispheric lateralization, the interpretation of alpha power). Second, it extends the review to dance, theater, sport, education, therapy, and professional practice, where behavioral, qualitative, and simulation-based studies predominate. Overall, the current evidence does not point to a universal neural signature of improvisation within music domain or other domains. We conclude with an outlook on wearable EEG--fNIRS sensing and closed-loop brain--computer interfaces for musical improvisation, the domain with sufficient evidence, formulated as an expertise-gated control problem and discussed as a possible complement to deliberate practice, and we list the evidence needed for other domains.

papers.title: Application of PDE emulators for a multi-material, multi-physics simulation problem
papers.abstract: Machine learning (ML) architectures are being developed for fast emulation of numerical simulators to accelerate both scientific discovery and engineering design. While these approaches are well-tested on popular PDE (partial differential equation) benchmarks, it is necessary to evaluate their performance on datasets that more accurately reflect industrial and engineering applications. We evaluate several computer vision-based architectures trained as surrogate models on a challenging computational physics task involving multiple materials, revealing significant implementation challenges for adapting certain pre-trained models, including transformer-based architectures. For such multi-physics multi-material datasets, our results underscore the importance of learning algorithms designed for sparse and imbalanced data, techniques for adapting spatial encodings and physical consistency metrics, in addition to methods for reducing the cost of generating sufficient training data.

papers.title: Preserving Safety During Sequential Fine-Tuning: A Factorial and Geometric Analysis of Replay
papers.abstract: Benign fine-tuning can erode safety alignment in large language models, and sequential adaptation substantially compounds this risk. Prior work mitigates this erosion by replaying harmful-prompt refusals and benign-compliance examples, while other work instead matches base-model logits via distillation. However, the individual contributions of supervised exposure and distillation to safety behavior and refusal geometry during sequential adaptation remain unclear. We factor these two strategies apart and study their behavioral and geometric effects during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B across diverse task sequences (code generation, German-language summarization, and science question-answering). Behaviorally, supervised replay exposure yields the largest reduction in HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) on Mistral, averaging 51.1 points below base, but at a substantial over-refusal cost, averaging 53.4 points above base on OR-Bench-hard. Logit distillation, without any supervised replay loss, largely prevents safety erosion at a fraction of this cost: an average 5.4-point ASR reduction against only a 5.1-point rise in over-refusal. Llama shows the same asymmetry between the two strategies. Combining exposure and distillation moderates exposure's over-refusal while leaving downstream task scores largely unaffected. Geometrically, the two models diverge: on Mistral, distillation preserves the base refusal direction more closely than exposure does, whereas on Llama, refusal behavior after exposure largely survives ablation of the extracted refusal direction. This dissociation between models indicates that preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety.

papers.title: What Can Firms Do in the Face of Model Distillation?
papers.abstract: Model distillation has become a major concern in the rapidly growing generative AI discourse. In its simplest form, distillation is the phenomenon where smaller firms can use data distilled from transcripts of conversations with powerful proprietary closed-weight models to train their own models, thus achieving reasonably high model quality but at much lower costs. Besides the legitimate safety and security concerns associated with distillation, another major issue is how it can also distort marketplace outcomes. This motivates us to initiate an exploration of the problem from an economic theory lens. We consider a setting with two players: an incumbent and a distilling competitor and characterize how the incumbent's model characteristics drive the incentives around how much the competitor should distill. We also consider the impact of distillation on key market outcomes like user-side surplus and the incumbent's utility. Our key contribution, however, is to study interventions for preventing or limiting distillation attacks. In this context, we study two settings: i) when it is possible, with a certain probability (which grows in the extent of distillation conducted), to detect an attack on the incumbent's model; and ii) when a distillation attack cannot be reliably detected. In the first setting, we show that penalty-based regulations can be very effective in completely deterring distillation, although it can have potentially adverse effects on market competition and user surplus. In the latter setting, we show that the incumbent can use self-distillation as a mitigation strategy. Importantly, the effectiveness of self-distillation depends on how cost-efficiently the incumbent can deploy a new self-distilled model on the market. On the positive side, self-distillation can preserve market competition thus protecting user surplus to some extent.

papers.title: Post-Training Large Language Models with LLMON
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) treat all context tokens uniformly, lacking explicit separation between executable instructions and passive data. This leads to prompt injection vulnerabilities, ambiguous instruction binding, and unreliable execution control. We present a post-training methodology using LLMON (LLM Object Notation), a framework that enables separating instructions from data and requires explicit identifier-based execution. We construct a large-scale structured training corpus of 4.6B tokens spanning general, RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation), and tool-calling data, augmented with distractor-infused variants in which competing instructions and irrelevant data segments are present in context but not referenced. Post-training two Granite-4.1 base models (3B and 8B) through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning, we show that LLMON-structured supervision reduces attack success rates on indirect prompt-injection benchmarks from 53-100% to 0.02-5.6% while preserving general capabilities. We further introduce attention-based interpretability metrics that diagnose failure modes at individual transformer layers for structured inputs, revealing how our approach reshapes internal attention patterns. Our results demonstrate that explicit execution semantics can be taught through standard post-training without architectural modification.

authors.name: Yada Zhu
authors.institution: IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center

papers.title: MiniMMD: Minimization of MMD for Sampling, Inference and Integration
papers.abstract: Many problems in computational statistics and machine learning can be formulated as approximating a target distribution by minimizing a discrepancy over a restricted class of candidate distributions. This minimum-discrepancy viewpoint appears, for example, in numerical integration, sampling, generative modelling, and statistical inference, but these instances are often studied separately in the literature. This thesis develops the first unified treatment of these many problems through the minimization of the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), a kernel-based discrepancy between probability measures. The central theme is that MMD is not only a statistically meaningful distance between probability distributions, but also a tractable optimization objective to design practical and efficient algorithms. This thesis summarizes the recent theoretical and empirical advancements of such minimum-MMD based algorithms.

papers.title: SkillCT: A Multidimensional Benchmark and Execution-Free Baseline for Agent Skill Assessment
papers.abstract: Agent skills package instructions, scripts, and resources for specialized tasks and are increasingly distributed through public Web repositories. However, existing skill benchmarks primarily focus on downstream task execution, insufficiently assessing specification quality, behavioral robustness, semantic alignment, and responsibility boundaries. Their reliance on task-specific tools, environments, and repeated executions limits scalability and pre-deployment assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillCT, a benchmark that broadens skill assessment from downstream utility to a multidimensional characterization of skill quality. SkillCT evaluates skills across nine complementary dimensions spanning three aspects: Static Assessment, which captures intrinsic properties of the skill specification; Dynamic Assessment, which measures whether the induced behavior remains stable across backbone models and request variations; and Human-Assisted Assessment, which examines behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. These dimensions provide a broader view of skill quality than execution success. Applying SkillCT to a public skill corpus establishes a reference benchmark for analyzing quality weaknesses and relationships across dimensions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an execution-free quality evaluation baseline that predicts the multidimensional quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving and leveraging similar reference skills, without executing the skills under evaluation. This reduces token consumption and evaluation time, while preserving consistency with the full assessment. Furthermore, SkillCT-guided optimization improves downstream task success and execution efficiency, demonstrating its value for skill refinement. These findings highlight the effectiveness of SkillCT in supporting scalable skill assessment, optimization, and repository maintenance.

authors.name: Ziyuan Yang
authors.institution: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

papers.title: From Natural Language to Real Schematics: An Automated Workflow for Power Electronics Schematic Synthesis
papers.abstract: Designing power electronics converters traditionally requires intensive human expertise across topology sizing, commercial component selection, circuit simulation verification, and schematic drafting. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise in electronic design automation (EDA), applying standalone LLMs directly to board-level power electronics schematic synthesis suffers from severe engineering hallucinations, including inaccurate analytical sizing, fabricated or mismatched component part numbers, violated voltage derating margins, and broken topological connectivity. In this paper, we propose a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that translates natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables. Our workflow integrates six stages across three functional columns: (1) requirement parsing and knowledge-driven power stage synthesis covering non-isolated (Buck, Boost) and isolated/resonant (Flyback, DAB, half-bridge LLC) topologies; (2) contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection grounded in distributor APIs and OEM datasheets, coupled with closed-loop ngspice transient verification and stress feedback; and (3) modular control hardware integration and multi-format deliverable generation featuring native KiCad netlist round-trip verification. End-to-end case studies on a 24-36V to 12V,2A Buck converter (29 positions, 83 verified terminals) and an isolated 48V to 24V, 0.5A, Dual-Active Bridge (DAB) converter (87 positions, 341 verified terminals), alongside comparative evaluations against a Vanilla LLM baseline, demonstrate that our framework improves component verification coverage from 22.2 to 98.6, nominal value consistency from 0 to 97.7, and SPICE simulation pass rates from 0 to 100.

authors.name: Jiahua Ying
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Power System Operation and Control

papers.title: Age-Resolved Vertical Motions in the Milky Way Warp: A Localized Enhancement in Intermediate-Age Populations
papers.abstract: Determining how the Milky Way warp evolves provides constraints on the formation and dynamical evolution of galactic disks. Using Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment Data Release 19 (APOGEE DR19) spectroscopy, we estimate ages for 222,355 red giants. With Gaia astrometry and geometric distances, we analyze 168,824 of these stars in five age bins spanning $0$--$10$ Gyr. The warp-related radial vertical-velocity ($V_Z$) profile of young red giants ($0$--$2$ Gyr) is broadly consistent with those of classical Cepheids and young open clusters. Over $9\leq R<12$ kpc, we find that the mean $V_Z$ values of the intermediate-age red giants ($2$--$4$ and $4$--$6$ Gyr) are $1.48\pm0.46$ and $1.49\pm0.52$ km s$^{-1}$ higher than that of the young population, respectively. By contrast, at $R\simeq12$--$13$ kpc, the $V_Z$ profiles of the $0$--$6$ Gyr red giants are consistent within their uncertainties. The intermediate-age enhancement persists across our robustness tests and may reflect smaller effective kinematic warp onset radii for the intermediate-age populations. The observed velocity differences may arise from the combined effects of earlier perturbations and the present-day warp, or from differences in vertical structure among stellar populations.

authors.name: Haifeng Wang
authors.institution: Changchun University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks
papers.abstract: Chemical kinetics determines molecular stability, reaction selectivity and the evolution of reacting mixtures, but discovering the underlying reaction networks remains challenging. Here we introduce ReactNexus, a generative framework for kinetic-guided network exploration starting solely from reactant graphs. Generative models propose transition states and predict the full reaction trajectories connecting reactants and products, while calculations using a machine-learned interatomic potential verify connectivity and evaluate electronic barriers. On an in-distribution benchmark of 10,000 generated candidates, 80.8% connect to the input reactant after density functional theory (DFT) optimization and intrinsic reaction coordinate verification. The resulting networks uncover lower-barrier cooperative pathways and competition between catalyst release and catalyst-bound branches. In the examined carbocation cascades, coverage of known product precursors saturates after limited expansion and distinct entries converge onto shared intermediates, indicating a compact accessible reaction space. Network-derived candidate structures further assist mass-spectral interpretation of a complex nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Together, these results establish a generative approach to reaction-network discovery and mechanistic analysis without predefined products or reaction templates.
