papers.title: On separators in $K_t$-minor-free graphs
papers.abstract: This manuscript presents a proof of the Alon--Seymour--Thomas conjecture developed under the author's guidance using ChatGPT 6pro. The author has checked every formula and theorem by hand and used Codex to assist with writing. GPT 6.1 Sol (Max) was also used to check the proof repeatedly and to generate numerous examples for verification. More precisely, for every integer $h\geq3$, every $n$-vertex $K_h$-minor-free graph has a vertex set of size at most $\min{n,21h\sqrt n}$ whose deletion leaves every component with at most $2n/3$ vertices.

papers.title: Counterfactual Public Opinion Projection for Intervention Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Effective public opinion intervention requires forecasts of how the same event would evolve under alternative actions. Existing methods mainly capture observational associations and inadequately address treatment selection bias. The paper proposes a counterfactual public opinion projection framework for intervention decision making. Each intervention is represented by its timing, type, content and intensity. Causal triggering structures are inferred from propagation event sequences. Counterfactual trajectories of attention, sentiment and polarization are generated from adversarially balanced representations. Candidate interventions are then compared through repeated rollouts. Semisynthetic experiments yielded an overall F1 comparable to a direct structure learning baseline and a recall of 0.698 for causal edges linking semantically dissimilar content. Representation diagnostics showed that the gradient reversal layer reduced treatment information leakage from 0.163 to 0.140. Bootstrap analyses of real data further revealed intervention specific model effects on attention, sentiment and polarization.

papers.title: How Hard Is It to Compute Cover Time?
papers.abstract: It is $\#\mathrm{P}\text{-hard}$. Even for connected simple undirected unweighted graphs, deciding whether an expected random-walk cover time is at most a given rational threshold is $\#\mathrm{P}\text{-hard}$ under polynomial-time Turing reductions, both from a specified starting vertex and when maximized over starting vertices. Both families have a universal vertex, called the hub, and diameter two. Deleting the hub leaves a planar bipartite graph, and every non-hub vertex has degree at most five. A shared construction encodes an Euler-tour count in rare covering walks. For specified starts, a number of fractional bits linear in the queried graph's vertex count suffices for recovery. For the maximum-start problem, a fixed cube attachment makes the maximizing starts known, and one interpolation of expected cover times recovers the count. Both reductions use polynomial-size graphs and polynomial-bit threshold queries. For general graphs, both comparison problems can be solved in polynomial time with access to an $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{PP}}$ oracle.

Rational transition probabilities give rational expected cover times in the finite irreducible setting [15].

We combine ordinary cover-time expectations to isolate walks that cover the subdivided graph before reaching the hub. Each walk is weighted by its probability and the expected time from its final vertex to the hub. The Euler trails contribute the Euler-tour count multiplied by an exactly computable coefficient; we call this an Euler contribution. A subdivided edge can have all its internal vertices visited from its two ends without ever being traversed end to end. Our principal estimate accounts for these possibilities and bounds their total weighted mass. Choosing the subdivision length to be a large enough multiple of the number of edges makes the error, after normalization, less than 1/161/16. We compute the exact normalizing coefficient by rational linear algebra. Approximating the expected cover times accurately enough then lets us recover the integer Euler-tour count by rounding.

papers.title: Berry curvature dipole circuit quantum electrodynamics
papers.abstract: Quantum three-wave mixing is an important resource in superconducting quantum circuits. The traditional implementation uses Josephson junction arrays and is activated by magnetic flux. Here we introduce the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) quantum circuit element, which achieves quantum three-wave mixing without breaking time-reversal symmetry. This quantum three-wave mixing results from the BCD nonlinear Hall effect in noncentrosymmetric quantum materials taken to a dissipationless, quantum coherent few-photon regime. We show how nonlinear Hall materials can be integrated to superconducting microwave circuits to accomplish multiphoton vacuum Rabi splittings and dynamical stabilization of bosonic Schr\"odinger cat states. Such BCD circuit quantum electrodynamics are a concrete exemplar of a physical resource for quantum information processing enabled by nonlinear response in quantum materials.

papers.title: Seeing and Imagining as One: Unified Video Generation and 4D Perception for Embodied World Modeling
papers.abstract: Embodied world models should not only imagine plausible futures, but also perceive the geometric, semantic, and motion structure of the evolving world. We present GenSight, a unified embodied world model that brings future video generation and dense perception into a single pretrained video diffusion transformer. GenSight uses a unified spatiotemporal representation for video, depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow. Built on a shared DiT backbone, GenSight uses lightweight task modulation to predict all modalities within the same architecture. All tasks are jointly optimized within a unified velocity prediction space. At inference, GenSight supports two complementary modes: multi-step future video generation with aligned dense predictions and single-step dense perception from an observed video. By unifying modality representation, model architecture, and prediction space, GenSight avoids separate modality-specific pipelines and couples appearance, geometry, semantics, and motion in a shared representation. It promotes cross-modal consistency and allows dense perception to benefit from the spatiotemporal priors learned through video generation. Trained on embodied manipulation data spanning multiple robot embodiments and human-hand interactions, GenSight demonstrates strong performance in both video generation and dense 4D perception, highlighting the effectiveness of unifying seeing and imagining for embodied world modeling.

authors.name: Hexiang Wei
authors.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Satisficing Regret Minimization in Bandits with Knapsacks
papers.abstract: We study satisficing regret minimization in bandits with knapsacks (BwK), where a learner sequentially selects randomized policies, i.e., distributions over arms, to obtain mean rewards above a satisficing threshold as frequently as possible while respecting finite resource budgets. The performance is measured by satisficing regret, the cumulative deficits of the selected policies' mean rewards below this threshold. Resource constraints introduce two difficulties: an algorithm can incur linear satisficing regret even with small standard regret as deficits to the threshold cannot be compensated, and random consumption can cause early resource depletion even when policies are feasible in expectation. To address these challenges, we propose SELECTwK, a general algorithmic template that uses a BwK learning oracle algorithm with sub-linear expected (standard) regret upper bound to search for and test candidate satisficing policies (i.e., policies whose mean rewards exceed satisficing threshold and whose expected resource consumption is feasible over the time horizon). Our regret analysis, supported by an LP-duality argument, establishes that SELECTwK attains constant expected satisficing regret when a satisficing policy exists. We further introduce a stronger regret condition that bounds the expected sum of positive reward deficits to the optimal one at each time step, under which SELECTwK achieves a sharper constant bound together with a sub-linear bound in the time horizon. As a complement, SELECTwK still preserves the oracle's sub-linear expected standard regret bound if the satisficing threshold is unattainable. Finally, we establish the oracle conditions and corresponding satisficing regret bound for existing finite-armed BwK and dynamic pricing algorithms, and conduct numerical experiments on dynamic pricing with limited inventory to demonstrate the empirical performance of SELECTwK.

papers.title: Micro-Edits: Computational Support for Fine-Scale Edits in Film
papers.abstract: In film editing, every frame matters. While macro, content-level edits shape the high-level narrative of a film, small local edits often control timing and direct visual attention. For example, editors can adjust the precise timing of clips to control the length of a meaningful silence, or cut to shots that highlight a specific character's reactions to important moments. These small, detailed edits are slow and tedious to make in standard editing tools because users have to map high-level narrative goals to low-level frame-by-frame adjustments. At the same time, these fine-scale adjustments, which we call micro-edits, can be nuanced and expressive, with different choices serving different creative goals. In this work, we start by conducting a formative study with professional editors to understand the structure of micro-edits and how they are used. We then derive a mathematical formalization for this structure to develop tools that leverage AI and optimization to make exploring micro-edits simpler and more efficient for users. Finally, we validate our tools in multiple user studies and a wide range of video examples.

papers.title: DOSE: Dominance-Guided Ordinal Severity Estimation from Sparse Relative Annotations
papers.abstract: Medical severity estimation commonly relies on absolute grade annotations, which are fundamentally ordinal, yet existing methods often treat the grades as independent categories. Learning-to-rank methods, which can be trained using relative annotations based on severity comparisons of image pairs, can provide continuous severity rankings but cannot directly predict discrete severity grades. We propose Dominance-guided Ordinal Severity Estimation from Sparse Relative Annotations (DOSE), a framework for learning ordinal medical severity from sparse pairwise comparisons without using absolute annotations. DOSE aggregates the observed comparisons through a global comparison graph to estimate a dominance score for each image. Differences between dominance scores set cumulative margins in the embedding space, so that pairs with larger estimated severity differences are separated more strongly, and also generate pseudo-pairs that supervise a scalar severity head alongside the observed comparisons. The learned continuous severity axis is converted into discrete grades via label-free score calibration, with tie-anchored segmentation as the main calibration method. In the experiment, DOSE consistently outperformed pairwise-ranking baselines on ACNE04, IDRiD, and LIMUC under different pair budgets. Code is available at https://github.com/TushirSahu/DOSE

authors.name: Tushir Sahu
authors.institution: Indian Institute of Information Technology Design and Manufacturing Jabalpur

papers.title: Silhouette-Based Gaitomics for Frailty Assessment in Older Adults
papers.abstract: Walking offers a window into physical function that may support interpretable video-based frailty assessment. We developed silhouette-based "gaitomics" to connect frailty predictions with measurable patterns of body configuration and movement. In 66 older adults assessed using the Fried Frailty Phenotype, standardized silhouettes and gait energy images yielded 90 descriptors of shape, temporal variation, motion, and texture. Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection using the mutual information difference criterion prioritized informative features while limiting redundancy. Each classifier was evaluated using nested stratified cross-validation with five outer and three inner folds at the participant level, with feature ranking and feature-count selection confined to training partitions. Shapley additive explanations examined contributions to held-out predictions. Bilateral silhouette difference led the aggregate feature-selection rankings for three-class classification and both comparisons involving frail participants. Attribution profiles differed across tasks, with texture and consecutive-frame silhouette differences prominent in three-class classification. Among classifier-specific evaluations, CatBoost achieved the highest mean three-class micro-AUC of 0.647 \pm 0.085. Leading pairwise mean micro-AUCs were 0.833 \pm 0.249 for frail versus nonfrail, 0.765 \pm 0.168 for frail versus prefrail, and 0.554 \pm 0.129 for prefrail versus nonfrail classification. These findings connect model predictions to explicit gait characteristics while revealing task-dependent feature priorities and limited separation of prefrail and nonfrail participants. The framework provides an interpretable basis for further investigation, with larger independent studies needed to establish reliability and clinical relevance.

papers.title: A logarithmic error term for subset sums of zero-sum-free sets
papers.abstract: For a positive integer $k$, let $f(k)$ be the minimum number of distinct nonempty subset sums of a zero-sum-free $k$-element set, where the minimum is taken over all finite abelian groups. We prove $f(k)\ge \frac{k^2}{2}-13k\log(k+1)-116k$. Together with the classical upper bound, this gives $f(k)=k^2/2+O(k\log k)$, with the optimal leading coefficient. As a consequence, the Olson constant of every finite abelian group $G$ satisfies $\mathrm{Ol}(G)\le\sqrt{2|G|}+O(\log|G|)$. The argument combines a triangular lower bound for repeated supports, a count using blocks of two and three copies, and a greedy expansion argument. No restriction is imposed on the order of the group or on the stabilizer of the set of subset sums.

authors.name: Chao Liu
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: Davenport constants with growing binary rank
papers.abstract: We study the correction to the standard lower bound $D^*$ for Davenport constants of finite abelian groups with a growing elementary two-component. For every fixed nontrivial abelian $p$-group $H$ of odd order, we prove $D(H\oplus C_2^r)=D^*(H\oplus C_2^r)+(D(H)-1)\log_2 r+O_H(1)$, with a uniform version for varying $H$. For $C_3\oplus C_2^r$, we determine exact values on explicit infinite intervals of ranks. More generally, the correction is logarithmic or smaller precisely when the fixed group has at most one odd prime divisor. We show that the two-primary part affects the logarithmic coefficient: for $C_{24}\oplus C_2^r$, the ratio $(D-D^*)/\log_2 r$ has limsup at least $2.4933231\ldots>2$, whereas for $C_3\oplus C_2^r$ the limit is $2$. These upper limiting coefficients are unbounded even with the odd prime fixed. The proofs use binary codes and finite-field Fourier analysis.

authors.name: Chao Liu
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: Tikhonov-Regularized Dynamics and Inexact Algorithms for Nonlinear Saddle-Point Problems
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study a Tikhonov-regularized second-order primal--dual dynamical system for smooth nonlinear convex--concave saddle-point problems in real Hilbert spaces. The dynamical system incorporates a vanishing damping coefficient $\alpha/t$, a Hessian-driven term, and a critical Tikhonov regularization coefficient $c/t^2$. By constructing suitable Lyapunov functions, we establish strong convergence to the minimum-norm saddle point and fast convergence rates under the same parameter conditions, without imposing any eventual inside/outside-ball condition. Specifically, the primal--dual trajectory converges strongly to the minimum-norm saddle point, while the primal--dual gap and the velocity norm decay at rates $o(t^{-2})$ and $o(t^{-1})$, respectively. Furthermore, we propose an inexact primal--dual algorithm with a computable relative residual criterion and prove strong convergence of the generated sequence to the same minimum-norm saddle point, together with an $o(k^{-2})$ convergence rate for the primal--dual gap. Finally, numerical experiments on nonlinear and bilinear problems of different dimensions illustrate the minimum-norm selection property and compare the performance of the proposed dynamical system and algorithm with related methods.

authors.name: Hong-lu Li
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

authors.name: Yi-bin Xiao
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Convergence rates of mixed primal-dual dynamical systems with implicit Hessian damping and Tikhonov regularization
papers.abstract: We propose a mixed-order primal--dual dynamical system with implicit Hessian damping and Tikhonov regularization for linearly constrained convex optimization, and derive a corresponding fast primal--dual algorithm. The proposed dynamical system couples a second-order primal equation with a first-order dual equation without requiring twice differentiability of the objective function. An energy analysis establishes $\mathcal{O}(t^{-2})$ convergence rates for the augmented Lagrangian gap, feasibility violation, and objective residual along an extrapolated primal trajectory. For the proposed algorithm, we construct discrete energy estimates and establish the corresponding $\mathcal{O}(k^{-2})$ rates at the extrapolated primal iterates. In particular, in the critical regularization regimes $\epsilon(t)=a/t^2$ and $\epsilon_k=a/k^2$, these accelerated rates hold simultaneously with strong convergence of the primal trajectory and primal iterates to the minimum-norm solution, respectively, under suitable parameter and trajectory conditions. Numerical experiments illustrate the convergence behavior of the proposed dynamical system and the corresponding algorithm.

papers.title: $H^2$-based equilibrated residual error estimates
papers.abstract: We develop a framework for equilibrated residual a posteriori error analysis of finite element methods, based on decomposing vector- and tensor-valued Sobolev spaces into $H^2$ and $H^1$ spaces. To estimate the residual functional acting on $H^2$ component, the method reconstructs symmetric and piecewise polynomial tensors on vertex patches in broken $H(\operatorname{div}\operatorname{div})$ spaces. We apply the proposed framework to conforming finite element discretizations of biharmonic equation, Poisson's equation, and linear elasticity in mixed form. As a result, we obtain several novel equilibrated residual a posteriori error estimates, providing guaranteed error control for energy error of biharmonic equation, $L^2$ norm error of Poisson's equation, and stress error of mixed linear elasticity. They also serve as the first polynomial-degree-robust a posteriori lower bounds of discretization errors. Numerical experiments illustrate the effectiveness of the $H^2$-based error estimators.

authors.name: Kexin Ding
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: The Liouville property for geometric graphs in the plane
papers.abstract: We show that every bounded discrete harmonic function with respect to the cotangent Laplacian on a Delaunay triangulation of the Euclidean plane is constant; equivalently, the cotangent-weighted triangulation has the Liouville property. Our main theorem establishes this property for a more general class of connected weighted geometric graphs in the plane. Furthermore, we show that a planar Delaunay triangulation with cotangent weights could be transient but is recurrent if edge lengths are uniformly bounded.

authors.name: Kuijun Liu
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

authors.name: Yanwen Luo
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Zhenghao Rao
authors.institution: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

papers.title: A Sharp Uniqueness-Nonuniqueness Dichotomy for Neutral Vortex Arrays in $2$D Euler Equations
papers.abstract: We establish a sharp uniqueness--nonuniqueness criterion for the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equations within a class of stationary arrays of disjoint neutral vortices. Let $\Theta$ be any finite nondecreasing envelope for the vorticity $L^p$ norms, and set $I_\Theta=\int_{p_0}^\infty \Theta(p)^{-1}\,dp$. If $I_\Theta=\infty$, every array in the corresponding class admits a unique Euler evolution, even among bounded energy-admissible weak velocity solutions. If $I_\Theta<\infty$, there exists a compactly supported array in the same class admitting two distinct unforced Lagrangian Euler evolutions from the same initial datum. The criterion holds for arbitrary nondecreasing envelopes $\Theta$.

papers.title: Nonuniqueness of the $2$D Euler Evolutions with $L^1\cap L^p$ Vorticity
papers.abstract: For each prescribed $1<p<\infty$, we construct a compactly supported initial vorticity in $L^1(\mathbb{R}^2)\cap L^p(\mathbb{R}^2)$ that admits two distinct evolutions under the unforced two-dimensional incompressible Euler equation on $[0,1]$. Both vorticities are strongly continuous in $L^1\cap L^p$ and are transported exactly by their respective almost-everywhere invertible, measure-preserving regular Lagrangian flows. The construction couples unstable four-vortex configurations across increasingly small spatial scales, realizing them through concentrated signed vortex patches. At each finite cutoff, a prepared reference evolution remains close to rotating configurations, while a second evolution differs initially only at the finest scale. In the second evolution, the finest configuration consists of separating dipoles whose remote strain activates the instability of the next larger configuration. This process propagates through successive scales with summable transition times. As the cutoff tends to infinity, the two families of initial data converge strongly, along a subsequence, to the same datum, while a nonzero difference survives at a fixed larger scale and is detected by a fixed smooth observable at a positive limiting time. Quantitative concentration and relative comparison estimates establish this cascade for exact Euler patch solutions. Strong compactness through inverse-flow stability then preserves both exact vorticity transport and the positive-time distinction between the two limiting evolutions. The initial datum and construction parameters may depend on $p$.

papers.title: Topological defect trains excited by a boundary discontinuity in the two-dimensional complex Ginzburg-Landau equation
papers.abstract: With numerical simulations of the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation in a two-dimensional space, we find that a stationary but non-zero Dirichlet boundary condition with a discontinuity can drive a periodic train of evenly spaced topological defects that drift along and in proximity to the boundary.

papers.title: Evidence for a charged vortex lattice in an exciton superfluid
papers.abstract: Lattices of quantized vortices are a defining property of rotating superfluids and of type-II superconductors in magnetic fields. Realizing an analogous vortex lattice in an exciton superfluid-formed from bound electron-hole pairs-has remained challenging because excitons are electrically neutral. Building on previous theoretical studies of the low-energy excitations in an exciton superfluid, recent theory has predicted that in a strong magnetic field, a weakly charged exciton superfluid can stabilize a vortex-antivortex lattice arising from the mutual repulsion of fractionally charged vortex cores. Here we report evidence for this predicted vortex lattice in a bilayer exciton condensate by imaging its charged vortices with the scanning tunnelling microscope. The condensate forms between Landau levels of two graphene layers separated by a thin hexagonal boron nitride barrier in a perpendicular magnetic field. We find that the vortex lattice periodicity scales with the total excess charge and is insensitive to its distribution between the two layers, in quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions. Our observations provide evidence for phase coherence in an exciton superfluid system.

authors.name: Allan MacDonald
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge -- and when they improve generalization -- is challenging, since training is nonlinear and non-convex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer's feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth. We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization -- an "anti-shrinkage" mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters -- notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment. Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure.

papers.title: Compartment-driven Gaussian processes for uncertainty quantification of pharmacokinetic exposures
papers.abstract: Pharmacokinetic modeling is a crucial part of drug development. An important goal is to estimate patients' total and peak exposure to a drug over time, quantified by the area under the concentration--time curve (AUC) and the maximum concentration ($C_{\max}$) respectively. Such exposure assessment is essential to balance efficacy and safety in medications that offer therapeutic benefits but carry risks of toxicity, such as chemotherapy drugs. Uncertainty quantification for exposure quantities, however, remains challenging, since they are functionals of an often sparsely observed concentration--time curve with measurement errors. We propose a compartment-driven Gaussian process framework that propagates uncertainty in concentration--time curves to pharmacokinetic exposure functionals. Our approach uses pharmacokinetic compartmental models to specify a mechanistically informed prior and Gaussian processes to accommodate departures from the assumed pharmacokinetic dynamics. The framework can accommodate both individual-level and group-aggregated concentration--time data commonly seen in practice. We provide straightforward computational procedures for drawing posterior inference on AUC and $C_{\max}$. Simulations across a range of observation schemes demonstrate robustness to departures from the assumed compartmental dynamics. We apply the method to patient-level datasets on warfarin and theophylline, and aggregated data from a chemotherapy study of 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine in patients with normal or impaired hepatic function. The chemotherapy analysis quantifies drug-specific exposure differences between groups with differing liver function, with potential implications for informing dosing decisions.

papers.title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/

papers.title: Robotic Data Inoculation
papers.abstract: Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover. Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it. In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves during data collection to collect more useful data. We propose Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make. These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human's continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, "inoculating" the dataset against the learner's future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.

authors.name: Qiyang Li
authors.institution: Gansu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

authors.name: Zhiyuan Zhou
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Fast rigid rotational alignment of voxelized 3-D density maps in sliced Wasserstein distance
papers.abstract: We develop a fast method for the rigid alignment of voxelized three-dimensional density functions over $\mathsf{SO}(3)$ using sliced optimal transport. Our approach efficiently transforms each density map into a tensor of one-dimensional quantile functions, taken from central slices over the unit sphere, such that the Euclidean distance of the transformed volumes approximates the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance. Our formulation is therefore compatible with existing, fast, voxel-based Euclidean alignment algorithms. We provide theoretical analysis and numerical experiments demonstrating that the sliced 2-Wasserstein distance is a robust metric for comparing three-dimensional shapes and for computing their rigid alignment.

papers.title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
papers.abstract: Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing. The fidelity of entangling gates mediated by Rydberg interactions has improved rapidly and is increasingly constrained by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions, which shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states that can cause correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude. However, realizing a universal gate set in such an environment has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic $^{133}$Cs atom array, with a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.970(2)% and a raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity of 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg $P$ state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling. The gate operates at a modest Rabi frequency of $2\pi\times4.3$ MHz. The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$. These results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant computation.

authors.name: Junlan Jin
authors.institution: Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology

papers.title: Mapping Stellar Obliquity Across Space and Time
papers.abstract: The angle between a star's rotational angular momentum vector and the orbital angular momentum vector of its planets---stellar obliquity---encodes the initial conditions and dynamical history of planetary systems. Variations in obliquity with orbital separation may arise from either primordial disk structure (e.g., broken or warped protoplanetary disks with misaligned inner and outer regions) or subsequent dynamical interactions with planets or external perturbers. Comparing obliquities across orbital distance therefore probes the spatial imprint of these processes, while comparisons across age constrain their temporal evolution. To test for signatures of obliquity evolution in both space and time, we compare stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single Sun-like stars spanning four samples that probe distinct regimes of orbital separation and age: 49 protoplanetary disk systems, 24 debris disk systems, 21 warm Jupiter systems, and 20 hot Jupiter systems. We find minimum misalignment rates of $33^{+7}_{-6}$% for protoplanetary disk systems, $21^{+9}_{-7}$% for debris disk systems, $23^{+10}_{-8}$% for warm Jupiter systems, and $20^{+9}_{-8}$% for hot Jupiter systems. These rates are consistent within 1$\sigma$ across all samples. The absence of significant variation in minimum-obliquity distributions with either orbital separation or system age suggests that stellar obliquities for Sun-like stars may be largely established at formation with limited subsequent evolution in both space and time. These results are consistent with post-formation inclination evolution being either infrequent, confined to small misalignments, or restricted to regions of parameter space not examined here---such as systems with close stellar companions, hot host stars, small planets, and long-period giant planets.

authors.name: Brendan P. Bowler
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: crush: Extensible Proof Automation for Lean
papers.abstract: Lean's rich expressiveness supports higher-order functions, inductive datatypes, and user-defined abstractions, making it challenging to translate proof obligations into first-order Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) queries and reconstruct kernel checked proofs. We present crush, an extensible SMT-backed proof automation framework for Lean. To bridge the gap between Lean's higher-order constructs and the solver's first-order logic, crush uses defunctionalization to encode function values and their applications. We formalize this translation for a supported higher-order fragment and prove its soundness. Moreover, crush provides metaprogramming interfaces for extending both Lean-to-SMT translation and the reconstruction of Lean proofs from solver certificates without modifying the translation pipeline. We implement crush as both a tactic and a backend for other third-party automation systems. We show that across four such use cases that target verification and general proof automation, crush discharges more obligations than the competing backends and reconstructs more kernel-checked proofs than the baselines.

authors.name: Dexin Zhang
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Global Well-Posedness of Landau Equation in Bounded Domains
papers.abstract: We prove global well-posedness of the Landau equation near a Maxwellian in bounded $C^3$ domains with in-flow or diffuse-reflection boundary conditions for $-3\leq\gamma\leq1$, including Coulomb interactions. Small compatible Gaussian perturbations generate global strong solutions, with uniqueness and continuous dependence among weak solutions. The proof combines energy estimates, the comparison principle, interior and weighted boundary estimates for velocity derivatives up to second order, and a logarithmic estimate for solution difference.

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Parallel Implementations of Short-Time Fourier Transform
papers.abstract: The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) computes the Fourier transform of a short-duration window of a longer signal, which characterizes how a frequency changes over time. While the Fourier transform algorithms, particularly the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm, has been well developed to take advantage of parallel computing, there is limited work on understanding the performance of parallel short-time Fourier transform algorithms. In this study, two parallel short-time Fourier transform algorithms, one is FFT-based and the other a quasi-parallel feedforward algorithm, are implemented and analyzed in comparison with each other. It is found that while the quasi-parallel algorithm outperforms in runtime under low concurrency settings, the FFT-based algorithm scales better and has lower memory usage. For each algorithm, three parallel approaches, shared-memory, distributed-memory and hybrid distributed-shared-memory, are tested. Profiling results show that all implementations are compute bound except for the hybrid feedforward algorithm, and that the distributed-memory variants incur significantly higher communication cost. Overall, this study presents a deeper and more comprehensive analysis and demonstrates the defining characteristics of different families of parallel short-time Fourier transform algorithms, in which the FFT-based approach uses less memory while the quasi-parallel feedforward algorithm has lower runtime but higher serial fraction.

papers.title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has become a standard for evaluating large language models, yet most approaches implicitly assume that a single judge prompt functions as a stable evaluation instrument. Prior work has primarily explored deliberate prompt modifications such as scoring rubrics, role descriptions, or chain-of-thought reasoning in order to optimize accuracy. In contrast, we investigate whether validated prompt variants intended to preserve evaluation semantics while differing in surface realization (\textit{paraphrastic rephrasings}) yield consistent judgments under a fixed evaluation task. We introduce \textit{Prompt Lottery}, a phenomenon in which paraphrastic rephrasings produce different LLMaJ judgments. Across a large-scale study spanning diverse evaluation tasks, judge families, and model backbones, we find that these variations can alter evaluation outcomes and, in some settings, reverse relative model rankings. A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies. This indicates that single-prompt evaluation is insufficiently robust for model ranking. Finally, we show that multi-prompt aggregation substantially improves robustness by emphasizing judgments that remain consistent across prompt variants.

papers.title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.

papers.title: A Differentiable, GPU-Accelerated Finite-Element Formulation in JAX for Large-Deformation Shells with Contact: Application to Patient-Specific Aortic Valve Simulation
papers.abstract: Patient-specific aortic-valve models can help assess how tissue properties and geometry influence leaflet deformation and coaptation, with potential to inform intervention planning. Large deformations, near-incompressibility, and evolving contact make these simulations computationally demanding and can challenge nonlinear convergence. Differentiable, GPU-accelerated methods offer efficient derivative evaluation and parallel computation, but their matrix-free application to soft-tissue shells with contact remains less established. We developed a forward solver using tatva's energy-based finite-element framework in JAX. The solver combines finite-strain extensible-director shells, hyperelastic constitutive models, and a finite-range repulsive contact energy. Nonlinear equilibrium is solved using a regularized, matrix-free Newton-Krylov method with two-level preconditioning. Automatic differentiation evaluates tangent-vector products without forming or storing the primary tangent matrix, while GPU execution parallelizes element and quadrature-point computations. Constitutive, shell, contact, and self-contact responses were assessed against analytical, semi-analytical, and published benchmarks. At a contact-free plate equilibrium, implicit sensitivities of the converged apex displacement to constitutive parameters, thickness, and pressure agreed with finite differences from independent nonlinear simulations. Simulations of three patient-specific aortic-valve models (two tricuspid and one bicuspid) achieved final relative equilibrium residuals below 10^-4. Median GPU runtimes were approximately 15-25 minutes, with 5.3-6.5-fold speedups relative to corresponding CPU runs on the tested hardware. These results provide component-level verification and demonstrate GPU-accelerated forward valve simulation in the tested cases, supporting future gradient-based inverse studies.

authors.name: Wensi Wu
authors.institution: University at Buffalo, State University of New York

papers.title: Multistable nematic liquid crystal pores as reconfigurable optical vortex metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Nematic liquid crystals confined in cylindrical pores adopt multiple stable director topologies --- radial, escaped, and arches --- each imprinting a distinct optical signature on transmitted circularly polarized light, with topological charge set by the projected director winding number, $\ell = 2m$. Using Landau--de Gennes and Jones-calculus modeling validated against micron-scale experiments, we show that this mechanism persists as the pore diameter shrinks toward the optical wavelength. However, full-wave Maxwell simulations of periodic sub-wavelength pore arrays reveal that the resulting vortex is a near-field phenomenon only: each topology imprints a distinguishable phase-singular signature --- differing in core multiplicity, core width, and ring amplitude --- directly below the pore array, but this signature does not survive propagation into the far field, where diffraction and inter-pore interference erase it within about one wavelength. Landau--de Gennes simulations further demonstrate that an applied electric field switches the pore between topologies, and hence between their near-field optical signatures. Because each topology is locally stable, sub-wavelength NLC pore arrays constitute an electrically reconfigurable, non-volatile platform for topology-encoded near-field optical readout, with potential application to optical labeling and anti-counterfeiting.

papers.title: 3D Occupancy-Language Fields from mmWave Radar
papers.abstract: Radar systems can recover scene geometry and recognize predefined categories, but these outputs do not provide a persistent spatial representation for open-ended language queries. Such queries require linking observations from different viewpoints to the same physical locations. We present TextRadar, a framework that constructs a scene-level 3D occupancy-language field from panoramic radar observations. The field combines occupancy with scale-dependent language features at surface locations, allowing the reconstructed scene to be queried with new descriptions. A single-frame radar distillation model predicts aligned ranges and language features from each radar observation. Using radar-estimated poses, we register these predictions to reconstruct the field from radar alone in a new scene. Experiments on approximately 20k synchronized observations across seven buildings demonstrate scene-level natural-language querying and prompt-free semantic visualization. Analysis of camera-to-radar concept transferability shows stronger agreement for structures, materials, and human poses than for colors and printed text.

authors.name: Mingmin Zhao
authors.institution: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

papers.title: L-PASSO: Adaptive Log-penalized Variable Selector, with Sparse Selection and Robustness to the Pilot Estimator
papers.abstract: We study L-PASSO, a penalized least-squares regression method based on the logarithmic penalty $\lambda\sum_j\log(1+|\beta_j|/\tau)$, and its two-stage adaptive form, in which the scales $\tau_j$ come from a pilot estimator. Although this concave penalty has been proposed previously, its variable-selection properties and sparsity relative to other popular penalties have not been fully characterized. We derive the exact orthogonal-design solution, and show that the single-stage estimator selects the true model under a weighted irrepresentable condition that holds for every design once $\tau$ is small. We further establish that, under matched tuning, the two-stage estimator possesses the oracle property and has half the asymptotic bias of the adaptive LASSO. Our main theoretical contribution concerns the robustness of the two-stage procedure to the pilot estimator. We show that two-stage L-PASSO remains selection consistent even when the weights associated with relevant variables are as small as $\exp\{-o(1/\zeta_n)\}$, whereas the adaptive LASSO fails to retain relevant variables whose pilot weights are sufficiently small relative to its tuning parameter $\zeta_n$. We establish that both thresholds are sharp. In high-dimensional settings, we prove support recovery for a local minimizer without imposing any lower-bound condition on the weights of relevant variables, and provide conditions under which this local minimizer is also the unique global minimizer. We additionally establish the selection consistency of a BIC-based tuning-parameter selection procedure. Finally, simulations comparing L-PASSO with the LASSO, SCAD, MCP, SELO, uniLasso, and the adaptive LASSO show that L-PASSO most frequently recovers the true support. Two real-data examples further illustrate the method.

papers.title: RainCheck: Harnessing Historical Weather Data with Machine Learning for Rainfall Forecasting in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Machine-learning rainfall forecasts are often evaluated by shuffling station records into random training and test sets. For rainfall, this lets a model see what happened at neighbouring stations on the very day it is asked to forecast, and it hides the fact that a seasonal lookup table already explains most of the variance. We quantify both effects on 618,650 station-days from 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations (1948-2014). We compare random, temporal (train <=1999, test 2005-2014) and spatio-temporal (unseen stations and unseen years) evaluation, calendar-only versus antecedent-rainfall features, and six learners against climatology, persistence and SARIMA. Three findings stand out. First, a station-month climatology alone classifies high-rainfall months with 88.4% accuracy (AUC 0.950), and no learner improved on it by more than 0.8 points under temporal evaluation. Second, a calendar-only random forest reached a next-day wet-day AUC of 0.889 under a random split, higher than any model with real predictors under temporal evaluation, yet fell to 0.835, below climatology (0.859), on future years. Third, models with lagged rainfall add genuine but modest skill for next-day forecasts: a Brier skill score of 0.074 (95% CI 0.064-0.088) over climatology, rising to 0.091 when station and year inputs are removed and to 0.131 when other stations' same-day observations are added. A GRU sequence model matches but does not exceed gradient boosting, and skill disappears beyond a two-day lead. For monthly totals, no learner beat climatology significantly. We release a leakage-aware protocol and code so that future station-based studies report skill against climatology on held-out years.

papers.title: Disparity Laundering: Consensus Without Fairness in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Clinical large language models are increasingly fielded as multi-agent teams, on the assumption that deliberation averages out individual error. It does not average out bias. Across a full factorial of five model families and four aggregation topologies on 120 real MIMIC-IV emergency cases under counterfactual demographic swaps, no configuration neutralizes the disparity: all 20 cells commit the direction of their agents' independent answers, giving Black patients more acute triage. Every model has a topology that amplifies its baseline gap, but which one varies by model, so no design is reliably safe or reliably amplifying: the disparity is relocated, never removed. Late-stage fixes fail: fairness instructions and demographic masking leave the gap untouched, and per-agent self-debiasing widens it, because the bias is already encoded in the agents' ordinary clinical numbers. We call this disparity laundering; the audits now applied to clinical AI, per model, per output, per version, can certify the parts but never the committed decision. Interventions close the gap exactly when they make counterfactual versions visible inside the system and pool them, through deliberation, into the committed decision. A diverse-perspective ensemble does both while keeping the team, with no retraining or architectural change: the disparity falls by 67 to 94% where all five perspectives pool at every round, and the one topology that never pools them is the one it cannot reliably repair. Medical multi-agent systems do not filter demographic bias; they launder it into plausible decisions no single-version audit can catch, and the only defense is to make the bias visible.

papers.title: HALO: Human-Grounded Granular Evaluation of Proactive Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive agents must decide whether, when, and how far to assist without an explicit request. Existing evaluations often rely on automated scores or binary verdicts, offering limited human diagnosis of evidence use and intervention quality. To address these gaps, we introduce HALO, Human-Grounded GrAnular EvaLuation of PrOactive Agents. HALO-Arena covers 4 proactive need types, Dependency, Blockage, Risk, and Opportunity, across 10 everyday domains and 50 personal environments. Scenarios require agents to retrieve evidence from structured databases or unstructured documents before judging whether assistance is warranted and choosing its scope. On HALO-Arena, we construct HALO-8K, a dataset of 8,000 responses from 10 models across 400 scenarios, annotated by 20 experts for action level, acceptability verdicts, and human diagnosis. For rejected responses, human diagnosis covers timing, intensity, and other issues. Recorded reasoning tokens and retrieval rounds measure the effort behind these responses. The best proprietary and open-source models achieve 72.88% and 56.63% acceptability, respectively. Our central finding is that over-proactivity is the dominant observed failure mode, with Premature timing or Excessive intensity accounting for 61.20% of rejected responses. Further analyses yield complementary findings on the balance between intervention and restraint, evidence acquisition, and the calibration of timing and intensity.

authors.name: Wenqi Pei
authors.institution: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)

authors.name: Jie Sheng
authors.institution: Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System
papers.abstract: Under Major League Baseball's automated ball-strike (ABS) challenge system, players must weigh the value of overturning a call against the risk of losing a challenge they may need later. We develop a policy that values an overturn through its effect on expected runs, accounting for the count, outs, and runners on base. Using pitch tracking and game records, we reconstruct challenge opportunities, including calls that players let stand. A Bayesian model represents players' imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions. Dynamic programming compares the expected gain with the future cost of losing a challenge, accounting for the stage of the game, the number of challenges remaining, and opportunities on both offense and defense. We develop the policy using games before the 2026 All-Star break and evaluate it without refitting on 983 games played afterward. Along the recorded sequence of opportunities, the policy recovers 0.536 modeled correction runs per game across both teams, compared with 0.452 under observed decisions, an improvement of 18.5%. The gain is 0.084 runs per game, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.065, 0.103]. The policy makes more challenges and recovers more value per successful review despite a lower overturn rate. These results show why overturn rate alone can be a misleading measure of challenge strategy.

papers.title: Witnessed Boolean Contracts: Sound Local Distance Guarantees for Approximate Implicit CSG
papers.abstract:
Hard min/max operations preserve the sign of exact implicit solids but generally destroy signed-distance semantics. Arbitrarily small, sign-preserving value perturbations can rotate the normalized gradient by nearly a right angle and displace a gradient-projected boundary witness by a finite amount. We formalize this as the absence of a value-only stability modulus for witness projection.
  We introduce a witnessed Boolean contract checking value and gradient errors, positive reach, active-branch separation, and a Lipschitz visibility margin at the approximate witness. A sharp normalization lemma bounds the normal-direction error. An enlarged neighborhood permits transfer of the inactive operand's bound between the approximate witness and the true foot point. Under the stated analytic and domain assumptions, passing the checks identifies a true point on the union boundary and bounds distance deficiency by the active operand's pointwise value error. Failed or unavailable checks return Unknown. The argument extends to finite hard unions by testing every inactive operand.
  An executable proof-chain audit finds no violations on 75,738 certified samples. A broader analytic stress test covers spheres, capsules, ring tori, three Boolean operators, and a four-leaf union. Of 96,000 narrow-band samples, 87,469 pass with zero oracle violations; per-case coverage ranges from 72.67% to 98.30%. Removing visibility admits 75 truly invalid witnesses, showing that branch separation alone is insufficient. Non-union cases remain empirical tests, not new theorems.

papers.title: Symmetric Structure and Motivic Transformation in Melodies, Phrases, and Themes
papers.abstract: Transposition, inversion, and retrograde are fundamental operations in music theory, from Schoenberg's twelve-tone technique to Forte's set classes and Lewin's transformational theory, yet their use in melodies has rarely been quantified. We read a melodic line through the orbits and stabilizers of its windows of $m = 3-6$ notes under the group generated by these operations and cyclic shift. The window entropy splits into an orbit entropy (motivic vocabulary) and a within-orbit entropy normalized by orbit size (deployment), and the group elements relating windows of one orbit give the motivic transformations. In 852 keyboard pieces spanning four centuries, at least 97% of melodies have lower orbit entropy than surrogates preserving their pitch content, spectrum, or one-step transitions ($m \geq 4$). Periods differ in vocabulary and symmetry types; musical forms differ in deployment. Recurring motifs are transposed 1.6 times more often than in random permutations of their forms, and transposed by a fifth or fourth 2.8 times more often, a preference that weakens from the Baroque to the 20th century and from Bach's fugues to Shostakovich's. Folk phrases and instrumental themes are rarely symmetric (2-10%), but are 1.6-5 times more often symmetric than note rearrangements. The framework extends to any symbolic sequence with a symmetry group.

papers.title: Conformal ordering: Distribution-free predictive inference for orders and rank
papers.abstract:
We study distribution-free predictive inference for the ordering and ranking of multiple unobserved outcomes. Although numerous methods, such as conformal prediction, have been developed for prediction and predictive inference of unobserved outcomes, extending them to provide inference for the ordering of multiple outcomes with an interpretable guarantee is not straightforward. To this end, we develop a framework and methodology for uncertainty quantification in predictive ordering.
  Our approach begins by reformulating the problem of determining an ordering among multiple objects as a graph inference problem. Our method adopts a multiple-testing-inspired approach and constructs an uncertainty graph, where each edge represents a confidently inferred pairwise ordering. We develop a distribution-free procedure for constructing a consistent uncertainty graph while controlling either the family-wise error rate or the false discovery rate. Moreover, we show that the resulting graphs naturally yield risk-controlling prediction intervals for the ranks of the outcomes. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed procedure achieves the target guarantees tightly while maintaining reasonable power and prediction-interval widths.

papers.title: Beyond Selected Breakthroughs: Evaluating Language Models on Randomly Sampled Mathematical Conjectures
papers.abstract: The last year has seen a shift in AI-assisted mathematics, with frontier language models producing proofs of and counterexamples to long-standing open conjectures. However, studying only the current set of major breakthroughs provides an incomplete picture of LLM capabilities and the computational resources needed to achieve reported results. To address this, we introduce a new dataset, OpenConjecture, which collects conjectures from mathematics papers published on the arXiv since February 2026. We use these conjectures as a source of open mathematical problems, and apply frontier GPT models to a random sample of 200 of these conjectures over three passes using a reproducible protocol without problem-specific mathematical guidance. Rather than attempt expert verification of these candidate solutions, we analyze the types of problems for which LLMs produce solutions and the characteristics of these solutions. The models we test produce candidate solutions for roughly 60% of the conjectures, with counterexamples about 1.3 times more common than proofs. We estimate solution novelty, assess how solutions cite and relate to existing literature, and analyze whether the proposed resolution relies on either an error in or underspecification of the conjecture. We find that models sometimes propose resolutions that are outside the authors' intent (e.g., proposing the trivial group as a counterexample) and that a number of proofs follow closely from existing results, but that some resolutions exhibit at least moderate novelty. Our findings underscore the need for evaluations that go beyond correctness to assess fidelity to the intended statement, attribution, and the nature of the mathematical contribution.

papers.title: Cross Lingual Abstractive Summarization for Marathi
papers.abstract: Text summarization is an important task for advancing natural language processing (NLP) research and applications in Indic languages. Despite progress in extractive and abstractive summarization, both monolingual summarization (MS) and cross-lingual summarization (CLS) remain relatively underexplored for these languages. Recent advances in Transformer architectures, pretrained language models (PLMs), and dataset availability offer new opportunities to address this gap. In this work, we construct cross-lingual training data from the monolingual Marathi MahaSum corpus and combine it with the smaller cross-lingual PMIndiaSum dataset to fine-tune IndicTrans2, an Indic neural machine translation model. We evaluate the resulting models using ROUGE, chrF and chrF++ metrics, focusing primarily on Marathi-to-English summarization due to computational constraints. We also discuss the applicability of our approach to the English-to-Marathi direction. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging a pretrained translation model yields substantially better summarization performance than the IndicBART and mBART-50 based baselines reported in previous work on cross-lingual summarization.

papers.title: On End-Semidualizing Modules
papers.abstract: We introduce and study the notion of End-semidualizing modules which are generalizations of semidualizing modules in the classical sense, and also extend the notion of $S-R$ semidualizing bimodules studied by Holm-White and Wakamatsu. By constrast with these notions, End-semidualizing modules exist abundantly. We characterize these modules by the inclusion of projective and flat modules in their Auslander class, or injective modules in their Bass class, and give criteria for when these Foxby classes satisfy the two-out-of-three property. Over commutative Noetherian rings, we prove base-change and duality results, and characterize local depth inequalities by the inclusion of all modules of finite flat or injective dimension in the corresponding classes.

authors.name: Luigi Ferraro
authors.institution: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

papers.title: The residue field as an infinite syzygy
papers.abstract: Let $(R,\mathfrak{m},k)$ be a commutative Noetherian ring which is either local or positively graded over the field $k$. We provide a method based on liftings for constructing free coresolutions of $k$ over $R$. We apply this method to twisted trivial extensions of the node $k[u,v]/(uv)$ to build a family of positively graded $k$-algebras of dimension $1$ over which $k$ is an infinite graded syzygy, resolving an open question of Iyengar in the negative. We also prove a formula for alternating sums of lengths of Ext modules when $R$ is positively graded, and use it to show that a graded free coresolution of $k$ cannot dualize to a resolution unless $R$ is Artinian Gorenstein.

papers.title: Identifying Scientifically Interesting Galaxies with Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Anomaly searches in large astronomical image datasets aim to identify rare objects for follow-up investigation. Yet the objects that are most statistically unusual are not necessarily those of greatest scientific relevance. We investigate whether pretrained vision-language models can directly assess scientific interest from natural-language instructions, enabling galaxy images to be ranked without labeled examples. We evaluate models on a 20,000-image Hubble Space Telescope sample that includes 167 reference anomalies previously identified through machine learning and expert inspection. By scoring images for scientific interest, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite places 98.2% of the reference anomalies within the highest-ranked ~2,000 images, at a present-day inference cost of approximately $5.05 per 10,000 images. We recover known gravitational lenses, jellyfish-galaxy candidates, and galaxies with visible jets, and release 102 high-scoring candidates for further investigation. These results show that an off-the-shelf vision-language model, without any training on the target data, offers a practical way to rank large image datasets by scientific relevance rather than rarity. The project code is available at https://github.com/TheCheng2005/Galaxy-Anomaly-Search/

papers.title: Meta-Altermagnetism and Enhanced Spin-Splitting
papers.abstract: Altermagnets are collinear magnets with zero net magnetization and spin-split electronic bands. Here, we explore whether altermagnetism can exhibit a discontinuous jump, a phenomenon we refer to as meta-altermagnetism. We show that meta-altermagnetism can emerge in 2D systems when magnetic-order-induced band reconstruction drives spin-split van Hove singularities (vHSs) across the Fermi level. Using mean-field theory for an extended $t$-$J$ model on a two-sublattice square lattice including anisotropic hopping integral, we find that a first-order meta-altermagnetic transition produces an intermediate altermagnetic regime with reduced staggered magnetization but strongly enhanced magnetic octupole and time-reversal-odd spin-splitter conductivity. We further show that the first-order transition line terminates at a quantum critical endpoint, giving rise to a rich phase diagram as the chemical potential and anisotropic hopping strength are varied. Our results identify the spin split vHSs as a route to enhancing spin-splitter effect for spintronic applications.

papers.title: Structured Security Explanations for Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection
papers.abstract:
Software vulnerability detection remains difficult because existing approaches rely on predefined analysis rules, learn vulnerability patterns implicitly from code and labels, or use large language models (LLMs) to make the final security judgment. It remains unclear whether structured descriptions of security-relevant program behavior can improve supervised detection.
  We present VulnLens, an explanation-augmented framework for binary C/C++ vulnerability detection that separates program-behavior analysis from the final decision. A label-blind LLM-based Explainer examines each function from seven fixed perspectives: data flow, memory access, object lifetime, arithmetic and type behavior, control flow, shared state, and external-resource access. Without receiving vulnerability labels or CWE information, it generates structured explanations. A supervised Detector combines source code and explanations through sequential cross-attention.
  We evaluate VulnLens on a PrimeVul-derived dataset covering ten CWE categories and test transfer to SecVulEval without retraining. On the 526-function PrimeVul test set, VulnLens achieves 75.5% accuracy and 77.2% F1, exceeding DeepSeek V4 Pro by 4.2 percentage points in accuracy and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 2.2 points in F1. Matched explanations improve F1 by 7.3 points over a separately trained code-only detector. On SecVulEval, VulnLens achieves 66.4% accuracy and 65.8% F1, outperforming DeepSeek V4 Pro by 7.6 points in accuracy and 20.0 points in F1, and Gemini 2.5 Pro by 16.6 points in accuracy and 7.8 points in F1.

papers.title: Understanding Large Language Models as Numerical Optimizers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as potential tools for numerical optimization. Despite promising results, their intrinsic optimization capabilities and limitations remain poorly understood, particularly in high dimensions. This paper investigates the ability of LLMs to exploit mathematical problem structures and generate feasible, near-optimal solutions. We develop an evaluation framework that distinguishes solution quality from execution failures, including numerical inaccuracies, constraint violations, and output-format errors. Using representative problems from convex optimization, fractional programming, and constrained projection, we assess LLM performance against deterministic reference solvers across different dimensions. Our results reveal that LLMs can capture useful optimization structures and produce near-optimal solutions, even when their outputs fail to satisfy numerical or formatting requirements. However, reliability deteriorates with increasing problem dimension and depends strongly on the underlying optimization structure. To further investigate the limitations, we deploy an iterative refinement mechanism that provides targeted feedback on feasibility and solution quality. The results demonstrate that iterative refinement substantially improves reliability and extends the range of problem dimensions over which LLMs produce valid solutions. Nevertheless, persistent numerical and structural errors limit their applicability as standalone optimizers. These findings provide insights into the capacity and limits of LLM-based optimization and motivate hybrid approaches that combine LLM reasoning with deterministic numerical verification.

papers.title: Infrastructure and its Discontents: Contestations of Power in Canada's AI Governance Scaffold
papers.abstract: This paper develops a critical theoretical framework for understanding national Artificial Intelligence (AI) strategies through the lens of "Governance as Infrastructure." Integrating insights from Infrastructure Studies, Science and Technology Studies (STS), this paper employs Black Feminist Technoscience (BFTS) to reveal how AI governance infrastructures are assembled, maintained, and contested, and whose forms of knowledge, labour, and experience are rendered visible or invisible in these processes. We analyze the Canadian AI governance landscape through in-depth interviews with bureaucrats, civil society advocacy groups, academic researchers, and industry actors. Our inductive thematic analysis reveals how AI governance infrastructure enacts specific configurations of power, particularly through the politics of expertise; how actors navigate profound ambiguities related to AI's opacity, often involving strategic ignorance; and how mechanisms for justice and accountability struggle to address AI-related harms. We contend that a BFTS perspective highlights the limitations of current governance approaches and points toward alternative infrastructural designs prioritizing care, maintenance, participatory democracy, and adaptive temporalities to foster more equitable and accountable technology governance.

papers.title: Non-associative Hopf Algebra on Dyck Paths Arising from the Shuffle-insertion Product
papers.abstract: In this paper, we define a shuffle-insertion product and a cut-box coproduct on the vector space spanned by Dyck paths, where the product is commutative but non-associative. We prove that the product and coproduct are compatible, making the space a non-associative bialgebra. This bialgebra is connected and bigraded by path degree and peak number, and hence is a non-associative Hopf algebra. Its primitive subspace is spanned by atoms, and associators of primitive elements are primitive. Furthermore, we provide closed-form formulas for its left and right antipodes. We also define the convolution product on the space of linear transformations of the non-associative Hopf algebra, which equips this space with a non-associative algebra structure. Finally, we construct a one-parameter deformation preserving the cut-box coproduct. Its zero specialization is the ordinary shuffle Hopf algebra, which is also the associated graded algebra for the atom filtration, while every nonzero specialization is isomorphic to the shuffle-insertion algebra.

papers.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
papers.abstract: I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects of research studies pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry and the Open Science Framework. I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM models extract forecasting questions from the pre-registrations or pre-analysis plans. These questions elicit forecasted treatment effects; not all resolve in the subsequent papers, but those that do can be used to consider forecast accuracy. Forecasts were elicited for 889 treatment effects from 39 papers with results disclosed in January 2026 or later, or 673 from 33 papers after screening. Forecasts were elicited in raw units but I focus on those that could be standardized and therefore compared across papers. Currently, the median absolute forecast error is 0.054 SD for the best model, the average absolute error is 0.093 SD, and the MSE is 0.0218. The AI forecasts perform substantially better than benchmarks forecasting 0 effect or forecasting the mean effect of other papers' results in that time period. Overall, these results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to be of value in informing policy and research.

papers.title: Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
papers.abstract: Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.

papers.title: Mean Field Games of Optimal Trading with an SPDE Model of the Limit Order Book
papers.abstract: We develop a mean field game model for optimal trading in which the interaction among traders is mediated by the dynamics of the limit order book. The bid- and ask-side order densities are modelled as stochastic processes with values in infinite-dimensional function spaces that solve stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) with stochastic order submission rates and multiplicative infinite-dimensional noise. This extends an existing limit order book framework to capture the aggregate impact of the strategic traders on the order densities. Trading activity affects the order densities, which determine the market depths near the best quotes and hence the mid-price, and the mid-price in turn affects the traders' decisions. We establish the well-posedness and regularity of the resulting density-price system and use it to formulate an $N$-player optimal trading game in which the traders' market orders enter the book through their aggregate order flow. We then study the corresponding mean field game as the number of traders tends to infinity, characterize the mean field equilibrium as a fixed point of the associated consistency condition, and prove its existence and uniqueness under suitable conditions. Finally, we show that the mean field equilibrium induces an $\epsilon_N$-Nash equilibrium for the finite-player game, with $\epsilon_N=O(N^{-1/2})$, and provide a numerical illustration of the equilibrium dynamics.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models Dramatically Outperform Bespoke Photometric Redshift Estimators
papers.abstract: Estimating galaxy redshifts (a proxy for distance) from imaging data alone, also known as photometric redshifts (photo-$z$'s), is essential for studies of extragalactic astrophysics and cosmology. However, data-driven estimators rely on spectroscopic training datasets, which are scarce and systematically biased toward bright and easily observed galaxies. In this work, we show that tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose synthetic pretraining amounts to a learned prior over regression problems, can outperform bespoke estimators using only in-context learning.
