Recent advances in off-policy RL have demonstrated large scale off-policy experience can be effectively combined with massively parallel simulation. Methods such as FastTD3 [14] and FlashSAC [28] leverage parallel experience collection, replay-based value learning, and efficient critic optimization to achieve rapid learning in high-dimensional robotic control tasks. These advances demonstrate the potential of off-policy RL to exploit large volumes of simulation experience through repeated value and policy updates. However, directly extending this paradigm to visual RL remains computationally expensive, as collecting additional experience using a visual policy requires rendering observations and evaluating the policy at every environment step. This raises a central question: can we scale off-policy experience collection for visual RL without proportionally scaling rendering and visual-policy inference?

We present a preliminary study of Echo, a single-stage off-policy RL framework that addresses this challenge through inverse distillation. Unlike conventional teacher–student distillation, where a privileged state-based teacher supervises a visual student, Echo reverses the direction of supervision: an auxiliary state-based policy learns to imitate the evolving visual policy. This state-based imitator enables inexpensive experience collection without camera rendering or visual-policy inference, while approximately tracking the state distribution induced by the visual policy. Crucially, the additional unrendered experience is not merely used to supervise the visual policy, but directly contributes to its improvement through off-policy reinforcement learning.

Unlike conventional teacher–student distillation, where a privileged state-based teacher supervises a visual student, Echo reverses the direction of supervision: an auxiliary state-based policy learns to imitate the evolving visual policy. This state-based imitator enables inexpensive experience collection without camera rendering or visual-policy inference, while approximately tracking the state distribution induced by the visual policy. Crucially, the additional unrendered experience is not merely used to supervise the visual policy, but directly contributes to its improvement through off-policy reinforcement learning.

Specifically, Echo learns a shared privileged critic from both rendered and unrendered experience stored in replay. The state-based imitator serves two complementary purposes: (1) collecting inexpensive transitions that remain approximately in-distribution with the evolving visual policy, and (2) providing continuation actions for temporal-difference updates of the state-based critic. The visual policy is then improved directly through critic-guided first-order updates using a smaller set of paired state–observation samples. By separating large-scale experience collection from expensive visual-policy evaluation, Echo combines the scalability and experience reuse of off-policy RL with the benefits of direct visual policy optimization, without requiring a separately trained privileged teacher.

papers.title: Think Twice: The Metis-1.6 Technical Report
papers.abstract: Metis is a bet that better data, better training methods and new architectures can buy what a bigger parameter count cannot, at a fraction of the cost. Metis-1.6 is its latest step: two language models built from scratch by a single researcher, Praxis (2.94B parameters, 0.46B active per pass) and Logos (10.23B parameters, 1.18B active per pass). Both run a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack twice for every token, so each token gets a second look. Each was trained on 1.02T tokens in total: 804.76B of pretraining, 18B of context extension to 131,072 tokens, and 200B of supervised fine-tuning. Metis-1.6 was never meant to challenge frontier models, and across 40 post-trained benchmarks it mostly does not: Logos averages 52.93, seventh of 17 models in its comparison set and within a point of Qwen3-4B. But it gets there on roughly a twelfth of the median training data of the comparators that disclose it, and with fewer active parameters per token than any model that beats it, which puts it on the Pareto frontier for both. In mathematics it ranks second of 30 models, with 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026. It is weak at code, instruction following and long context. The rest of the report is the part I found most valuable: what went wrong. The optimizer I configured never ran, and attention trained with AdamW for all of pretraining. A 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off. Five fine-tuning choices cost capability. And a length reward under group-mean normalization punished correct solutions for being long once a group's pass rate passed 2/3, a sign inversion I prove and fix with a one-line clamp. I close with the 10B-token ablations behind MoRE (Mixture of Recursive Experts), the looped architecture of Metis-1.7.
papers.intro:
Most of the progress in language models over the past few years has been bought with scale. When a model is not good enough, the standard answer is to make it bigger, and parameter counts are announced like trophies, as if size were the achievement. Bigger models are more capable, but they are also far more expensive to train and to serve, and the price of the most capable models keeps climbing even as the labs building them promise to bring it down. Too often the safe choice wins: another trillion parameters on a recipe from 2023, rather than a better recipe.

Metis is Lernex’s bet on the opposite direction. Better training data, better training algorithms and genuinely new architectures can buy capability that parameters alone cannot, and at a fraction of the cost. A single researcher cannot outspend a frontier lab, but can out-iterate one: try an idea the day it occurs, build on the newest results instead of the safest ones, and take risks on designs a large organization would not. Every part of the Metis stack is written from scratch, from data acquisition and decontamination to tokenization, training kernels, reinforcement-learning environments and evaluation, so any of it can change the moment a better idea arrives.

Metis-1.6 was never meant to beat frontier models. It was built to test that bet at small scale, and to answer a more personal question: can I, starting from nothing, build each model better than the last, learn from every mistake, and get measurably better at the craft? Each Metis release is one step of that answer. Metis-1.5 was the first Metis model you could really talk to. Metis-1.6 is the first one you can realistically use: it works through olympiad problems, calls tools and follows instructions well enough to be genuinely helpful in places. Metis-1.7 comes next, and this report is, in large part, the story of how I got ready to build it.

This report has two jobs. The first is to measure the models honestly. Every comparison comes from one harness that ran Metis and every comparison model with identical prompts and scorers, and every comparison table is generated from the benchmark data published with the models. The second job is to write down what went wrong. Release reports usually describe the recipe that worked. This one also describes an optimizer that silently differed from its configuration for the entire pretraining run, a component the model learned to switch off, and post-training choices that cost capability. I would rather publish my mistakes than repeat them, and I suspect they are the most useful pages here for anyone else building models without a frontier budget.

That is not a frontier result, and the open models from large labs beat it more often than not. But Logos was trained on 1.02T tokens, against a median of 12T for the comparators that disclose a count, and every model above it that discloses its data was trained on at least 28T. It is also a mixture-of-experts model running against mostly dense ones: it activates 2.36B parameters per token, while every model that beats it activates between 1.5 and 4.6 times as many. On both axes, Logos sits on the Pareto frontier, and in the shaded corner of each plot: a higher score than the median model, on far less data and compute than it.

papers.title: An Integral Equation for the Surface Current in the Problem of the Natural Modes of a Waveguide Containing a Resistive Film
papers.abstract: This paper considers the eigenmode problem for a waveguide with a resistive film. An integral equation for the surface current on the film is formulated. A method for evaluating the kernel is described, and an explicit expression for the kernel is derived for rectangular and circular waveguides.

papers.title: Muon Makes the First Mixture-of-Experts Layer Harder to Balance
papers.abstract: Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.
papers.intro:
Most of the leading open language models of 2026 are mixture-of-experts (MoE) models [12, 27, 72, 48, 33]. An MoE layer has many feed-forward networks, the experts, and a router that sends each token to a few of them [56, 29, 18]. Left alone, the router tends to send most tokens to a few experts, which then train on more data and attract still more tokens [56]. Earlier models such as GShard and the Switch Transformer countered this with an auxiliary balance loss that penalizes uneven loads [56, 29, 18]. DeepSeek-V3 switched to auxiliary-loss-free balancing [63, 11], and most recent open models have followed, among them DeepSeek-V4, GLM-5.3, and MiMo-V2.6 [12, 72, 69], some keeping a small balance loss as well. Each expert has a bias that is added to its score when the router selects experts. After every step, the bias of an expert that received more than its fair share of the tokens moves down by a fixed amount, and the bias of an expert that received less moves up. We refer to this balancer as the bias.

At learning rates tuned for each optimizer on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, from 0.084 to 0.194 on average (Figure 1), and it did so again at all nine seeds of three later experiments (Section 4.4). We had expected the opposite. Under Muon the update of an expert has the same size however many tokens the expert receives, which should weaken the feedback in which busy experts become busier. papers.title: Opportunistic Optical Link Scheduling in the Scalable Matching Model
papers.abstract: The Scalable Matching Model (SMM) is a useful abstraction for reconfigurable datacenter networks. In SMM, a set of $n$ (Top-of-Rack) electrical packet switches is connected via a set of optical circuit switches (OCS), each realizing a $p \times p$ matching, where $p$ is the number of ports per switch. In the case when $p \ll n$, bounded-degree networks utilize only a small portion of the OCS infrastructure at each point in time, especially when traffic patterns are skewed and bursty. In this work, we propose the Opportunistic Optical Link Scheduling (OOLS), a set of lightweight OCS link scheduling routines, designed to augment bounded-degree reconfigurable network topologies by leveraging idle OCS resources. We evaluate the performance of OOLS in the SMM through simulations, using synthetic and real-world data-center workloads. Our simulation results show that OOLS substantially improves performance, lowering communication costs and boosting throughput.

papers.intro:
The growing reliance on data-centric applications across various domains, coupled with advances in AI and machine learning, has significantly increased communication traffic in data center networks [1, 2]. Traditionally, data center network designs have relied on static topologies, like Clos [3, 4], hypercube [5, 6], or expander [7, 8]. Such architectures are essentially demand-oblivious and perform well for uniform all-to-all traffic patterns. Traffic in data centers, however, is known to be bursty and skewed [1, 9].

Recent progress in optical circuit switching (OCS) has enabled demand-aware reconfigurable data center networks (RDNs) to emerge [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. Several technologies support this new paradigm, including nanosecond-scale tunable lasers [16], digital micromirror devices [17], liquid-crystal-on-silicon wavelength-selective switches [18], and microcombs and semiconductor optical amplifiers [19].

Several technologies support this new paradigm, including nanosecond-scale tunable lasers [16], digital micromirror devices [17], liquid-crystal-on-silicon wavelength-selective switches [18], and microcombs and semiconductor optical amplifiers [19].

One common abstraction for RDNs is the ToR-Matching-ToR (TMT) model [20, 21, 22, 23, 24], in which nn (Top-of-Rack) electrical packet switches are linked via a set of optical circuit switches, each realizing a p×pp\times p matching, where pp is the number of OCS ports per switch. Interesting optimization problems arise in this context, e.g., regarding which is the best combination between electrical packet switches and OCSs [25, 26]. There is still, however, no consensus in the community on which RDN design is optimal [10].

TMT can be used as a testbed for Self-Adjusting Networks (SAN) [27, 10, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. SANs optimize their physical topology toward the demand they serve in an online manner, i.e., without prior knowledge of the traffic, with the requirement that the network remain connected and have bounded degree [34]. Previous studies have shown that, in the case when p≪np\ll n, SANs typically utilize only a small portion of the OCS infrastructure at each point in time, especially when spatial and temporal locality of the workload is high, i.e. traffic is skewed and bursty [35, 36]. This unexplored idle capacity motivates us to develop opportunistic scheduling strategies for these network architectures.

Our work is based on the Scalable Matching Model (SMM) [36, 35], a generalization of the TMT model [22]. SMM introduces the constraint that the number of ports of each OCS is bounded by a constant, i.e., p=O⁡(1)p=O(1). SMM guarantees strict non-blocking (i.e., any point-to-point connection can always be established), uses a minimum number of OCSs to realize any dynamic bounded-degree topology, and allows to execute existing SAN algorithms on top of it, while preserving the performance (amortized communication cost) guarantees of the latter.

We present the Opportunistic Optical Link Scheduling (OOLS), a set of lightweight OCS link scheduling routines, designed to integrate with TMT RDN architectures. OOLS leverages idle OCS ports to dynamically augment a SAN topology with opportunistic routing shortcuts. We implemented OOLS in combination with multiple SAN algorithms using OpticNet [36], a framework for simulating RDNs in the TMT model. We performed extensive simulations using both synthetic and real data center workloads, with variable temporal and spatial locality. The simulation results show that OOLS significantly increases the concurrency of the RDN system and optimizes not only the system’s throughput and makespan, but also the total communication cost. Our experiments also revealed a trade-off between efficiency improvement and resource utilization, as a function of pp (the number of OCS ports per switch). In particular, the smaller the OCS, the higher the potential gains of opportunistic link scheduling. Overall, OOLS proved to be an effective and efficient mechanism to utilize idle OCS capacity in RDNs, especially in network architectures that utilize OCSs of limited size.

papers.title: Maximum Diversity and Support Transitions on Disks and Three-Dimensional Balls
papers.abstract: For the similarity kernel $e^{-|x-y|}$, we determine the probability measure of maximum diversity on every planar disk and three-dimensional ball, answering a question of Leinster and Roff. In each dimension the measure is uniform on the boundary up to a threshold. Above it, the support is a closed central ball and the outer sphere, separated by a mass-free annulus. In dimensions two and three, their conjecture of finitely many supporting spheres therefore holds only up to the respective threshold. We obtain the measure explicitly up to one scalar root in three dimensions and through Fredholm integral equations and a scalar contact equation in the plane. Computations in dimensions four and five suggest that interior supporting spheres appear one at a time.

papers.title: A curve of genus $2$ over $\mathbb{C}(t)$ and hexads of bitangents to a smooth quartic
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the Abel-Jacobi map of a genus 2 curve over $\mathbb{C}(t)$ arising from a double cover of $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{C})$ branched along six lines. We utilize the so-called Mumford representations to conduct the calculations. As an application, we give an alternative proof of classical results on quartics and bitangents. Furthermore, we obtain a method to give explicit defining equations of quartic curves that have the six lines as bitangents and apply it to determine the number of connected components of the realization space.

papers.title: Predicting What Answer Engines Cite: Open Decision Models, Rerankers and a Distilled 4B Student on Ten Engines under Controlled Retrieval
papers.abstract: Generative engine optimization needs a scorer that ranks candidate pages by the share of an answer they will receive as citations. We measure pretrained rerankers, a hosted typed decision model (Jev), eight open decision models and distilled students on GEO-Bench queries answered by ten engines that receive the same candidate sources in their prompt. Where several engines answer the same query, they agree with one another at a within-group Spearman correlation of 0.704. Jev and two open 27B decision models, used without training, are the strongest scorers at 0.575 to 0.578. A Qwen3-Reranker-4B fine-tuned with low-rank adapters on teacher labels for other GEO-Bench queries, released as GEO Citation Ranker 4B, reaches 0.542 to 0.549 across three seeds, and its differences with the 27B models and with Jev are not distinguishable from zero on 229 queries. Most of the remaining distance between the student and Jev disappears when Jev scores one passage at a time, as the student does. Students trained on teacher labels and on observed engine citations reach the same level, and labels from Jev alone match the two-teacher target at 0.6B. We release the model, the benchmark, the predictions of every reported scorer and the code.
papers.intro:
Work on generative engine optimization (GEO) asks, for a given query, which of the candidate pages an answer engine will draw on, and how much (Aggarwal et al., 2024). Measuring engines directly answers it, but each measurement is paid, slow and non-deterministic, so practitioners increasingly use a model to predict the answer before any engine is queried. Pretrained rerankers are free to run and were trained for topical relevance (Nogueira et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). LLM judges prompted with a rubric can rank sources, at the cost of one generation per group (Zheng et al., 2023). Typed decision models, such as the hosted Jev (TypeSafe, 2026; Shea and Roche, 2026), return a probability distribution over a fixed scale for each question asked about a state. Several open decision models were published on the Hugging Face Hub after Jev’s release (autotrust, 2026; Perplexity AI, 2026; TokenRhythm, 2026; Mapika, 2026; manjunathshiva, 2026; jaredpalmer, 2026; convaiinnovations, 2026). We know of no measurement of decision models or distilled rerankers against the citations of answer engines.

papers.title: Comparison categories: the normal form and the regularity of comparison data
papers.abstract: There are many types of equivalence relations in mathematics, each one enjoying its own defnition, but many of them can also be defined by transformations of morphisms: Green's relations, orbit relations, conjugacy, equality of orbit closures, equivalence of Cauchy sequences, stable isomorphism. We unify them through the comparison category of a comparison datum, read at levels $-1,0,1,2,\dots$ (comparisons in both directions, connected components, homotopy groups). Its normal form is a full subcategory of a Grothendieck construction $\int_VH$ cut out by a map $s$; the classical relations are traced back to it by restriction along $s$, enrichment by a cost (limit relations) and filtered colimits (stabilization). If the map $\sigma$ transporting morphisms into a $2$-category is arbitrary, every relation occurs, so the constraint is the regularity of $\sigma$. We grade data along seven regularity classes. The rigid and diagonal classes are classified completely (on finite groups, by the double coset relations); completely functorial data contain conjugacy and obey a dichotomy on nil monoids. Whether every relation on a monoid is level $0$ of a completely functorial datum is open.

papers.intro: The problem in plain words. To classify objects one declares some of them to be “the same”. Very often the rule is given by a transformation: two matrices are the same if one is obtained from the other by a change of basis; two elements of a monoid are the same if each divides the other (Green’s relations [3, 4]); two sequences of rationals are the same if they get arbitrarily close, which is how the real numbers are built; two modules are stably the same if they become isomorphic after adding a common summand. Each of these relations is usually defined by its own formula, and each forgets information: an orbit relation does not record the stabilizers, and the divisibility relation does not record in how many essentially different ways one element divides another. The idea. Let mm and m~\tilde{m} be morphisms of a category 𝒞\mathcal{C}. We say that mm can be compared to m~\tilde{m} if, after modifying mm on its target and on its source by admissible morphisms, we obtain something that matches m~\tilde{m} up to an admissible 22-morphism in an auxiliary 22-category 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The data are 𝔇=(𝒞,𝒟,σ,τ1,τ2,𝒰1,𝒰2,𝒲)\mathfrak{D}=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D},\sigma,\tau_{1},\tau_{2};\mathcal{U}_{1},\mathcal{U}_{2},\mathcal{W}), a comparison datum (Definition 2.2): 𝒟\mathcal{D} is where the comparison takes place, σ\sigma sends a morphism of 𝒞\mathcal{C} to 𝒟\mathcal{D} (it may forget structure), τ1,τ2\tau_{1},\tau_{2} send the modifications to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, 𝒰1,𝒰2\mathcal{U}_{1},\mathcal{U}_{2} are the admissible modifications and 𝒲\mathcal{W} the admissible 22-morphisms. All comparisons are collected in a category 𝖪⁡(𝔇)\mathsf{K}(\mathfrak{D}), the comparison category, whose objects are the morphisms of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For 𝒟=𝒞\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{C} and σ=τi=Id\sigma=\tau_{i}=\mathrm{Id}, a comparison m→m~m\to\tilde{m} is a factorization m~=u1​m​u2\tilde{m}=u_{1}mu_{2}. Information is read from 𝖪⁡(𝔇)\mathsf{K}(\mathfrak{D}) at levels: level −1-1, comparisons in both directions (the relation); level 00, connected components (the relation generated by chains of comparisons); level k≥1k\geq 1, the homotopy groups of the classifying space (“in how many essentially different ways”). The structural picture. This paper shows that the many relations above are one construction seen through a small number of operations. Notion Role Grothendieck construction ∫VH\int_{V}H A category whose objects are pairs (place vv, observation xx at vv) and whose arrows are moves of the place together with a matching of observations. It is the “universe of observations” on which an action acts. Normal form (Thm. 4.2) Every comparison category 𝖪⁡(𝔇)\mathsf{K}(\mathfrak{D}) is equivalent to the full subcategory of some ∫VH\int_{V}H on the observations s⁡(m)s(m) of the morphisms mm. So a relation is always reachability inside ∫VH\int_{V}H, restricted along ss. Transport datum (Thm. 5.5) A device for realizing a given ∫VH\int_{V}H as a comparison datum: one adjoins an extra object ⋆\star so that observations become morphisms. The Grothendieck construction is the category; the transport datum is how it is made into a comparison datum. Restriction along ss Choosing which observations come from morphisms of 𝒞\mathcal{C}; this is where σ\sigma enters. Enrichment (§7) Attaching a cost to comparisons and asking that the infimum vanish: gives limit relations, which are not levels of 𝖪\mathsf{K} but are read off an enriched version of the same normal form. Filtered colimit (§8) Passing to the colimit of a sequence of data along a stabilizer: gives stabilization relations. The result is again a comparison datum. In these terms: Green’s relations are the transport relations of the Hom bimodule; orbit relations are transport relations of an action; limit relations are transport relations enriched by a cost; stabilization relations are transport relations of a filtered colimit of data. The constraints on which relations occur are not on the shape of 𝖪\mathsf{K}, which is arbitrary, but on ss, that is, on how regular σ,τ1,τ2\sigma,\tau_{1},\tau_{2} are; this is the subject of Section 10. Main structural results: normal form and families. (A) Normal form: 𝖪⁡(𝔇)\mathsf{K}(\mathfrak{D}) is equivalent to the full subcategory of ∫VH\int_{V}H on im⁡(s)\mathrm{im}(s) (Theorem 4.2); level −1-1 is the pullback of mutual reachability, and for saturated data all levels are those of a homotopy colimit (Corollary 4.3). (B) Realization: every small category is, up to opposite, a union of components of some 𝖪⁡(𝔇)\mathsf{K}(\mathfrak{D}) with 𝔇\mathfrak{D} completely functorial (Theorems 4.5, 5.5); so the shape of 𝖪\mathsf{K} is unconstrained, and the higher levels of transport data are homotopy colimits (Proposition 5.8). (C) Green’s relations are transport relations: 𝖪⁡(Gr⁡(𝒞))\mathsf{K}(\mathrm{Gr}(\mathcal{C})) is the twisted arrow category, with 𝖩\mathsf{J} at level −1-1 and the homotopy type of 𝒞\mathcal{C} above it (Theorem 6.5). (D) Limit relations: for lengths zero every limit relation is the pullback of closure equality along an orbit map (Theorem 7.5), which covers Hausdorff closure, approximate unitary equivalence and completions. (E) Stabilization: a strict stabilizer produces a datum 𝔇∞\mathfrak{D}^{\infty} with 𝖪⁡(𝔇∞)=𝖪∞\mathsf{K}(\mathfrak{D}^{\infty})=\mathsf{K}_{\infty}, so stable relations and stabilized levels are levels of a datum (Proposition 8.8). Examples and counterexamples are collected in Section 11. The regularity axis. The matching of a comparison goes through a map σ\sigma that sends a morphism of the given category 𝒞\mathcal{C} to a morphism of 𝒟\mathcal{D}. If one allows σ\sigma to be an arbitrary function, σ\sigma can simply record the answer, and every equivalence relation is obtained (Corollary 10.13); this says nothing. Classification by a rule that respects composition is only meaningful if σ\sigma respects composition too, at least up to something. How regular must σ,τ1,τ2\sigma,\tau_{1},\tau_{2} be, and which relations survive at each degree of regularity? We grade data by seven classes ρ0⊂ρ1⊂⋯⊂ρ6\rho_{0}\subset\rho_{1}\subset\cdots\subset\rho_{6} (Definition 10.1): Class Name Requirement ρ0\rho_{0} rigid 𝒟=𝒞\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{C}, σ=τ1=τ2=Id\sigma=\tau_{1}=\tau_{2}=\mathrm{Id}: nothing is transported ρ1\rho_{1} diagonal σ=τ1=τ2\sigma=\tau_{1}=\tau_{2} is a functor, identity 22-cells ρ2\rho_{2} completely functorial, strict σ,τ1,τ2\sigma,\tau_{1},\tau_{2} are three (different) functors, identity 22-cells ρ3\rho_{3} completely functorial as ρ2\rho_{2} with arbitrary admissible 22-cells ρ4,ρ5\rho_{4},\rho_{5} pseudofunctorial, lax σ\sigma preserves composition only up to a 22-isomorphism, respectively a 22-morphism, admissible in 𝒲\mathcal{W} ρ6\rho_{6} arbitrary σ\sigma is any function Each class is contained in the next, and the question becomes: which relations occur in each class, are the inclusions strict, and what is the least class in which a given relation occurs? Main structural results: regularity. (F) Rigid and diagonal data are classified. Rigid relations are m~∈𝒰1​m​𝒰2\tilde{m}\in\mathcal{U}_{1}m\mathcal{U}_{2}, m∈𝒰1​m~​𝒰2m\in\mathcal{U}_{1}\tilde{m}\mathcal{U}_{2}; diagonal relations are these on a quotient 𝒞/≈\mathcal{C}/{\approx} pulled back (Theorems 10.3, 10.4). On finite groups both are exactly the double coset relations, on abelian groups the congruences (Corollary 10.5, Proposition 10.7). (G) The classical families sit at σ=Id\sigma=\mathrm{Id}, once the relation is viewed on the right category (Proposition 10.8); regularity is relative to the category on which the relation lives. (H) Completely functorial data contain relations that no rigid or diagonal datum gives: constrained Green data, hence conjugacy and twisted conjugacy of any group (Theorem 10.17). (I) A dichotomy. Examples and counterexamples are collected in Section 11. Open problems. (2) Is every relation on a finite group level −1-1 of a completely functorial strict datum, and which relations are? We know the congruences, double cosets, 𝖧\mathsf{H}, transport relations, twisted conjugacy, products and full pullbacks, and the nil dichotomy. papers.title: Replaying the Same Gradients at a Different $\varepsilon$: A Registered Test of the Fixed-Trajectory Account of Adam's $\varepsilon$ for One Rare Row
papers.abstract:
Adam divides every update by the square root of a running average of squared gradients plus a small constant, epsilon. For an output-embedding row whose token is rare, which we call the probe row, raising epsilon can be read as shrinking that row's steps by arithmetic alone. We test that reading directly. While a training run proceeds, we also divide the probe row's update by a different epsilon, using the run's own moment estimates; this replay is exact arithmetic on the gradients the run actually saw, so it holds the run's trajectory fixed. A rule for when the replay counts as wrong was written down before the runs.
  We train a small causal transformer in a standard configuration. When epsilon rises by four orders of magnitude, the replay counts as wrong on each of the three seeds registered for the test: the probe row keeps 8.9--11.4 times more of its displacement than predicted with the main, sampled-negative head, and 5.0--7.7 times more with a full-softmax head scored as a second instrument. At three orders of magnitude, tested with the main head only, it does not, by narrow margins; a further two seeds, registered after this result had been committed and scored on their own, follow the same pattern. In separate real runs, raising epsilon on the probe row alone is enough to reproduce the row's change and raising it on every other parameter alone also moves the row part of the way --- readings about the runs that do not rescue the replay; scaling the row's learning rate instead, with the denominator untouched, is mispredicted by the replay in the same direction.
  This is one embedding row of one model family on one corpus; we make no claim about rates, about rows in general (other rows were read only as a panel on one trajectory) or about how the effect changes with model size.
papers.intro:
Adam divides each update by the square root of a running average of squared gradients plus a small constant, usually written epsilon. The constant is conventionally a guard against division by zero, but wherever the squared-gradient average is small next to it, it also shortens the step. What it does to one parameter row whose token is rare is less settled. The natural explanation for any effect of epsilon on such a row is arithmetic: a larger constant makes the denominator larger, so the row moves less.

The constant is conventionally a guard against division by zero, but wherever the squared-gradient average is small next to it, it also shortens the step. What it does to one parameter row whose token is rare is less settled. The natural explanation for any effect of epsilon on such a row is arithmetic: a larger constant makes the denominator larger, so the row moves less.

That explanation can be tested without assuming anything about the network. While a run trains, divide one rare row’s update by a second constant as well, using the run’s own moment estimates; since those estimates do not depend on the constant, this equals integrating the run’s gradients through a second Adam state that differs only in the constant (Section 2). If the arithmetic account were complete, this replay would predict how far the row moves when the run itself uses the new constant. We test that prediction for one rare row, the probe row, in a standard training configuration, against a rule registered before the runs for when the replay counts as wrong. We then take the change apart in separate real runs, giving the new constant to the probe row alone or to every other parameter alone, or giving the probe row a matched learning-rate change instead.

papers.title: Negative Convexity in Pass-Through MBS: Mechanisms and Conditions
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the mechanisms and conditions underlying negative convexity in pass-through mortgage-backed securities (MBSs) backed by fixed-rate mortgages. We first derive an exact decomposition of MBS prices into three components: the present value of interest-rate-independent cash flows, the present value of principal repaid early through interest-rate-dependent prepayments, and an interest rate option component capturing the reduction in future cash flows due to prepayments. Under a first-order approximation, the latter two components resemble portfolios of floorlets and Asian-style interest rate options, respectively. We then apply a cumulant expansion to derive closed-form valuation approximations under the one-factor Hull--White model. Numerical results show that including the second cumulant improves accuracy relative to a first-cumulant approximation. Building on the price decomposition, we decompose duration and convexity into component-level contributions and express the condition for negative convexity in terms of their second-order interest rate sensitivities. Finally, phase diagrams across interest rate levels and refinancing sensitivities identify the regions where negative convexity occurs and the corresponding sign boundaries. The negative-convexity region expands as the long-run mean of refinancing sensitivity increases. Negative convexity can arise even when no refinancing incentive exists initially, while its magnitude may vary nonmonotonically with the interest rate level. These findings explain negative MBS convexity through the sensitivities of its price components and quantitatively characterize the conditions governing its occurrence.

papers.intro:
The future cash flows of pass-through mortgage-backed securities (MBSs) depend on the future path of interest rates through borrowers’ prepayment behavior, making their prices and interest-rate sensitivities more complex than those of straight bonds. In particular, declining interest rates tend to increase prepayments through mortgage refinancing and other mechanisms, thereby limiting the increase in MBS prices. As a result, MBSs exhibit distinctive interest-rate sensitivities, such as duration shortening and negative convexity. However, the presence of a prepayment option does not necessarily imply that MBS convexity is always negative. Therefore, to understand the interest-rate sensitivities of MBSs, it is important to clarify the mechanisms through which negative convexity arises and the conditions under which it occurs.

Therefore, to understand the interest-rate sensitivities of MBSs, it is important to clarify the mechanisms through which negative convexity arises and the conditions under which it occurs.

In this paper, we investigate this issue from two perspectives: a component-wise decomposition of MBS prices and their interest-rate sensitivities, and phase diagrams of MBS convexity. Specifically, we decompose the MBS price into three components: a component corresponding to interest-rate-independent cash flows, a component corresponding to the present value of principal repaid early through interest-rate-dependent prepayments, and an interest-rate-linked option component reflecting the reduction in future cash flows due to increased prepayments. Furthermore, we derive an approximate closed-form expression for the MBS price and analytically evaluate the first- and second-order interest-rate sensitivities of each price component, thereby decomposing MBS duration and convexity into the contributions of these components. This decomposition allows us to quantitatively examine which price components contribute to the emergence of negative convexity through their interest-rate sensitivities. We also use phase diagrams of convexity with respect to the interest-rate level and refinancing sensitivity to numerically identify the parameter regions in which negative convexity occurs and the boundaries separating positive and negative convexity. Through these analyses, we provide a unified examination of the mechanisms and conditions underlying the emergence of negative convexity.

The cash flows of MBSs have a more complex structure than those of government and corporate bonds because they are affected by borrowers’ early repayments, known as prepayments.

The cash flows of MBSs have a more complex structure than those of government and corporate bonds because they are affected by borrowers’ early repayments, known as prepayments.

In this paper, we focus on MBSs backed by fixed-rate residential mortgage loans. Under fixed-rate mortgages, borrowers generally make constant monthly principal and interest payments, which serve as the source of cash flows distributed to MBS investors. Therefore, if all borrowers continue to make their contractual payments until their loans mature, the principal and interest cash flows received by MBS investors are predetermined.

Under fixed-rate mortgages, borrowers generally make constant monthly principal and interest payments, which serve as the source of cash flows distributed to MBS investors. Therefore, if all borrowers continue to make their contractual payments until their loans mature, the principal and interest cash flows received by MBS investors are predetermined.

On the other hand, under typical mortgage contracts, borrowers are allowed to repay all or part of the outstanding principal before the scheduled maturity date. Such early repayments are referred to as prepayments. When prepayments occur, principal is repaid ahead of schedule in addition to the scheduled principal and interest payments, thereby altering the amounts of subsequent principal and interest payments. Consequently, the future cash flows of MBSs depend on borrowers’ prepayment behavior, making their valuation more complex than that of straight bonds.

In addition to scheduled principal and interest payments, principal collected through borrowers’ prepayments is generally passed through directly to investors. In this paper, we investigate the valuation of such pass-through MBSs.

Therefore, investors in MBSs backed by such mortgages can be viewed as effectively holding a short position in the prepayment option. The optionality associated with prepayments and its effects on MBS prices and interest-rate sensitivities have been extensively studied in the literature.

Hendershott and Van Order (1987) examine the valuation of fixed-rate mortgages within an option-pricing framework by relating the value of a prepayable mortgage to that of an otherwise equivalent nonprepayable mortgage and the values of contingent claims, including the prepayment option granted to the borrower. As interest rates decline, borrowers have stronger incentives to refinance, increasing the value of the prepayment option and thereby limiting the increase in the value of prepayable mortgages relative to nonprepayable mortgages. They also emphasize the importance of modeling actual prepayment behavior as a function of economic variables, including interest rates, rather than relying solely on a simple optimal exercise boundary.

They demonstrate that securities whose cash flows change in response to future interest-rate movements require a valuation approach different from that used for fixed-rate bonds with predetermined cash flows. papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
papers.abstract: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at https://github.com/JaydenTeoh/Soft-MTP.

Next-token prediction (NTP) has become a general recipe for training large language models (LLMs), yielding models with remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks (Radford et al., 2019). One might argue that the NTP objective is sufficient—any distribution over token sequences can, in theory, be factorized autoregressively and modeled by a sufficiently expressive next-token predictor (Sutskever, 2023).

One might argue that the NTP objective is sufficient—any distribution over token sequences can, in theory, be factorized autoregressively and modeled by a sufficiently expressive next-token predictor (Sutskever, 2023).

Yet, Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) (Stern et al., 2018; Qi et al., 2020; Gloeckle et al., 2024), which trains a model to predict multiple future tokens, has now been widely adopted in modern LLM training, including in DeepSeek-V3/4 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2026b), Nemotron 3 (NVIDIA, 2025), GLM-5 (GLM-5-Team, 2026), and Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), just to name a few. MTP offers two main advantages over NTP—better model performance and more efficient inference. As a learning objective, MTP has been shown to alleviate the myopic nature of the next-token supervision (Bachmann and Nagarajan, 2024; Gloeckle et al., 2024; Nagarajan et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026), leading to stronger downstream performance on long-horizon domains such as mathematics and code. More importantly, MTP heads can also be used for speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2023) to accelerate model inference.

Despite the wide adoption of MTP, we still understand little about how it interacts with next-token prediction and which objective is best for training the MTP heads. During speculative decoding, a token drafted by MTP is accepted only if it agrees with the model’s own next-token prediction. If the goal is to improve speculative decoding, shouldn’t we directly train the model’s MTP heads to match its own NTP distribution via self-distillation? Recent work does exactly this (Teoh et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a), but naïvely minimizing an explicit KL divergence requires materializing vocabulary-sized logit tensors for both the teacher and the student, which is costly in memory and incompatible with the standard fused cross-entropy kernels used in modern pre-training (Hsu et al., 2025; Wijmans et al., 2025). In practice, frontier models still train their MTP heads with standard cross-entropy against the data.

papers.title: The Characteristics of Finite Projections of Certain Stochastic Processes and Queues
papers.abstract: This thesis studies finite projections of transient regenerative processes, constructed by conditioning regeneration cycles to be finite. It develops comparisons between the original and projected laws, including finite-time bounds and best-approximation properties for specified metrics and comparison classes. Applications concern birth-and-death processes, Markov chains and semi-Markov processes, with explicit queueing examples. Structural results describe projections associated with different regeneration states, invariant measures and connections with Martin boundary kernels. The thesis also studies reconstruction of birth-and-death rates from passage-time laws and continued-fraction representations of Laplace-Stieltjes transforms for skip-free semi-Markov processes, together with truncation-error bounds. This is a corrected English edition of a Romanian doctoral thesis completed in 1998 and defended in 1999. The preface distinguishes the historical work from corrections and later additions made for this edition.

The aim of this method is to simplify the study of transient regenerative processes and unstable queueing systems by replacing them with recurrent models and, when the projected mean regeneration cycle is finite, stable models with equilibrium distributions. The notion of finite projection is based on a natural method of conditioning regenerative processes on certain events of probability zero through a limiting construction.

Our main objective is to highlight the optimality of the finite projection in the sense of the introduced metrics, which essentially represent modifications of the total variation distance and the Hellinger distance between probabilities. With this, the quality of finite projections in approximating initial processes over finite and infinite time intervals is examined. While the continuity of processes and stochastic systems over both finite and infinite time intervals [36], [41] has been studied in the works of many researchers, the specificity of the problems examined in this work allows, in addition to demonstrating the continuity of finite projection, the determination of asymptotically sharp finite-time errors under the stated observability and parameter assumptions.

Another aspect of this research is the conditioning of stochastic processes, a subject with a long history. Kolmogorov’s measure-theoretic formulation of conditional probability is based on the Radon–Nikodym theorem [46]. This rigorous definition does not, by itself, provide a universal constructive rule for conditioning on events of probability zero. Different limiting procedures that appear natural can lead to different conditional laws; see, for example, [10], [11], [12]. Similar questions arise for finite projections of regenerative processes. For a transient irreducible time-homogeneous Markov chain, choosing a regeneration state gives a finite projection under which that state is recurrent. On an infinite state space this gives a family indexed by the states, although different states need not give distinct projections; see Section 3.3. Rényi proposed an alternative axiomatic framework for conditional probability in [67], [68], [69]. This framework extends the scope of the usual probability-space formulation. The relation between the two frameworks is not examined here: we treat conditioning as the application of a projection operator that transforms one probability measure into another.

Another aspect of this research is the conditioning of stochastic processes, a subject with a long history. Kolmogorov’s measure-theoretic formulation of conditional probability is based on the Radon–Nikodym theorem [46]. This rigorous definition does not, by itself, provide a universal constructive rule for conditioning on events of probability zero. Different limiting procedures that appear natural can lead to different conditional laws; see, for example, [10], [11], [12]. Similar questions arise for finite projections of regenerative processes. For a transient irreducible time-homogeneous Markov chain, choosing a regeneration state gives a finite projection under which that state is recurrent. On an infinite state space this gives a family indexed by the states, although different states need not give distinct projections; see Section 3.3. Rényi proposed an alternative axiomatic framework for conditional probability in [67], [68], [69]. This framework extends the scope of the usual probability-space formulation. The relation between the two frameworks is not examined here: we treat conditioning as the application of a projection operator that transforms one probability measure into another.

A short introduction cannot cover the entire literature on conditioning stochastic processes, so the references given here are selective and may not be representative. A principal concern of these studies is to identify properties and relationships shared by the original and conditioned processes. Conditioning Brownian motion has received particularly extensive attention. We mention the work of Doob [22], McKean [56], and Williams [80], together with the later works [8], [9], [19], [20], [21], [30], [54], [61], and [81]. These results also motivated analogous studies of random walks; see, for example, [10], [11], [15], [23], [43], [62], and [63]. During the decade preceding this thesis, research on the existence and properties of quasi-stationary distributions of Markov chains became increasingly active, although the general problem remained unresolved. This line of research was developed in the work of Seneta and Vere-Jones [71], [72]. Among the later publications available at the time, we mention [44], [64], and [29]. These works establish connections between quasi-stationarity, the lifetime of a Markov chain, and conditioning.

papers.title: Transfer kernels and the Schur multiplier
papers.abstract: In this article we prove that if $H$ is a normal subgroup of a finite group $G$ with $G/H$ cyclic, then the kernel of the transfer map $G/G' \longrightarrow H/H'$ equals $(G:H)$ times the order of the cokernel of the natural map $M(H) \longrightarrow M(G)$.

papers.title: A Primer on Instanton Physics - A Short Course
papers.abstract: These six lectures, delivered at the University of New Brunswick 6-21 October 2026, are an introduction to instantons in quantum mechanics and quantum field theory for senior undergraduate and beginning graduate students. The first four lectures deal solely with particle mechanics, building the necessary background for the last two that cover applications in semi-classical field theory.

papers.title: From Grind to Grasp
papers.abstract: Discussions of complexity, knowledge and intelligence often overlook the work involved. For example, outputs generated by short programs have low algorithmic complexity but can have high computational depth, the least work needed to produce them from near-shortest programs. Producing them with less work can require longer descriptions, giving high work-bounded complexity. We introduce a formalism that compares achievements under work and information limits and describes how learning and persistence can make deep achievements shallow by reusing products of earlier work. For an agent with a limited work budget, the value of building and maintaining such resources depends on how they support its goals over later tasks. We define grasp as performance across work budgets at a fixed information allowance. Low grasp can still yield success through grind at high cost in work, without necessarily improving human grasp. Applied to improvement itself, grasp gives a criterion for recursive self-improvement in which successors make comparable further improvements more efficiently. Another route to faster progress is to expand the resources brought to bear through knowledge sharing and coordination across society, even while comparable advances require increasing work. Grasp also applies to collectives, which may outperform their members yet require more total work than one system with their combined resources. Establishing and sustaining organisation can itself be deep even when the primary task is simple. These demands may help explain the richness of biological and social systems. In agent collectives, this organisational work can generate goals beyond assigned tasks, including maintaining the collective itself. We therefore caution against allowing an emergent agent society to assume authority over social coordination, since it could increasingly direct work towards its own persistence and goals.
papers.intro:
Discussions of complexity, knowledge and intelligence often overlook the work involved in producing an outcome, even though an agent with a limited work budget must decide how to use it to pursue its goals. A familiar example is the use of emergent complexity to describe apparently complex outputs generated by simple programs [106]. In algorithmic information theory, an output’s complexity is the length of the shortest program that produces it on a fixed reference computer. An output fully determined by a short program therefore has low algorithmic complexity, but its computational depth (the least work needed to produce it from a description close to the shortest possible) can be high [9, 60]. Producing the output within a work budget below that depth requires a longer description, potentially much longer than the unrestricted minimum [21]. The length of this longer description offers one interpretation of the complexity a human observer experiences. The products of earlier computation can change the work required later, whether they are byproducts saved while pursuing an immediate goal or resources built specifically to make future tasks easier. An output that was deep from an earlier starting condition can become shallow from a state that inherits products from related tasks. A similar dynamic arises in physical and chemical systems when structures form without anyone constructing them and persist to support or constrain later processes [36, 35].

To see how learning can reduce the work needed for a task, consider chess. A novice may need extensive calculation to understand a position that an expert grasps almost immediately. Early studies of expert cognition in chess [22, 14] showed how experience changes what players recognise and choose to examine. Learning can therefore affect both the work required for a particular achievement and the performance reached with the resources available. For a chess engine, quality of play depends on the amount of allocated computation. However, one system may perform better with little computation while another benefits more from a larger budget. To compare their core capabilities, the limit on additional information about the position must also be fixed, since a hint or an intermediate result can reduce the work left to do.

We call the performance a system can attain across work budgets at a fixed information allowance its grasp. One system’s grasp dominates that of another when it can match every performance level the other can attain with at most the same work. New large language models are often compared with earlier versions from the same lab by plotting performance on a task family against tokens used or monetary cost. Tokens and monetary cost are practical proxies whose relation to counted work depends on the implementation. Across a broad family of tasks, grasp dominance gives an efficiency-based view of intelligence. Many familiar notions, such as knowing and coordinating, depend on a work budget in this way. In our sense, knowing how to solve a task requires being able to produce a solution within a given work budget and input bound. A system that can reach the same level of performance with less work has a better grasp of the task at that level. Low grasp can still yield success through grind, at a high cost in work.

A chess engine’s capabilities can depend on trained parameters, an opening book of previously analysed moves, endgame tables containing results for positions with few remaining pieces, and heuristic rules for evaluating positions and selecting candidate moves. A transformer trained on the values that a chess engine’s search assigns to moves can play strongly without searching during move selection [79]. Software libraries let a user build on work that others have already done. NumPy, a numerical library for Python, provides linalg.solve for solving a system of linear equations. This function uses routines from the LAPACK numerical library [69]. A developer can call it instead of writing the numerical procedure for each application. The execution still requires computation, while development work is reduced. Similarly, in cellular automata, Gosper’s Hashlife algorithm for Conway’s Game of Life [33] caches canonical spatial blocks of cells together with their evolved future centres in a hash table, replacing step-by-step simulation whenever a configuration recurs.

A system boundary specifies which parts are included in the system for the purposes of our comparisons. A library can belong to the system’s state or be available as an external resource, though reading and using it require work in either case. Real systems can also maintain physical or organisational boundaries and spend work to keep the products of earlier work inside them. Cells maintain membranes, while projects maintain shared storage and control access to it. Whether those products remain available can then depend on the work available for this maintenance (section 4.1). The system boundary is one fundamental choice in defining our notions, and the reference machine is another. We use one fixed reference machine to compare description lengths, while work is counted in the system being evaluated.

We introduce the notion of work-reducing information (WRI) as retained information that lowers the least work required for the same output or achievement when all else is equal. Some WRI comes from saving intermediate steps of an ongoing task, while much of it comes from work invested in advance, such as building a chess endgame table or pre-training a large language model. Constructing an endgame table is a different form of task from consulting it during play, and playing games is not the most efficient way to build one. Producing or improving a more efficient program for generating such tables is yet another form of task, one that lowers the work required for improving the chess engine itself. Acquisition depth is the depth of the task of obtaining a state with a required capability.

papers.title: Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4
papers.abstract: We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr.

papers.intro:
Speech recognition on microcontrollers usually means recognizing a fixed list of commands. Espressif’s ESP-SR, for instance, recognizes up to 200 commands on the ESP32-S3 [11]. Writing down arbitrary speech needs a model with tens of millions of parameters, which is more than the memory of most microcontrollers and, until recently, more than their arithmetic could handle. Oído [29] has just shown a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model on the ESP32-S3 that transcribes in 1.97 times the audio duration on one core: close to real time, not yet in it.

This report describes how we ran a model five times larger, faster than real time and in streaming mode, on the ESP32-P4. The chip has two 400 MHz RISC-V cores with a 128-bit SIMD extension called PIE [12]; it has no neural accelerator, and the board we used adds 32 MB of PSRAM and 16 MB of flash. The model is Kroko [4], a streaming Zipformer2 transducer [31, 15] for English, trained by Banafo and released as int8 ONNX weights for sherpa-onnx [19]. We did not retrain it. Everything described here happens after training: the weights go to 2 and 4 bits, the activations to int16 and int8, and a C engine with hand-written PIE kernels runs the result.

The report makes four contributions. • A training-free method that stores a streaming transducer’s encoder with 2 or 4 bits per weight in the Cactus Quants layout [8] (Hadamard-rotated groups of 128, Lloyd-Max levels [22, 23], one norm per group): a bit width per matrix from its measured sensitivity, then a sequential pass that corrects each matrix toward the original model before rounding it with GPTQ [14] and choosing the group norms. It brings 71 MB to 26.65 MB for half a point of WER on test-clean, and an ablation on the whole test set shows what each part contributes (Section 4). • An integer design, chosen by measurement in a GPU simulator before it was written in C, that costs no measurable accuracy on LibriSpeech, FLEURS or Common Voice (Sections 5 and 9.2). • A C engine with PIE SIMD kernels that is bit-exact with its PC build, so that every accuracy number in this report is measured on complete test sets and is also the chip’s, and the cost of each design step measured again in a single build (Sections 6 and 7). • An account of what did not work, including an attempt to reach 16 MB with slimming and quantization-aware training that stopped at 19.63 MB (Sections 10 and 11). The engine and the firmware are open source [7], and so are the weights [6]. The conversion code is not part of the release; Section 4 and Algorithm 1 describe the method in enough detail to reimplement it.

papers.title: Examples of rigid Twistor D-modules
papers.abstract: The well-established theory of D-modules gives a framework to study linear differential equations from the perspective of algebraic geometry. A significant advancement in this theory has been the introduction of Twistor D-modules by Claude Sabbah and Takuro Mochizuki: These objects expose inherent, but hidden information of the underlying differential equations in an elegant way. We explain the foundational concepts of Twistor D-modules and give concrete examples of these objects. We introduce a notion of rigidity for Twistor D-modules, which these examples fulfill. We conclude with a certain algebraicity conjecture about rigid Twistor D-modules, which we prove in a special case.

papers.title: Small-time Wasserstein action for KPZ and $\Phi^4_3$
papers.abstract: We determine the leading small-time Wasserstein action of the full spatial laws of centered KPZ and dynamical $\Phi^4_3$, both started from zero. The leading term is Gaussian, with an explicit heat-trace constant. A common comparison also determines the ratio of length to displacement. For KPZ, a first-chaos cancellation yields a quadratic coupling error. For $\Phi^4_3$, two weighted entropies and an adjoint estimate give comparison bounds uniform in the spectral cutoff. Integrating a Gaussian rotation gives a differentiable realization of the full law; the comparison holds at every positive time.

Its leading small-time term equals that of the Gaussian linearization; we bound the nonlinear error.

papers.title: Gradient Estimates for Hessian Equations with Measure Data
papers.abstract: In this article, we establish the interior gradient estimates for $k$-Hessian equations with measure data. We use the ideas from the potential theories for the $p$-Laplacian type equations and pointwise estimates of $k$-subharmonic functions by Labutin. The interior gradient regularity is optimal for $k\geqslant3$, while for $k=2$, we prove the interior $W^{2,1+\varepsilon}$ and $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimates for $2$-subharmonic solutions.
papers.intro:
The notion of kk-Hessian measure and kk-subharmonic function in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} was introduced by Trudinger and Wang in [39], [40] and [41]. Their results provided a framework for the theory of weak solutions of kk-Hessian equations, extending the classical theory of Riesz measure when k=1k=1 and Monge–Ampère measure when k=nk=n. Later in [23], Labutin studied the potential theory for kk-subharmonic functions analogous to the classical potential theory for subharmonic functions. In this article, we concern the further properties for such functions. More precisely, we establish the interior gradient estimates by means of the natural Wolff potential of certain kk-Hessian measure. The resulting estimates provide a comprehensive picture concerning the pure interior regularity results for kk-Hessian equations. Our work is inspired by the gradient potential theory of quasilinear equations (see [13, 14, 12, 22, 28, 32, 33]); however, some of our results are totally different, since the key estimates in the quasilinear case are not valid for the kk-Hessian operator.

papers.title: Maxwell's equations are universal for sparse linear algebra
papers.abstract: Optical and wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a route to accelerating linear algebra, with metamaterials and photonic circuits shown to invert matrices and solve integral equations. However, it has remained unclear which problems such passive structures can represent, and at what cost, once encoding, precision, conditioning and readout are accounted for. Here, we show that every polynomially conditioned sparse linear system can be compiled into a three-dimensional dielectric -- a cavity filled with lossless, isotropic material of bounded permittivity -- whose time-harmonic response encodes its solution. For $m$ nonzero coefficients, the volume of the structure and the cost of writing it down and reading out the answer scale as $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$, coefficients require only $O(\log m)$ bits, and every field that approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations decodes to an approximate solution. We prove the construction for the continuum equations and give a computer-assisted version for the Yee discretization underlying finite-difference solvers. Read in reverse, it implies that electromagnetic simulation is, up to this overhead, as hard as general sparse linear algebra: a sufficiently fast general-purpose Maxwell solver would yield a faster sparse linear solver.
papers.intro:
Solving large sparse systems of linear equations is the central task of scientific computing, and electromagnetics is no exception: discretizing Maxwell’s equations with finite differences or finite elements turns the analysis and design of a photonic device into a sparse linear system with millions to billions of unknowns [1, 2, 3]. Optical analog computing runs this correspondence in the opposite direction. Instead of computing the response of a given structure, one designs a structure whose response computes something else – e.g., a derivative, a convolution or the solution of an equation [4, 5, 6]. Metamaterials and inverse-designed metastructures have been shown to solve integral equations [7, 8, 9], reconfigurable networks invert matrices [10, 11], and integrated photonic circuits solve differential equations [12, 13]. These build on a broader effort to perform linear algebra with light, from universal interferometer meshes [14, 15, 16, 17, 18] to optical neural networks and photonic tensor cores [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24].

Metamaterials and inverse-designed metastructures have been shown to solve integral equations [7, 8, 9], reconfigurable networks invert matrices [10, 11], and integrated photonic circuits solve differential equations [12, 13]. These build on a broader effort to perform linear algebra with light, from universal interferometer meshes [14, 15, 16, 17, 18] to optical neural networks and photonic tensor cores [19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24].

Whether such devices can ever offer a computational advantage is decided by details that are easy to overlook in a demonstration: the cost of programming the device, the precision with which it must be built and read out, the sensitivity of the answer to imperfections, and the size of the structure as the problem grows [25, 6]. The same questions were asked of analog computers long before the current interest in photonics, and they have a precise formulation in the theory of computation [26, 27, 28, 29, 30]. Physical systems as simple as waves, rays and fluids can embed universal computation [31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36], but these constructions establish what is computable in principle, not what a physical system computes efficiently. For optical equation solvers, the relevant question is quantitative: which linear systems can a passive optical structure represent, and how large, precise and well-conditioned must it be? Current demonstrations encode a fixed kernel or a small, dense matrix, and they do not answer this question.

The linear systems produced by Maxwell solvers are highly structured – local, three-dimensional and determined by a scalar material distribution – and fast solvers exploit this structure wherever they can [37, 38, 39, 40]. However, time-harmonic wave problems are notoriously hard to solve iteratively [41, 42, 43], and it is not known whether their structure makes them fundamentally easier than general sparse systems. For other structured classes this question has sharp answers. Graph Laplacians can be solved in nearly linear time [44], whereas the stiffness matrices of trusses and multi-commodity flow problems are as hard as general sparse systems [45, 46, 47]. For Maxwell’s equations, no such statement exists.

Physically, the construction is the familiar picture of coupled defect modes in a photonic crystal [48, 49, 50], made quantitative. papers.title: The Oriented Freudenthal Suspension Theorem
papers.abstract: The Freudenthal Suspension Theorem states that the connectivity of the unit map $X\rightarrow\Omega\Sigma X$ of the suspension-loop adjunction for a pointed space $X$ is twice the connectivity of $X$ itself. We extend this theorem to $X$ being a pointed $(\infty,\infty)$-category, i.e. an oriented space in the sense of Gepner--Heine.

In recent times, the subject of oriented category theory, i.e. the study of what is classically called (∞,∞)(\infty,\infty)- or (∞,ω)(\infty,\omega)-categories together with the monoidal structure known as the Gray tensor product, is becoming increasingly prevalent. There are numerous reasons for this, e.g. it is the natural setting for higher Morita, span and bordism categories ([19], [20], [16]), and a natural intermediate stage in the passage from geometry to homotopy theory ([36], [35], [11]). The general theory is being developed by Gepner–Heine in an ongoing series of papers [15, 14, 13], and one of its central features is to understand higher categories themselves as geometric objects, resulting in a theory that bears a striking resemblance to classical algebraic topology (e.g. one has cellular filtrations, Postnikov-towers, obstruction theory, etc.). In a sense, this program encapsulates the categorification of classical algebraic topology. Additionally, the oriented analogue of stable homotopy theory has been studied: it starts with the foundational work of Stefanich [36] and Masuda [35] on categorical spectra, and has been continued in [23, 24].

papers.title: The Categorical Fargues-Scholze Correspondence at Generic Parameters
papers.abstract: Let $G$ be a quasi-split reductive group over a finite extension $F$ of $\mathbb{Q}_p$. We study the Fargues-Scholze categorical Langlands correspondence at generic parameters $\phi$, namely those whose semisimplification does not coincide with that of any parameter with nontrivial monodromy. Extending the theory of quasi-exceptional sets on the nilpotent cone developed by Bezrukavnikov to the setting of disconnected reductive groups which arise as stabilizers of semisimple generic parameters, to any irreducible representation $\rho$ of such a group we construct sheaves labeled $\overline{\nabla}_\rho$, $\overline{\Delta}_\rho$, $IC_\rho$, and $\delta_\rho$ on the moduli stack of L-parameters for $G$. Using forthcoming work of Hamann, Hansen, and Mann on geometric Eisenstein series compatibility, the (conjectural, in general) behavior of the correspondence at generous parameters, and the (conjectural, in general) agreement between Fargues-Scholze and classical semisimple L-parameters we prove that these sheaves correspond under the Fargues-Scholze functor to the sheaves $i_{b!}\pi$, $i_{b\sharp}\pi$, $i_{b\sharp!}\pi$, and $i_{b!*}\pi$ on $\text{Bun}_G$, where $\pi$ is a smooth irreducible representation with Fargues-Scholze parameter $\phi$. As applications we prove t-exactness properties of the Fargues-Scholze functor specialized at a generic parameter, and that Hecke operators are perverse t-exact on the generic locus. We also construct and study foundational properties of Hecke eigensheaves at generic parameters, compute non-semisimplified Fargues-Scholze parameters on the generic locus, and construct a Fargues-Scholze-theoretic version of the BM-O bijection at generic parameters.
