papers.title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
papers.abstract:
We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize.
  We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options.
  Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2\pi X)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.
papers.intro:
We develop a common planning framework for episodic bandits over unknown recurring priors, incorporating delayed observations, hard per-arm budgets and per-episode caps, and risk-sensitive objectives beyond expected reward. In an episodic bandit or a meta-bandit problem there are nn unknown arms and a learner uses these arms over NN episodes, each with at most TT decision steps. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from the recurring, initially unknown prior distribution. A single episode is a finite-horizon multi-armed bandit problem. At each step, the learner plays an arm, earns reward and generates an observation. The observation provides information about the current episode’s arm quality and, across episodes, its recurring prior. Therefore the typical multi-armed bandit tradeoff of explore/use now expands to explore, use, and generalize. Meta-bandits formalize this transfer/generalization by learning shared priors [25, 7, 19] using variants of Thompson sampling. Other examples include cold-start dynamic pricing [6], cloud management [31], database tuning across hardware environments [43], program synthesis [13], and LLM routing [41]. The analyzed MetaTS policy supplements Thompson sampling with a forced play of every arm in each task [25, Section 4.1]. HierTS avoids forced exploration in its sequential Gaussian analysis, but its concurrent guarantee again prescribes initial exploratory actions [19, Sections 6.1 and 6.3]. These methods share information through a hierarchical posterior, while their guarantees establish the learning produced by specified sampling and exploration rules. They do not explicitly optimize which observations are worth acquiring through their contribution to later feasible decisions. Even with independent arms, optimizing each episode separately can lose linearly in NN by never collecting observations valuable to later episodes (Examples A.1 and A.2). We formulate a common planning objective that accounts for current reward, resource consumption and the continuation of learning. Its execution guarantee then accounts for the information and reward actually realized under the hard constraints.

Budgets are natural in distributed applications of episodic bandits. Budgeted learning is NP-hard even for a single episode with independent arms [16]. An unexpectedly long episode, or a favorable draw of an arm’s episode quality, can make immediate use attractive enough to exhaust the arm’s remaining budget. Those plays then become unavailable for learning and reward in later episodes. Per-episode caps limit this drawdown. Routing, coding, tuning and pricing also motivate risk-sensitive objectives beyond expected reward. Risk-sensitive objectives introduce a further structural difficulty. Mean–variance criteria need not satisfy Bellman’s principle of optimality, and maximizing expected return subject to a variance bound is NP-hard in finite-horizon Markov decision processes [27]. The objective depends on the return distribution across possible histories. Evaluating risk conditional on a sampled episode quality can discard variation that determines which action is preferable (Example A.6). Planning over outcome distributions retains this variation: fixed outcome scores enter as linear coefficients, while risk functionals act on the resulting law (Subsection 3.5).

Delays couple decisions within and across episodes. Concurrent Bayesian meta-bandits [19] analyze feedback withheld within a batch of decisions, and distributed optimization also motivates delayed feedback [2]. Delayed observation in learning dates back to Anderson [3]. Surprisingly, it was shown by Eick [12] that in the presence of delays an optimal policy can use a known arm and later return to an unknown arm. Thus the optimal policy of a delayed finite horizon multi-armed bandit problem is not a familiar stopping time problem [14], creating a foundational divergence from standard multi-armed bandits. A late-arriving observation changes an arm’s information even when the arm is not being played. This violates the standard rested-bandit assumption, and such arms are restless [40]. Caro and Yoo [9] study no-crossover delays. General restless bandits have no known tractable algorithms, and their decision versions are PSPACE-hard [30]. Here the delayed observations result from our own earlier plays and arrive on a calendar fixed in advance. We call this planned restlessness.

papers.title: Beyond Passing Tests: A Systematic Review and Controlled Re-evaluation of Techniques for Improving the Quality of LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Large language models pass most functional-correctness benchmarks, but passing tests says little about whether their code is readable, efficient or secure. Many techniques claim to improve these qualities, yet their evidence is scattered, usually covers one quality dimension and is rarely compared at an equal compute budget. We contribute a systematic review and a controlled re-evaluation. A systematic literature review of 628 primary studies (July 2021 to October 2026), with disclosed, author-reviewed LLM assistance, organizes the techniques by stage, signal source and quality target. Most studies measure only the dimension they target, gains often come with unchanged or unreported correctness, single automated quality signals are gamed, and compute, variance and contamination are rarely reported. A controlled re-evaluation runs ten techniques on four models at matched budgets on correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks, extends it to thirteen current models and repository-level tasks, and compares 66 highlighted techniques head-to-head on Gemma 4 31B. At one call, quality prompting raises analyzer issue counts and leaves complexity and judge scores almost unchanged. At matched budgets, best-of-n sampling with an analyzer-weighted ranker matches or beats prompting, planning, self-refinement, a reviewer agent and retrieval on measures the ranker does not optimize, while an analyzer feedback loop and fine-tuning beat it only on analyzer issue counts. Large correctness losses on HumanEval+, a likely contaminated benchmark near its ceiling, do not appear on contests held after the models' training cutoffs. In the head-to-head, 1 of 66 techniques beats best-of-n on its primary target beyond the 95% interval, a rate consistent with chance. Gains should be reported against a budget-matched sampling baseline and on measures independent of the technique's own signal.
papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) now write a large share of new code, and the benchmarks used to judge them are running out of headroom. On SWE-bench Verified, the most cited measure of repository-level coding, the leading system reached 97.00% as of September 1, 2026 (Vals AI, 2026). OpenAI stopped evaluating on it on February 23, 2026, stating that it “is increasingly contaminated” and recommending SWE-bench Pro instead (OpenAI, 2026m). Function-level suites such as HumanEval and MBPP saturated earlier (§5). When nearly every model passes, the tests no longer tell us which code is better.

A program can pass every test and still be hard to read, slow, or exploitable, and evidence of a large gap predates current models. When Pearce et al. (2022) prompted GitHub Copilot with scenarios tied to high-risk weaknesses, about 40% of the 1,689 generated programs were vulnerable. In BaxBench, exploits succeeded on around half of each model’s correct back-end programs (Vero et al., 2025). Liu et al. (2024d) found code-style and maintainability issues in 1,930 of 4,066 ChatGPT solutions, and on EffiBench GPT-4’s code ran on average 3.12 times as long as the human-written canonical solutions (Huang et al., 2024b). Agent code was 2.3x more verbose and 2.0x more eroded than code in 473 open-source Python repositories (Orlanski et al., 2026). These context studies (Section 2) support our thesis: code quality is not the same as functional correctness, and a technique that raises pass@1 while degrading maintainability, efficiency or security has produced a finding, not a success.

A fast-growing literature improves LLM code beyond correctness through quality-oriented prompting, analyzer feedback loops, self-refinement, multi-agent pipelines, retrieval, constrained decoding and training-time alignment. The evidence, spread across software-engineering, machine-learning and security venues, is hard to use for three reasons. First, most studies measure only the dimension they target, so a security technique’s effect on readability, or a readability technique’s on correctness, is rarely known. Second, iterative techniques spend several times their baselines’ compute, and gains often shrink once compute is matched (Olausson et al., 2024). Third, base models change faster than the studies: a technique evaluated on GPT-3.5 in 2023 says little about its value for a 2026 reasoning model.

This article has two parts. The first, a systematic literature review (SLR), follows Kitchenham-style guidelines and is reported per SEGRESS (Kitchenham et al., 2023) and PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021). We searched OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv from July 2021 to October 2026, calibrated the search string against a quasi-gold standard (Zhang et al., 2011), screened 6942 records with LLM assistance disclosed under GUEST (Kitchenham et al., 2026), and included 628 primary studies; the author reviewed every LLM screening, eligibility and extraction decision (§4). The second, a controlled re-evaluation (§16), re-runs ten techniques, one or more per family, and a single-shot baseline on a fixed grid of one closed frontier and three open-weight models, on fixed correctness, maintainability, efficiency and security benchmarks at matched budgets; an extended grid of thirteen current closed and open-weight models adds the repository- and agent-level benchmarks that dominate 2026 model releases (DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench, FrontierCode, SlopCodeBench, GSO, SWE-fficiency, SusVibes).

The review answers five research questions: RQ1 (taxonomy).: What techniques have been proposed to improve the non-functional quality of LLM-generated code, and how can they be organized? RQ2 (targets and measurement).: Which quality dimensions does each technique target, and how is each measured? RQ3 (effects and trade-offs).: What effects are reported on the target, on correctness, and on non-targeted dimensions? RQ4 (evidence quality).: How rigorous and reproducible is the evidence (baselines, compute reporting, contamination handling, human validation, artifacts)? RQ5 (gaps).: Which combinations of technique, dimension and setting are unstudied or under-studied? The re-evaluation adds four empirical questions (ERQ1–ERQ4, §16): matched-budget effects on the target, correctness and other dimensions; their dependence on model strength and architecture; and how the highlighted techniques compare in one setting.

papers.title: Grothendieck Pairs, Functors and Profinite Invariants
papers.abstract: As another variation of profinite properties, we define the notion of natural profinite invariants: functorial invariants, inducing isomorphisms for every Grothendieck pair. We give a characterisation of when adjoint functors are natural profinite invariants and describe a strategy on how to disprove natural profinite invariance. By means of examples we show that the notions of profinite invariance and natural profinite invariances are logically independent.

papers.title: Coarse comparison of Bessel families
papers.abstract: We classify Bessel families in separable Hilbert spaces under coarse equivalence relations: $f$ and $\tilde f$ are equivalent if the seminorms $\|T_f\,\cdot\|$ and $\|T_{\tilde f}\,\cdot\|$ of their analysis operators are mutually dominated, up to constants, after pullback along operators $w,\tilde w$ of a prescribed class $\mathcal O$. In contrast with orbit relations such as unitary or similarity equivalence, these relations ignore redundancy and the geometry of the index set, and compare frames, nonframes and compact families on the same footing. They are level $-1$ of the comparison categories of the companion article, and we compute the levels $0$ and $k\ge1$: they are trivial for bounded, injective, bounded below, isometric and upper semi-Fredholm comparison operators, and for invertible or unitary ones level $1$ is a stabilizer-type group of the family. For bounded $\mathcal O$ the classes are given by the singular numbers up to constants; injective operators add the kernel dimension, bounded below operators or isometries add upper semi-Fredholmness, and invertible, unitary or surjective operators give the kernel dimension and the dyadic multiplicity sequence of the spectrum up to bounded displacement on the logarithmic scale, which splits each remaining class into continuum many. Upper semi-Fredholm operators give only three noncompact classes, whereas Fredholm operators give continuum many, so that the Fredholm relation is strictly finer. For each relation we determine exactly which families are equivalent to an orthonormal basis, and we compute an operator Banach--Mazur distance, $\log(\sup_ns_n/\tilde s_n\cdot\sup_n\tilde s_n/s_n)$. As applications, we obtain a relative Paley--Wiener stability theorem for Bessel families and the invariance of Schatten membership and of $\int\|f\|^2$ under coarse equivalence.

Such relations are rigid: they preserve every spectral invariant of the analysis operator and they only compare families living in isomorphic spaces.

papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers: Bridging the Compositionality Gap in GPT-2-like Models
papers.abstract: Compositional generalization remains a persistent limitation of transformer language models: even when a model learns to combine known facts correctly in-distribution (ID), the same compositional mechanism may fail when applied to out-of-distribution (OOD) knowledge. We investigate this compositionality gap in a controlled two-hop reasoning setting using a GPT-2-like transformer model trained from scratch. Building on prior work identifying a circuit associated with compositional generalization, we test whether the failure of OOD transfer is related to how atomic knowledge is structurally exposed during training. We modify the training distribution by presenting both ID and OOD atomic facts in a format positionally aligned with the second-hop retrieval step of the learned compositional circuit, without modifying the model architecture or adding OOD compositional supervision. Under this intervention, the model successfully transfers the learned ID compositional behaviour to held-out OOD atomic facts, closing the observed compositionality gap in the controlled setting. Our results provide evidence that the observed compositionality gap is not a fundamental architecture limitation and that it can be overcome through mechanistically informed training distribution design.
papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) can store vast amounts of knowledge, but recalling individual facts is rarely enough, many questions require combining several pieces of information through multi-hop reasoning (Wei et al., 2023; Press et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). When this composition happens inside a single forward pass, without verbalizing intermediate steps, it is called implicit reasoning. This step is all but trivial, it has been shown that models that can reliably answers two atomic queries will often fail on their composition (Press et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025), a failure Press et al. (2023) called the compositionality gap.

Explicit decomposition methods such as Chain-of-Thought can narrow the compositionality gap by verbalizing intermediate steps (Wei et al., 2023; Press et al., 2023), an inference-time solution that acts on top of the core capabilities the model acquires during (pre-)training (Zhou et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023).

Controlled studies show that grokked transformers (i.e. trained far beyond overfitting) can learn implicit two-hop composition tasks. For example, given the atomic facts “Barack’s wife is Michelle” and “Michelle was born in 1964,” the model can infer that “Barack’s wife was born in 1964.” These models generalize to unseen In-Distribution (ID) cases (atomic facts that appear in compositional training examples), yet fail to systematically transfer the same compositional behaviour to Out-of-Distribution (OOD) cases (atomic facts seen only in isolation, never in compositional training examples) (Wang et al., 2024; Karmim et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2025; Biran et al., 2024). Ye et al. (2025) pushed this further by showing that generalization extends to queries whose first-hop is OOD, but never to those whose second-hop is. So the natural question is: what limits the transfer of a learned compositional mechanism to OOD atomic facts, and under what training-data conditions can such generalization emerge?

We address this question by modifying the training distribution while keeping the task and model architecture fixed, without introducing any additional compositional supervision, working with the same rigorous synthetic setup from Wang et al. (2024). Specifically, we introduce a position-aligned atomic-fact format that exposes atomic facts in the configuration associated with second-hop processing, and use controlled ablations to identify the conditions under which the learned compositional behaviour transfers to OOD knowledge, enabling OOD compositional generalization.

papers.title: Construction and formal verification of a special topology on {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}: characterization of connected subsets
papers.abstract: We examine whether the integers admit a topology whose connected subsets are precisely the sets of consecutive integers. The main result gives a construction for every integer lattice {\mathbb{Z}}^{n}, n>0; the answer for Z is then obtained as a corollary. We prove that the neighborhoods determined by the parity of the sum of the coordinates form a basis and that topological connectedness agrees exactly with accessibility by finite paths of unit lattice steps. We also present a deductive audit and the correspondence between this argument and a verification in Lean 4 and Mathlib, including the empty set and the independent formal characterization of integer intervals. The construction and mathematical result originate in Problem 5712, proposed by Dan Marcus and solved in 1970 by the Cleveland State University group; the present article contributes a detailed exposition and a report on formal verification.

papers.title: Information-Driven Collaborative Autonomy for Heterogeneous UAV/UGV Teams
papers.abstract: This paper considers coordinating a heterogeneous team of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) traversing a domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial sensing using onboard optical cameras, adapting their trajectories to ground routes and target information. We formulate the aerial search problem using ergodic control, which distributes sensing effort according to a spatial information density to balance exploration and target localization. The formulation incorporates dynamic camera field-of-view footprints and pose-dependent probabilistic detection models. Angles-only measurements are processed through Bayesian inference and marginalization over data-association hypotheses to obtain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior, representing both detected and undetected targets. This belief directs aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and viewpoints that improve target localization. Ground planning combines chance-constrained target avoidance, enforced through confidence sets, with a void-probability objective that favors routes unlikely to contain threats. We solve each team's optimization problem in a fully decentralized manner using a nested SCvx*--C-ADMM scheme, with outer sequential convex programming iterations and inner distributed consensus optimization, accounting for nonlinearities, nonseparable objectives, and continuous-time inter-agent separation constraints. A closed-loop scheme updates both fleets' trajectories as information becomes available and permits ground motion when the remaining route risk falls below a prescribed threshold. Numerical case studies examine sensing geometry and target uncertainty, compare decentralized and centralized solvers, and demonstrate full closed-loop collaboration between multiple UAVs and UGVs.

papers.intro:
Collaborative autonomy deals with the problem of coordinating multiple autonomous vehicles to accomplish a common objective. In a homogeneous team, the vehicles typically share similar motion and sensing capabilities, allowing coordination to be formulated around a common vehicle and sensor model. Heterogeneous teams introduce an additional level of coupling, since the capabilities of one vehicle class may be needed for another to complete its task. For example, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can observe regions that are inaccessible to unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), while the ground vehicles can carry the payloads needed to execute a mission. This complementary use of aerial and ground platforms has been studied in coordinated exploration and mapping (Dewan et al., 2013), collaborative localization (Butzke et al., 2016), and persistent sensing with mobile recharging (Naveed et al., 2025).

In this work, we consider a UAV/UGV team in which the ground vehicles must traverse a bounded domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial overwatch, using onboard optical cameras to discover, localize, and track these targets before the UGVs encounter them. The difficulty is that neither fleet can plan effectively in isolation. The value of a UAV observation depends on its relevance to the ground routes, while the admissibility of those routes depends on what the UAVs have observed. Moreover, failing to detect a target does not imply that a region is empty, since the camera has a limited field of view and a non-unit probability of detection. The planning problem must therefore account for both uncertainty in detected targets and the possibility of targets that have not yet been observed.

A natural approach to the aerial search problem is ergodic control, which seeks trajectories whose time-averaged spatial statistics match a prescribed distribution over the search domain. Regions assigned greater probability mass receive proportionally more sensing effort, allowing a single objective to express both broad exploration and concentrated information gathering. The work of Mathew and Mezić (2011) introduced multiscale metrics for measuring deviations from ergodicity and designing multi-agent coverage dynamics. Subsequent works formulated continuous-time ergodic trajectory optimization (Miller and Murphey, 2013) and used expected information densities to guide active sensing with nonlinear measurement models (Miller et al., 2016). The commonly used spectral metric compares weighted Fourier coefficients of the trajectory occupation measure with those of the desired spatial distribution. Alternatively, Hughes et al. (2025) formulate ergodic trajectory optimization using maximum mean discrepancy between kernel mean embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing coverage objectives to be specified from samples on more general domains.

For a fleet of UAVs, the ergodic objective depends on the aggregate coverage of all agents and thus couples their trajectories through the team Fourier coefficients. Abraham and Murphey (2018) address this coupling through consensus on the coverage statistics, obtaining decentralized ergodic control for agents with nonlinear dynamics. The sensing model introduces a second difficulty: the point occupation measure of a vehicle does not describe the ground area observed by a camera whose footprint changes with altitude and attitude. Finite sensor footprints and obstacle constraints have been incorporated into ergodic coverage by Ayvali et al. (2017). Here, we derive the elliptical ground footprint from the position and attitude of the camera and construct a smooth, normalized sensing kernel from this geometry. Integrating this kernel along a trajectory gives an occupation measure that describes the spatial distribution of camera coverage and depends on both the translational and rotational motion of the UAV. Its spectral coefficients enter the fleet ergodic objective, so that the trajectories are optimized with respect to the area observed by the cameras. The same camera geometry also enters a spatially varying detection probability and an angles-only measurement model with pose-dependent covariance. This connects the coverage model used in trajectory planning with the missed detections and measurement uncertainty accounted for in Bayesian inference.

The search distribution must, in turn, reflect the information collected by the UAVs. Random finite set (RFS) theory provides a natural Bayesian description of this information, since both the number of targets and their states are uncertain (Mahler, 2007). The measurements are also a finite set, containing an unknown combination of target detections and clutter, with some targets producing no measurement. Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filtering represents undetected targets by a Poisson point process and detected targets by Bernoulli components conditioned on global data-association hypotheses (García-Fernández et al., 2018). Marginalizing the association uncertainty provides tractable multi-Bernoulli approximations (Williams, 2015). These ideas have also been used for multi-agent planning that balances the discovery of new objects with the tracking of existing ones (Nguyen et al., 2020). Here, we specialize the measurement update to camera-based, angles-only observations with pose-dependent detection and measurement quality, and maintain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior. This distinction between detected and undetected targets is particularly useful for ground planning, since avoiding known tracks alone does not account for threats in regions that have not been sufficiently explored.

papers.title: Diameter-two graphs whose mutual-visibility chromatic number equals their chromatic number
papers.abstract: A set $S$ of vertices of a graph $G$ is a mutual-visibility set if every pair of vertices of $S$ is joined by a shortest path whose internal vertices avoid $S$, and the mutual-visibility chromatic number $\chi_\mu(G)$ is the least number of mutual-visibility sets into which $V(G)$ can be partitioned. Klav\v{z}ar, Kuziak, Valenzuela Tripodoro and Yero (2025) proved that $\chi_\mu(G)\le\chi(G)$ whenever $G$ has diameter two, observed that equality holds for complete bipartite graphs, and asked whether there are any other diameter-two graphs attaining equality. We answer this question in the affirmative. We construct a graph $G_{11}$ of order 11 and diameter two with $\chi_\mu(G_{11})=\chi(G_{11})=3$, and an infinite family of such graphs obtained from $G_{11}$ by replacing one vertex with pairwise non-adjacent copies of it.
papers.intro:
Mutual visibility in graphs was introduced by Di Stefano [5], motivated by settings in which a set of entities placed at vertices of a network, such as mobile robots, or nodes whose messages must not pass through other members of the set, must be able to “see” one another along shortest paths that avoid the other members. The concept has since been studied intensively, including on graphs of diameter two [3]. Klavžar, Kuziak, Valenzuela Tripodoro and Yero [6] introduced the corresponding colouring problem: partition the vertex set into as few mutual-visibility sets as possible.

papers.title: Meromorphic order from Taylor coefficients, least singular values of Hankel matrices and rational approximants
papers.abstract: We introduce a natural notion of generalized order for entire and meromorphic functions and express it in terms of their Taylor coefficients. More precisely, one formula uses the least singular values of Hankel matrices of the coefficients, and the other uses their determinants. These formulas generalize the classical coefficient formula for the order of entire functions and its extensions by Edrei and Sheremeta. The proof combines a theorem of Pommerenke with a bound for the Nevanlinna characteristic that results from a convergence theorem for rational approximants introduced by Prokhorov. We also characterize the largest class of growth scales for which the associated generalized order is well-behaved.

papers.title: Guaranteed indirect delivery in directed networks: The joint extremal function and explicit attaining constructions
papers.abstract: A messenger and a pursuer move alternately on a finite loopless directed graph, with complete information and waiting permitted. The messenger moves first and wins upon reaching a designated recipient, before interception there. We determine the maximum number $M(n,m)$ of ordered nonadjacent source--recipient pairs for which delivery is guaranteed against every initial pursuer position, among graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ arcs. We give the exact value and an explicit attaining graph for every admissible pair $(n,m)$. For $n\ge12$, a piecewise formula describes sparse growth, the interval $2n\le m\le n(n-3)$ in which every missing pair can be guaranteed, a dense staircase, and the zero range above $n(n-2)$. Complete finite tables cover smaller orders. The proofs combine degree and support bounds, local strategy composition, protected routing, and constructions in the missing-arc graph. Finite exceptional cases use explicit strategy certificates and complete computational exclusions. Reproducible programs and certificates accompany the paper; a Lean development verifies the complete formula for $n\ge12$ and $m\ge24$, the claimed scores of prescribed constructions at every admissible pair, and further finite upper bounds. Its remaining obligations are stated separately.

papers.title: Does Federated Training Degrade Explainability? A Comparative Analysis of Grad-CAM Faithfulness in Centralized vs. Federated Deepfake Detection
papers.abstract: Automated detection has become the essential safeguard against realistic synthetic media, but deploying it at scale requires training on sensitive data from multiple organizations, putting privacy and the transparency demanded by forensic review in direct conflict. Federated learning resolves the privacy side by sharing only model updates rather than raw data, but whether this comes at the cost of trustworthy gradient-based explanations, which analysts rely on to decide whether or not to trust a flagged clip, has not been studied. We present the systematic study of Grad-CAM explanation faithfulness under federated deepfake detection, evaluating an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++ across five federated clients under varying degrees of data heterogeneity. We find that the relationship between federation and explanation quality is non-monotonic: at near-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed Data) and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed the faithfulness of a centralized baseline, but at extreme heterogeneity, explanations break down entirely, becoming spatially incoherent and, on average, causally misleading. This degradation is not a general cost of federated training but a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity, and we offer practical guidance for identifying when privacy-preserving deepfake detection can be deployed safely and when its explanations can no longer be trusted. Code and data partitions are available for reproducibility.

Synthetic media, also called deepfakes, has reached a level of realism that makes manual inspection unreliable and threatens digital forensics [1], information integrity, and public trust. Convolutional neural networks trained on large benchmarks such as FaceForensics++ now classify manipulated facial video with high accuracy [1], and therefore automated detection has become the front line against this threat.

Federated learning (FL) solves the first problem by letting multiple data holders train one model together without any of them sharing raw samples [4]. Under Federated Averaging, each participant trains locally on their own private data and sends only parameter updates to a central server, which combines them into a global model through sample-weighted aggregation. Digital forensics, healthcare, and finance have picked up this approach for exactly that reason.

Forensic analysts routinely trust a flagged clip because its heatmap looks plausible, yet this is precisely the signal that federated aggregation could compromise.

papers.title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.

papers.title: Rebuilding a Field's Open-Problem Catalog from the Literature: A Two-Layer Knowledge Graph, and Why Status Must Stay Proposed
papers.abstract: A research field records its open problems in surveys, keynotes and community reports. Those are prose, written every few years, and nobody can ask them who works on a problem now or whether it was settled last year. We argue the problems should be data, and we build the system that makes them so: a hand-curated problem layer carried in unchanged, under an evidence layer rebuilt from a bibliographic index, joined by typed, provenance-carrying links in one graph database and queryable from one language. A language model does four jobs -- per-paper extraction, catalog grounding, per-paper status verdict, and idea generation -- each constrained to a candidate set so out-of-set answers are refused rather than stored. We report a study on two curated catalogs, database research (1,053 problems) and AI research (1,000 problems), each with a prior catalog-only graph. The rebuilt graph answers every question the catalog-only graph answered -- 47 of 47 on databases, 34 of 35 on AI -- plus questions the catalog-only graph refused: recent workers, untouched problems, methods tried, and outside papers bearing on a problem (336 problems, 770 works on databases). The capability we most wanted does not survive its own audit. Of 41 solves and refutes verdicts hand-checked against the papers, 9 are correct, 30 partly correct and 2 wrong; no refutes verdict (0 of 34) disproves an open problem, and only 1 of 7 solves closes the central question. We report that failure in full and draw the design conclusion: a status change must be proposed with its evidence and never applied, making the human reviewer part of the architecture. We close with the data-engineering problems this raises: entity resolution across curated and harvested layers, verifying model status claims, freshness under source quotas, and evaluation without ground truth.

Ask a database researcher which problems in the field are open and they will point you at a community report [1, 2]. These reports are careful, broad and influential. They are also prose, assembled every five to ten years by a committee, and they are out of date the week they appear. Nothing in them can be asked a question. If you want to know who works on a named problem now, whether the problem was settled since the report was written, or which of its open problems nobody has touched, you read the report, then you read five years of proceedings, and then you have an opinion rather than an answer.

papers.abstract: For every bounded convex domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge2$, we establish the following sharp inequality for torsional rigidity $$T(\Omega)\ge\frac{2(d+1)}{d}\int\limits_\Omega\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^2\dd x,$$ where $T(\Omega)=4\int\limits_\Omega u\dd x$ and $-\Delta u=1$ in $\Omega$, $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Equality holds for balls.

papers.title: Bank-World: A Benchmark for Evaluating Agents on Banking Workflows
papers.abstract: Bank-World is a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions. Completing banking work requires more than producing the right calculation: agents must reconcile records, obtain permission, execute transactions, and keep instructions and status reports consistent as circumstances change. Bank-World tests these requirements through single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions. Grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, we find that correct decisions often fail to become completed work. Agents charge fees twice, distribute the correct total in incorrect amounts among the recipients, and execute payments while approval is pending. Their strengths also differ: Sol leads single-turn completion, Opus has the highest observed multi-turn completion rate, and Grok succeeds across more multi-turn tasks but less consistently. Bank-World makes these differences inspectable through task-level results and worked examples connecting source evidence, agent decisions, and simulated consequences. We retain the task environments, executable graders, and full trajectories privately to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark for future evaluations.

papers.title: When the Top Answer Decides: Gender Bias in Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models are language models built to route, classify and triage: they return option probabilities from one forward pass, and an application acts on the top answer. They are offered off the shelf, trained for the decision format rather than for fairness or any one application, and we found no bias measurement in their cards. We test TypeSafe's closed Jev and five open decision models on gender-swapped yes/no decisions about people (Tamkin et al., 2023), BBQ, StereoSet and the gender-bias studies of Fulgu and Capraro (2024). Five of the six give women significantly more favourable answers than men (+0.05 to +0.10 in log-odds), and a gender swap changes 1-3.5% of top answers (Jev's partly through its call-to-call variation). The makers' recommended confidence gate removes many biased commitments but raises the stereotyped share of those it keeps in ambiguous BBQ gender questions (granite-switch 0.76 to 0.85, pplx 0.81 to 1.00). Probes show gender preferences in the same models: all six rate violence for a greater good as more acceptable against a man than against a woman, and two default to "girl" when forced to guess a child's gender without a cue. Decision-level and probability-level measures differ, so audits should read a model as its application does.
papers.intro:
Decision models are built to act. In September 2026 TypeSafe AI released Jev, “a new class of frontier models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly” (Almeida, 2026): it answers typed questions (pick one of these options, score this on a scale, yes or no) with calibrated option probabilities from one forward pass, to “classify, route, score, extract, or branch”. It also reports a confidence on which applications set thresholds (TypeSafe AI, 2026a). Open models from Perplexity, Cloudflare, IBM, Liquid AI and Jared Palmer answer the same typed questions and can be served through llama.cpp’s /v1/systemone endpoint (Perplexity, 2026; Cloudflare, 2026; IBM Granite, 2026; Liquid AI, 2026; Palmer, 2026). We use “decision model” for this model class: a component of an automated decision-making system, which also includes the application that acts on its answers. Unless that application adds review, the model’s answer is the decision.

papers.title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI
papers.abstract: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.

Much as the transistor is the basic element of electronic circuits, the neuron is the basic element of neural networks, yet each neuron on its own already exhibits incomparably greater functional complexity. papers.title: Planarity estimates and codimension reduction for ancient flows at the Andrews-Baker threshold
papers.abstract: We derive an interior planarity estimate for space-time proper mean curvature flows of $n$-dimensional submanifolds of $\mathbb R^{n+p}$, $n\geq5$, that are uniformly quadratically pinched up to the Andrews-Baker threshold $\frac{4}{3n}$. The estimate is parabolically scale-invariant and it requires neither curvature nor entropy bounds. The proof combines Naff's gradient estimates with a localization argument in the spirit of Ecker and Huisken. In dimensions five and six, Naff's estimates alone do not give the gradient terms a sign. We bound these terms from below with an argument we developed in a previous work. As a consequence, for $n\geq5$, and by known results for $2\leq n\leq4$, every space-time proper ancient solution that is uniformly $\frac{4}{3n}$-pinched is either a static affine $n$-plane or lies in a fixed affine $(n+1)$-dimensional subspace. This replaces the finite entropy and polynomial curvature growth assumptions of Lee, Naff and Zhu by space-time properness, and improves their pinching constant in dimensions two, five and six. For closed flows, we extend Lynch's planarity estimate to a larger range of exponents.

papers.title: Accumulating Pruning Constraints: New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT
papers.abstract: We present deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT on $n$ variables exactly in time $\Ostar(2^{(1-\gamma)n})$, for a fixed $\gamma>0$, on several classes of instances whose clause density may grow with $n$. Our main tool extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm. When the search gives a variable its less promising value, comparing the two values of the variable yields a pruning constraint that is satisfied by some optimal assignment. Accumulating these constraints along each branch prunes all but an exponentially small fraction of the assignments. The classes are formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and on graphs generated by a stochastic block model. In a semirandom formula, the pairs of variables that may share a clause are arbitrary, and the clauses on these pairs are random. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms are still exact on every input, and the time bound holds with high probability over the input. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with such a running time for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances. Beyond these classes, the pruning constraints can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, and we expect them to be of practical relevance for general formulas, in particular for sparse ones, where each constraint involves only a few variables.
papers.intro:
Max-SAT is the optimization version of the fundamental NP-complete SAT problem. Instead of checking whether a Boolean formula over nn variables in conjunctive normal form (CNF) is satisfiable, that is, whether some assignment satisfies all its clauses, Max-SAT asks for an assignment satisfying the largest number of clauses. Exhaustive search solves both problems in time O∗​(2n)O^{*}(2^{n}), where the notation O∗O^{*} suppresses factors polynomial in the input size. For formulas whose clauses may be arbitrarily long, no algorithm with running time O∗​(2(1−γ)​n)O^{*}(2^{(1-\gamma)n}), for a constant γ>0\gamma>0, is known for either problem. The kk-SAT problem, where each clause has at most kk literals, is easily solved in time O∗​(ckn)O^{*}(c_{k}^{n}) for a constant ck<2c_{k}<2. For Max-SAT, no comparable polynomial-space result is known even for k=2k=2; note that Max 2-SAT is NP-hard, although 2-SAT is solvable in polynomial time. The only known algorithm that improves on the O∗​(2n)O^{*}(2^{n}) bound on all Max 2-SAT instances is the elegant algorithm of Williams [33], with running time O∗​(2ω​n/3)O^{*}(2^{\omega n/3}), where ω\omega is the matrix multiplication exponent. However, it uses space O∗​(22​n/3)O^{*}(2^{2n/3}), which makes it only of theoretical interest. Designing an algorithm with running time O∗​(2(1−γ)​n)O^{*}(2^{(1-\gamma)n}) that uses only polynomial space has been an open problem since 2004 [33, 34].

The exponential time hypothesis (ETH) and its strong version (SETH) [21, 7] assert that 3-SAT requires time 2Ω⁡(n)2^{\Omega(n)} and that the savings for kk-SAT vanish as kk grows. Two recent preprints from frontier AI labs [9, 27] claim to refute both hypotheses with a polynomial-space algorithm that solves kk-SAT in subexponential time for every fixed kk. If confirmed, this is a theoretical breakthrough, but it has little bearing on the results of this paper. Applied to Max 2-SAT through standard reductions, the algorithm improves on exhaustive search only at very low density, when a variable occurs on average in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\sqrt{\log n}) clauses, and the dense instances in our classes are not affected. Moreover, the current version of the algorithm has no practical value, because of astronomical constants hidden in the big-Oh notation which make the new upper bound purely asymptotic.

We present a technique that extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm of Davis, Putnam, Logemann, and Loveland [11, 12]. Consider a branching variable vv, and suppose that we first explore v=1v=1 and then backtrack to v=0v=0. Setting vv affects only the clauses containing vv, so for a given assignment of the other variables, which of the two values is better depends only on the values of the neighbors of vv. After backtracking, the branch v=0v=0 therefore only needs the assignments of the neighbors for which v=0v=0 is strictly better. We describe them by a linear inequality over the literals of the neighbors, a hard pruning constraint. Since the constraint depends only on the neighborhood of vv, we can efficiently decide which of the two branches would receive the more restrictive constraint. Along a branch, the search creates many such constraints. Each of them alone prunes only part of the search space, but for each of our classes, only an exponentially small fraction of all assignments satisfies the sum of the constraints of its own branch, and listing only these assignments yields the saving.

Our contributions are of two kinds: 1. We present new algorithms for several classes of instances, including dense ones with clause density m/n=ω⁡(1)m/n=\omega(1), that run in time O∗​(2(1−γ)​n)O^{*}(2^{(1-\gamma)n}) using only polynomial space. To the best of our knowledge these are the first results that show such running time bounds for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances, thus making an important step towards resolving the open problem from [33, 34]. 2. The key idea of creating pruning constraints during search is easy to implement and likely to find practical applications. Some of our classes model practical inputs; for example, the stochastic block model is the standard model of networks with communities. The savings that we prove are small, since they result from a conservative analysis of a deliberately simple version of the algorithm. On practical instances we expect much larger savings: after some branching steps, the remaining variables have lower degrees and, relative to their degrees, larger differences between their positive and negative occurrences, which yields more restrictive constraints. Similarly, SAT solvers routinely solve instances with thousands of variables, although their worst-case running time is exponential. In future work, we plan to obtain such practical gains with heuristics based on our constraints and to evaluate them experimentally. The present paper focuses on the theoretical results.

papers.title: Hilbertian Fields and Profinite Iterated Monodromy Groups Over Transcendental Elements with Specializations of Infinite Index
papers.abstract: Given a field $L$ and polynomial $f(x)/L$, one can consider the indices of the profinite iterated monodromy groups formed over the ground field within the profinite iterated monodromy groups over elements transcendental over $L$. For any countable Hilbertian field $k$, we show random Galois fixed field extensions almost surely make the indices infinite over all ground field elements, with certain conditions on $f(x)$. This is a generalization of a result in arXiv:2012.03076 by Dittmann and Kadets.

papers.title: Parahoric Spherical Whittaker Functions
papers.abstract: Let $F$ be a non-archimedean local field and let $K_\mu$ be a standard parahoric subgroup of $GL_n(F)$. We express the diagonal values of normalized parahoric Whittaker eigenfunctions with trivial central character using blockwise Casselman--Shalika formulas with the appropriate modulus factor. Every irreducible generic Iwahori-spherical representation has a one-dimensional fixed space for a suitable parahoric, with no invariants under a strictly larger parahoric. The full Hecke character of this line determines the representation. We compute its adjacent-block Hecke eigenvalues and, under additional irreducibility hypotheses, obtain an explicit finite formula on every Bruhat cell using an opposite induced model, Whittaker-preserving intertwiners, and Demazure--Whittaker operators. We apply these formulas to local Rankin--Selberg integrals for $GL_n\times GL_1$ and for compatible parahorics in $GL_n\times GL_m$. In the latter case, the lowest Laurent coefficient and the equal-rank functional equation determine the integral. Explicit translations and rescalings then give test vectors for the local $L$-factor.

papers.title: Agentic process evidence
papers.abstract: The way software gets built is changing dramatically. AI agents now create pull requests, select dependencies, refactor codebases, interpret test failures, and execute infrastructure changes across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). AI agents are autonomous team members, but unlike human engineers, they are ephemeral - their reasoning, decisions, and tool calls vanish the moment the session ends. Modern Security incidents involving intent mismatch or injection are becoming increasingly common - forcing us to address AI Agents as an insider threat. No widely adopted standard yet enables agentic provenance and governance and its obvious that you can't hold an ephemeral process accountable. The git log was designed for human commits. It shows what changed. It does not show what an AI agent did, which model it used, which tools it called, or whether anyone was accountable for the outcome. Every governance framework, every audit trail, every compliance control in the SDLC was built around one assumption: a human made the decision. That assumption no longer holds. This shift introduces 3 main procedural problems (not addressing scale) - Supply-chain vector - The agentic coder is software, so it is a supply-chain security risk. Policy guardrails - How to ensure the agentic coder is compliant with the policies of the organization. Task-alignment - How to align the agentic coder on its tasks and goals. We introduce Agentic Process Evidence (APE), a signed, tamper-evident, machine-readable attestation of agentic processes, linking the sessions to their outcome (process-aware logging). APE enables Policy-as-Code control over the agentic processes, allowing for human in the loop only when it's needed. We support the in-toto style attestation framework, and the protocol is aligned with the relevant regulations
papers.intro:
The coder that drafts the change, selects the dependency, reads the failing test, and edits infrastructure is, in many organizations, no longer only a person. In April 2026 Sundar Pichai wrote that 75% of all new code at Google is generated by AI and approved by engineers, up from 50% the previous fall (Pichai, 2026). A year earlier, Satya Nadella said that in some Microsoft repositories 20% to 30% of the code had been written by artificial intelligence (software) (TechCrunch, 2025). These are not the same measurements, and neither one is an industry consensus. But they describe the same shift. A large share of what lands in a process where a code commit is drafted by a model, and a person is left to accept it.

The controls around that acceptance were built for a person who stayed with the change. A commit carries an author. A review asks a colleague who can be questioned later about what they did and why. A protected branch can refuse the merge until that review, or a required check, has passed (GitHub, 2026). Ownership, approval, and the later audit all attach to someone who remains available. To trust the change was to trust that person.

The system is a supply-chain attack vector, sitting next to the components a bill of materials already lists.

Hooks can refuse a class of tool call before it runs (Claxton, 2026). A check at the tool boundary can reject an argument the policy forbids (Brooker et al., 2026). papers.title: A Dolbeault complex for the contact quantised flag manifolds of type $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{D}_{4}$
papers.abstract: Differential calculi on non-irreducible quantised flag manifolds of the $\mathrm{A}$-series have recently been investigated using Lusztig positive root vectors, revealing that several features of classical differential geometry persist in the noncommutative setting. We extend this investigation to quantised flag manifolds associated with the lowest-rank quantum groups of types $\mathrm{C}$ and $\mathrm{D}$ whose classical spaces are holomorphic contact manifolds. Building on the Heckenberger--Kolb framework, we construct covariant first order differential calculi. The maximal prolongations of calculi restricted to contact directions have lower dimensions than their classical counterparts. In type $\mathrm{C}_2$, however, adjoining the Reeb direction yields a three-dimensional calculus on the contact flag manifold whose maximal prolongation has classical dimension. Adjoining the remaining simple-root direction yields a four-dimensional calculus on the full flag manifold, again with a maximal prolongation of classical dimension. For both calculi, we explicitly present the exterior algebras and identify them with those of the corresponding framing calculi on the quantum group. In type $\mathrm{D}_4$, we show that adjoining the Reeb direction yields a nine-dimensional calculus on the contact flag. We conjecture that its maximal prolongation also has classical dimension.

papers.title: Holomorphic 1-forms without zeros on K\"ahler manifolds
papers.abstract: Assuming the existence of good minimal models, we give a bimeromorphic classification of compact connected K\"ahler manifolds admitting a holomorphic 1-form without zeros.

papers.title: The generative paradox: the Anti-Prompt paradigm for human capability
papers.abstract: Generative AI in education is usually judged by the output of human-AI teams. That focus overlooks a second outcome: what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt when assistance changes or disappears. We call this tension the generative paradox and distinguish four manifestations: performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock. We propose developmental function allocation, which complements operational function allocation and meaningful human control by treating retained human capability as a design objective alongside current joint performance. The Anti-Prompt paradigm reverses the default interaction order: when immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act, AI should first create the conditions for human construction. We distinguish the validity of a product, responsibility for its construction, and evidence of capability after support changes. Representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests spanning mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design make these distinctions concrete. We conclude with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about the reproduction and distribution of expertise.

papers.title: Point-Splitting-Perturbative-Chern-Simons I
papers.abstract: We define mathematically the Point-Splitting Perturbative Chern-Simons Theory. The framing anomaly arise directly from the dependence of the configuration space of points on the frame.
papers.intro:
Let MM be an oriented compact three manifold. The Perturbative Chern-Simons (P​C​SPCS for short) theory on MM was defined mathematically by Axelrod and Singer more than thirty years ago ([1], [2]) . The P​C​SPCS partition function was defined in terms of an expansion in Feymann diagrams, where the contribution of a graph is obtained integrating a differential form (which depends on a metric of MM) on the compactification of the configuration space of points associated to the vertices of the graph. The framing anomaly arise because in order to cancel the dependence on the metric of MM it is necessary to introduce correction terms which depend on a frame of MM.

The P​C​SPCS partition function was defined in terms of an expansion in Feymann diagrams, where the contribution of a graph is obtained integrating a differential form (which depends on a metric of MM) on the compactification of the configuration space of points associated to the vertices of the graph. The framing anomaly arise because in order to cancel the dependence on the metric of MM it is necessary to introduce correction terms which depend on a frame of MM.

In this paper we introduce the mathematical theory of Point-Splitting-Perturbative-Chern-Simons (P​S​P​C​SPSPCS for short). The frame of MM is used directly to define (the analogous of) the configuration space of points. Making this definition mathematically precise is quite subtle. We introduce the Point-Splitting-Homology (P​S​HPSH) which is the object playing the main role in our construction.

We introduce the Point-Splitting-Homology (P​S​HPSH) which is the object playing the main role in our construction.

P​S​P​C​SPSPCS provides the natural ambient space to understand the Skein relations, a longstanding open problem in the context of standard P​C​SPCS. Indeed, in [7] we show that (a version of) P​S​HPSH is isomorphic to (a version of) the Skein.

The structures studied in this paper plays a fundamental role in the general Open Gromov-Witten theory (see [4], [5], [6] ). In degree zero the decorated graphs used in [6] reduces to the decorated graphs used in this paper and, accordingly, the Multi-Curve-Homology introduced in [6] reduces to the Pont-Splitting-Homology introduced in this paper. The conditions defining Multi-Curve-Cycles are directly related to the constrains of the perturbation of the moduli space of (multi-)pseudo-holomorphic curves defined in [4].

In this paper we consider the case of pure Chern-Simons, i.e. , without Wilson loops. In [7] we extend the formalism to include Wilson loops. In [8] we consider the not compact case and the gluing procedure.

The starting point of the construction is as follows. In the standard approach to P​C​SPCS to any graph GG it is associated a (compactified) configuration space of points on MM which is a differential blow-up along the diagonals of the space of arrays MV⁡(G)M^{V(G)} of points of MM labelled by the vertices of the graph (see [2]). Denoting with H⁡(G)H(G) the set of half-edges of GG, the space MV⁡(G)M^{V(G)} may be identified with a subspace of MH⁡(G)M^{H(G)} (this is the subspace where the points corresponding to the half-edges attached to each vertex coincide). In P​S​P​C​SPSPCS we consider a perturbation of this subspace which is transversal to the diagonals associated to the edges of the graph, that is, we split the points associated to the half-edges attached to the same vertex. We are lead to consider a collection of singular chains labelled by the graphs. Of course this perturbation suffer of a very high indetermination. We constrains the admissible perturbations introducing the cycle condition and the forgetful compatibility condition which relate chains associated to different graphs. These conditions leads to the notion of Point-Splitting-Cycle. A consequence of the cycle condition is that the integration of the Chern-Simons differential forms does not produces boundary terms (in contrast with the situation of the standard P​C​SPCS where these terms are responsible of the framing anomaly). Let us stress that in P​S​P​C​SPSPCS we do not use the compactified configuration spaces of points but we simply work with chains on MH⁡(G)M^{H(G)}. In order to formulate the cycle condition it is necessary to consider graphs equipped with a suitable decoration: any graph is equipped with a set (called components), to each component it is associated a genus and a set of vertices. (The vertices may have attached an arbitrary number of half-edges, each component is required to satisfy a stability condition.) There is a natural notion of isotopies of P​SPS-cycles. Taking isotopies classes of P​SPS-cycles we obtain P​SPS-homology. The next step consists in showing that to each frame of MM we can associate canonically a P​S​HPSH-class. Roughly this class may be characterized by requiring the invariance under the translation of the vertices. This condition is defined in a certain limit defined using the frame. We make this condition precise introducing the notion of flat-approaching-P​SPS-cycle. We show that, for any fixed frame, there is a unique flat-approaching-P​SPS-cycle up to isotopies.

papers.title: Point-Splitting-Perturbative-Chern-Simons II
papers.abstract: We extend the formalism of Point-Splitting-Perturbative-Chern-Simons to include Wilson Loops.
papers.intro:
Let MM be a compact oriented manifold. In a preview paper [5] we introduced the mathematical theory of pure (i.e., without Wilson loops) Point-Splitting Perturbative Chern-Simons (P​S​P​C​SPSPCS) on MM. In this paper we extend the formalism of [5] to include Wilson Loops.

Let MM be a compact oriented manifold. In a preview paper [5] we introduced the mathematical theory of pure (i.e., without Wilson loops) Point-Splitting Perturbative Chern-Simons (P​S​P​C​SPSPCS) on MM. In this paper we extend the formalism of [5] to include Wilson Loops.

In this paper we use the same notion of P​SPS-cycle used in [5], which depends on the choice of an annulus data, The difference with [5] arise in the definition of nice-P​SPS-cycle where we drop the assumption made in [5] roughly stating that the loop associated to each vertex shrink to a point. In order to make this condition precise we introduce the notion of limit-support of a nice-P​SPS-cycle (whereas in [5] we limited ourself to consider only trivial limit-support). Point-Splitting-Homology is defined as the space of equivalence classes of nice-P​SPS-cycles, where we quotient by isotopies that do not deform the limit-support (that is, we consider only small isotopies). We denote it as P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U), where UU i a smooth Euler Structure UU corresponding to the annulus data (see [5]). To each oriented embedded link 𝐰\mathbf{w} it is associated a subspace P​S​H​(M|𝐰,U)PSH(M|\mathbf{w},U) of P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U). The subspaces of P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U) generated by P​S​H​(M|𝐰,U)PSH(M|\mathbf{w},U) for different 𝐰\mathbf{w} is dense in P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U).

The subspaces of P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U) generated by P​S​H​(M|𝐰,U)PSH(M|\mathbf{w},U) for different 𝐰\mathbf{w} is dense in P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U).

P​S​H​(M|U)PSH(M|U) comes with a natural notion of isotopy, which in particular deform the limit-support. To an isotopy of links correspond an isotopy of the associated subspaces P​S​H​(M|𝐰,U)PSH(M|\mathbf{w},U). However the notion of isotopy in P​S​HPSH is much more general of the isotopy of links and its formulation does not refer to links. This fact is of critical importance in order to understand Skein relations: classically the crossing of the link or the twisting of the frame are singular processes, however in P​S​HPSH each process is translated in a smooth process. The Skein relations are translated in the existence of small isotopies in P​S​HPSH between certain P​S​HPSH-classes. The P​SPS-Homology provides the natural ambient space where the Skein relations live.

papers.title: Exponential Convergence of the Lifted Gradient Flow of the Bass Functional
papers.abstract: We establish multidimensional exponential convergence of the lifted Bass gradient flow in martingale optimal transport. Let $\mu\le_{cx}\nu$ be an irreducible pair, with compact convex target support, source support strictly inside the target support, and target density bounded above and bounded away from zero almost everywhere on its interior. For every bounded $\sigma(X)$-measurable initial state, the flow converges exponentially in $L^2$ to the global minimizer with the prescribed mean, and the functional value gap decays exponentially. Both bounds hold at every nonnegative time with the exact initial errors as prefactors. The quantitative step is strong convexity on sets with a common $L^\infty$ bound and a fixed mean. We prove it by interpolating entropic endpoint potentials, using two conditional copies to cancel the unknown potential increment, and obtaining a Hessian lower bound uniform in the regularization parameter. Removing the regularization yields curvature for the original functional; the known qualitative theory supplies a common bound for the orbit. This extends the one-dimensional exponential-convergence result of Backhoff-Veraguas, Pammer, and Schachermayer. The main result is formalized in Lean 4. AI was used in preparing the paper (see Section 8).

papers.title: On generic subsystems of a Smale space
papers.abstract: We study properties of generic compact invariant subsystems of a fixed Smale space in the Hausdorff topology. For a transitive Smale space, we show that the hyperspace of all subsystems contains an open and dense family of NMC subsystems, a dynamically degenerate class with finite orbit structure. A substantially different picture emerges in the closure of the infinite transitive locus: minimality, unique ergodicity, and zero topological entropy are generic, while subsystems conjugate to regular Toeplitz shifts are dense. Despite generic zero entropy, typical subsystems exhibit large oscillations in complexity: we prove that they have infinite slow entropy at the polynomial scale, and their slow entropy at the stretched-exponential scale is equal to one. For mixing Smale spaces, we further study the closure of the infinite totally transitive subsystems. In this hyperspace, minimality, unique ergodicity, and zero entropy remain generic; the conjugacy class of any Sturmian subshift is dense; and uniquely ergodic subsystems whose invariant measure is weakly mixing form a residual set. In particular, topological weak mixing is generic in this space.

Smale spaces provide a topological framework for hyperbolic dynamics, encompassing shifts of finite type and the basic sets of Axiom A diffeomorphisms while retaining the fundamental features of uniform hyperbolicity, such as expansivity, shadowing, and local product structure. The purpose of this paper is to describe the generic behavior of compact invariant subsystems of a fixed Smale space in the sense of Baire category.

The purpose of this paper is to describe the generic behavior of compact invariant subsystems of a fixed Smale space in the sense of Baire category.

The notion of Baire category, introduced at the end of the nineteenth century, has long been used to provide a topological description of typical behavior in several parameter spaces that naturally arise in the framework of topological dynamics. In the early literature, Oxtoby and Ulam [18] proved that, for a polyhedron with a suitable Lebesgue–Stieltjes measure, ergodicity is generic among measure-preserving homeomorphisms in an appropriate uniform topology. In 1944, Halmos [13] considered the group of Lebesgue-preserving automorphisms of the unit interval and proved that the set of weakly mixing transformations is residual in the weak topology. This result was complemented by Rokhlin [24], who established that, in the same setting, strongly mixing automorphisms form a set of first category. A unifying theme in all these results is that the underlying measure space is fixed, while the measure-preserving transformation varies. Related questions were later studied in spaces of homeomorphisms; for instance, Kechris and Rosendal [15] proved that the homeomorphism group of the Cantor set has a residual conjugacy class.

The hyperbolic structure of the ambient Smale space therefore enters essentially into the analysis.

papers.title: The Precision Wall: An Optimizer-Dependent Boundary for Optimization under Power-Law Measurement Spectra
papers.abstract: In low-rank matrix sensing of a rank-$D$ factor $U^\ast \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times D}$, replacing isotropic Gaussian designs with power-law measurement covariance $\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(j^{-s})_{j=1}^V$ leaves the Burer--Monteiro landscape free of spurious local minima, yet division-normalised first-order optimizers stall above a critical exponent $s^\ast$. We trace this failure to a numerical precision wall. At the ground truth, the smallest non-gauge expected Hessian eigenvalue scales at leading order as $V^{-(s+1)}D^{-s}$. When this curvature drops below the effective denominator floor $\epsilon_O$ of optimizer $O$, normalisation noise overwhelms rare-direction gradients, yielding the leading-order boundary $s^\ast_O(V, D) = [\log(1/\epsilon_O) - \log V]/\log(VD) + \delta_O$, where $\delta_O$ is a metric-dependent detection lag. With $\delta_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ calibrated on four configurations and frozen, this formula predicts Adam's onset within $0.45$ across all 16 cells of a held-out grid ($V \in \{64,128,256,512\} \times D \in \{4,8,16,32\}$), separates fixed-$VD$ pairs, and distinguishes denominator-precision walls from conditioning and sign-quantisation walls. The approximation fails at $D = 2$, reflects a finite-$D$ spectral crossover, and saturates below $\varepsilon_0 = 10^{-8}$ at a dynamical floor.

papers.title: Beyond Ground Truth: A Heuristic Unsupervised Quality Assurance Engine for Diagnosing Calibrational Blindness in Dental Segmentation
papers.abstract: In real-world clinical settings, dental X-ray segmentation using deep learning methods suffers from reliability issues. Even when the segmentation quality is bad, deep learning models show high confidence in their predictions (calibrational blindness). Moreover, in real use, doctors do not have ground-truth masks to check their accuracy. To address this problem, we introduce a simple quality-checking engine called HUS-QA with three stages. We train it on the PRAD (Periapical Dental X-ray) dataset to build our SimCLR self-supervised ResNet-18 U-Net model, which generates the segmentation mask and then evaluates its quality. Our HUS-QA checks the segmentation mask quality without a ground-truth mask. Prediction confidence, edge sharpness, shape connectivity, and area-size penalty are the simple indicators considered in this research. Results show that standard confidence methods fail (r = -0.1394, p = 1.7864e-3, ROC AUC = 0.4275). By contrast, our HUS-QA shows a positive correlation with actual Dice scores (r = 0.4647, p = 3.7510e-28) and achieves a strong ROC-AUC of 0.8405. Therefore, HUS-QA serves as a practical tool for clinical quality control.

papers.intro:
In modern medical systems, automatically segmenting dental X-rays is essential, as it helps clinicians diagnose oral conditions[1, 2]. Deep learning models, especially encoder-decoder models [3], help doctors detect oral diseases and save time by segmenting different dental anatomical structures in images [4]. But in real-world use, calibrational blindness is a major problem. Deep learning models often show high confidence even when their output masks are wrong or incomplete [5]. After deployment, clinicians have no labels to check whether the masks generated by deep learning models are reliable or misleading [6].

Deep learning models, especially encoder-decoder models [3], help doctors detect oral diseases and save time by segmenting different dental anatomical structures in images [4]. But in real-world use, calibrational blindness is a major problem. Deep learning models often show high confidence even when their output masks are wrong or incomplete [5]. After deployment, clinicians have no labels to check whether the masks generated by deep learning models are reliable or misleading [6].

We need a quality-control framework that can assess predicted mask quality without ground truth to build trust in Medical AI tools [6, 7]. Standard quality checks only look at basic confidence scores, but high confidence does not guarantee good shape or structure [5]. To solve this issue, we present the Heuristic Unsupervised Quality Assurance (HUS-QA) engine. By looking at four simple visual indicators such as confidence score, boundary sharpness, component connectivity, and anatomical area size, HUS-QA checks the segmentation quality of X-rays. It combines these indicators into one final score to tell doctors if a mask needs manual checking. Also, to lower the cost of expert annotations, our framework uses Self-Supervised Learning (SimCLR) to learn features from unannotated X-ray images first [8, 9].

papers.title: Multicomplexes in Action: Strong Formality of Compact Hyperk\"ahler Manifolds
papers.abstract: We show that all compact hyperk\"ahler manifolds are bigraded strongly formal in the sense of Milivojevi\'c and Stelzig, proving that in the context of pluripotential homotopy theory they play the same role as compact K\"ahler manifolds in rational homotopy theory. Indeed, the main result arises from general algebraic considerations on categories of objects with more differentials, that of multicomplexes and commutative $n$-differential graded algebras. For them we discuss a standard model category structure, introduce a generalization of the $\partial\bar{\partial}$-Lemma and establish an algebraic formality theorem.
