papers.intro:
In the 1960s, 1970s Daniel Quillen and Dennis Sullivan developed the so-called rational homotopy theory ([14, 23, 24]), a topological framework in which it is possible to completely understand the rational homotopy type (informally, "homotopy type up to torsion") of, say, simply connected topological spaces with rational homology of finite type in terms of the algebraic homotopy type of a specific cdga (commutative differential graded algebra) over ℚ\mathbb{Q} associated to every topological space, namely the algebra of polynomial forms AP​L​(−)A_{PL}(-). And this last weak equivalence class can be entirely recovered from the isomorphism class of another cdga, a "minimal one", that is, the minimal model of the topological space (this operation corresponds to taking the cofibrant replacement with respect to an appropriate model category structure in CDGA). The concept of formal space appeared for the first time in that context: a topological space XX is called formal if AP​L​(X)A_{PL}(X) is weakly equivalent to the cohomology ring H∗​(X,ℚ)H^{*}(X;\mathbb{Q}). Thus, for a formal space the rational homotopy information is encoded in the rational cohomology ring. Certain results from rational homotopy theory are actually invariant for field extensions ℚ⊆K\mathbb{Q}\subseteq K, so it makes sense to discuss the real homotopy type by looking at cdga over ℝ\mathbb{R}. We know that for a manifold MM we have a weak equivalence between the de Rham algebra Ad​R​(M)A_{dR}(M) and AP​L​(M,ℝ)A_{PL}(M;\mathbb{R}), therefore the more comfortable cdga to consider when we are dealing with manifolds is the cdga of forms, and the definition of formal manifold can be restated using Ad​R​(M)A_{dR}(M). A very important class of formal spaces is that of compact Kähler manifolds ([3]), thus establishing a conceptual bridge between complex geometry and rational homotopy theory. The presence of the holomorphic structure has remarkable consequences on the algebra of forms: indeed, it gets a bigrading and the differential dd splits into two components ∂,∂¯\partial,\bar{\partial} of bidegree (1,0),(0,1)(1,0),(0,1) respectively; such a structure is called commutative bidifferential bigraded algebra (cbba) (see [9, 22]). Moreover, the formality result in [3] for compact Kähler manifolds only relies on a property of the underlying bicomplex, the ∂∂¯\partial\bar{\partial}-Lemma. In light of the preceding discussion one could ask what the extra information on the algebra of forms and the homotopy type given by the holomorphic structure is. Answers to this question were found in [9, 22], which have produced a new, enlarged homotopical setting for the holomorphic category. This latter environment, called pluripotential homotopy theory, is a new tool for studying complex geometry from a homotopical point of view. In the pluripotential context, a weak equivalence is a map of cbba’s f:A→Bf:A\to B inducing isomorphism in Aeppli and Bott-Chern cohomologies, and a bigraded strongly formal cbba is a cbba connected to a cbba with trivial differentials via a chain of weak equivalences. A complex manifold MM is bigraded strongly formal if its cbba of forms is; informally, we could say that the "new" homotopy information is determined by the Bott-Chern cohomology HB​C​(M)H_{BC}(M). Although all compact Kähler manifolds and, more generally, ∂∂¯\partial\bar{\partial}-manifolds are rationally formal, it is not always the case in the bigraded context (see, for example, [18, 12, 7]). Therefore, a natural problem is the research of new theorems ensuring strong formality of classes of complex manifolds. We have answers in this direction; for example, the following classes of complex manifolds are strongly formal: • Compact Kähler manifolds with central cohomology of a certain width ([17]); • Complete smooth toric varieties ([13]); • Homogeneous compact Kähler manifolds ([13]); • Splitting type solvmanifolds ℂn⋉ℂm/Γ\mathbb{C}^{n}\ltimes\mathbb{C}^{m}/\Gamma satisfying the ∂∂¯\partial\bar{\partial}-Lemma ([16]); • Compact geometrically Aeppli formal manifolds ([20]); • Compact Kähler solvmanifolds ([19]). We could look at the question "Which classes of complex manifolds are strongly formal?" from a metric classification viewpoint. More precisely, suppose MM is a compact smooth manifold equipped with a Riemannian metric gg; if we exclude exceptional holonomy (in general, manifolds with exceptional holonomy need not be rationally formal, see [8]), we have the following three interesting cases: (1) Holonomy in the unitary group (equivalent to the metric being Kähler); (2) Holonomy in the special unitary group (equivalent to metric being Kähler Ricci-flat, in case of equality with the special unitary group we are in Kähler Calabi-Yau geometry); (3) Holonomy in the symplectic group (equivalent to the metric being hyperkähler). In the first two classes there are counterexamples to strong formality (in the Kähler case see [12], for Calabi-Yau see [7]), hence, if there is some hope in finding general results looking to the holonomy, only the last case Hol⁡(g)⊆S​p\mathrm{Hol}(g)\subseteq Sp (i.e., the hyperkähler case) is open. Another way of looking at compact hyperkähler manifolds is the following: compact hyperkähler manifolds are compact, holomorphically symplectic complex manifolds of Kähler type. Recently, in [15], it has been shown that if we eliminate the Kähler type hypothesis, compact, holomorphically symplectic complex manifolds are not necessarily topologically formal.
